commission. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i should first like to thank mr hubert pirker for his report, which deals not only with the commission's communication on the management of the external borders of the european union but also with the action plan adopted by the council. and it can be said that there is a very large overlap between the two documents, the commission proposal and the council action plan. i believe that the four fundamental objectives which were set out for us in laeken are also reflected in this action plan: to strengthen mutual trust between the member states in the control of the external border, which is a common external border, which means that weak control in one state has inevitably dragging effects on the security of all the other member states of the european union; to ensure the effectiveness of the fight against illegal immigration; to give special priority to the control of the external borders in order to prevent the entry of terrorist groups or agents; and finally to safeguard a high level of internal security in the european union, without which it is not possible to preserve freedom of movement and to abolish external border controls. as mr hubert pirker has pointed out, the objectives of this action plan are clear. i believe that rather than talking about objectives, it is important to set targets and to record what is actually being done. firstly, in the legislative field. we have an acquis, the schengen acquis, which, as mr hubert pirker has rightly pointed out, is applied very differently by the various member states. the conditions for the application of the schengen acquis should be harmonised. and we are doing this in two ways: firstly, by reworking the schengen common manual, and the commission will present in the first half of this year a proposal for the refounding of the schengen common manual. but secondly, by also establishing a code of good practice on the application of the common rules. the second objective is the training of border guards. i believe that at this very moment, as we are speaking, a meeting is taking place in vienna, with the commission taking part, to define a proposal for a common framework for the training of border guards. a project that is being led by austria and sweden. thirdly, the use of modern information technologies to improve external border control. in this context, the commission intends to present to the thessaloniki european council in july this year the feasibility study on the launch of the online visa system at european level. we shall also be putting forward the first proposals on the control of the european union's external maritime borders. objective 4: the definition of a common risk model for external border control. a model is already in place in this area, based on a proposal from the finnish government, and the danish presidency held the first meeting of the 'scifa+' body which coordinates the border control services of all the member states of the european union. the new body's work at european level has already made it possible to carry out two specific operations in 2002. the first, 'operation ulysses', was coordinated by spain and involved joint teams from several member states in the control of the mediterranean; and the second, a joint team operation led by germany in controlling its land borders. these two operations were financed in 2002 by the argo programme and new operational cooperation actions are already being presented for 2003. finally, the seville european council supported the principle of shared responsibility for external border control. it is a sharing of responsibility in financial terms, in terms of sharing equipment and also in terms of the prospect of creating, in the long term, a common border guard. the commission presented a first assessment of the financial situation. we must recognize that the data which the member states have submitted to us on the actual expenditure of each of them on external border control are very different, hardly comparable. the commission has therefore asked for further clarification and intends to present during the greek presidency a proposal for criteria for sharing financial responsibilities for the control of the external border of the european union. i hope that with the motion for a resolution tabled by mr hubert pirker, which will be voted on here tomorrow, parliament can give a decisive boost to this ambitious, demanding and urgent action programme for the control of the external borders of the european union in the name of strengthening the internal security of all the member states.

- question no 17 by mr cushnahan (h-0872/02): subject: recent maritime disasters following the series of maritime disasters in european waters in november and december 2002, namely the sinking of the prestige, from which oil continues to leak, causing black tides that seriously damage the coastline and marine life of galicia, to which is added the recent collision between the freighter tricolor and the kariba and a second collision between the wreck of the tricolor and the freighter nicola, does the commission accept that there is a clear need for concerted action? in addition, given the serious consequences of such maritime accidents, what is your view of the proposal i submitted to the convention on the future of europe in june 2002 (conv. 150/02) for the creation of a european coast guard corps?
commission. - mr president, on 3 december the commission adopted a communication on the measures to be taken following the sinking of the oil tanker prestige. the document sets out in detail a number of measures, in particular to speed up the implementation of the legislation adopted by parliament and the council after the tragedy of the erika oil tanker, the so-called erika i and ii packages. the transport council of 6 december last supported most of the initiatives proposed by the commission. on 20 december, the college adopted a proposal for a regulation, which has just been sent to the council and parliament, banning the transport of heavy oils in single-hull tankers to or from ports in the european union and speeding up the replacement of these types of tankers by double-hull tankers. the european union has not waited for the latest developments to have a concerted policy on maritime safety. a wide range of measures to ensure greater protection in this field already existed. the commission takes note of the contribution of the honourable members to the convention's work on the creation of a european coast guard as an effective means of combating the danger of pollution and maintaining maritime safety. the repetition of accidents such as the erika, the prestige and, not to mention, other minor accidents such as the vicky just a few days ago, shows that all of europe would benefit from having a european coast guard, especially since some of the future 25 member states of the union have no such protection or body at all. in any event, the first task of the forthcoming european maritime safety agency is to coordinate technically the application of community rules, and the commission will therefore consider what measures should be taken in the future, taking into account the experience acquired by the agency.
the commission (es) i cannot but agree with you, mr president, that among other things i cannot accept that citizens have fewer rights in europe than in the united states. that is what i said very clearly when i made the proposals with the erika i and erika ii packages. if the council had followed the proposal to remove single-hull vessels from community waters in the transport of oil, the prestige disaster would not have occurred, because it would have had to leave community waters several months earlier. i am sure that the commission will be able to give us a clear answer to this question. i do not understand why the united states can have a timetable for the year 2010 in which there will no longer be single-hull oil tankers in its ports and we cannot adopt a similar measure. in the end, as you know, a less ambitious timetable was adopted. what i have already put before this parliament and the council of ministers is to go back to the original commission proposal and to speed up the departure of single-hull ships in the transport of oil. and also to take the maximum safety measures, namely that the transport of heavy oil, heavy fuel oil, bituminous materials, tar, that is to say, the most polluting products, be carried out in the safest ships, which are those with double hulls. specific measures are being discussed in copenhagen. the commission is studying how to implement these specific measures after the prestige, including the possibility of promoting the construction and maintenance of two or three large skimmers, large suctioners, so that, in the event of a black tide - unfortunately there is no zero risk, although the risks must be reduced to the maximum - there are ships of maximum power, superior to those of ships existing today on the european coast, which can also act and operate at sea in times of storm and difficulty. the european response must be coordinated. the agency, which would be responsible for these ships and their placement at various strategic points along the european coast, also has to put in place a series of response plans in the event of a maritime accident of this nature. that will be one of its tasks: to provide for this collaboration between the various member states of the union in a pre-established way, the functioning of which can be improved, since it depends to a large extent on bilateral agreements rather than on an already perfectly coordinated action of a european type. as regards liability, as the honourable member knows, we are working on it and i hope that in the coming weeks we will be able to put forward, within the commission and for it to be adopted quickly, a proposal to make gross negligence in such accidents a criminal offence in all the member states of the union.
- madam commissioner, from the commission's written documents which you have inspired and from your words, at least from the words you occasionally utter, i conclude that there is a genuine political conflict between your position - that of the commission - and the position of the council as it was put in copenhagen. i have the document of 3 december, which i read with great interest, but the transport and environment councils held in the same month and the european council in copenhagen, as far as i am concerned, did not respond in any way to the urgency demanded by the commission. the commissioner wanted the commitments in the erika legislation to be respected and even to go beyond them, and the european council turned its back on those who were at that very moment collecting the oil with their hands. in a way, the council has disregarded the commission's positions, it is enough to recall that it has proposed only five million euros for galicia and for all the countries concerned, whereas the united states is currently claiming four billion euros for the exxon valdez accident. in this connection, commissioner, i would like to ask you why the commission is not drawing up a law like the oil pollution act in the united states, which will enable it to fight this problem effectively. moreover, will galicia be considered for the location of a european maritime safety science centre?
commission. - (es) mr president, you are very familiar with maritime safety issues; you have been a rapporteur and have had some very notable successes, for example the inclusion of black boxes, which was largely achieved thanks to your work, commitment and tenacity. he is also very familiar with the problem of maritime traffic. i think we have to work on this; we have seen in the canal problem that there are areas where progress can be made. as regards flags of convenience, the honourable members are aware that work is being done within the international maritime organisation to improve this situation. in any case, there are two types of flags of convenience: those which are flags of convenience for purely fiscal and economic reasons and those which, moreover, show very little responsibility with regard to the control and quality of the ships flying them. a distinction must be made between the two situations. the way forward is not to make a generic statement; that would be the easiest thing, but, when the time comes, it is difficult to put it into practice. we must make their lives difficult, impossible, in our ports, so that they stop coming. in this sense, the selective port inspections that we have proposed and approved here with the support of this parliament, and which the council also approved, clearly imply that whenever a ship flying that flag calls at a port in the european union, it will be thoroughly inspected. so, you're gonna have to be in condition. this type of action and control, especially in those countries and flags which pose risks, represents the most immediate way of acting. in any case, the honourable member is right, because it is not just a question of flags of convenience, but also of the responsibility of the classification societies, which are both judge and party, because they justify and certify the quality of a ship on behalf of the flag state but at the same time they work for the shipowner who owns it to issue certain types of certificates. we must analyse these chains and get to the bottom of the issues, supplementing all this with responsibility in the event of gross negligence.

- question no 21 by mr rübig (h-0879/02): subject: status of third party certifiers in the euethe european commission is currently working on a new approach to ce marking and its future configuration. from the point of view of european smes, it is particularly important that european third party certifiers can continue to affix their own symbols to all products. in particular, taking into account international competition and in the interest of consumer protection, the symbols of third-party certifiers should be easily identifiable by every citizen. non-european certifiers have the possibility, as third-party certifiers, to put their own name or logo on a product at any time after it has been checked. how does the european commission intend to take these considerations into account, which are aimed at strengthening european certification bodies, in its new approach to ce marking?
commission. – the objectives of the forthcoming communication on the new approach, enhancing the implementation and new approach are: firstly, to analyse the overall situation in the field of new approach directives which cover a wide range of products; secondly, to detect possible weaknesses; and thirdly, to outline remedial measures to improve the application of the new approach directives. ce conformity is one of the main points that have been identified as requiring strengthening. this marking, required by most new approach directives, is addressed to market surveillance authorities of the member states and symbolises the conformity of the product with the applicable community requirements imposed on the manufacturer. the communication will also address the issue of the relationship between the ce marking and voluntary markings. the commission has conducted an on-line survey of new approach stakeholders. as far as the ce marking was concerned, the commission has taken on board the opinions of the majority of those who replied, the main thinking being that the additional voluntary markings are not in contradiction with the ce marking, as long as they do not cause confusion or overlap in meaning or purpose with it. they also often provide added value for consumers, users, public authorities and all those being addressed. third party certifiers are in some sectors already involved in the conformity assessment procedures leading to the ce marking. it is also quite often stipulated that the identification number of the item should appear next to the ce marking. third party certification, in areas of conformity assessment where no harmonised directives apply, is permitted and even welcomed, since it indicates to the people to whom it is addressed that certain qualities of the product have been tested and certified by the body in question.
commission. – i thank mr rübig for his interest on this issue of conformity assessment. conformity assessment new approach directives are not usually included among the major policy issues which reach the front page. when we talk about smes or any entrepreneurs, whether small or large enterprises, these are key issues to enable a company to act in the internal market and globally. on the other hand, they also enable the proper weight to be given to the interests of the consumer. i hope parliament will create a system to deal properly with the communication which is coming in fairly soon.

- question no 24 by mr lund (h-0836/02): israeli military actions and loss of european union funds the european union has financed many projects in the palestinian state, notably to establish democracy and ensure respect for human rights. could the commission state which projects are being financed by the european union in the palestinian state and what damage has been caused to these projects by israeli military action? could it also indicate what the consequences of israeli military actions in the palestinian state are for israel's chances of obtaining community aid and for relations between the european union and israel in general?
commission. – as i suggested in response to the previous supplementary question, it may be that the destruction of some projects and some infrastructure has been an unfortunate by-product of legitimate, counter-terrorism activities, which are proportionate to the violence that they are seeking to contain. this may be true in some circumstances, but what has seemed surprising to us is the way in which one palestinian institution after another has been destroyed or badly damaged as though some people believe that the aim of the exercise should be to undermine the ability of palestinians to actually create an administrative structure for a future palestinian state. i will take two examples that i referred to earlier. how can destruction of the land registry contribute to the defeat of terrorism? how can doing a huge amount of damage to the central bureau of statistics in the palestinian territory be other than an example of needless destruction? it is not very sensible when most of the material contained in the central bureau of statistics can be found freely on the internet. it is difficult to see how those activities can be justified. this is a point i have made before; it is a point that the council of ministers has also made, and it is a point which the israeli authorities should address rather more intelligently and sympathetically than they have so far.

(es) mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, rapporteur, i should like to begin by congratulating mr mantovani on the quality of his report, which i consider to be serious and well thought out. i have heard that you cannot comment on the figures, and therefore we are not saying anything new when we note that the world demographic trends reveal the progressive ageing of the population. the rapporteur referred to the percentage of the european population over 65 years of age, 16%, an estimated 22% and 27.5% for the years 2025 and 2050, and to the fact that the number of people over 80 years of age will also increase from 3.6% in 2000 to 6% in 2025 and 10% in 2050. in the face of statistics, neither the ostrich attitude - to hide its head under the wing and wait to see what happens - nor the catastrophistic attitude is appropriate. obviously, the demographic situation is a success of society, attributable to medical care and the improvement of living conditions in general. older people are not a homogeneous group or group and therefore their needs are also different and diverse. policies for the elderly must be approached from the dual perspective of their needs and the care they require - and are entitled to - to meet them, but also from that of their potential and that of the services they can provide to society. no society - not even the european one - can afford to disregard the contributions that the experience, training and knowledge of its elders can provide. in addition to article 152 of the treaty, these policies are supported by article 21 of the charter of fundamental rights of the european union, which prohibits all discrimination - in this case on grounds of age - and article 25, which states that the union recognises and respects the right of older persons to lead a life in dignity and independence and to participate in social and cultural life. these principles would be devoid of substance if they were not accompanied by the policies which are to make them a reality. in this connection, the barcelona council of march 2002 already pointed out the need to initiate and develop cooperation between member states on these issues during 2002 and 2003, the need to exchange good practice and information and the need to launch a debate on common challenges at european level. health care systems face a threefold challenge. firstly, access to care for all, with the uniqueness of care for the elderly; secondly, a high level of quality; and thirdly, the financial sustainability of the systems. i believe that these are three necessary and minimum objectives, which are commendable and praiseworthy, and i would like to draw attention to their close connection. whatever the system of financing, monitoring or contribution, its achievement can and should also be promoted through the promotion of healthier lifestyles, prevention measures and awareness-raising among service providers and users about the correct application of therapies and medicines. this will allow a balance between the three objectives. the risk of prioritising the objective of financial sustainability can devalue and distort those of quality and accessibility, but also, without sustainability, quality and accessibility would only be possible in the short term.

- the agenda calls for the commission and council statements on afghanistan, one year after the bonn agreement. mr yiannitsis, president-in-office of the council, has the floor. transmission of texts of agreements by the council: see minutes
council mr president, i would like to thank the honourable members of the european parliament for the debate we had, for the support they have given to a number of ideas and proposals from the presidency and to the ideas and proposals of the european commission, although they are not in my competence. we have written down a number of helpful suggestions. i would like to say that i particularly hold the need for the expansion of the role of the government beyond the borders of kabul, so that there is greater stabilization and normalization in larger parts of the country, the need for the expansion of the mandate of isaf so that it can also operate in the same political direction, and thirdly the rights of people whether they concern women or they concern prisoners or opponents. we are interested in the respect of human rights for institutional, historical and cultural reasons. it is a historic tradition in the european area which must be respected wherever it is needed. the whole debate has shown that what we want to create in afghanistan, and this is of course well known, is a country where the values of democracy, freedom, the prospect of economic development, the prospect of trust can become a reality. historically, this has all been a tough, difficult and time-consuming process in any country. i know of no country in which such enormous changes have taken place in periods of time that were not long enough. we need a strong political will, we need economic, political and humanitarian support, but we also need pragmatism in terms of what can be done, how far we can go, what the conditions are, what the difficulties are for the people there, what balances need to be respected, what values prevail there and how we can help in the desired direction. we are far from the point where we can say that the game in afghanistan has been won. the time is short and we have a long way to go. developments in afghanistan will be influenced by many factors, both external and internal. we need to look at the individual elements, what's happening with the constitution, what's happening with humanitarian and many other things, but we need to look through a global perspective and a global strategy how we will influence developments there. success is not measured by one or a few criteria, which we can name and have named many of them, whether institutional or individual rights or economic successes. success will be measured by the parallel positive development of many elements that together concern the political, institutional, social and economic life of the country.
commission. – i will be very brief in responding to a debate which has ranged extremely wide. mr andrews' contribution covered not only afghanistan but iraq. if he had been able to stay until the end of the debate, i would have said that i fear we will have further opportunities to discuss iraq and he may be able to take part. i would like to thank members such as mrs fraisse who praised the work done by our officials in kabul and beyond. they do have a difficult job. it is not the easiest assignment to manage our programme there. i will certainly pass on the commendation of members. i would also like to express once again my agreement with mr van orden that we are in this for the long haul. there are no quick fixes in afghanistan. we have to go on repeating that. we cannot simply call what we have done so far success and move on to the next failed state. there is a great deal for us to do, not least, as mrs fraisse said, in helping to create a public service in afghanistan which will be able to deliver the sort of services we would want to see to the whole community. the quality of some of the members of the afghan diaspora who have returned to afghanistan gives one a good deal of confidence in what could be achieved in that country. i could mention mr ghani and many other afghans who have gone back to their country to help reconstruct it after the years of medieval ferocity to which its people of afghanistan have been subjected. so i can assure mrs fraisse that we shall continue to give proper attention to support and training for public services. we have, more than most other donors in afghanistan, provided budgetary assistance for the ordinary business of government. it is not a very attractive, or sexy thing for donors to do. donors typically like to have projects and like to have blue plaques on walls and flags over buildings. but unless there is a decent public administration in afghanistan, unless there are nurses and teachers and doctors and police officers, men and women, and unless those people are paid regularly, there will not be a government that can extend its authority over the whole country. so i continue to defend the priority that we give to that. one would have to be deaf not to recognise the concern the house has expressed about women's rights as part of a general concern about human rights. i could go through a list of the projects that we are helping to support, such as the park for women in kabul, but i will merely say that i think the best way of reflecting parliament's concern is to raise this issue at the meeting of the afghanistan development forum in march, when we should be monitoring progress. we will emphasise then that this parliament, which votes this money so intelligently and generously, wants us to ensure that the issue of women's rights is at the heart of the government's approach to development. let me just say one other word about donor coordination, because several speakers have referred to that and i only touched on it in general terms in my opening remarks. i fully agree that development aid to afghanistan must be used to maximum effect and that effective coordination is critical. the afghan government has now put in place the structures to coordinate donors. the october implementation group meeting in kabul agreed to move to a consultative group structure, which is the one that we typically put in place in countries receiving substantial assistance from the international donor community. we strongly support this initiative. it should ensure that donors are well-coordinated and that funds are targeted to the priorities agreed by the consultative group. we have also established an informal european donor forum to help develop a coordinated european union approach to key issues and meetings and there is also an informal donor network between the european commission and the member states, the united states and japan. through echo, the commission has had extensive experience of operating in afghanistan over the last ten years and has established close working relationships with non-governmental organisations. as the crisis in afghanistan unfolded, the key priority was to deliver humanitarian support quickly and effectively, but now looking to the future, it will be important to ensure that all donors operate within the framework and priorities set by the consultative group. so we are aware of these concerns. we want to do more about them and, as i said in my opening speech, i intend to pursue this when, god willing, i visit afghanistan next month.

council mr president, ladies and gentlemen, we are all aware of the serious impact this has had recently. i would like to stay on the questions that have been asked. the council had already had the opportunity last december, during a general debate on the prestige disaster, of discussing with the european parliament the problems arising from the continuing accidents of this kind. having expressed its regret at the disaster caused by the sinking of the oil tanker prestige off the coast of galicia last november, it now wishes to confirm the determination of all member states and the commission to improve their cooperation, generally aiming at the safety of ships and the prevention of pollution caused by them. the new european maritime safety agency is a good example of this. on 6 and 9 december, the council adopted measures in the form of council conclusions on both the maritime transport and environmental aspects. parliament and the council adopted, under the co-decision procedure, five of the six acts proposed by the commission in the 'erika i' and 'erika ii' legislative packages. the dates for the entry into force of these legislative acts were chosen to ensure their swift implementation and the development of port authorities' control capabilities - in the case of port state control. as regards the phasing out of single-hull tankers, the timetable set at international level in the international maritime organisation (imo) is followed, which was reinforced by the commitment of member states not to use the derogation provided by the imo. the european council in nice, wishing to strengthen the union's strategy on maritime safety, had already called on the member states to implement the measures to be adopted by the 15 before the deadline, provided that they did not require an international framework. in its conclusions adopted on 6 december 2002, and in particular in points 1, 5 and 8, the council 'urgently called on the commission to submit a proposal to accelerate the phasing-out of single-hull tankers', 'called on the member states to speed up the transposition of the amended port state control directive into their national law so that the enhanced control measures could be implemented as soon as possible and preferably before 1 january 2003', and 'urgently called on the member states to draw up plans for the identification of shelters for ships in distress as soon as possible and in any event not later than 1 july 2003'. the council wishes to emphasize that the measures adopted by the council and parliament apply to all ports of the member states of the community and to their territorial waters, including the azores, the canary islands and madeira.

question no 3 by mr nogueira román (h-0847/02) subject: erika legislative packages and the us oil pollution act 1990 for what reasons, after the erika oil tanker accident and even after the successive accidents off the coast of galicia, including those of the polycomander, aegean sea, urquiola and casón vessels, did the council never include in the initiatives of the erika legislative packages the strict measures imposed on shipowners and vessels in terms of financial guarantees and insurance under the oil pollution act adopted in 1990 by the united states following the exxon valdez accident ?
council following a series of very serious accidents involving the transport of dangerous goods by sea off the european coast in recent years, the council, in conjunction with the european parliament, took measures to eliminate the risk of such accidents happening again. the objective pursued was - and i stressed this in my previous answer - to achieve a high level of protection of the environment, in particular of habitats and biodiversity. as already noted, the council recognised in december 2002 that the transport of certain substances by sea still poses significant risks to the marine and coastal environment and to the populations dependent on it. additional measures should therefore be adopted. with regard to the question referred, which refers to the solution provided by the american law, the council draws the honourable member's attention to the proposal submitted last december to examine the possibility of creating a common mechanism whereby oil companies and the shipping companies used by them, shipowners, charterers and insurance companies, will provide the means not only to prevent but also to deal effectively with possible ecological disasters or accidents. the council also stressed the need to apply properly to maritime transport the precautionary principle, the principle that environmental damage must be remedied at source and the polluter pays principle.
mr president, mr president-in-office of the council, at this stage the whole of society is convinced that international maritime traffic is the domain of a rapacious capitalism which has no regard for the interests of society, and indeed of a criminal capitalism. rules must be established to prevent this disaster. there are different approaches to solving this problem: one is the one the united states adopted in the wake of the exxon valdez accident in 1989 and created the oil pollution act in 1990. i would remind you that the guarantee required from the ship owners is one billion dollars and the liability required is unlimited and that at this moment exxon mobil is being demanded $4 billion in compensation. the double-helmet, the coast guard, etc., etc., are all part of this approach. another is the erika package, legislation which, although it is a step forward, is not being applied by the council, by the states, which prefer to operate within the framework of the international mafias. on the other hand, there are countries like galicia, at the moment, which are suffering the consequences and whose populations, including fishermen and volunteers, have to fight the black tide with their own hands. i believe that the only solution is for the european union to create its own legislation (we could even call it 'prestige' legislation) in imitation of the united states. and from that point on, surely all international law would change. i wonder if you will take any steps to that end.
council i have already mentioned that these accidents, these disasters, create a problem to be tackled together; the commission's proposal is to be submitted to the council for adoption. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's fishing fleet is not affected by the catastrophic floods in the mediterranean. the council wants to promote and promote solutions, and i think it is very important that there are proposals and ideas from many sides to deal with this problem, a problem which is not just about ship technology, it is about a number of other issues: economic, social, institutional, organisational, about how these issues are dealt with at political level and at european union level.

(es) madam president, as you know, a year ago the european parliament decided, at the request of the socialist group, to draw up this own-initiative report on the external dimension of the cfp, that is to say, on the participation of the european union in the regional fisheries organisations and also in international fisheries agreements. during the procedure and after the adoption of this report in committee, we have seen the communication from the european commission in the framework of the reform of the cfp on the same subject and it is clear that the committee on fisheries will have to draw up a second report which i think will be along the lines of the resolution we are adopting here today. the committee on fisheries is calling for greater coordination and linkage between the external dimension of the cfp and other community policies, such as trade policy, development cooperation and foreign policy. because when the directorate-general for fisheries negotiates in multilateral bodies or when it negotiates international fisheries agreements, it does not seem to have the weight of the world's largest economic and commercial power behind it. and, conversely, when the european union negotiates association agreements, trade agreements or decisions in the world trade organisation, fisheries concerns are not being sufficiently taken into account. the fact is that the activity of the community fleet in non-community fishing areas supplies our market, which is, as you know, deficient in fishery products, and also helps to maintain activity in areas dependent on fishing, which are traditionally backward and have no other economic alternatives. the european union supports this activity, in accordance with the resolution of the council of ministers of 3 november 1976, which also covers other requirements arising from other fundamental pillars of the european union. the fact is that the european union has a very competitive fleet, for example, long-liners, tuna vessels and trawlers, which operate outside community waters and is considered the most advanced in the world, and is also a pioneer in the search for new fishing grounds and new species. it is a fleet with the technical know-how and processing and marketing tools to supply a market of 350 million consumers. unlike other fleets with which they compete on a global scale, european fishermen are not pirates, they do not engage in illegal fishing, they do not destroy local fisheries, they do not engage in social dumping, but are closely controlled by the european union through the member states and different control systems and they also respect the requirements of the fisheries agreements, the national regulations of the coastal states and the regulations of the respective rfmos. some 3 000 european vessels operate on the high seas or in the exclusive economic zones of other states: 2 100 in the north and some 900 in the south of the union. this represents almost 41 000 jobs for us, 83% of which are in the southern agreements. we catch 2.7 million tonnes a year, 40% of the total catches of the community fleet, and, surprise you, the total value of these catches is estimated at 614 million euros. this value is multiplied through manufacturing and through economic activity in related sectors such as shipyards and shipbuilding companies. the financial cost of the external dimension of the cfp is very small, at eur 276 million in 2000, representing 28% of the total cfp budget. the profitability of community assistance to this fleet is therefore well established: it is estimated that each public euro generates a turnover of three. although the european union - and i repeat the idea i expressed at the outset - has the economic, legal, legislative and political potential to lead and promote the principles of responsible fishing outside the union, the community's fisheries interests are not considered to be sufficiently supported. perhaps the underlying reason is the lack of resources allocated to this task by the european commission and the lack of a political strategy and the fact that, i repeat, this external dimension of the cfp is outside the cfsp and the international trade relations of the fisheries union. the european parliament has repeatedly criticised this, insisting that the commission and, in particular, the directorate-general for fisheries must adapt its organisational structure to deal properly with its responsibilities. ladies and gentlemen, the sea is the forgotten half of our planet. but until now, no one has shown that sustainable management of deep-sea fisheries is not possible. to do this, i think it is essential to adopt an ecosystem-based approach, to strengthen scientific research, to strengthen control and surveillance measures, to reduce bycatch and to be firmly involved in the fight against illegal fishing. at the same time, we must develop a legal framework for protected areas and thereby broaden our view of the causes of the decline in resources, which is not the result - i repeat - of fishing activity alone, but also - and this is the situation we are currently experiencing - of the discharges from oil tankers such as the prestige, which sink in the richest and most biodiverse part of our coasts, or the discharges from so many others which clean up their bottoms by wildly polluting the sea - today, moreover, with the greatest impunity - without forgetting other causes, such as the profound climate changes we are experiencing at global level or the massive use of substances which inevitably end up in the sea, such as fertilisers and pesticides for agricultural uses. i would like to stress the importance of social aspects in this type of fishing. we believe that all fishermen must be guaranteed their fundamental labour rights and that it is up to the european union to take action, such as the incorporation of a social clause in international agreements or the promotion of social dialogue by socioeconomic actors, so that fishermen too benefit from the protection of their rights and the european social model is finally implemented in fisheries.

council mr president, commissioner, honourable members of the european parliament, ladies and gentlemen, i am pleased to have the opportunity to refer to the community's preparations for the next session of the united nations human rights committee. the strengthening of the dialogue between the european parliament and the council on human rights issues is one of the objectives of the greek presidency. the conclusions adopted by the council on 10 december 2002 contain recommendations for closer cooperation with you in order to achieve a more open and transparent european human rights policy. it is important to refer to the basic principles of this policy which define the union's overall approach to a matter of great importance and sensitivity for all. on 25 june 2001, the council reaffirmed its commitment to promoting european human rights and democratisation policy towards third countries and set out a number of basic principles with a view to achieving a more credible, coherent and consistent human rights and democratisation policy. in particular, to ensure coherence between community action, the common foreign and security policy and development policy, in close cooperation and coordination between the relevant union institutions. to mainstream and promote human rights and fundamental freedoms in all policies and actions of the union. to open up european human rights and democratisation policy by strengthening dialogue with the european parliament and civil society. regularly identify and review the priorities for union action in implementing union policy. the european union has a long tradition and has succeeded in creating an area of legal certainty and inviolable freedoms of which we are rightly proud. the european union is not only a political union, but also a political union of the peoples of europe, and we are all aware of the fact that the european union is a political union, and that it is a political union of the peoples of europe. we hope that this will meet the expectations of citizens and increase their level of protection. the more obvious and unquestionable the respect for human rights within the union, the more solid and convincing our foreign policy on these issues will be. the european parliament has already expressed its views on the need to ensure that the european union is able to play a full part in the international community's efforts to achieve a peaceful settlement of the conflict in the middle east. you know that the abolition of the death penalty and torture, the prevention of discrimination against women, the protection of children from exploitation are our main priorities. respect for these principles must permeate all aspects of the union's foreign policy, even when it may have an economic or political cost. this attitude is a guarantee of our credibility. ladies and gentlemen, before going into the details of the preparations for the geneva summit, let me briefly outline the results of last year's summit, because this will give us some indication of the challenges we will face in march and april. you all know how hard we had it last year. this was partly due to the composition of the commission, with members with low human rights records. moreover, for the first time the united states did not participate in the commission, while the middle east dominated the discussions and overshadowed all other initiatives. the european parliament has been asked to vote on the draft resolution on the situation in chechnya, iran and zimbabwe, which was rejected. i would like to point out that this year, with the exception of the united states, the composition of the commission has remained more or less constant. i would also like to point out that the work of the committee on human rights illustrates the complex and difficult balance of power in which our action takes place. this was made clear last year during the commission elections, where the european union's soothing and balancing role demonstrated the value of a european approach, sober but also pragmatic, which would relieve tensions and avoid a painful or dangerous impasse. i would add that this situation may become more complicated in the near future with the possibility of unilateral intervention in iraq, a deterioration of the middle east and a possible resurgence of terrorism which will feed contradictory arguments to all the forces involved, as some will shift the burden of responsibility onto others. the european council has already made a number of recommendations on the basis of the conclusions of the european council in brussels. the cohom working group held its first two-day meeting two weeks ago to prepare the work of the commission. the meeting brought together representatives of the various geographical groups and presented the priorities for the year. with the help of experts, the cohom group has already managed to identify those states which are willing to agree to a number of actions. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the use of the term 'competent authority' to cover the whole of the eu. for all these countries, it requested reports from the heads of the community embassies on the spot. i would point out that no final decisions have yet been taken, and certainly no initiatives have been taken in the absence of decisions. the cohom group will decide on as many issues as possible at its meeting on 5 february. if highly controversial issues remain, they will be discussed in the political and security committee and, if necessary, referred to the council. so i would say that the timing of today's debate is ideal since cohom on 5 february will be able to draw on your ideas and comments. but i can inform you that there is already a provisional agreement in the working party to have a union resolution on item 9 of the agenda for five countries: sudan, the democratic republic of the congo, iraq, myanmar, and the israeli settlements in the occupied territories. the european union also urges that the regions of south-east europe should no longer be considered under article 9 of the agenda but should be moved to article 19, which will provide them with advisory services and expertise in the field of human rights. the commission's proposal for a regulation on the protection of the environment is a very important one, and i would like to thank the rapporteur for the work he has done. in its traditional reporting on the human rights situation in various regions of the world, the union will include countries of concern. the relevant plan has already been drawn up and i can tell you that we will try to refer to some twenty or thirty countries in order to give them greater weight. the commission's proposal is to be submitted to the council for approval, and the council will be able to accept it. the commission will be presenting a report on the implementation of the programme in the coming months. but i can already inform you that the relevant preparations have begun for resolutions on the death penalty and the rights of the child. finally, preparations have begun for supporting statements on topics which are major priorities for the union such as racism, racial discrimination and xenophobia, women's rights, modern forms of slavery and the strengthening and encouragement of all kinds of initiatives, individual or collective, towards the protection of human rights. the list is not exhaustive, but i believe i have given you an idea of the commitments and expectations of the european union for the next meeting of the commission on human rights in geneva. the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos is a very good one. it is about the importance which our presidency attaches to an organised approach to the wave of migration that is being smuggled into the union. we believe that this will also help to combat the most serious forms of crime and human rights violations, such as slavery, prostitution and often the destruction of the value of human life. in order to protect the human rights of migrants and refugees, our presidency believes that, in addition to the third pillar issues relating to this issue, it is important to make progress on issues relating to the social rights of these people within the union. finally, i would like to stress that, particularly at the present stage, the union must always strike the right balance between security and the unimpeded exercise of rights, between cooperation and pressure, between control and protection, between what it requires of third parties and what applies to its members. the road is hard, but it remains the only strong one. in this context, the council welcomes the entry into force of the statute of the international criminal court and believes that its operation will also contribute effectively to the protection of human rights and fundamental freedoms.
commission. – mr president, i welcome the opportunity to respond to parliament's resolutions on the forthcoming session of the united nations commission on human rights and the clear indication of parliament's country and thematic priorities for that session. eleanor roosevelt was unanimously selected as the first chairman of the un commission on human rights in 1946, which was charged with the drafting of the universal declaration of human rights. she might well have turned in her grave at the recent events in geneva. the election of a libyan chair to the primary un body dealing with human rights has rightly prompted wonderment at how this can be. it may simply be because the election of individuals to the commission on human rights bureau is based on nomination by regional groups: it was the africans' turn to nominate, and they chose an individual from libya. the secret vote called at the behest of the united states led to a common abstention by seven eu member states in the commission on human rights. the strong concern of many in the international community, including the eu, has rightly been registered at what is a significant blow to the credibility of the commission on human rights. the performance of the new chair will undoubtedly be closely scrutinised. it is now time for the eu to focus on the initiatives it will take in the 59th session. the challenges facing the eu constitute a decidedly uphill task. at the 58th session last year we saw the commission of human rights vote down eu initiatives on zimbabwe, chechnya and iran. those results prompted a bout of soul-searching as to how the eu could improve the prospects for its country and thematic resolutions. at the un general assembly – a third committee in new york – several innovations were put in place by the presidency: earlier preparation of drafts, more concise resolutions and improved burden-sharing amongst eu partners. these are important measures because they free up time for lobbying – diplomatic groundwork can, of course, make all the difference between failure and success. it is true that the eu will need all the diplomatic finesse it can muster in geneva when faced with an array of chr members with poor human rights records, many disputing the legitimacy of tabling country resolutions. the eu has rightly defended the need for country resolutions alongside thematic resolutions. in many instances, those resolutions form the basis for the mandates of the special representatives and rapporteur who, when permitted by the country in question, seek to illuminate the human rights difficulties requiring attention. this constructive system is not embraced by the vast majority of the international community, with over 150 states declining to issue a standing invitation to the un special mechanisms. i would add that, in view of this, it is interesting to note that the african nations have agreed to have the african union organise a peer review process which, whilst weaker and different from this, nevertheless represents a step towards arriving at a situation in which some collective measurement of performance in these areas is actually taking place. it is undoubtedly a difficult process to determine which countries should be subject to eu action in the commission on human rights. the eu has sought to develop its approach this year, with the council working group on human rights taking soundings from all relevant geographic working groups in the council as to which countries most warrant attention. discussions are set to continue at the cohom meeting on 5 february 2003. it should be stressed that no final decisions have been taken by the eu, but initiatives on the democratic republic of the congo, sudan, israeli settlements, burma/myanmar and iraq have been provisionally agreed upon and other countries remain under consideration. the european parliament's resolution on priorities for the commission on human rights will constitute an important contribution to that debate, as will the presentation of priorities by ngos at the forthcoming session of the human rights contact group. clearly, the eu's approach to iran and china at the commission on human rights will attract a great deal of interest. the eu is engaged in human rights dialogues with both countries, with the primary aim of achieving concrete progress on the ground. that is why we have designed a set of clear benchmarks to measure results. as the eu guidelines on human rights dialogues make clear, and as we have made fully apparent to the iranian government, such dialogues do not in any way preclude the tabling of resolutions in international human rights fora. that decision must be made on the basis of our assessment of the human rights situation on the ground. at the same time, however, the eu's decision on a resolution cannot be divorced from an assessment of the prospects for progress within the framework of the dialogue. for the first round of dialogue with iran, the initial assessment is cautiously positive. whilst the mandate of the special representative to iran, mr maurice copithorne, disappears with the defeat of the eu's resolution at the 58th commission on human rights, last year iran issued a standing invitation to the un special rapporteurs, and it has announced that it will accept visits by four un thematic rapporteurs during the course of this year. it is worth noting that mr copithorne was not allowed to set foot in the country to implement his mandate, illustrating that, in the face of intransigence on the part of a third country, resolutions do not always secure the progress sought. after a year's absence, the united states returns as a member of the commission on human rights. it is important for the eu and the united states to pursue their common interests in advancing human rights in the often hostile climate at the commission on human rights. it is true that there are several issues on which the united states and the eu do not see eye to eye, including such fundamental advances as the optional protocol to the convention against torture and the international criminal court. those differences should neither be artificially papered over nor allowed to block meaningful cooperation. that is why the eu and the united states have launched regular informal consultations on human rights which complement the existing human rights troika and include scrutiny of the language used in our respective resolutions and the thinking behind our approaches. the next round of consultations is scheduled for 6 february 2003. finally, i welcome the european parliament's intention to send a delegation to the 59th commission on human rights following last year's successful visit, which first of all, i would like to talk about the implementation of the reform. the commission has introduced a number of new instruments, such as activity-based management, the annual policy strategy planning (app) and the annual management plans. in 2002, for the first time, all directors-general submitted annual activity reports, including specifically on financial management. i cannot list all the measures here, but i would like to mention in particular the adoption of the new financial regulation, the drafting and adoption of the implementing rules, including the new financial regulation for the edf and the new financial regulation for the agencies, as the main priorities for 2002. the new financial regulation strengthens the budgetary principles, as the court of auditors has repeatedly pointed out, and i believe that this is essential for a financial regulation. it strengthens the role of the authorising officers and, above all, the responsibility of the various actors in financial operations, the rules for granting grants and contracts, the so-called procurement, are streamlined and harmonised. these are just some of the main points. in 2002, the main focus was again on the decommissioning of the technical assistance offices. we had the opportunity to discuss this at the last meeting of the committee on budgetary control. in addition, in order to make its internal financial management more efficient, the commission, with the support of the budgetary authority, has initiated a wide range of measures to modernise and improve the quality of the public service and has in particular submitted to the council proposals for a revision of the staff regulations. decisions were also taken on administrative and disciplinary measures and the commission's investigation and disciplinary unit (idoc) was set up. the commission has also reorganized its external services - another very important aspect of financial management. country and regional strategy papers have been developed to better align programming with policy priorities and a single entity, europeaid, is now centrally responsible for managing the entire project cycle. the commission has also increasingly delegated the powers of management of external aid to its delegations by means of what is known as decentralisation, in order to ensure a faster and, above all, more appropriate implementation of financial assistance. the second complex i would like to address is the budget surpluses - mr mccartin has also mentioned them. the discrepancy between the estimated payments and the actual payments made in 2001 for the structural funds and the cohesion fund is mainly due to the fact that the start-up phase of the programmes of the new programming period was slower than expected. in addition, the payment forecasts submitted by the member states to the commission are often very optimistic - to put it diplomatically. during the 2002 financial year, the commission reminded the member states on several occasions of their obligations in this respect, stressing in particular the importance of the most reliable estimates possible. i would also like to mention briefly the simplification of the rules on the structural funds, which mr mccartin has just mentioned. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. the commission has taken a number of horizontal and sectoral initiatives to simplify rules and procedures in general, and in the context of an ex ante impact assessment of legislative proposals, the commission will now examine in more detail which are the best regulatory instruments to achieve policy objectives. the commission will also prepare a comprehensive report on the achievement of its objectives, broken down by policy area, and forward it to the council and parliament. the commission has also recently adopted, just before christmas, a communication on improving the recovery of funds wrongly received from the european budget. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept the commission. madam president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you for your report. it is good that we have agreed on this directive. this is an important part of our overall strategy to reduce air pollution and greenhouse gas emissions. with the help of directive 98/70/ec we can ensure that leaded petrol is phased out. once adopted, the new directive will pave the way for the introduction of sulphur-free fuels that will be available throughout the eu by 1 january 2005. sulphur in fuels may reduce the efficiency of several existing and future technological solutions, such as three-way catalysts, oxidation catalysts, nitrogen oxide traps and particle traps. that is why it is so important to phase in sulphur-free fuels. the phasing-in of sulphur-free fuels shall be completed by 1 january 2009. this will enable manufacturers to exploit the full technological potential to reduce emissions of pollutants such as nitrogen oxides and particulate matter, which pose a major threat to air quality and human health. the adoption of this directive is indeed good news for the environment and health in europe. i would therefore like to thank the rapporteur, heidi hautala, and all the members who have contributed to the adoption of this act.

commission. - mr president, the debate you have put on today's agenda on the world economic forum and the world social forum gives me the opportunity to share with you, on behalf of the commission, some reflections on these two events which took place recently in davos and porto alegre respectively. i say reflections rather than observations, because i did not personally participate in either of these events because of a trip to brazil scheduled elsewhere to make contact with the new brazilian president and his government. there has been much echo of the two competing visions of globalisation that would characterize these two forums. however, there are several similarities between these two events. first, they have in common that they were both designed as places of thought and places of influence. secondly, they have in common that they have both been gradually established with a view to influencing economic and political developments on the planet. finally, they have in common that they are both products of a globalisation that they are fuelling, even if the visions of what that globalisation is and should be are different. and these differences exist not only between these two forums, but also within each one. the commission therefore believes that it would be a mistake to analyse these two events solely in terms of their differences, their opposition and their confrontation. it is interesting to note that the main themes of each of these events also have something in common. at the world social forum, for example, debates focused on democratic world order, antimilitarism and the promotion of peace. the theme of davos was 'security and geopolitics'. the debate in porto alegre on what was called principles, values, human rights, diversity and equality is not entirely unrelated to what is called in davos a debate on trust and values. thus, although the terms used are different, there is a certain convergence between these two conferences on the nature of many of the problems affecting our world. i would add that this year some people were even warmly welcomed in both chambers. i am thinking in particular of the new president of brazil, mr lula da silva. it is clear that the world economic forum in davos continues to attract an international elite from the business community, but also from politics, media, ngos now, academia and religious groups. in quantitative terms, this represents 2 000 participants and it is clear that there is a disproportion in relation to the 100 000 people present in porto alegre, themselves five times as many as at the first edition of this forum in 2001. as politicians, we cannot but take a popular expression of such magnitude seriously. this expression, in my view, reflects a deep sense of dispossession that a significant number of citizens in all countries of the world feel towards the process of globalisation. there is a clear message behind all these mobilizations: citizens tell us that they do not want to be subjected to globalization. they want it regulated, they want it controlled, they want it framed, they want it controlled. they want globalization to be a project that does not divide but integrates the entire planet. what is this globalization that we have been talking about so much this year in porto alegre and in davos? at the outset, this globalisation is not a project, it is a movement, it is the product of a convergence of technological, economic or political processes, the pattern of which is becoming increasingly clear before our eyes. i don't think there is a conspiracy behind globalization. there is a logic that is the one that dominates our world: market capitalism. the instability and injustice that have been deplored, both in davos and in porto alegre, are one of the consequences of the efficiency of this market capitalism. in the absence of global regulation and adequate domestic policies, these injustices, instabilities and volatilities are reappearing today, deepening inequalities and, in a number of cases, widening the north-south divide, while continuing to threaten the environment. the commission's position on this is clear. to those on either side who would like us to choose between growth and justice, we say that we refuse to choose between growth and justice or justice and growth. we need both. we must embrace market-based globalisation, because it offers enormous potential for development. however, we must give it a global regulatory framework to ensure that this development is more equitable and sustainable than it is in our eyes. from this point of view, the multilateral negotiations initiated in doha in november 2001 within the wto are part of this dual perspective of opening up markets on the one hand and rules and integration of the countries of the south on the other, by ensuring that they have wider access in practice to the countries of the north, depending on the degree of preferential treatment. this global regulation is, in a way, the synthesis we are trying to achieve between porto alegre and davos. this synthesis is difficult and painful. there are at least two reasons why this is taking so long. the first is that it is in conflict with powerful interests, as illustrated by the ongoing battle in geneva for developing countries' access to essential medicines, which we will discuss further in a moment. the second is that regulation implies, if we are serious, a convergence of collective preferences on issues such as the environment, health, workers' rights, the place of public services or cultural diversity. we know that the discussions on this subject are sometimes heated in this parliament. it is therefore easy to see that addressing these issues in order to reach an international agreement is a long-term undertaking. it is the task of organizations such as the international labour organization, fao, the wto and various environmental, health and cultural diversity standards bodies to reconcile freedom of trade with respect for minimum standards. we must therefore ensure that the multilateral system is developed, strengthened and built more solidly, so as to allow for different acculturations of market capitalism. so developing countries could be pursuing effective, heterodox, catch-up strategies in a number of cases, while we, more advanced economies, could be moving faster along the path of social justice and environmental protection. i believe that this is the message that we europeans have received this year, both from porto alegre and from davos.

developing countries in our concessions and ensure that concessions and therefore disciplines are equitably distributed. there is no question of the union accepting, as a developed country, policy. there is a debate on our positions at the world trade organisation and there is a debate between us on the reform of the common agricultural policy. the reform of the common agricultural policy is not being discussed in geneva, tokyo, washington, sydney or cancún. we debate it amongst ourselves, for reasons that are our own. yes, we are debating in brussels and strasbourg the positions we take in the world trade organisation, but that is the way it is going. it is true that the commission has put on the table a proposal which, if adopted, will bring further reforms in the management of our common agricultural policy. we shall see if and when decisions are taken and, moreover, how many of these decisions we shall use and when we shall use them as negotiating credit. that is not the case at the moment, and i am clearly telling mrs doyle that the 36%, 45% and 55% that franz fischler and i have put on the table, we are now, with the council's approval, doing so within the reforms already adopted and without encroaching on the potential credit for other reforms. so, is what we've put on the table too ambitious or not enough? i think you have all answered this question, some of you thinking that our proposals are not ambitious, others that they go too far. mrs mcnally has indicated that she thinks we could have gone further. to this i reply that i do not believe that, at this stage at least. if every single one of the wto contracting parties would today sign up to the kind of commitment that we have put on the table, we would all have taken a very big step towards better discipline for agricultural subsidies around the world. have we gone too far? that is what i thought i understood when i heard mr hyland's position. i do not think so either, except to consider - and perhaps that is what he means - that we have already gone too far in the reform of the common agricultural policy in recent years. that is not, as you can imagine, the commission's position. mr van dam, mr graefe zu baringdorf and mrs erika mann rightly raised this food security issue, starting from the very fact that in agricultural trade only 10% of production is traded internationally, which is quite different from what happens in other sectors. they are right and that is why we have incorporated a new feature which has been noticed in many places. the concept of food safety, of safeguard clause, of food safety box, which, as i said in my introductory speech, was inspired by various sources, in particular by european non-governmental organizations. i would like to conclude by answering mr mulder. yes, mr mulder, the rules of the 'everything but arms' initiative contain extremely strict requirements as to origin, so that products, and only products, from the least developed countries benefit from the 'zero right, zero quota' that we have decided in their favour. these are very restrictive rules and some of these countries find them too restrictive. so it's good that they are. in conclusion, i would say that we have learned two things from this debate. the first is that mr. martinez may have ontological anxiety, which, in itself, is excellent news. the second is that, for once, he has excellent reasons for having ontological anxieties. i happen to agree with him for once that agriculture is not just about having it but about being it, and i am sure that is also the position of my colleague mr fischler. he is right on this point: agriculture is a commodity that circulates, that we produce, that we find on our plates, or on the plates of others, but it is also a service, which circulates less. the "goods" part is found in the market, in the sales circuits; it's bought and sold. the service part, the part which is made up of safety, the part which is made up of the environment, the part which is made up of welfare, that part does not circulate and is generally poorly remunerated by market mechanisms. it is the coexistence of this goods and services part, it is the coexistence of this circulating part, which we can imagine is subject to the same rules as socks, tyres or shoes, and of a part which is not comparable to the trade in tyres, socks or shoes, that is to say the services part, the part which makes us have a particular relationship with what we eat or produce in our countryside, it is this coexistence which makes the whole difficulty of the subject. it is for this reason, and because this is our concept of agriculture, that we in europe have a balanced position on this point, going in a number of directions, but not to the point of destroying what we consider to be the collective price of agriculture. it is this combination of the two that we will pursue in the discussion and i already tell those of you who are interested or passionate about these issues that i would only see advantages in our taking up this discussion as a whole, and if possible on the whole negotiating programme rather than piece by piece as we did tonight, at some point before cancún. in any case, franz fischler and i are ready for it.
