commission. – madam president, firstly i would like to thank the rapporteur, mr santini, and the committee on citizens' freedoms and rights, justice and home affairs, for this very positive report. the report concerns a long-awaited proposal for a directive which is crucial for facilitating the free movement of persons and which takes into account the work carried out at the end of the 1990s, in particular by the high level panel chaired by mrs simone veil, on citizenship of the european union. this proposal lays down the conditions governing the exercise of the fundamental right of free movement and residence, which is conferred directly to every eu citizen by the treaty and enshrined in the charter of fundamental rights of the european union. in this respect the proposal represents a first step towards defining a strong concept of citizenship of the european union, as confirmed by the basic aim of the proposal. eu citizens should mutatis mutandis be able to move between member states on similar terms as nationals of a member state moving around or changing their place of residence in their own country. in particular the directive should facilitate the exercise of the right to free movement by reducing administrative formalities to what is absolutely necessary, by better defining the situation of family members, by introducing a permanent right of residence after four years of uninterrupted residence in the host member state, and by further restricting the scope for refusing or terminating residence on grounds of public order. the proposal also introduces important innovations by comparison to the existing acquis. in particular it extends from three to six months the period during which citizens are not subject to any formalities other than the possession of a valid identity card or passport. it suppresses the obligation to obtain a residence permit for european union citizens, replacing it with straightforward registration with the competent authorities, which is already the case in some member states. it establishes a system in which the european union citizen has simply to declare that he fulfils the conditions linked to the exercise of the right of residence. finally, it introduces after four years of uninterrupted residence a permanent right of residence which is no longer subject to any conditions. as is rightly underlined in mr santini's report, the right to free movement is still subject today to many obstacles. this has been confirmed in the repeated judgments of the court of justice on the matter. this proposal incorporates the clarifications made by the court's recent decisions and, once adopted, it should considerably simplify the exercise of the fundamental rights of every european citizen.
the commission has also proposed that the council should adopt a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos. (es) madam president, european citizenship was one of the great achievements of the treaty on union adopted in maastricht in 1992. in accordance with the case law of the court of justice, the rights of european citizenship, including the right to move and reside freely within the union, were rights which were inherent in european citizens and whose recognition did not require any legislative development. in accordance with this legal basis, the committee on legal affairs and the internal market considered that there was no reason to introduce administrative restrictions on entry into a country or on freedom of movement and residence. the schengen agreements have made great progress in the area of legislative organisation, but the truth is that some countries are still reluctant to take part in these developments and remain outside them. the committee on legal affairs and the internal market therefore hoped that this proposal for a directive would be a real step forward in removing all administrative and substantive restrictions on the possibility for a community citizen to establish himself in another community country. this was the spirit of the amendments adopted by the committee on legal affairs and the internal market. the amendments of the committee on legal affairs and the internal market were not accepted by the committee responsible, the committee on civil liberties, and the rapporteur would naturally be interested in their being retained, but he did not insist on them, so as not to go against the agreements reached in this area. however, i would like to draw attention to an amendment which could to some extent address these concerns of the committee on legal affairs and the internal market, namely amendment no 23 - which introduces a new article 4b - which says that 'this directive shall not lead to the abolition of existing rights established by union legislation or by decisions of the court of justice of the european communities'. in my view, this amendment is essential if we do not want to reduce the rights of european citizens within the union.
(es) madam president, on behalf of my colleague, carmen cerdeira, who has been the alternative rapporteur for this report and who unfortunately cannot be here, i will try, as far as possible, to speak on behalf of my political group. citizenship of the union - institutionalised and created as such by the maastricht treaty and later modified by the treaty of amsterdam - confers a number of rights and duties on nationals of all member states. it aims to involve citizens in the process of european integration by giving them greater involvement, strengthening the protection of their rights and promoting the idea of a european identity by creating a feeling of belonging to the union among citizens. these citizenship rights and the union as a whole will only have credibility for citizens if they can be applied in the practice of their daily lives. in the context of citizenship of the union, one of the fundamental rights conferred by it is set out in article 18 (1) of the treaty, which confers on every citizen of the union the right to enter, move and reside freely within the territory of the member states. the same right, with virtually similar wording, is conferred on the european citizen by article 45 (1) of the charter of fundamental rights, and this seems to us to be very relevant. these rights are therefore constitutive and not declaratory, i.e. they are acquired independently of the granting or any permit issued by the member states. we welcome the commission's proposal, which we really consider to be a step forward. the movement of citizens of the union between member states should take place, mutatis mutandis, under conditions similar to those for citizens within a state. in fact, madam president, the citizens of the union have internalized this right much more quickly and solidly than their governments. they've internalized it and they're exercising it. i can assure you that in my part of the union, on the coast where i spend several days, there are many european citizens who are illegally resident and who simply go back and forth between their two homes, one in the country of origin and the other in mine, whenever they want and without filling out any paper. it is impossible to prove whether these gentlemen have returned to their home in the last six months, because sometimes it is 60 km from the neighbouring country. the euro will make this even easier and more possible and i hope that we can move in the direction of the commission. that is why my group has tabled amendments which seek to remove once and for all the consideration of the economic status of individuals, giving priority to that of citizens, and to recognise that at this moment citizens and their families, as they are, already exercise freedom of movement within the european union.
commission. – madam president, i wish to begin by thanking the rapporteur, mrs terrón i cusí, and all those who have contributed to this very positive report which we are considering today. by way of the proposed directive, we put forward a framework which, once approved, will lead member states to be open and transparent about their immigration policies. this is very much a step forward. nowadays, member states do not know what each other's immigration policy really is. many of the national immigration policies have in the past been simply conducted by stealth. what the public knows is that those who come in illegally, end up having their situation legalised by member states in one way or another. our proposal is a first step aimed at ending such a pattern. immigrants must be able to come in legally and be given work permits and a set of rights, if there are jobs - and we are increasingly aware that there are - that cannot be filled by the domestic job market. in this respect, it must be pointed out that such rights do not cover the right to stay unemployed in the european union. the proposal further helps to streamline cumbersome procedures and to bring about clarity and legal security. however, as we clearly stated in our communication on migration policy of november 2000, we do not intend to decide by directive the number of immigrants that our economies and societies are prepared to absorb. the proposed directive leaves that decision to the member states who, together with their civil societies and, above all, their local and regional authorities, know how many they are capable of integrating. i therefore emphasise that, as i have always said, this proposal does not allow one single entry of one single immigrant into the labour market of the european union. the commission is certainly not creating a subjective right to immigration. its aim is simply to harmonise the procedure for admission and it believes such harmonisation is necessary. we simply want member states to inform each other and the commission of what is happening so that everybody can learn from each other's experience and find out what the added value of european responses might be. all the more so as we mostly live in a border-free area where decisions affect our neighbours. the european union must primarily mobilise its existing human resources, including migrant workers currently residing legally in the european union. more must be done on training, bringing older people and women into the labour market. in this respect, the proposal gives a clear preference to the domestic labour market. there is, therefore, no incompatibility between the fight against unemployment and the proposal. our unemployed have four weeks in which to show up and take jobs free from the competition of foreign workers. however, given that our unemployed are not always willing or capable, the effect of an ageing population and the related skills gap means that restricting legal migration risks jeopardising our economic health. as i have said before, even if member states were to face labour market shortages, they would be free to cap the total number of migrants they are ready to admit, if they consider, for instance, that their society is already facing too much of an integration burden. immigration numbers are one of our citizens' priorities, and one of the areas where they clearly expect us to tackle the problem at european level. i hope that this debate and its impact on the council will allow us to move forward.
the rapporteur. (es) madam president, we have repeated a thousand times in this house that a comprehensive european immigration policy must be based first on the establishment of legal immigration rules and then on strong instruments to enforce those rules. we are discussing today a proposal for a directive which would be the cornerstone of this policy, a directive on which the council has of course not made much progress. parliament should have spoken long ago, but we are always dragging our feet on these issues. i have chosen this moment to present my report because, for the first time in a long time, the greek presidency has put the issue of legal immigration back on the political agenda, which i welcome. the commission proposal for a directive aims to harmonize the conditions of entry and residence of third-country nationals who wish to enter a member state for the purpose of employment. it allows entry of workers from a third country when a post cannot be filled by a national worker or by a worker from another member state of the union or by a resident of a third country with a right of access to the labour market. the proposal provides for a contract of origin for immigrant workers, except for those who are legally resident in the european union for other reasons. the residence and work permits would be a single document. the adoption of this directive would mean recognition of the need for legal channels for immigration and would create a more transparent framework with simpler procedures, thus making it easier for economic operators and at the same time strengthening the rights of immigrants. i welcome the commission's proposal. i only regret that the commission, no doubt in an exercise of realism, has not been able to reflect in this proposal for a directive some of the ideas it put forward in previous communications, because i sincerely believe that we cannot continue to copy immigration control models tested during the last century, in the height of industrial society, but must be able to imagine new procedures adapted to our world, to a society and a labour market that operate in very different ways from those of the post-war decades. some of the measures considered by the commission, such as mobility, were going in the right direction and reality will force us to return to them. this, madam president, is just an opinion report. i would have preferred to have made a resolution rather than a package of amendments - which will hardly be read or taken into account by anyone with real decisionmaking capacity. but for procedural reasons we have had to table a package of amendments, and these must point to two fundamental issues. firstly, a strong will or a strong signal in favour of a european immigration policy. we need clear rules that can be followed. we have therefore rejected the amendments, especially those tabled by the ppe group, which sought to turn the directive into a kind of recommendation which the member states could or could not comply with. we have also not accepted amendments which introduced requirements other than those of employment and which were difficult to verify. if we accept that the possibility of working is what legitimizes entry and residence in the union, then we must make sure that this system works. by requiring immigrants to have a contract or a firm offer from the source, we are already regulating access according to the labour market. even in a situation of unemployment, this pathway would simply be paralysed. secondly, we must establish rules that can be enforced, thereby encouraging the arrival of immigrants through regular channels and avoiding illegal contracts; preventing immigrant workers from falling into a situation of irregularity, for bureaucratic reasons, once inside the union; and discouraging, to the maximum extent possible, the entry of illegal immigrants. we have sought three things in this connection: that persons who are legally resident in the union, or who are legally present for any reason, or who have entered with a residence permit and have lost it, can regain their legal status and not remain in an irregular situation forever, and that the states can, if they wish, establish a six-month visa to seek employment. we have also introduced the question of strengthening equal conditions for workers, with a view to avoiding any discrimination, and the creation of a second-class labour market, which would be the victim of both immigrants and native workers. we also want to see equal rights and obligations for workers, free movement of workers within the member state - for obvious reasons i do not think we need to go any further - and, in general, to reduce the time and bureaucratic obstacles to the establishment of this immigration policy. as our citizens and their representatives, as employers and trade unions, i hope that we will have clear rules based on criteria of effectiveness and not on ideological problems, which do not help much.

commission. – mr president, the european council of seville of 21 and 22 june 2002 fixed a certain number of priorities in the fight against illegal immigration, and revision of regulation 539/2001 on visas before the end of 2002 was definitely one of them. the commission has a monopoly on initiatives in this field but considered it appropriate to profit from the experience of the member states and collect from them, via a specific questionnaire, relevant information regarding the criteria on the basis of which third country nationals are subject to, or exempt from, visas. the answers of the member states converged essentially on two factors: a significant rise in illegal immigration from ecuador and respect of the reciprocity principle as regards visas. in this last respect, it was noted that certain third countries exempted from visas do not grant, or grant in only a limited way, visa exemptions to nationals of certain member states. taking into account these two aspects, the commission proposed transferring ecuador to annex 1 of regulation 539/2001 which lists the third countries whose nationals are subject to the visa obligation. in addition, we propose to submit a report to the council and the european parliament on the implications of reciprocity as regards visas. the commission is very pleased with the collaboration of the european parliament, which dealt with this proposal promptly, and appreciates very much mr hernandez mollar's report confirming our approach. we congratulate the rapporteur.

(es) mr president, commissioner, the proper management of migration flows by all member states, including the states of origin and transit, the fight against human trafficking mafias and illegal immigration, and the need to reconcile the pressure of immigration with the capacity of the host society, are essential aspects that we have been advocating from many quarters - (es) mr president, with the completion of the process of enlargement and european construction following the convention and the new treaty of 2003, the union will have new frontiers which will require not only a new form of economic, social and cultural partnership and collaboration with these new neighbours, but above all a common foreign and security policy which is firm, far-reaching and effective. the reasons depend on the entity of these new neighbours, from ukraine and georgia to belarus, in which the presence of the giant russia plays a major role. it is therefore a challenge for the european union to decide how to develop relations with these countries. one of these countries, belarus, borders latvia, lithuania and poland and, until 1996, its development had been more or less similar to that of the other former members of the ussr, but since then it has settled into an authoritarian drift restrictive of human rights and democracy, with elements of abusive social control, which prevents the establishment of mechanisms of relationship, association and collaboration such as those developed by the european union with the rest of these countries. so much so that the three european institutions which have followed developments in belarus, the osce, the council of europe and the european union itself - the parliamentary troika - have not hesitated to declare that the events in belarus are incompatible with the minimum democratic requirements and have suspended relations with the republic until those minimum democratic conditions are met. the presentation of this resolution has been considerably delayed by the need to convert an initial draft report on the european union's relations with belarus into an own-initiative resolution by the committee on foreign affairs, because of the worsening conditions for the exercise of democracy and the enjoyment of human rights in that country. in 1995, the european union had prepared an agreement on trade and commercial cooperation based on the one between the ussr and the european economic community which had existed since 1989, and lukashenko's victory had also given rise to some hope. but everything came to a halt when president lukashenko himself put the brakes on the democratization process in 1996. lukashenko's authoritarian trajectory has been characterized by the adoption of mechanisms to harass the opposition, eliminate critical voices and create a client network through the springs of power and, in turn, has attempted a greater rapprochement and dependence on russia, which, recently, putin has curbed. the various electoral processes held since 1996 have been described by the parliamentary troika as lacking in effective guarantees for the exercise of democracy. this has led to the emergence of a democratic opposition platform which has matured and which covers a wide range of parties, from the right to the left - the communist party, for example - which agree on basic aspects such as the implementation of democracy, association and, where appropriate, integration into the european union. in the belarusian society itself, there is a growing awareness of the need for democracy and more and more members of the current belarusian parliament are in favour of democratic reforms that bring the legal framework of freedoms closer to those prevailing in the european union. the recommendations which we, the european union, have to make and which we are proposing in this resolution therefore combine two approaches: on the one hand, the categorical refusal to reach an association at this stage, because it would legitimize the current authoritarian regime and put the achievement of democracy at risk, and on the other hand, an increase in initiatives which would be a clear sign of collaboration and solidarity - for example, those affected by chernobyl - or of cultural, social and trade union rapprochement and which would facilitate the democratic conquest, and this is the direction in which the proposal we are presenting is going. we must not forget the important role that russia can play in this process. i would like to end by thanking the committee on foreign affairs, all its members, for their important cooperation and, finally, it must be acknowledged that, for the reasons i have just mentioned, i do not accept some of the amendments proposed by my own group.

commission. – mr president, first of all, i feel in many respects that i should be taking second place to the honourable member, mr salafranca sánchez-neyra, in discussing this subject, because he has played such an important role in achieving what we are discussing today. he is in a sense - if this is not regarded as blasphemous - the john the baptist for this agreement. we have both had the pleasure in the past of addressing conferences on this subject, speaking on this subject in santiago and elsewhere. it is extremely important to recognise the role that he and other members have played in this important and happy occasion. we are considering today a very important proposal on the adoption of the association agreement that we signed with chile in november last year. this agreement is not only crucial for european union-chile relations, it is also extremely important in the context of latin america as a whole. indeed, the agreement is a very tangible expression of the european union’s willingness to establish a strategic partnership with that continent, despite its present economic problems and its political turbulence and the violence which some countries in the region are still suffering, not least from terrorism - a subject about which the honourable member has understandably expressed considerable concern. we both come from countries that have suffered from mindless and vicious terrorism in the past and our sympathies go out to those countries, like colombia, that are suffering from terrorist madness today. it is more important than ever for us to send a positive signal of support to the region - from the european union to latin america. parliament has played an active and supportive role throughout the negotiation of this agreement. in november 2001, parliament adopted a resolution inviting the commission to conclude the negotiations of the eu-chile agreement at the second eu and latin america and caribbean summit in madrid in may 2002. i am pleased to note that the commission met this objective and managed to negotiate a very ambitious agreement. we worked very closely with the spanish presidency in the first semester of last year to achieve this, and it was a very important step forward. this association agreement is firstly a political agreement – indeed it is important for the european union to establish privileged links with those countries like chile that share common values and objectives. chile, as we know, is a constructive player on the international stage and endorses the same values and policies that we defend in the european union. for example, it is not surprising that last year chile ratified the kyoto protocol. there are many other examples. we certainly want to deepen the political dialogue with chile and to define converging positions on issues of common interest. i am pleased that chile is keen on closer political relations with the european union. this is shown in the almost unanimous support that the chilean congress gave to the agreement in january, less than two months after the agreement was signed in brussels. the european union-chile agreement is also a comprehensive free trade agreement which, according to the very important sustainable impact assessment study carried out by the commission, should generate additional growth for chile’s gdp of about 0.5% and which should contribute to raising the standard of living of the chilean people. the european union has been for a long time chile’s first trade partner; this agreement should further consolidate and increase our trade relations. let me point out as an example that after only two years of implementation, the eu-mexico agreement - which in many respects set the pattern for the eu-chile agreement - has already led to an increase of 28% in bilateral trade. the agreement should allow us to overcome obstacles and to build an operating framework for entrepreneurs which allows more predictability, confidence and bigger trade flows. not only did chile and the european union agree to liberalise gradually over 97% of our bilateral trade in goods, but we also agreed on a whole set of rules to facilitate trade, on the establishment of a free trade area in services, on the liberalisation of investment and on the reciprocal opening of government procurement markets. the bulk of the trade chapter entered into force on 1 february; i trust that entrepreneurs and consumers on both sides will soon reap the benefits of the agreement. however, the eu-chile partnership will extend well beyond politics and trade: it will intensify our cooperation in a number of areas and stimulate social, economic and environmental development. the cooperation strategy devised jointly for the period 2000-2006 with the chilean authorities may need to be adapted so as to take into account rather better the recommendations of the sustainable impact assessment study and to accompany the implementation of the agreement. let me say a final word about the institutional framework of this association agreement. the agreement singles out the need for an increased involvement of civil society - this should materialise through regular meetings of representatives of chilean and european civil societies so as to allow an exchange of views on the implementation of the different parts of the agreement. i would also like to highlight the establishment in the agreement of an association parliamentary committee, which will be a discussion forum for members of the european parliament and members of the chilean congress. i hope that honourable members of this parliament will participate actively in this committee. judging by the enthusiasm with which they have pressed us to make this agreement, that should be no problem. once again, i would like to thank parliament for the leadership it has shown in this issue. i am sure the beneficiaries will be not only the people of the european union and chile but also the overall relationship with such an important and dynamic continent.
the rapporteur. (es) mr president, commissioner, i would first of all like to thank the political groups in this house for their collaboration in the preparation of this report, which was unanimously adopted by the committee on foreign affairs, human rights, common security and defence policy, and i would like to stress this collaboration precisely because it is not a very frequent occurrence. secondly, i congratulate the commission on the impeccable negotiation of this association agreement with chile - as commissioner patten reminded us - taking up the suggestions made by the european parliament as regards the timetable and overcoming the difficulties involved in the negotiating directives. commissioner patten asked us to trust his judgment in overcoming the shortcomings in the timetable and the facts have proved him right. the result, mr president, is that we are faced with the most innovative, ambitious and comprehensive agreement the european union has ever concluded with a third country which is not a candidate for accession. the commission itself has rightly described it as an agreement for the 21st century, an agreement of the fourth generation plus. i think we should be pleased that this agreement has been concluded with a country like chile, because this agreement is in some ways a recognition of the high civic maturity of the citizens of that country and their strong commitment to openness and trade. as commissioner patten said a moment ago, this agreement is also a message of hope to a region which is currently going through a difficult situation: instability in venezuela, crisis in argentina, the hopes and challenges raised by the election of president lula da silva in brazil, poverty in the subcontinent and also the phenomenon of violence in colombia. i would like to thank mr patten in particular for his words, who will also be sending a message of solidarity on behalf of our institution, the european parliament, to the colombian authorities for the attack which caused many deaths in bogotá last weekend. this agreement - as the commissioner very rightly pointed out - is in line with the association agreement with mexico, which has indeed led to an increase in trade since its entry into force, and it is an agreement which goes far beyond these requirements, since it provides for a 100% liberalisation of trade, going far beyond the forecasts set out in the negotiations of the world trade organisation. i would like to stress one aspect which i consider particularly relevant, namely that chile has concluded this association agreement with the european union before finalising its agreement with the united states. i would also point out that the commission has stated that this agreement goes beyond commercial logic, since the association agreements seek to establish a strategic partnership based on the principles and rights deriving from the democratic clause for both parties. this agreement is very rich in terms of trade liberalization. it covers almost 100% of products, not just agricultural products but all kinds of products, it lays down provisions on agreements and technical clauses, it lays down the greatest liberalization ever in an agreement in the services sector and it also lays down, mr president, the most generous treatment ever granted to a third country by chile, and for the first time in the negotiations with the european union, it lays down the accessibility of foreign investors in an agreement of this kind. i believe that this agreement completes the network of agreements currently being negotiated. the only one left is mercosur, and we are waiting for the negotiating directives for the political dialogue and cooperation agreements with the andean and central american community, which we hope - as parliament has repeatedly called for - can be transformed into association agreements. i believe that this will enable us, mr president, to respond to the difficult situations in which some latin american countries find themselves and to build a broad network of relations between our two regions which could culminate - this is parliament's wish - in the next summit of heads of state in mexico, and we hope that these agreements will pave the way for a strategic and bi-regional partnership which can give rise to the global partnership we seek. this agreement, mr president, therefore covers the geographical links between the two regions, which are called to be political, commercial and strategic partners, and increases the tools with which to respond to the challenges and uncertainties posed by the globalised world in which we live. i would like to thank all the political groups for their positive and constructive cooperation in the adoption of this assent to the association agreement.
(es) mr president, commissioner, i would first of all like to express the satisfaction of the group of the european people's party - and my own in particular - at the conclusion of this association agreement between the community and its member states and chile, the most ambitious, innovative and comprehensive agreement ever negotiated by the european union with a non-candidate country, in the words of the european commission itself, along the lines of what, as has already been said, should be the bi-regional strategic partnership between the european union and latin america proposed by this parliament. i also want to and must congratulate mr salafranca on the work he has done to make this work a reality and the commission for the efforts and the direction it has given to the conclusion of this agreement, which was started practically as soon as chile regained its rights and freedoms, and which would not have been possible without the political vision and tenacity shown by the chilean leaders, from president elwin to the current president, president lagos, and which reflects the will of chile and that of the european union and its member states to establish privileged relations in the political, commercial and cooperation fields covered by the agreement and to strengthen the ties, the fruit of shared values, that bind them together. in the context of market liberalisation, the benefits that economic and trade relations based on reciprocity can bring to economic growth and sustainable development are undeniable, as are the benefits of political dialogue aimed at promoting democracy and developing common responses to the major challenges of the new millennium. i am therefore convinced that this agreement - to which my group will give a resounding yes - is a very positive step not only for relations between chile and the european union but also for the economic and social well-being of the chilean people as they walk down the path of democracy, which has so far been so exemplaryly recovered, and that it should serve, indeed serves, as an example to latin america in these difficult times that some of its countries are experiencing.
(es) mr president, commissioner, we must congratulate ourselves on the establishment of this agreement between the european union and the republic of chile and i think it is right to congratulate the rapporteur, mr salafranca, on his efforts and the results achieved. it is a very broad agreement which will undoubtedly increase trade between the european union and chile, and that is a positive thing, precisely at a time when latin america is going through particularly difficult times in many of its states. it should be noted that all import duties from chile on industrial products will be capped in 2006 and that in the agricultural sector this will occur in 2012. the agreement also opens up wide possibilities in the areas of services and financial services, as well as in all investment-related matters. it is also good that it includes a protocol on fishing companies. i have read the report of the international federation for human rights on the indigenous populations in chile. they account for 4.4% of the total population, or 13%, depending on the statistical source. among these populations the mapuche people are, by percentage, the most important. the problems of the indigenous population are related to logging and the construction of large hydroelectric dams. it should be remembered that these problems were aggravated extraordinarily during the period of the pinochet dictatorship. we welcome the fact that the report makes explicit references to the protection of human rights and that it specifically mentions the rights of indigenous minorities. we hope that this agreement will facilitate greater transparency and mutual understanding, and that it will also recognise the rights of indigenous peoples. finally, as a citizen of catalonia, i cannot help thinking of the welcome that chile once gave to catalan exiles who came fleeing the franco dictatorship.
mr president, most of the previous speakers have praised this agreement, the rapporteur first. i wish i could add my voice to that almost unanimous chorus, but i must confess i am puzzled. the real question, the only question worth asking, is this: will this agreement make the people of this state less poor, better educated, better cared for tomorrow? will they be able to surf the internet or travel if they wish? i'm not sure. there is one people, at least, who have doubts like me, and that is the mapuche people. firstly, the chilean government has not yet ratified the ilo's indigenous peoples convention 169. multiple acts of arbitrary police violence against indigenous communities often go unpunished. secondly, the agreement states that one of the principles that inspired it is that of sustainable development, while the mapuche land is suffering from blind exploitation of its natural resources: deforestation and construction of dams that flood ancestral lands, as a result of national hydrological plans. finally, i am not sure that the all-round liberalism of the agreement will allow the harmonious development of the economies of this state. economic and monetary dependence can lead to an argentinization of the country. those are the risks and those are my doubts. i'll abstain on this agreement.
commission. – mr president, this debate has been slightly livelier than some of us might have anticipated. i would associate myself entirely with mr linkohr's remarks in response to mr lang, who may be living on the right planet, but it is certainly a different planet to the one i live on. speaking for the bureaucratic superstate, i should like to respond firstly to mr sakellariou on the important point which he raised about the international criminal court. he will know that chile participated actively in the preparatory work on the statute of the international criminal court. on 22 january last year the chilean chamber of deputies approved the text with a large majority, but the senate asked for the opinion of the constitutional court in chile. that court indicated that it was necessary to modify the chilean constitution before approving the treaty. since modifying the constitution is a lengthy procedure, as it requires a two-thirds majority in congress, the treaty cannot yet be ratified. however, ratification of the treaty remains high on the political agenda of the chilean government, since it is entirely consistent with its external policy of promotion of respect for human rights. if there is one country which should understand the arguments for the international criminal court, as the honourable member and i would agree, it is chile. he also said that he hoped that as a member of the security council the chilean government would try to coordinate its response to the crisis in iraq with european member states. i hope he does not regard it as lèse-majesté on my part to say that i hope the member states of the european union will try to coordinate their policy in the security council in dealing with this terrible crisis in iraq. (applause)there is article 19 of the treaty and there is the maastricht treaty, but perhaps i should not be drawn down these boulevards. it is interesting that in the convention we are discussing how much further we can go in coordinating a common foreign and security policy when we are not even using and implementing the provisions of the maastricht treaty. in any case, i am using what he said about chile merely as a trigger to fire off some of my thoughts on this subject. several honourable members raised the question of indigenous peoples, which is always a particularly important issue on these occasions. difficult as these issues are, the chilean government is trying to handle them in a sensitive and democratic way. they have set up a public agency to try to handle some of these challenges. they have taken at least 16 concrete measures to help deal with some of the problems, of which members have been informed. my view is that we can help with the efforts that the chilean government is already taking through, for example, co-operation projects that are paid for by the funds voted by this parliament. on the question of fisheries – and i realise what a controversial issue this can be – i should like to remind members who have spoken that the association agreement does not include a fisheries agreement, although we would be interested in concluding one. there is the protocol, which has been referred to. community fishing companies will be allowed to own up to 100% of chilean fishing companies. however, that is under exactly the same conditions as chilean investors. that implies that they will have to respect, for example, the catch quotas defined in chilean laws. there is an elaborate regulatory framework in chile to address the issue of stock depletion since a serious decline in catch levels of certain species, mostly due to over-fishing, was registered toward the end of the 1990s. it is not right to say that the implementation of the agreement will lead to over-exploitation of fishing resources. the current dynamism of the artisanal fishing sector in chile is something all of us should recognise, and it needs to be underlined in debating these matters. this sector is the main supplier of seafood products to the domestic fresh fish market. it currently provides 25% of export income from fisheries products. a significant increase in the artisanal fishing sector has been recorded over the past years, and the interests of the sector have been preserved in the recently adopted fisheries law. if there is to be a loss of artisanal fishing employment in the long term – and this may well happen since artisanal fishing is a highly labour intensive, but not capital intensive business – it would probably occur with or without the agreement we are discussing today. without any reservation whatsoever, i commend this agreement to the chamber. i am sure that the vice-president of the commission would also warmly endorse all that we are trying to achieve with this important agreement. once again, i wish to thank mr salafranca sánchez-neyra and his colleagues, mr linkohr and others, who have taken such an active interest in this matter. this is a model of this sort of agreement. it is the sort of agreement that will not impoverish the world, that will not bring people the 'joys' of north korean economics – which some people endorse – but that should make the world a more prosperous place, that should ensure that we better protect our environment and that we have greater political stability than would otherwise be the case.

validity. we are looking - i repeat - for a transitional regime so that austria, which is in the eco-points system, can join the other 14 countries - 24 within a few months - in a common system and - question no 46 by mr sacrédeus (h-0902/02) subject: demographic issues, family composition and working life for several years now, the number of people who have stopped working because of illness has been increasing dramatically in sweden and there are also signs of a worrying trend in other member states of the european union. at the same time, the birth rate in european countries is lower than ever and, therefore, a considerable decline in population is to be expected over the next 50 years, particularly in germany, italy and france. as the population ages, the financial balance of pension and social security schemes will become increasingly difficult to maintain. the european summit in stockholm in march 2001 had identified demographic issues as one of the union's priorities for the future. what lessons can be drawn from this worrying development and what initiatives has the commission taken to promote a better overview of family composition, birth rates, demographic issues, the increasing number of people withdrawn from work for reasons of illness and the sustainability of pension schemes?
the commission. i agree with you that at the moment, the integration of older workers over 55 into the labour market is an urgent need in europe. the numbers are really disturbing. in europe, only 37% of those over 55 are in the labour market. for years in most countries early retirement has been a tool for restructuring. this has taken a large proportion of the workforce out of the labour market and, of course, because of the current restructuring of the information society, unemployment is hitting these ages first and foremost. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. this is an economic approach and a necessity in too many countries, but at the same time we cannot raise the retirement age without having specific policies and incentives, as you said, so that these people can enter the labour market. that is why, at least at european level, in the employment strategy, and now in the review of the strategy we have made, we are putting the over-55s as one of the priorities. there is the barcelona target, whereby all countries have committed themselves to reaching 50% by 2010, so that people over 55 are in the labour market up to 50%, and secondly, all countries have committed themselves to ensuring that in their training policy and lifelong learning policies, they have percentages that are relevant to people over 55, that is, that there are incentives, tax incentives or subsidies, to get these people into the labour market. and of course there is the large social sector, which you mentioned, where someone is not full-time, but provides social services with some specific motivations. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the social partners are able to take part in the work of the european social fund.

commission. – it is my pleasure to be here, particularly when the discussion is so interesting and there are so many participants. the provisions of the recently adopted directive 2002/73/ec define for the first time, in a binding community text, harassment on the basis of sex and sexual harassment as discrimination in the work place and, therefore, prohibit them. moreover, member states have to take the necessary measures to encourage employers to prevent harassment and sexual harassment in the work place. these provisions concern the private and public sectors and include the armed forces. the new directive reinforces protection for victims of discrimination based on sex with specific provisions reflecting the case-law of the court. in order to comply with the provisions of this directive, all member states, including spain of course, will have to take implementing measures and bring them into force by 5 october 2005 at the latest. by this date, these measures, including those on harassment and sexual harassment, should also cover the armed forces. member states should guarantee by this date that all necessary measures have been taken to eliminate discrimination on the basis of sex in all matters covered by this directive.

commission. – mr president, because the directive has yet to be implemented, the commission cannot operate in an effective way. i believe that it is very important to tell the minister about a very specific instrument that he can use before the implementation of the legislation. this instrument is the code of practice of the commission, annexed to the commission's 1991 recommendation. it is a code of practice concerning the need to prevent sexual harassment or harassment in the workplace. it envisages specific policy measures. these include informing workers, communicating to workers the main messages; training them; training the middle managers on this issue and then taking responsibility. the employer must take the responsibility for creating an environment which prevents sexual harassment. the employer must give the employee the opportunity and the right to complain and to discuss with a particular person in management his or her particular problem. they can put in place these first steps to prepare the armed forces for the implementation of the directive. it will be a pleasure for me to send the code of practice to the minister. it may be helpful to the armed forces in spain.

commission. – mr president, let me first thank the rapporteur, mrs redondo, for her report concerning the commission's 'forest focus' proposal for a regulation on monitoring of forests and environmental interactions the proposal aims to contribute to the protection of the community’s forests by means of monitoring. it builds on the achievements of the two council regulations on the protection of the community's forests against air pollution and fires, which expired at the end of last year. however, the proposal broadens the scope to include new environmental issues such as biodiversity, climate change, carbon sequestration and soils. the protection of forests and the enhancement of their multifunctional role are matters of particular importance and urgency in the union. the community and the member states are committed to implementing internationally agreed activities and to set up monitoring and reporting systems. sound political decisions have to be based on reliable information. we need harmonised and comprehensive long-term monitoring of forests at community level. it is essential in order to provide information on the temporal and spatial variation in the condition of forests. experience from the previous forest monitoring scheme shows that the harmonisation of data collection is of major importance. there are two key issues which deserve special attention. firstly, comitology. the report considers whether the principle of subsidiarity needs to be reinforced in the context of forest focus, and proposes strengthening the role of member states in the proposed monitoring scheme. experience from the previous community scheme shows that close cooperation between the commission and the member states is indeed needed to set up an efficient monitoring scheme. that is why the commission proposed strengthening the comitology arrangements by incorporating a management committee. this is an approach which balances the evident need for greater involvement of the member states, whilst being proportional to what, in community terms, is a relatively modest scheme. our view is that the characteristics of the scheme proposed closely fit the criteria for management committees set out in the council decision on comitology. secondly, i would like to address the important aspect of forest fire prevention measures. fires have affected forests in many parts of the community, but in particular in the southern parts of the community. the commission takes this seriously and will ensure that all forest fire related measures introduced by the now lapsed council regulation (eec) no 2158/92 will continue to be covered in future by community legislation. the proposal for 'forest focus' and the regulation on rural development together meet these requirements. the activities that were not already covered by the provisions of the regulation on rural development, such as specific studies, and the forest fire information system, are now addressed by 'forest focus'. the commission fully understands parliament's concerns, which are reflected in those amendments concerning forest fire prevention measures. however, the commission regrets that the incorporation of forest fire prevention measures within the 'forest focus' proposal cannot be accepted. our two institutions share the objective of preventing forest fires, but this duplication of measures already covered by the rural development regulation would lead to legal and budgetary uncertainty which may impede our attainment of those objectives. i should like to reassure members that the approach proposed by the commission will allow the continuity of the forest fire prevention measures. the commission has already urged member states to incorporate any necessary amendments to their national or regional rural development plans. the question of the budget increase is linked to the issue of fire prevention measures. it follows that just as the commission does not support additional fire prevention measures within the proposal, nor does it support the proposed budget increase.
the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. the forest focus replaces two regulations which were in force until december 2002 and whose legal basis, which was changed from the old article 130 to the current article 175, was changed on 25 february. that is to say, it was passed by codecision. this report looked at both fire protection and air pollution and will now include actions on biodiversity, climate change and carbon sequestration. actions under the sixth framework programme for environmental action which the european commission and the community are obliged to implement. the proposal, however, removes the bulk of the fire prevention measures in the old regulation (eec) no 2158/92. now, the commissioner has just told us that these measures are included in the rural or regional development programmes he mentioned. i have to tell you that the member states have already submitted the plans for the rural development regulation, which was adopted in 2000, but they have not been able to take account of the fire prevention plans. it does not therefore seem serious to ask the member states to guess that in 2003 or at the end of 2002, as it should have been, this parliament and the commission will be debating the replacement of the regulation and that it was to be transferred to the rural development programme and, moreover, that it was to be transferred with a budget reduction of eur 5 million, because this amount does not appear in the rural development programme. it will therefore have to appear to balance the 2002 budget. that's 18 million a year. now, commissioner, we are spending 18 million euros. this is what has been balanced and consolidated in 2002. the commission proposes €13 million. it does not seem serious that we want to take the same measures, plus those relating to biodiversity, climate change and carbon sequestration, with such a significant reduction in the budget. i think that there has been a great deal of effort, both by the council and by this parliament, to reach a transactional agreement, with transactional measures ending in 2006. it seems that the commission has not been able to reach this agreement. i am very sorry, commissioner, but this is a regulation which is decided by codecision in this parliament and therefore i think that the proposal which was on the table at the time has been withdrawn by this rapporteur in amendment no 44 so that we can all discuss it on equal terms. i think we all have to make a move here, it is not just a matter of this parliament making a move. the rapporteur accepts amendment no 48 from the amendments tabled by the group of the party of european socialists. amendment no 47 cannot, however, be accepted, because it would be contrary to the spirit of this report. there are other amendments tabled by the rapporteur: two of them are legal clarifications, and a third one in which we simply want to introduce into the article the idea already included in the recitals of extending the scope of the european forestry information system. i would have liked to have introduced some more ideas, such as the idea of prioritizing some methodological projects and also enhancing the 'old' activities, so to speak, and not just as proposed in the new modules. i also think that the most advisable periodicity should be the annual one, in which there is a forward-looking part, which needs to take into account the frequent interactions by the experts. i think it is not a good idea to both the budget and the harmony of these regulations. i think we have an obligation to do that.

- the next item is the report (a5-0063/2003) by mr friedrich, on behalf of the committee on economic and monetary affairs, on the recommendation of the european central bank concerning a council decision amending article 10.2 of the statute of the european system of central banks and of the european central bank (6163/2003 - c5-0038/2003 - 2003/0803 (cns)).
the commission - mr president, i will be brief. i think there are two different issues in the debate. the first is the system proposed by the central bank on the basis of the application of the enabling clause: is it logical or is it not logical and can there be a better system? second, what system could be better? it could be the one in the friedrich report or any other. however, what we are talking about now is the use of the enabling clause, established in nice, which governments put forward to authorize the central bank to make a proposal which has to be approved unanimously or a proposal from the commission which also has to be approved unanimously. the enabling clause only allows either for all members of the central banks to be present and all to vote, or for a limited voting system to exist which necessarily has to be a rotation model. obviously, if there is a rotation pattern, it means that not everyone is involved in everything, and the problem that arises is what is the rotation pattern. the central bank has proposed a model in which, without any doubt, a certain balance is established between some countries and others in accordance with their economic and financial dimension and which, logically, gives a very important role, in accordance with this dimension, to the smallest countries. the commission considers, however, that this rotation system is not sufficiently justified and has therefore only proposed to amend this rotation scheme. what has the commission done? propose to use only and exclusively the criteria currently held by the central bank to define its voting system. it's true that this system changes with respect to everyone's presence, but that's what the enabling clause allows. it was not worthwhile to make an additional proposal for another rotation model, instead of making an amendment to the proposal of the central bank. what you are saying is that the enabling clause does not solve our problems, that we want to go to a more ambitious position. i understand perfectly well that this has been the commission's position in some cases. but if we vote or decide on the basis of the use of the enabling clause, then obviously the proposal of the central bank, with certain amendments, can be perfectly useful and solves the transition problem that could arise. any other model - let us not forget - also requires unanimity and ratification and will not be an easy model to implement.

- the agenda calls for the commission's statement on 'the neighbours of an enlarged europe: a new framework for relations with the eastern and southern neighbours'. ladies and gentlemen, i'm here to inform you of a slight change in our schedule. we shall now move on to the commission's statement and the debate will continue until 5.45 p.m., at which time we shall move to question time.
president of the commission. mr president, i will make a very brief comment on the document on neighbourhood policy presented today: the european council in madrid in december last year adopted a resolution on the future of the european union. the enlargement process has indeed generated great expectations in our neighbouring countries, but it has also generated frustrations, tensions that can be summed up in some very clear remarks, very understandable to the eastern countries excluded from enlargement. they have reproached us for simply moving the iron curtain eastwards; the mediterranean countries have reproached us for turning our attention mainly to the east and not to the mediterranean countries. our neighbours have high expectations and i have always believed that they cannot be disappointed, but that we should also formulate a serious policy towards them, in their interests and in the interests of the union. the communication on neighbourhood policy adopted by the college today responds to this need to create a framework within which to develop ever closer relations with our neighbours to the east and south; the european union is a great example of the kind of cooperation that can be achieved by the european union, and i think that the european union should be able to do that. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. the ambition is to develop a policy for those countries which require a special relationship with the union but for which the union does not envisage an enlargement strategy, at least in the near future. in this context, therefore, it is clear that the countries of the western balkans are not included, for which the prospect of enlargement, although the date is not yet known, has already been agreed. the framework we have outlined in the communication is complementary to, and not a substitute for, the union's relationship with any single country or group of countries. the intensity and, above all, the speed with which relations between the union and the individual countries will develop within this framework will obviously be adapted to the capacities of the individual country, i.e. the principle of differentiation will also apply here. the aim is twofold: first, to create, together with our partners, an area of prosperity and stability, based on the principle of economic integration, the strengthening of political links and cultural cooperation, and on the latter - cultural cooperation - i insist; secondly, to link the development of these preferential relations to the progressive approximation of these countries to our rules and values, both in the economic and political fields. we therefore want to develop, with each country, on the basis of experience and our existing contractual links, an agreed action plan outlining the path we intend to take together. these action plans will contain objectives, timetables, methods and monitoring mechanisms involving both sides on an equal footing. in this context, we will therefore consider the possibility of creating a specific contractual instrument, the neighbourhood agreement, and an ad hoc financial instrument, the neighbourhood instrument. in concrete terms, we will work with our neighbours to create a single market, promote the free movement of people, goods and services, strengthen cooperation in tackling common threats, strengthen our cooperation in conflict prevention and crisis management, promote human rights, intensify dialogue between cultures and religions, integrate transport, energy and telecommunications networks and create a wider research area: the european union is a great example of the european union's ability to act in a democratic way.
commission. – mr president, we have just had an extremely interesting discussion in the commission in which the leitmotif of most of the contributions - the strongly-held argument of most of those who spoke - was that it was absolutely imperative that we give the question of the relationship with our new neighbours the priority which in the past we have given the whole process of enlargement; that, in other words, it becomes part of everybody's responsibility to promote the concept of an institutionalised ring of friends to whom we can offer ways of sharing in our security, stability and prosperity. the honourable member will see from the communication we are publishing today the practical ways in which we try to give expression to this notion. it is not easy. we have tried it in the past. to some extent it has been like the philosopher's stone; we have never quite found a way of expressing our views about our neighbours that does not involve offering them all membership of the european union. that is not the subject of this communication. however, the honourable member will see from our proposals that we have put forward sensible and concrete ways in which we can encourage our neighbours, both on our land and our sea borders, to share in our market, to share in our policies, not to share in our institutions but to share in the prosperity and political stability which have been the hallmark of the european union. the simple answer to his question is that there is no disagreement. the commission believes that this is a responsibility for the whole commission and that responsibilities will have to be shared between us.

commission. – mr president, i think the house is going to have the benefit of the president after the external affairs commissioner has made one or two points. firstly, i should like to assure mr beazley that there is no question of us seeking to create another iron curtain in europe. indeed, part of the intention of this communication is to prevent any notion of a fortress europe being created with the 25 member states. when one talks about easing visa regimes, it is important to consider the conditions under which interior ministers are likely to regard that as a tolerable option. one of the things that they look at is not simply the border between the country making the application and europe, but the other borders for which that country is responsible. when, for example - i hope after we have concluded a re-admission agreement with the russian federation - we begin discussing the question of visas, one question which will be raised again and again is the security of the thousands of kilometres of borders which russia has with other countries. there are a number of conditions precedent to any serious discussion of visas. the honourable member also asked whether we were going to try to involve the applicant countries which have not yet joined, and whether we were involving those countries in the debate. we have the democratic process to go through, as the honourable member said a moment ago, but the simple answer is 'yes, we are'. a number of applicant countries, for example poland with its recent discussion document on the eastern dimension, have made very sensible and thoughtful proposals. from april the candidates for accession will be sitting in the meetings of the general affairs and external relations councils and listening to the debates, so i hope that will inform their contributions in due course. i am aware of mr tannock's concern about the ukraine which he has expressed on a number of occasions. as mr prodi said, this document itself is not a definition of the geographical boundaries of the european union, but i hope that our friends in the ukraine will recognise the real efforts that we have made to help create a common political and economic space which will be to their advantage. i would wish that we were able to have a closer and more benign relationship with belarus. it is not our fault that does not exist. the honourable member knows the style, objectives and policies of the regime in belarus which led to the unfortunate visa ban not long ago. at the moment we can still provide belarus with support for civil society developments, and i look forward to the day - perhaps after the next elections if they are conducted freely and fairly - when we can develop our relationship with that country. we do not want any country on our borders to be isolated by its own will, or by the will of its regime. i have attempted to answer the honourable member's point about a buffer zone. one has to take account of all the borders of other countries. finally, i say to the honourable member - whose interest in these matters i readily acknowledge - that he should recognise that many of us believe passionately that when we discuss enlargement we are not just talking about a matter of money. we are not just talking about commercial, economic or even geostrategic interests. for many of us the case for enlargement is a moral one. the honourable member should not worry too much if we think it is worth expressing that case as vigorously and as comprehensively as possible. though i have intervened in their debate myself, i do not believe that the people of malta, who have a certain reputation for courage and independent-mindedness, are likely to be swayed by the occasional advertisement in one of their newspapers, or even, i must confess, by the occasional interview with the commissioner for external relations. they might be much more swayed by interviews with the commissioner for enlargement who has a much more silver tongue than i do, but i hope, as this democratic process rolls across europe, that the honourable member will see one country after another voting to come home. president of the commission. just two additional remarks because the commissioner has given a broad answer to almost all the problems. i insist . this offer, this proposal, this political project does not imply enlargement for these countries, it does not imply membership of the union: it does not imply or exclude that. i would also like to say very clearly that i do not accept - that is, i accept to a certain extent - that the assumption of membership of the union helps the democratic process, helps the internal development of these countries. i am very pleased about this, it is useful, but it is certainly not enough to judge whether a country should be a member of the union or not. membership of the union also means sharing specific political objectives, sharing roots, sharing identities, sharing much more than just democratic sentiments. this was my observation about new zealand: i never said new zealand is more european than ukraine. i simply said - and i repeat - that if we look only at democratic criteria, i see no reason why new zealand cannot be part of the union. but there are geographical, historical facts, there are political objectives to be shared in order to be members of the union. so it is clear that this perspective must be given when these objectives emerge, become strong and are shared by them, but they are also shared by us. that explains my anxiety to see the debate on the union's borders opened up. finally, i would like to reassure mr flautre that the objective is precisely the opposite of what has rightly been highlighted as a danger, namely the creation of detention centres for immigrants from these countries. the immigration aspect has a different ethical content: with cooperation with these countries, the issue of immigration can also be dealt with in a more humane, more serious, more shared and less traumatic way. it is clear that this can only be done through the circle of friends, whereas we know that immigrants are now coming to europe from countries that are very far away. it is extremely important to have a group of countries with which we can cooperate also in these sensitive matters, and it is our task, of course, to ensure that this happens in a way which respects the rights of immigrants. it is much easier to achieve this objective when there is cooperation than when there is no cooperation.

- question no 50 by mr newton dunn (h-0095/03): subject: press announcement of national quotas for football players in the esui british newspapers, some of which are known for their inaccuracy and sensationalism in their statements about the eu, are believed to have reported that "an agreement is in sight between uefa and the european union" to limit the number of "foreign" players in each team to 50%. some football clubs in the member states of the union may therefore be obliged to form teams comprising at least 50% of nationals of the member state concerned. could the commission confirm that this information is inaccurate, as such an agreement is contrary to the fundamental principle of free movement of eu citizens?
commission. – the commission is not aware of the united kingdom press reports to which the honourable member refers. as far as any enforced limit on the number of foreign players is concerned, i should like to recall the following. the application of the community rules on the free movement of workers in sport was decided by the european court of justice in the 1974 walrave case, in which the court held that sport was subject to community law when it constitutes an economic activity, whether by professional or amateur athletes. this was confirmed by the court in its now famous 1995 judgment in the bosman case. in this case-law the court also held that nationality clauses could only be justified in relation to specific official matches between teams representing countries - such as the olympic games - or certain world or european championships.

the commission is not prepared to accept the amendments tabled by the committee on budgets. the subject of your oral question is exactly the same as that of a formal complaint which we have received. the formal complaint was lodged by the media observatory czech republic and the company media print & kappa pressegrosso joined the complaint. the case concerned alleged infringements of ec competition law in the czech republic. i myself and the eu delegation in prague have also been made aware of the matter through contacts with the chairman of media observatory czech republic. and i can tell you that immediately afterwards i had the opportunity to raise this issue with the czech government at the highest level. the commission considers, provisionally, that the czech competition authorities and courts have primary jurisdiction in the matter, as it concerns mainly distortions of competition on the czech print media market. the commission services have nevertheless contacted the czech competition authority. the czech supervisory authority is currently investigating the case and has recently issued a provisional injunction against prvni novinova spolecnost and its parent company for possible infringements of czech competition law. i hope i pronounced that right. i'm not sure. czech is a difficult language! the enforcement of the legislation by the czech competition authority will be closely monitored before accession and the commission will continue to follow the matter in this context.

- question no 56 by mrs van lancker (h-0125/03) subject: accession negotiations with slovakia and the roma minority in its resolution of 20 november 2002 (paragraph 114), the european parliament called on the slovak government to take decisive action to overcome the problems of discrimination against roma minorities and to eliminate possible discriminatory practices by public institutions and authorities. at the end of january 2003, the centre for reproductive rights published an investigation report stating that cases of forced sterilisation of roma women were found in the slovak health system. does the commission share the view of the author of this question that these practices constitute a violation of the copenhagen criteria and of articles 1, 3, 4 and 7 of the charter of fundamental rights of the european union? will it call on the slovak government to carry out a thorough investigation and take action against these practices of forced sterilization, which constitute a serious violation of human rights?
the commission is not prepared to accept the amendments tabled by the committee on budgets. i am a little surprised by your question, because there is hardly a subject on which i have reported to the european parliament so often as the situation of the roma in the slovak republic, the czech republic, hungary, bulgaria and romania. there is hardly any subject which i and the commission are concerned with as much as this question. first of all, i should like to remind you that discrimination against roma is a sad social reality not only in the future member states but also, unfortunately, in a number of member states. it is only because there are not so many of them in the member states that the numbers do not stand out. the crucial point here is whether or not the constitutional system, the legal system and the administrative practice of the state in the future member countries actually discriminate against the roma. our investigations - in agreement with the council of europe and many, many human rights organisations - show that discrimination against roma is not built into the constitution, legislation or administrative structures of these countries. what we find is a deep-rooted, traditional, social discrimination which has taken on dramatic proportions in some areas of these countries. but it's -- i have to say it again -- nothing new. our efforts have focused on ensuring that these countries develop a strategy to reduce discrimination against roma. we have made it a political condition for the conclusion of enlargement negotiations that such strategies exist and are in force. but i have always said - and i have said this in this house - that we cannot expect that when the new member states join, there will be no social discrimination against roma in reality. nor can we say that there is no discrimination in the member states today. i could mention a number of cases of discrimination in our present member states where we do not say that it is a breach of the treaty that people are discriminated against here, but we say that european community law requires that measures be taken to put an end to this discrimination. this is the situation we find in these countries. the commission has responded very strongly to the needs of the roma minority in its pre-accession instruments. it has invested a lot of money, a lot of human resources, a lot of consultancy to help the future member states to develop and implement such a strategy to combat discrimination against roma. i don't think you'll find anyone who knows the reality of roma in these countries better than i do. i shall not let a visit to these countries pass without dealing with this problem directly and on the spot. i do this not because i think that by visiting a roma settlement, a roma school or wherever, i can solve the problem, but i do it to make a strong and symbolic contribution to the awareness building. i want the people of these countries to see on their television screens that when the commission comes to their country, it does not regard the roma as untouchable, but as a population group requiring special attention and special attention.
