the rapporteur. - (es) mr president, welcome to the sitting, mr commissioner, and my first words of thanks to all the parliamentary groups who have worked closely together so that we can today offer parliament a clear text, which focuses on action and not words, on speeding up and not delaying the strategy agreed in lisbon, gothenburg and stockholm to restore confidence in european markets and thus be able to accelerate our growth with a very clear objective, underlined in the first paragraph: increasing job creation, which is the necessary condition to compensate for ageing and to maintain our social model. secondly, i would point out three strict limits to demand policies, which are included in short-term policy: maintaining macroeconomic stability, maintaining european competitiveness in an increasingly globalised world and reducing public debt, thus freeing up resources which should be allocated to investment and providing a window for future social provision. the second key idea is to increase coordination, which is why we welcome strategies to examine economic and employment guidelines together, but we would also like to integrate budgetary and supply policies, which remain in national hands, to create a framework which could serve as a basis for discussions on budgets, both european union and national. the report stresses that the european central bank should continue to monitor price developments in view of the underlying inflation in the services sector. but it says something else, it says that everyone else, especially national governments, must do their duty: keep wage developments linked to productivity, introduce measures on price transparency and reform their structures to increase productivity, to give the european central bank room to manoeuvre, an additional room, in the event that it is deemed necessary to reduce interest rates, especially if exchange rates are to be adjusted to the needs of european exports. the message is equally clear in the field of budgetary policy. parliament stresses its commitment to the stability and growth pact, which it has maintained over time. secondly, it welcomes the commission's efforts to interpret this pact, to assess the budgetary situation of each of the member states, taking into account the volume of debt and the quality of expenditure, especially when it is investment expenditure, consistent with the lisbon, stockholm and gothenburg strategies. thirdly, it regrets the lack of implementation, the lack of diligence on the part of the wasteful governments, which, bordering on the danger of excessive deficits, seem unwilling to make any effort to reduce structural deficits. finally, as an express appeal to the commission, i urge it to play a more vigilant role in the good times to prevent the storm. as regards structural reform policy, we stress that the lack of investment is the key, the most definitive explanation for our lagging behind the united states, especially investment in new technologies. we therefore call for quantified objectives for public and private investment to be set in the economic guidelines and for private sector investment in these technologies to be encouraged, mainly through tax deductions linked to the obtaining of benefits and not subsidies, which are not well known for what activities they are used. the call for a new industrial policy is made, because man does not live on services alone, and there is also an effort to develop renewable energy sources, which i do not have to stress given the international climate. the commission is urged to pursue the objectives of the feira charter in the field of small and mediumsized enterprises, to facilitate their creation within 24 hours through new technologies, to advocate tax deferral in the first few years of operation, to simplify their operation, especially in the administrative environment, and to exercise strict supervision of financing in the basle ii negotiations, to strengthen the role of the european investment fund and to establish a network of guarantees to enable them to access markets. in the field of market liberalization, transposition and, therefore, strengthening the mechanisms for sanctioning non-compliant states, increasing competition in the privatised sectors, liberalizing energy networks and especially their connection. in financial markets we are in substantial agreement. we welcome the efforts in the field of taxation and call for further efforts to achieve vat at source and a consolidated corporate tax base and we call for the stronger representation of the euro in international forums and a denomination in this currency for energy. i hope that the message is clear and well received. i thank all the groups and the president again for their patience. commission. – mr president, i should like to add the following to what commissioner patten has just said. the new american law requiring airlines operating flights to, from or through the united states to grant electronic access to their passenger name records raises a number of policy issues: firstly, the fight against terrorism; secondly, the right to privacy; thirdly, the ability of our airlines to compete; fourthly, the security and convenience of legitimate air travellers; fifthly, the relationship between europe and the united states in general. it is necessary to pull all these strands together and to strike an appropriate balance. it is also necessary to be practical and not theoretical. my first message is that we should work together for an outcome that achieves the best possible results, responding to the need to combat terrorism while respecting data protection in practice, without damaging the commercial interests of our airlines and without inconvenience for legitimate air travellers. the commission very much welcomes the opportunity to address parliament on this matter. underlying the technical issues are some fundamental questions about security and civil liberties which all democracies have to ask themselves. discussions amongst elected parliamentarians on such issues is essential. the motion for a resolution before parliament criticises the commission for not informing and consulting parliament sooner. the commission accepts this reprimand. it had no intention to conceal. it was more a question of when to bring this matter to the attention of parliament and in what form. we only have a short time. rather than making a lengthy factual statement i will draw the attention of parliament to two documents which the commission has made available. the first document is the joint statement which is the agreed account of the outcome of talks between senior officials of the commission and us customs on 17 and 18 february 2003. the second document is the statement by us customs of 4 march which gives undertakings as regards the handling of sensitive data. it is necessary to correct a misunderstanding. as my distinguished colleague commissioner patten has just said, many reports referred to an agreement or a decision. i stress that there is no agreement, there is no decision. it follows that, at this moment, there is no legal basis. there have been discussions and the us side has given certain assurances. this is the first step in the process. both sides are committed to finding a more legally secure solution in due course. these discussions are necessary. why are they necessary? because of information received about new us requirements, the commission found it necessary last november to inform eu airlines and the related reservation systems that it was not clear whether they could provide the information required by us law without being in breach of their data protection obligations under eu law. in order to answer that question, it was necessary to obtain information from the us side, in particular as regards the use of the data and the conditions under which they would be processed. unfortunately the american side was very slow to respond to these requests for information and they only started to take our concerns seriously in december 2002. in the absence of discussions with the united states, the airlines – as commissioner patten has already explained – would have been left in an impossible situation. they would have faced a whole range of penalties, starting with the practice of secondary inspections of arriving passengers. that indeed had already started. that meant very long delays at arrival points for hundreds, if not thousands, of legitimate travellers. that is an option, but is it what we really want? it is certainly not what the airlines wanted, and there was every likelihood that these airlines would have complied with american requirements anyway. i strongly agree with members who expressed the view in the committee on citizens' freedoms and rights, justice and home affairs on monday that the american way of proceeding by unilateral action and threats of penalties is unacceptable. but not having discussions with the american side would have left them with the data and no means for the european union side to influence their handling of it. it would have left the airlines open to either us or member states' enforcement action when they – the airlines – are the wrong target. if we want to bring pressure to bear it should be on those who can deliver a solution – and that is not the airlines. our aim has thus been to open up a process of dialogue through which we can influence us practices and obtain assurances from them that will ensure that data is adequately protected. the commission considers that the outcome of the february talks was positive for data protection for the following two reasons. firstly, we secured us agreement on the further steps to be taken to reach a mutually satisfactory solution that would and can provide legal certainty to all concerned. the second reason is that the united states made a number of significant, unilateral undertakings of immediate application. for example they made undertakings on what data they would not use and how they would handle the data they do use. they confirmed in particular that their data gathering would be limited to flights to, from or through the us. clearly we need more time and information from the united states before we can say that we have a solution. we can only be satisfied when we have an arrangement which provides a maximum amount of legal security for all concerned. there are in the meantime transfers of data. are such transfers legal? only the courts can answer that question in a definitive way, but i would like to make two points in this respect. firstly, the airlines have to meet their obligations as data controllers and they must inform passengers fully, in line with article 10 of the directive, and obtain their consent for the processing of sensitive data in line with article 8. secondly, legality has to be examined from the angle of the need for adequate protection for data that is transferred to a third country. transfers may however benefit from one of the exceptions in article 26(1) of the directive. for example, certain transfers may be necessary in order to fulfil a contract with a data subject – in other words the contract to fly the passenger to the united states. – since such an exception could be challenged, however, this solution lacks legal security. moreover, although exceptions may be legal for specific transfers, they offer no guarantees that the data will subsequently be protected. article 25(6) of the directive, on the other hand, provides for a finding by the commission that a third country ensures adequate protection for transfers of personal data from the european union. an article 25(6) decision by the commission is therefore much to be preferred to relying on the exceptions to the adequacy rule because it means that the data go on being protected. the prospect of such a decision and the legal security that it brings allow the commission to engage the third country concerned in discussions about the protection provided, and hold it to ensuring a high standard. moreover, article 25(6) decisions always contain safeguard clauses which can be triggered if protection does not in practice match up to the standards expected. they can also be unilaterally abrogated if necessary. finally, an article 25(6) decision is a community procedure, producing a result that is binding on all member states. it is very much to be preferred to leaving member states to act in dispersed order. it is worth mentioning that one or two member states have or are planning measures very similar to those in place in the united states. on my own behalf and also on behalf of my colleague mr patten, i should like to invite the house to take a positive view of the commission's actions of 17 and 18 february. the american side has committed itself to a process which recognises our legitimate interest in their data protection practices, under which they subject their arrangements to our scrutiny according to our standards. that i think is a major step forward. of course the united states still must provide the elements needed for the commission to make such an adequacy finding. as a comitology decision, an adequacy finding under article 25(6) is always brought to parliament before being finalised, as was also explained by mr patten. i certainly look forward to discussing this further with members of parliament on a future occasion.

commission. – mr president, i shall do my best to answer the most important questions and remarks addressed to me. it is difficult to be brief as this is a complicated and important subject. so far we far from it. we have not yet achieved an agreement. the discussions with the united states will continue, i hope as quickly and as energetically as possible. it is premature to say that the commission has failed and that it should have achieved more than it has. on behalf of commissioner patten and commissioner de palacio, who deals with transport, i must reject those criticisms. that is not to say that there is not more to do. it has been pointed out that, although there is no agreement as yet, the effect is nonetheless that data is being accessed where it was not accessed before. that is true. is a very important point which may have been overlooked in the heat of the debate. it is not simply a question of letting the data be transferred or preventing this, much of it is flowing anyway. therefore it seems to me that the suggestion which has been made that we should take the airlines to the european court of justice is not a very productive suggestion. it is happening now. the airlines are, as baroness ludford said, between a rock and a hard place. they know that the american side is serious about imposing penalties, including some that could put their transatlantic traffic at risk. the counterbalancing threat – namely that the commission would start infringement proceedings, legal action for breaches of the data protection rules – was a serious concern for the airlines. however, some of them have said that is not life-threatening, whereas the american threats are. i would beg members to understand the very difficult position in which the airlines find themselves, which will have an effect on transatlantic traffic of 10 to 11 million passengers a year, as commissioner patten has explained. a number of speakers have mentioned the supply of information to european union citizens. under data protection law, as i am sure members know, the first duty to inform data subjects lies with data controllers. in this case that is the airlines and possibly travel agents. on friday 14 march there will be a meeting to ensure that they understand their obligations to inform passengers and aircraft crews about what will happen to their data and why. a duty of information also lies with the american government. most of us would find it hard to argue that a country such as the united states does not have the right to determine the conditions under which it allows people to enter the country. they also have a duty to inform the public so that potential travellers can make an informed choice. baroness ludford made a very pertinent point about the data systems that would be based in the european union and the way in which the united states would access those data systems. it concerns the direct application of the directive to us customs that give the european directive a clear extraterritorial effect. the commission is at present undertaking a thorough legal analysis of the various implications of that question, for example with regard to the scope of the directive and to the exercise of state power by us customs within the territory of member states. the judgment is awaited from the european courts in a case that may throw some light on the directive's precise scope but no date has yet been fixed by the courts. in any event this question only arises when us customs have direct access to the airlines' databases. it would not arise if the airlines were to send the data to us customs and this method of transfer, that is the push method, is certainly much to be preferred if it can be organised from a technical point of view. furthermore, the question has been raised in particular by mrs buitenweg and also by other members of parliament about meals taken on aircraft. it is important to realise that the us screening process does not use data such as meal orders, but those data are in passenger name records and they are downloaded with the rest. that is bad practice in terms of data protection. the fact is that the united states neither requires airlines to change their data collection practices nor asks them to separate relevant data from irrelevant data, which makes the exercise less costly for the airlines. mr santini and mr jarzembowski referred to this aspect of the case. even our directive says that certain efforts are not mandatory where they are disproportionate to the results they achieve for data protection. we shall certainly pursue our talks with the airlines with the view to their installing filters that separate us flights from the rest and possibly also filters that separate sensitive data from other data which the us side say they do not need or use. these are some of the more substantial points which were raised by members of parliament. in addition to these points, with respect to a suggestion made by mrs paciotti, the possibility of using 25(6), i.e. a finding of adequacy, is of course available. if the commission should come to the conclusion that there is adequacy in this area it will and it must inform parliament and a proper discussion can then take place on the basis of this finding of the commission. a question has also been raised about discussions to be held at political level. i am sensitive to that suggestion and i shall certainly discuss it with commissioner patten – who begs to be excused for the reasons that he mentioned – and commissioner de palacio, since she, for obvious reasons, is very much involved. on the other hand i would like to say that it is not always the political input that provides a solution. after all, the staff – certainly in the cannot be excluded and i am therefore sensitive to this suggestion. various members of parliament have spoken about the suspension of the american measures. i am sorry, but in view of what i said council i would like to reply to the honourable member that the council considers that maritime transport is a sector of a particularly global nature and that it is therefore desirable that the rules governing it should be applied as widely as possible. i therefore agree with the honourable member that it is desirable, as far as possible, that the candidate countries for accession to the union, as well as other neighbouring countries, including russia, should be able to apply principles similar to those applicable in the european union. the council, and in particular the transport, telecommunications and energy council, on 6 december 2002, followed exactly this approach in the conclusions it adopted. it adopted conclusions on ship safety and pollution prevention following the sinking of the oil tanker prestige off the coast of galicia. it noted the commission's intention to take the necessary vigilance measures, in cooperation with the member states, to ensure that the applicant countries and other neighbouring countries, including russia, organise the transport of heavy oil products only by double-hull tankers. the council also supported the commission's efforts to explore the possibility of drawing up technical cooperation programmes to assist neighbouring countries, in particular the candidate countries, russia and the euro-mediterranean countries, in their efforts to improve maritime safety and pollution prevention and in particular to strengthen the effective application of appropriate port state control procedures. finally, the commission pointed out to the council at the same meeting that it considered that it was in a position, within the framework of existing cooperation with the countries i mentioned above, to carry out this project.

the rapporteur. - (es) mr president, commissioner, the objective of equal opportunities for women and men was introduced into the treaty of amsterdam, and thus provided a legal basis for the community's commitment to work in all structural fund programmes towards this objective. it was also incorporated into the structural funds regulation for the period 2000-2006. equal opportunities are an objective in all programmes and actions co-financed by the funds. despite these clear objectives and their obligatory nature, we have seen that, with the exception of the european social fund, they are not being met, even when they are included in the programme to be implemented. the european social fund, in the field of employment, vocational training and promotion, is the only one to achieve this objective through specific programmes aimed at achieving equal opportunities; but other important areas, such as infrastructure, transport, the environment, local and urban development, rural development, research, etc., do not include equality among their objectives. although the european social fund focuses on promoting employment, important actions remain to be taken, such as reducing segregation in the labour market, pay gaps for equal work, as well as promoting women's participation in new information and communication technologies, entrepreneurship and new employment opportunities and decision-making. we call on the commission to take more specific and effective measures to remedy these shortcomings. we also feel that there is a clear lack of political will in the member states to push the equality objective in the structural funds. it is true that progress has been made in developing sex-disaggregated statistics, which gives us a better understanding of reality, but the indicators for monitoring programmes have not improved in relation to previous programming. member states are responsible for programming and we ask them to make an effort to support specific policies and actions to achieve the goal of equal opportunities by selecting projects that meet this objective. infrastructures such as childcare centres or day centres for the elderly or disabled can be developed; these are usually tasks which women take on in the family environment and with the right infrastructures we could achieve better integration of women into working life and reconciliation of work and family life, better organisation of working time and reintegration into working life after a long absence, and greater awareness of the equitable distribution of tasks between women and men within the family. special attention should be given to women who have the most difficulty in achieving equal opportunities, such as women with disabilities, migrants and heads of households. the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to carcinogens at work is a welcome step towards this objective. but training and awareness-raising on equal opportunities should not be directed at women alone, but at society as a whole. let us take advantage of the opportunities that the treaty and the structural funds regulation give us to advance equal opportunities with projects that meet these objectives. the mid-term evaluation to be carried out this year at the end of the programme will examine the achievement of this objective: the nature and amount of the appropriations allocated to the specific measures on equal opportunities in order to make the necessary changes for the second programming period. the importance of these measures in the candidate countries, which will join in just over a year's time and which are experiencing difficulties in administrative and economic restructuring, particularly affecting women, should also be taken into account.
the rapporteur. - (es) mr president, on 27 may 2002 the council adopted regulation (eec) no 881/2002 with a view to transposing a number of resolutions of the united nations security council. in united nations sanctions committee for these purposes. the european parliament took a decision on this on 11 april 2002 under an emergency procedure and adopted the resolution with 14 amendments. in december of that year, the un security council adopted resolution 1454 of 2002, which recognized certain exceptions to the obligation to freeze funds and financial assets. on the basis of this, the european commission has put forward the proposal before us today, which almost word for word takes up the text of the united nations. the aim is to authorize the release of appropriations in respect of the persons listed, with the aim of covering basic human needs such as food, medical treatment, lawyers' fees, rent, etc., in line with what the european parliament itself called for in its resolution of 11 april 2002 cited above. however, the european parliament's plenary also proposed other amendments which were not included by the council in regulation (eec) no 881/2002 or by the commission in its current proposal. in this connection, the committee on civil liberties voted a number of amendments which are included in the report which has reached the house today and which i propose we should support as a whole. these are five amendments which seek to include explicitly in the community regulation the procedure for removing names from the list of terrorists currently in force at the united nations, to require that the european parliament be fully associated and informed, and to stress the need for the life of the regulation to be in line with the period of validity remaining speaking time to make a more general reflection on the reason why this type of international and european legislation has had to be adopted, namely the persistence of terrorism. indeed, and especially in the last year and a half, the bloody brutality of terrorism has shocked the whole world. the european union is not a terrorist organization, but a terrorist organization. if we are all really in agreement that we want to achieve the creation of an area of freedom, security and justice, it is vital that we work to ensure that its three components are fully developed and with equal intensity throughout the territory of the european union. but it is no use talking about a european area of this kind if, in practice, not all of europe is fair, secure or free. and the main cause of that is the persistence of terrorism within the european union. it is not something outside our borders but something that lives within them. the european authorities have therefore set about adopting a whole range of legislation to combat the scourge of terrorism. although all action in this direction could be questioned and, of course, subject to evaluation, i would also like to denounce those voices that have emerged, much more concerned with safeguarding the rights and freedoms of terrorists than with remembering the damage, suffering and despair that they cause to their victims, not to mention the injustice and powerlessness that such acts imply. i therefore look forward to concrete actions in the future to promote the rights and freedoms of victims of terrorism and their families. in this context, and with the commission here today - and i do not think the council - i would like to take this opportunity to put forward an idea which is already beginning to circulate in the corridors and which i hope will be answered shortly: i am referring to the possibility of studying the possibility of creating a european solidarity mechanism which would provide for formulae for compensating european citizens who are victims of terrorist attacks on the territory of the union. - the common position of the council on the proposal for a council regulation amending the staff regulations of officials of the european communities and the conditions of employment of other servants of the european communities (com (2002) 213 - c5-0262/2002 - 2002/0100 (cns)); oral question (o-0019/2003 - b5-0087/2003) to the commission on the reform of the staff regulations.
the rapporteur. (es) mr president, first of all i would like to thank mr harbour for his kind remarks. i think that the two rapporteurs have indeed worked together to try to do the best we can. we were two speakers from two different countries, from two different political forces, with different sensibilities, which has enabled us to approach the subject with fairly impartial. but the starting point was the work of commissioner kinnock, who also made some fairly balanced proposals to us, aimed at making the administration more flexible, at the possibility of recruiting good staff, of promoting them on the basis of their merits and qualifications, and i think that it was easy to continue working from that starting point. we, the rapporteurs, had the opportunity to meet with representatives of civil servants and the institutions and we found that the work done by the commission was good, and at the moment i have the impression that this package, which is a very well thought out and very well worked out package, could really be adapted to the needs of the civil service in the european union. i would like to make an appeal and remind you of the work that officials have done in the european union. the european union currently has 25 000 officials to administer a budget which is not excessive but important in a community of 15 countries with a population of 380 million. the number of officials in the european union is far less than that of a large municipality, with a budget perhaps much larger than that of a large municipality. i therefore believe that the union's civil servants have done a great job and that at this stage it would make no sense to make regulations which would harm the position of civil servants or create situations which would give rise to conflict in the workplace. i therefore refer, in the same terms as mr harbour, to statements by the council which seem to be aimed at cutting the pension scheme in a healing way, in total contradiction, moreover, with the proposals coming from the commission. that said, the amendments to which mr harbour has referred are amendments which i believe are reasonable, which are due. mr harbour has referred in particular to one, namely the correction coefficients; it makes no sense that when a person retires from the community institutions, having the possibility of choosing to reside in any country, his allowance should be fixed in the country in which he decides to reside. the european union, like any administration, must pay all officials the same allowance and let them decide where their permanent residence is going to be, which may be colder, hotter, cheaper or more expensive, but let the official decide freely what he wants to do. i would also like to refer to another clause which is quite important to me, namely that we had in the staff regulations an anachronistic rule, a kind of ecclesiastical nihil obstat, under which an official of the institutions could not write a work without the authorization of a hierarchical superior. i think that we are living in a society that is free enough and that officials are responsible enough to know what they have to write about, and if they do something that harms the institutions, it will be seen whether it is criminal or whether it is simply a matter of observations to which they are entitled. i do not think that it is time to introduce prior censorship and i also think that it is practically impossible, because i do not see commission officials reading the works and papers of their subordinates on subjects that can be as pedestrian as the structure of the commission or the structure of the european parliament. there are also some proposals for amendments to the statute concerning gays and lesbians, that is to say people with a different sexual orientation. we have sought a formula of flexibility to prevent, as a result of the application of very strict legal criteria, an official with a certain sexual orientation from being unable to obtain the benefits of cohabitation with another person because of that sexual orientation. i think, mr president, that our proposals are balanced, that parliament could adopt them without any difficulty, and that both the commission and the council should see in them a spirit of collaboration on the part of parliament, so i hope that the council will finally adopt the package taking into account the amendments we propose. i am grateful to the commissioner for his attention, and i hope that tomorrow's presentation on the oral question will shed some light on the situation regarding this threat to the pension system of community officials.

- the next item is the report (a5-0061/2003) by mrs van brempt, on behalf of the committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy, on a thematic strategy on the sustainable use of pesticides (2002/2277 (ini)).
commission. – mr president, first of all, i would like to thank the european parliament, and in particular the rapporteur mrs van brempt, for the work that has gone into this report in reaction to the commission’s communication 'towards a thematic strategy on the sustainable use of pesticides'. the sixth environment action programme introduced the new concept of thematic strategies and requires the commission to develop them in close consultation with all relevant parties. the commission launched this broad consultation with the communication. more than 150 comments were received via internet and following a stakeholder conference with almost 200 participants, the council adopted conclusions in december 2002 and the european economic and social committee did so in january 2003. with this report of the european parliament, the consultation process will be concluded. the commission welcomes the parliament’s broad support towards the general approach and the main objectives presented in the communication. the numerous detailed comments and requests contained in the resolution will be fully taken into account in the development of the future thematic strategy. however, i would like to draw the attention of the parliament to three particular issues raised in the resolution, where the commission could face some difficulties with implementation. these issues are also addressed in the amendments tabled for the plenary. the first one relates to the scope and goal of the future thematic strategy. the parliament calls on the commission to extend the scope to include all uses of plant protection products, agricultural and others, and also biocides. i can assure you that it has always been the commission’s intention to cover all uses of plant protection products. but for the reasons already explained in the communication, the commission thinks that for the time being actions should be focused on plant protection products. only these are also specifically referred to in the sixth environment action programme. secondly, the commission takes note of the emphasis that parliament's report puts on an overall quantitative reduction of the use of pesticides, whilst the communication puts more emphasis on reducing the risks. i would like to underline once more that there is no direct link between the quantities of pesticides used and the risks they can pose to health and environment. in fact, there are cases where substances are much more active and can be used at lower volumes, but because of their higher activity they pose higher risks to the environment. nevertheless, the commission recognises the interest of seeking a reduction in use as one possible tool to achieve reduction of risks. given that the member states are setting out from very diverse starting points due to efforts made in the past, it is extremely difficult to establish overall quantitative use reduction targets. such targets should, however, be considered by the member states when they establish their national action plans. lastly, parliament's report urges the commission to develop a regulatory framework for taxes and levies on pesticides. as outlined in the communication, this is a very complicated area – in particular the calculation of the real externalities of pesticides – and the effects of introducing such levies in some member states have been more limited than originally expected. the commission will, therefore, have to examine the problem further before making any proposals. in conclusion, i would like to emphasise again that i consider the parliament’s resolution to be a very important contribution in the consultation process. we can now get to work and start the development of the details of the strategy. i am confident that i can count on the parliament’s continued support in our efforts to further improve the sustainable use of pesticides in the eu.
agri (s). - (es) mr president, commissioner, the thematic strategy for the sustainable use of pesticides presented by the commission and which the commissioner has just outlined is undoubtedly a programmatic statement of the actions which the commission intends to take in the near future, either by means of its own provisions or by means of legislative proposals to the european parliament and the council of ministers of the european union. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the pesticides are used in a safe manner and that they are not used in a way that is harmful to the environment. the commission proposal, however, has important shortcomings and has received a large number of comments which the community executive will have to take into account when proposing concrete measures in black and white. among the various comments made, i would like to highlight a few points which are relevant to me. firstly, the commission's draft does not deal with the problems arising from the use of pesticides in the various regions of europe in a differentiated way. the current undifferentiated treatment leads to false conclusions when applying them to the different areas. secondly, it is not clear whether organic farming is the objective which the commission intends to develop in the future as a model of agriculture which should be extended to the entire territory of the european union. ladies and gentlemen, we should demystify organic farming. i don't want to remind anyone of the nitrophen case. naturism is often confused with environmental protection. oil, strychnine, hemlock and even anthrax are natural, but unacceptable if they are spilled into the environment. organic farming is naturist farming, but that is not why it is the most desirable and the most desired at all times. nor is there any mention in the commission proposal of any concrete idea of what the community policy should be with regard to so-called integrated production, an important path which cannot be overlooked, especially in the use of plant protection products. the proposal does not take into account the potential we have in our hands to reduce the use of pesticides significantly by using gm products which undoubtedly require very transparent legislation in order to ensure the absence of negative side effects. in conclusion, i would like to draw attention to another point on which the commission has not yet responded. this is the guideline for establishing appropriate indicators to measure the effectiveness of the various measures envisaged the commission. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i have to say that i am very pleased with the way the commission has been working. in the discharge procedure, the commission and the other institutions are accountable to the freely elected european parliament for the use of the community budget. parliament, on behalf of the citizens of the union, shall monitor such use. in 2001, this budget was used to spend eur 79.4 billion. in addition, expenditure from the european development fund and the coal and steel community was increased. i should like to thank the lead rapporteur, mr casaca, for his very thorough and intensive work. i should also like to thank the rapporteurs, mr staes, mrs avilés perea, mr blak, mr sørensen and mrs langenhagen, on behalf of the commission, for their thorough and conscientious work, and i should also like to pay tribute to the chairman of the committee on budgetary control, mrs theato, for her leadership of this difficult process, and to thank all the members of the committee on budgets for their hard work. finally, in addition to the several hundred pages of annual accounts, the rapporteurs and the committee also examined the court of auditors' annual report and hundreds of pages of replies to the 267 questions put to the commission, and the committee held hearings with eight commissioners. the european budget covers a wide range of spending programmes, from promoting the marketing of dairy products to beef slaughter premiums, promoting beekeeping, restructuring measures in the fisheries sector, youth exchange programmes and promoting biotechnology research, to helping girls to go to school in afghanistan or providing food aid in southern africa. all of this is subject to different rules. different actors manage the programmes and resources and are exposed to different risks of error. the court of auditors' and parliament's audit work has taken account of the full range of these diverse tasks. i must, however, concentrate on a few points which played the greatest role during the discharge process, namely the accounting rules and the accounting system, the statistical office contracts and the question of the rate of implementation of the budget. as regards the accounts, the court of auditors found that the 2001 accounts also accurately reflected revenue and expenditure, and this was also reiterated in mr casaca's report. he has again called for reforms in the accounting of assets. the report by mr casaca gives a detailed account of the forthcoming reform. we have had the opportunity to discuss the concept of reform and the concrete steps to be taken in this reform in great detail in the committee on budgetary control. it is a project that involves all departments and all bodies. in some respects we are already exemplary in accounting in terms of publication, namely that we publish the figures of the cash-based budgetary accounts on the internet on a monthly basis. i mention this because the commission's proposal to require public limited companies to publish quarterly reports has sparked a lively debate on the reasonableness of this. the commission itself publishes its figures on budgetary management on a monthly basis. we also need not hide from the fact that some of the elements in the balance sheet are comparable to those in the member states. but is that enough? no, it's not enough. the accounting system must be able to identify whether a payment is a final payment or an advance payment which can be recovered if a programme does not work well. in the accounting system, an entry in the assets and liabilities must be made as soon as, for example, a commitment has been made, and not only after payment has been made. we need to keep the books in chronological order. and the services that manage the funds must have direct access to the account balances for their programmes. that is the only way to ensure that the budget is properly managed. this is of course a challenge to the underlying information and technology system. the commission will of course be happy to comply with the committee on budgetary control's request to report on progress in reform every quarter. we also agreed to follow the suggestion of the rapporteur, mr casaca, to include in a pilot project the fact that the beneficiaries of payments are informed in writing as soon as the authorising officer has made the request for payment, in order to ensure greater transparency here too. it should be remembered that only 20% of the budget is managed by the commission and that practically the bulk of the budget remains in the treasuries of the member states, even in cash. the commission's cash management is audited annually by the european court of auditors. we shall nevertheless submit to the court of auditors parliament's request for a specific external audit. we will also base the reform on the standards set in 2000 and 2001 by the international federation of accountancy. i would also like to make a fundamental comment. in old europe - to put it briefly - it was the case, and so is the case in the european union, that the main accounting rules were and are laid down by public law and not by the standards of such an association alone. the question is whether we want to abandon this practice. i think that the public legislator should retain the right to decide on the principles to be applied to the accounting of the public budget. we also have the great advantage, of course, of having the european court of auditors as an independent public authority as our external auditor. in the united states, for example, at a time when the public audit authority is being strengthened in relation to private auditors as a consequence of scandals such as enron, it is clear that it is advantageous to have a public auditor who is committed to independence. in response to your chief rapporteur's questions on contracts with eurogramme, the commission has agreed to suspend all payments for eurogramme and to review all contracts concluded with eurogramme. in all cases where this does not involve additional costs, the contractual relationship will be terminated. they also ask the commission to review all contracts concluded by the statistical office since 1999 by july this year: 2 660 contracts. that's not possible until july. but precisely because we want to meet parliament's concerns, we must find a feasible solution here, for example on the basis of a sample. the commission will present a review of these contracts to the committee on budgetary control at one of its next meetings and will propose a further procedure for its examination. the operations concerning eurogramme or eurostat have also shown that cooperation with olaf in the field of information needs to be put on a clearer basis. olaf is and remains the owner of the information resulting from its investigations, and olaf's independence must of course be safeguarded at all stages, but it has also been shown that it is necessary to ensure that olaf's findings are made available to the intermediate bodies in good time, so that timely measures can be taken to protect the budget against fraud. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council and parliament. as regards the sapard programme, the commission has given its commitment to the committee on budgetary control and to parliament to give the highest priority to improving the implementation of the programme. the commission has already taken some of the steps it has promised to take in the committee on budgets. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. mrs the rapporteur. (es) mr president, the european union has 12 million legal immigrants from third countries. entry and residence for the purpose of family reunification is the main legal channel of immigration for third-country nationals in almost all member states of the union. this family immigration includes both family reunification in the strict sense - the reunion of family members with the third-country national already resident - and family formation when family ties are established after the entry of the third-country national. the percentage of persons allowed to enter as family members of immigrants varies between 40 and 50%, with even higher values in some member states of the union such as france or the united kingdom. without ignoring the quantitative importance of this aspect of legal immigration, it is also important to emphasize the fundamental role played by family reunification as a necessary means of achieving the integration of third-country nationals legally residing in the european union. the presence of family members contributes to greater stability and integration of these people, by allowing them to lead a normal family life. most family members who are admitted on the basis of the exercise of the right to family reunification enjoy a great advantage compared with other types of immigrants, as they maintain very close ties with a person - the person who is being reunited - already established in the host country, which greatly facilitates the possibility of their integration. the legislation on family reunification should be governed by two principles which should also apply to all immigration legislation. these principles, which have been reiterated on other occasions, are equality and security. i will not go into the whole history of this proposal for a directive again, because i take it for granted, but i cannot help but mention the first political agreement on legal immigration which was reached at the last meeting of the justice and home affairs council on 28 february on the council directive on the right to family reunification. an agreement which is in many respects far from what this parliament is proposing. i am aware of the difficulties in reaching agreements on such sensitive issues as those relating to immigration, the approach and legal regulation of which are very different in the member states. the proposal as it is before this house today for approval includes as family members the spouse of the person being reunited, as well as the common-law partner recognised in the member state, irrespective of sex; the minor children of the person being reunited and their spouse, including adopted children; the minor children, including the adopted children of the person being reunited or their spouse where one of them has custody and is responsible for them; but we have not accepted the exception concerning the child over 12 years of age for whom the member state could examine whether he or she meets integration criteria before authorising entry and residence under the directive. first-degree ascendants in difficulty in their country of origin have been included when they have no other family support. and older children with health problems have also been included. the time limit for communicating the decision adopted is reduced from 9 to 6 months and from 12 to 9 months in exceptional cases. with regard to the conditions for exercising the right to family reunification, we maintain the grounds of public policy, public security and public health when granting the exercise of the right to family reunification. the renewal of the permit may not be refused for reasons of illness after the permit has been issued. and refugees are exempt from the requirement to prove a condition for supporting their relatives. i have withdrawn all the amendments relating to subsidiary protection in exchange for a commitment by the commission to present as soon as possible a directive harmonizing this figure in the european union. as regards the entry and residence of family members, we propose to align the right of access to education, employment and vocational training with that of the family members of the person being reunited and not with that of union citizens. this will avoid differences in treatment within the same family. in the event of widowhood, divorce, separation or death, you can obtain a residence permit for yourself if you have been a resident for at least one year. in general, there are some aspects which i consider positive, such as: the exemption of refugees from having to prove conditions for supporting their relatives, the adoption of flexible criteria for refugees with regard to the proof of kinship and the authorisation of alternative means of proof where documentary proof is not possible; the granting of the same residence rights to relatives as to the head of the family, the granting of the same rights to family members with regard to access to education, employment and self-employment, and family guidance, and the recognition of the special needs of unaccompanied minors. however, i must say that the political agreement reached on 28 february falls far short of what this parliament proposed in certain areas, because it narrows its scope and requires a well-founded perspective of obtaining a right of permanent residence. finally, i would like to reiterate that i have decided to withdraw all the amendments which included persons in receipt of subsidiary protection in return for the council's commitment to adopt the directive presented by the commission on 12 september 2001 on minimum standards on the conditions and status to which third country nationals and stateless persons may be entitled to be refugees or beneficiaries of other forms of international protection, which would include the right to family reunification. for these reasons, and for the reasons which we have explained at length in the committee on civil liberties, justice and home affairs, i ask the house to support this report.

- question no 32 by mr bowe (h-0154/03) subject: sale of goods via the internetdoes the commission accept that the fact that eu regulations allow companies with headquarters in countries outside the community to sell goods via the internet and then deliver them directly to the buyer without the latter having to pay vat if the value of the goods remains below the minimum threshold determined by the commission appears to be a completely unfair practice? does the commission not agree that this represents a serious threat to business and employment in the eu? if she won't admit it, why? if it does, what steps does the commission propose to take to remedy the situation?
commission. – i would like to reply to mr bowe's very understandable question by firstly saying that i recognise the problem, but that on the other hand we should welcome the sale of goods through the internet. in itself it is a welcome phenomenon of the internal market and therefore we should try to further such commerce. the problem then arises of the payment of vat and excise duties, and thus the problem to which mr bowe referred. as i said earlier, we cannot really propose a useful course of action until and unless we have analysed the situation and that analysis is based on the investigations of member states into the size of the problem. only then, when we have that analysis, can we propose something useful. mr bowe will be interested to know that member states will be gathering details until july of this year, so in a few months' time the intelligence ought to have been gathered and then the commission can propose a useful course of action – but only if it is decided that there is a distortion of the internal market; and secondly, of course, we want to target only those commercial consignments which really present a problem. after all, if one asks people to comply with certain requirements, it needs to be checked that these are correct and this implies a cost for the governments concerned; that is basically the reason for the de minimis rule. there may be exceptions and it may quite possibly be that mr bowe's constituents form such an exception, but i would ask mr bowe to give us until the end of june or july of this year, and then we will come back to the matter if mr bowe so desires.
subject: abolition of the scheme of generalised tariff preferences for certain sectors for the countries of central america and the andean community, by means of graduated tariff reductions does the commission consider that the abolition of tariff preferences (as a result of the adoption of proposal com/2003/0045 final for a council regulation implementing article 12 of regulation (ec) no 2501/2001 oj l 346, 31.12.2001, p. 1) in respect of the perennial plants, flowers, vegetables and edible fruits sector in colombia, resulting from the application of the graduation mechanism, is likely to help a country of approximately 26 million poor people, with 30 000 violent deaths per year and 10 hostage-takings per day, in its fight against drug production and trafficking? does the commission not consider that the above measure is likely to jeopardize the fragile economic, social and ecological progress made by costa rica in a sector of activity concentrated in the less favoured regions of the country, often affected by natural disasters, and which provides employment mainly to women, heads of households and immigrants from nicaragua? does the commission not consider that the application of the graduation mechanism to the beneficiaries of the 'gsp-drug' risks distorting the objectives which led to the creation of what is arguably the most beneficial trade mechanism the eu has ever adopted in relation to developing countries and which is vital for the andean and central american countries, at the very moment when they are going through a regional crisis? does the commission believe that the situation in these countries will improve during the months in which the entry into force of the regulation has been delayed? does it not think that this may be a discouraging signal for these countries, whereas the madrid summit has opened up prospects for free trade for central america and the andean community? what was the reaction of the countries concerned?
commission. - i would remind you that the graduation mechanism, which is the subject of mr salafranca's question, has existed in our system of generalised preferences since 1995. the aim of this system is to encourage the economic development of the countries benefiting from preferences by enabling them to increase their exports to the community and by targeting these tariff preferences on those countries which need them most. the aim of this system is to encourage the development of exports from countries benefiting from preferences, with the corollary that preferential treatment must cease as soon as this objective is achieved. this system of trade preferences cannot be extended indefinitely; the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the gsp is not used in a way that would be contrary to the common interest. this graduation is based on objective and neutral criteria which are set out in our regulations and are directly linked to the specialisation of the exports of the countries concerned. the commission understands the concerns expressed by mr salafranca, which coincide with those expressed by a number of beneficiary countries. we are not prepared to accept the commission's proposal to introduce a new system of graduation, but we are prepared to show a certain degree of flexibility in this respect. in the case of colombia, which is the subject of the first part of the question, most of the exports concerned are cut flowers and the exports are mainly to the us market. a slight increase in european customs duties is therefore unlikely to affect the level of colombia's overall exports of cut flowers. in the case of costa rica, where both plants and cut flowers are involved, we do not share the concerns expressed here and there. costa rica is a country that is developing relatively well. the overall economic situation has improved and in terms of specialization, which in some ways defines the competitiveness of a sector in the country compared to the same sector in other countries, costa rica remains clearly competitive. as regards the impact of the graduation mechanism on the countries benefiting from the special preferential regime which are fighting drug culture, it is true that when the graduation mechanism was created it did not apply to the gsp-drug. the situation was changed in 2001 with the council regulation establishing the new preferential regime 2005 and aligning the gsp-drug to the normal scheme. why the change ? because we wanted to avoid the discriminatory nature of this gsp-drug being called into question at the wto. it was not lost on india, which brought a case against us before the wto over this matter. i think we should be able to defend ourselves. finally, let us see what has been the result of the application of graduation in the past. we note that the withdrawal of preferences has not generally impeded exports of the products concerned from the beneficiary countries. if we look at what has happened in the region mentioned in the question, in chile and mexico in particular, the introduction of graduation has not prevented the further increase in exports from these countries. it is also true that as customs duties are gradually being reduced as multilateral negotiations progress, their importance and the importance of preferences are becoming less and less significant. finally, it should be remembered that if this preferential treatment is withdrawn, it is the european importer who has to pay the duty in question, possibly by reducing his margin a little, which, as we know, is generally comfortable in the case of the importer. so for colombia and costa rica, they meet the objective conditions in our regulations for the graduation mechanism to be applied and we do not share the analysis that this would cause a considerable shock to their economies. graduation is not a punishment. quite the opposite. it means that the country's exports have reached a level which can be sustained without the support of the preferential system and that the objectives of competitiveness and economic maturity which we wanted to promote have been achieved. the commission has accepted a certain amount of flexibility in response to the concerns expressed by several members of parliament, a number of our member states, certain economic operators and, of course, the countries concerned. the graduation mechanism, which was due to come into force at the end of 2002 as provided for in the regulation, has not yet come into force and therefore the countries have been able to continue to benefit from the gsp. the final date is still under discussion and should be decided by the council of ministers in the near future. so, although we do not share all the concerns that have been expressed, we have begun to show flexibility in this case.

commission - it was not lost on me, mr salafranca, that the commission is supposed to be a political rather than a technical institution. however, whatever its policy, it is aimed at implementing the treaties, regulations and legislation which the european union has adopted. if we do not do this, we are failing our duty, and that is a political matter, not a technical one. will costa rica and colombia be severely and permanently affected by this modest reduction in the customs duty on cut flowers? we don't believe that. you can express a contrary opinion. the only thing that can separate us right now is the precedent. however, as we have seen from the previous cases, there is no major danger. however, it is because of its political sensitivity that the commission has accepted a delay in implementing this graduation. until what date? we are discussing this with the council of ministers, which, as is often the case in trade policy, has the last word on this matter. would a specific derogation for agricultural products be welcome? we do not believe this for the simple reason that it would further weaken the compatibility with the wto of our gsp, which, as you know, is being challenged by india, on the grounds that it does not benefit from the gsp for drugs. we do not want to add to the troubles of those who want to be killed by this regime. finally, what will happen in 2004? the scheme is due to expire at the end of 2004 and we will decide next year on two options that are currently possible: either to change the scheme from 1 january 2005 or to extend it for some time. the choice between these two scenarios will depend on the state of progress of the negotiation cycle, since it would be useful to know the general evolution of the level of tariffs before determining exactly the preferences. the commission will take a decision on this during the course of the next year.

the commission. mr president, i would like to thank you. mr lund, this is a very, very complicated procedure. at the same time, it is important for the eu to play a role in the international context. this is clearly a cross-border problem. it is important that we stick to the oecd framework and that we try to develop these methods. i do not think anyone would want to delay this work. on the contrary, we all feel the need to move quickly and to ensure that we have as quickly as possible the testing methods and systems to work with these endocrine disruptors. we can only promise to do all we can to ensure that a good result can be achieved in the work. the point we are discussing now in connection with the new chemicals legislation is that as long as we do not have clear definitions and clear test methods and agreed systems to deal with them, we have to do it on a case-by-case basis. the discussions we have had so far have at least mentioned the endocrine disrupting substances group, which points in this direction. then we just have to work as fast as we can to come up with agreed methods of dealing with them.
- question no 38 by mr dhaene (h-0197/03): subject: establishment of a european civil protection body the creation of a european civil protection corps is an urgent necessity: further proof of this is the prestige disaster. these 'green helmets' under the european banner will be able to be used in disasters throughout the european union and will be equipped with specialised equipment, which not all member states can afford. could the commission state where it is in the preparation of this proposal? which member states have already pledged their cooperation? when will the commission submit this proposal to the council?
commission. – i should like to thank you for that question, because actually the case of the prestige is a clear illustration of the added value of the response centre. immediately after the accident on 13 november 2002, the centre was first activated by the spanish authorities and subsequently by the portuguese and french authorities as well. altogether, eight requests for assistance were registered and their immediate treatment through the response centre made it possible to organise and channel the offers made by all the other european countries. thus, following the accident, an impressive range and quantity of resources – including 15 oil-combating vessels, more than 20 kilometres of booms and several specialised surveillance aircraft – were put at the disposal of the national competent authorities affected. the response centre also coordinated the assistance offered to the three countries, it sent a group of community experts immediately following the accident and has offered to co-finance, with spain, an environmental study on the consequences of the accident. what if one of the new member states requests our assistance? of course the response centre will be used in the same way and we will offer assistance from all member states. now we can mobilise and coordinate the help and assistance of all member states. in addition, we are cooperating on a regular basis with those national authorities and services that deal with civil protection, so we can learn from each other. we also have exercises whereby we can actually simulate a major accident, even with biological or chemical weapons. this has improved our capacity considerably, but it is perhaps not so well known. it is time to make it more visible and time to ensure that we actually intervene immediately after accidents. all the new member states know about our response centre and we offer the support of all member states in cases like this.

(es) mr president, i would like to congratulate the commission, because i have the impression - from its answers to various questions - that so far it has been able to distinguish between technical and legal problems in the spanish national hydrological plan. however, given the pressure and harassment of certain members who believe that politicians have the right to enter into the intimate relationship between countries and the commission in informal relations and, above all, to interfere in the role of the technicians, i ask the commissioner: are you prepared to guarantee the freedom of work of the experts at the ispra meeting, which is technical - as you have said - and to avoid politicization by particular and concrete interests? because we could also get involved in issues like nitrates in the netherlands and others. my question is: are you prepared to guarantee the freedom of the experts to work and their privacy so that their work is not interfered with or subjected to pressure?

question no 40 by mr posselt (h-0139/03) subject: common border protection how does the commission assess the recent efforts to establish common border protection with the applicant countries, and what are the measures planned in the near future to achieve border protection at the level of the european union?
commission. – the seville conclusions are balanced conclusions. they emphasise the need to fight against illegal immigration, and that is definitely an issue that concerns us all, but at the same time they emphasise the need for the ever better integration of immigration policy into our external relation policies, including the development of a partnership with countries of origin and transit in order to cooperate and have better control of illegal immigration. in the communication that the commission issued a few months ago on immigration and development policy, it tried to give you a picture of everything it is doing in the field of development policy that is relevant for migratory flows, not only fighting poverty but also guaranteeing the rule of law and respect for human rights, and guaranteeing there are no 'pull' factors inducing people to leave their own country and travel, sometimes illegally, to the european union. such an approach has been not only a balanced but also a realistic approach. we are developing all the elements of the action plan, not only the operational part, but also the legislative one, and in several areas that you have mentioned, such as asylum legislation, we have been adopting the necessary rules that were provided for by the tampere programme. it is probably happening more slowly than some political rhetoric might lead one to expect, but at least i can assure you that we are progressing on a solid basis.
- question no 41 by mrs ludford (h-0141/03): subject: crime: european-wide prevention measures against the theft of mobile phones theft of mobile phones within the european union, often by international gangs, is likely to be in the millions each year. in this connection, a recent eurobarometer survey shows that between one fifth and one third of the population in the member states fear being victims of such theft. in the uk, it is now illegal to reprogram a stolen phone and uk operators, brought together in the gsm association, cooperate through a common database of imei numbers of stolen phones, which can be unusable. some european operators have joined the association, but only 20 of the 500 or so operators on the continent are members. what action has the commission taken to encourage the creation of a european-wide imei database, similar to the uk one, which would put an end to the theft of telephones by preventing their further use? does the commission intend to make a proposal under article 34 of the eu treaty for a community decision establishing the reprogramming of stolen mobile phones as a criminal offence?
commission. – i am willing to receive any information that the honourable member can give us on the economic implications of these criminal activities. i recognise that the figures are impressive: i recognise that 48% of all robberies in central london involve mobile phones and that the rate in paris is about 40%. i am very much aware of the fact that last year approximately 700 000 phones were stolen in the uk, 150 000 in france and 130 000 in spain. i do not deny that there is an important cross-border dimension to this kind of criminal activity. the issue is how to prioritise the actions that should be taken. my view is that priority should go to operational cooperation. i do not see any need for harmonisation of legislation. therefore we will go on discussing a european network of crime prevention and what concrete operational activities should be developed to fight this kind of crime. the imei approach has already been discussed. we can only decide by unanimity and the member states are split on this issue. however, we will definitely not drop the issue.
- question no 42 by mr krivine (h-0174/03): subject: french-german charter on monday, march 3, 2003, france and germany collectively deported 54 senegalese and ivorian nationals on a charter of the company euralair horizons. on board this aircraft chartered by the two governments were 30 ivorian nationals and 23 senegalese nationals, who were not admitted to french territory or whose applications for political asylum in france were rejected and who were kept in a waiting area in roissy, and a senegalese who had arrived by road from germany, from where he had been expelled. does the commission consider that article 4 of protocol no 4 to the european convention on human rights and fundamental freedoms and the first paragraph of article 19 of the charter of fundamental rights, ratified at the nice summit, have been respected? does the commission consider that the second paragraph of article 19 of the same charter of fundamental rights has been respected in respect of ivorian nationals who have been returned to a country currently experiencing a situation of unrest and that the asylum application procedures guaranteed by the geneva convention of 28 july 1951 and the protocol of 31 january 1967 relating to the status of refugees have been respected? what steps does the commission intend to take to ensure that the treaties are respected, in particular the provisions on the right of asylum and protection in the event of expulsion, deportation and extradition?
commission - with pleasure, congressman. firstly, a joint flight is a flight organised by at least two member states. it is at this level that there is a combination of wills, in this case those of france and germany. both countries have gathered together in one place a number of people who were to be deported and these were part of the same flight. it's a joint flight from an organizational standpoint. from the point of view of collective expulsion, which is prohibited by the european convention on human rights, the question is: when does collective expulsion begin? a collective expulsion decision is not taken for each individual who makes up the group, but it is a single decision that applies to a whole group of people, without taking into account the specific situations of each individual who makes up the group. that's the difference. a mass expulsion is prohibited. nothing in the european union allows that. on the other hand, if you have ten individual expulsion decisions and you see these ten people together, they are in a group, no doubt, they may be part of a joint robbery or not, but it is not a collective expulsion. that is the main difference, in my opinion.
