(es) mr president, commissioner, i would like to thank everyone for their participation in this debate. the report before us is intended to be parliament's response to the commission's communication of 2 july 2002 on an information and communication strategy for the european union. to present the report briefly, i would point out that one of its first features is that it places information as a condition of citizenship. i hope that in the future, after the recognition of the european union's legal personality, this right of citizens will be combined with the european union's right to express itself, what we would call the right to the image of the european union, the right for the european union to explain what it is and what it does, and the combination of these two rights will allow us to have a firm legal basis on which to develop a genuine information and communication policy. the report is firmly committed to consolidating interinstitutionality in all three phases of the process, i.e. in the drafting of messages within the interinstitutional information group, in implementation, using the commission representations and the offices of the european parliament, as well as national, regional and local authorities and interinstitutionality, and in evaluation both within the interinstitutional information group and by organising an annual debate on information and communication policy. in relation to the conditions of information, i shall only dwell on the analysis of information languages and accessible language. the languages should not only be the official ones, but also the co-official ones and all those in which the message can reach more directly, with the participation of local, regional, national and community authorities, according to the scope of their competence. as for the content, i will only focus on two points. on the one hand, the content should show the influence of the european union on the daily life of citizens, rejecting the image, which is often held, of the european union as a field of confrontation, with conflicting interests of the individual member states. on the other hand, a permanent flow of basic information for the citizen should be consolidated. it is difficult to associate citizens with the priorities i shall be discussing later if they are not familiar with the basic and elementary workings of the european union. as regards the current priorities, we are assuming those already included in the prince programme, i.e. enlargement, the future of europe, the area of freedom, security and justice, the introduction of the euro, or the role of the european union in the world. and it draws attention to the proximity of the 2004 elections which have symbolic value because it is the first time that 25 countries will elect their direct representatives in this house. the analysis of the report raises some critical questions. on the one hand, the question of the legal basis. the time is not ripe for formulating a legal basis for the preparation of the programmes, but the opportunity of the convention and the future intergovernmental conference makes it possible to support the idea that the right of citizens to be informed, to be authentic and true citizens, should be enshrined in the future constitution - within the democratic life of the european union. secondly, i would like to refer to the question of sectoral information, which - as i am fully aware - as the commission representatives have shown, is the commission's exclusive domain. the fact is, however, that the image of the european union is either enhanced or damaged directly by the actions emanating from the various sectoral policies. the coordination of the various sectoral policies, the direction of sectoral policies towards a common objective - the development of the european union - is what should be the subject of the interinstitutional information body, not of decision, of course, but of consideration. thirdly, the question arises as to whether systematized, basic, pedagogical information is better or the impact of spectacular campaigns that allow citizens to be alerted and then to look for the basic elements. finally, there is the filter of the national authorities. citizens perceive europe through their national authorities, who see what they have achieved as successes in relation to the rest of europeans and as a detriment what they find negative. the partnership and integration of the member states and regional and local authorities is essential for this purpose.

council the council is closely following the situation in western sahara. the european union calls on the government of the drc to take all necessary measures to ensure that the situation in the drc is resolved as quickly as possible. the union also fully supports, for this reason, the efforts of the united nations, and in particular the efforts of the personal envoy of the un secretary-general, mr james baker, to find a viable solution in full respect of international law. on 16 january 2003, mr baker submitted a proposal for a political settlement of the conflict, ensuring self-determination in accordance with security council resolution 1429 of 30 july 2002. it presented this proposal to the parties concerned and to the neighbouring countries during a visit to the region from 14 to 17 january 2003. the mandate of the united nations referendum mission in western sahara was subsequently extended twice. once by 31 march and once by 31 may, to give the parties concerned sufficient time to examine the proposal and formulate their replies. the presidency of the council of the union, in its contacts with the representatives of the parties, including recently at the meeting of the association council with morocco last february, has strongly urged them to give favourable consideration to mr baker's proposal. as noted in the report of the united nations secretary-general of 16 january, the united nations and the security council have been making active efforts over the past 20 years to help the parties involved find a solution to the dispute. all possible solutions have been presented to the parties concerned. it is now up to them alone to show the necessary political wisdom and seize this new opportunity to improve the future of the people of western sahara. the recent announcements of increased contacts between morocco and algeria, and the expressed willingness of both sides to discuss all issues, including western sahara, are a source of hope. given that the discussions on the final settlement of the sahara issue are taking place within the united nations and are now at a critical stage, the council does not consider it appropriate to take a position on the issue of exploiting the natural resources of western sahara. irrespective of the political settlement of the conflict, the issue of human rights is of fundamental importance to the union and a source of constant concern to it. in seeking to separate the humanitarian dimension of the conflict from its political dimension as far as possible, the european union has always encouraged the parties involved to take measures of a humanitarian nature to facilitate the re-establishment of trust between the people and the affected populations. the union has repeatedly made representations to the parties concerned to this effect. these efforts were again successful with the release of 100 moroccan prisoners of war on 26 february from the polisario front. the european union welcomed this development. the eu also called on the parties to the conflict to take all necessary steps to ensure that the peace process in the region is not disrupted by the threat of war. humanitarian issues related to the conflict in western sahara, including the issue of missing persons, are also systematically included in the political dialogue conducted by the union in the framework of the association agreements concluded with its partners in the southern mediterranean. at its last meeting in brussels on 24 february, the association council with morocco stressed the need to respect human rights and fundamental freedoms in western sahara. the european union is also calling for the immediate release of all political prisoners and for the immediate release of all political prisoners. the council also reiterated its attention to united nations security council resolution 1359, which urges the parties concerned to clarify the issue of missing persons and to comply with the requirements of international humanitarian law. the council has no information on the question of the el ayun black prison, nor sufficient evidence to rule on the actual circumstances of the arrest and conviction of the sahrawi prisoners. the european union, through the european community humanitarian aid office, is the main donor of humanitarian aid to the sahrawi population. for more information on the exact amount of union assistance, the honourable members are invited to contact the commission.

- question no 18 by brian crowley (h-0164/03):on: alternative energy research and development funddoes the council not think that, in view of the high oil price on world markets, it is now time to set up a european alternative energy research and development fund with ample appropriations and, if so, will it invite the commission to submit the necessary proposals to this effect for the 2004 budget and subsequent budgets?
council the honourable member is reminded of article 163 (3) of the treaty, which states that: all community actions under this treaty in the field of research and technological development, including demonstration projects, shall be decided upon and implemented in accordance with the provisions of title 18 concerning research and technological development, and in particular the multiannual framework programme referred to in article 166. research and development in the field of alternative energy is therefore carried out and financed under the framework programme. the current framework programme was established by decision 1513/2002 for the sixth framework programme of the european community for research, technological development and demonstration activities, with a view to contributing to the creation of the european research area and to innovation, and covers the period 2002-2006. the framework programme, under the priority theme 'sustainable development, planetary change and ecosystems', provides funding for research and development of sustainable energy systems in the following areas: clean energy, and in particular renewable energy sources and their integration into the energy system, including storage, distribution and use; energy saving and energy efficiency, including through the use of renewable raw materials; alternative fuel engines; electric fuel cells and their applications; new technologies for energy transmission and storage on a european scale, and in particular hydrogen technology; advanced and intensive research on renewable energy technologies linked to the significant long-term potential of clean coal-fired power plants, which requires a more ambitious energy future. an indicative amount of eur 810 million has been allocated to these research activities over the duration of the framework programme. it is also recalled that the 6th framework programme of the european atomic energy community, again for 2002-06, has an indicative budget of eur 750 million for research on controlled thermonuclear fusion, which could contribute to long-term energy supply and thus to the requirements of sustainable development for reliable central baseload electricity generation. further details of the research to be carried out and specific budget allocations are included in the specific programming decisions. the council, in agreement with the european parliament, has therefore, i believe, allocated substantial resources to research into alternative and renewable energy sources, as well as energy saving and efficiency.
council i would like to point out again that i have no new question here. but i would also point out to the honourable member that the us government's expenditure on alternative energy sources should not be compared with the european union's expenditure on the same purpose. we must add to the european union's expenditure the national expenditure of the governments of the 15 countries today or the 25 countries tomorrow for the same purpose, so that we can have a comparable size. it is well known and widely agreed that alternative energy sources must be promoted in order to deal with the problems of pollution and other pressures on the environment.
council i think that this issue has to do with proposals from the european commission on how these initiatives can be taken into account and beyond that, as in other matters, if there is no consultation with the members of the council, the presidency cannot give a positive or negative answer to something that has not been discussed.

- question no 20 by liam hyland (h-0167/03):on: older farmers and the debate on population trendsthe commission has expressed its concern about the impact of population ageing on the labour market and potential growth issues and says that there must be a clear economic incentive for people to stay in the labour market. the heads of state or government have set a target for europe to become a dynamic area by increasing the potential growth rate to 3% by 2010. will the council state whether it considers that the agricultural sector and older farmers fit into this debate on population trends?
council taking into account the impact of population ageing on labour markets and its potential impact on growth and the sustainability of social protection systems, member states agreed in stockholm to increase the employment rate of older workers to 50% by 2010. the barcelona european council called for a further progressive increase of around 5 years in the effective average age of retirement from the labour market by 2010. according to the 2002 joint employment report, all member states consider older workers to be the most important source of labour force and efforts have been made either to discourage early retirement or to provide incentives for longer stays on the labour market, while creating a framework to facilitate a gradual exit from economic activity, combining both approaches. in its contribution to the spring council of 21 march 2003, the council included increasing the supply of and participation in work by all groups and promoting the prolongation of active working life as one of its nine priorities, in order to achieve the three overarching objectives of the european employment strategy. the council expects the commission to include this priority in the employment guidelines and the commission is expected to present the employment guidelines in april 2003. the council also recognised the importance of maintaining agricultural activities in order to achieve balanced territorial development in the european union and to prevent depopulation in rural areas.
council i think the honourable member is expressing a thought which could be studied. i think we all know how complex the situation is, where on the one hand we have to see how to reduce the protection of the rural sector without this leading to an exodus of the population from the rural sector, and on the other hand how to deal with the issues of retirement age, because there is an ageing population on our continent, which is undermining the foundations of the pension system. there are various problems with the employment rate, which we are seeking to increase on the other hand. i have mentioned, by way of example, a number of situations which are not easily reconciled. you'd have to find golden meanings to say that. the proposal that has been heard, as i understand it, is in this direction, and i am sure that the commission will be able to assess and evaluate it in its proposals for the employment guidelines. the commission's proposals will also be a major overhaul of the employment guidelines agreed five years ago in luxembourg.

- the next item is the report (a5-0103/2003) by mr liese, on behalf of the committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy, on the proposal for a european parliament and council directive on the establishment of standards of quality and safety for the donation, procurement, testing, processing, storage and distribution of human tissues and cells (com (2002) 319 - c5-0302/2002 - 2002/0128 (cod)).
(es) mr president, first of all i would like to underline the excellent work of our colleague, mr liese, who has completed and improved the commission's proposal, which i think is very appropriate both in its approach and in its scope. it was during the spanish presidency of the european union that this directive was promoted. it is not in vain that spain has continued to be a world leader in donations and transplants for the tenth consecutive year in 2002. we are therefore very well aware of this issue, as well as the whole problem of tissue, cell and organ transplants, which have seen very significant technical advances in recent years, as well as increased awareness among the population of the need to become potential donors. all this makes it desirable to have specific legislation at european level to regulate these activities and to ensure that they are carried out within an appropriate framework in all member states, from the ethical, health and social point of view. the procedures of donation and transplantation are, as has already been said, the result of general solidarity, of the effort of all those who collaborate in an altruistic and disinterested way in the donation system and, therefore, it is so important to maintain and even to motivate and increase the voluntary nature to become a donor free of charge and, above all, for the donor's family to respect his will, when the time comes. there has been a lot of debate about the desirability of including organ transplantation in this directive. i think that there is a need for community regulation of organ transplantation, but to include it in this directive would be a mistake, because it would require substantial amendments to the directive, with uncertain results for the proper treatment of organ transplants. i therefore believe that amendment no 6 offers an appropriate solution and that it is a good opportunity for the commission to present a proposal on this subject in 2003. on the contrary, i think that, in relation to the commission's original proposal, which excluded cells to be used in the manufacture of medicinal products from the directive, amendment no 21, which includes them, is more appropriate. but perhaps the most controversial aspect of the directive is indeed the use of tissues and cells from cloned human beings, because of the important ethical and moral implications. i believe that amendment no 30 sets out basic conditions of respect for human dignity which should prevail in all member states, irrespective of whether each one is more or less strict, on the basis of this common basic commitment. finally, i would like to express my full support from this parliament to all those anonymous european citizens who, by donating tissues, cells or organs, make possible the miracle of giving a sick organism a breath of life and hope.
commission. – mr president, this interesting debate has highlighted the importance and the sensitivity of this proposal. i note that many of you, including mr liese, are disappointed that the commission has not offered to go further on the ethical issues. this is not because we do not consider ethical standards to be important – quite the contrary. it is precisely because ethical standards are so important to our citizens that we must not overstep the mark. the commission is the guardian of the treaties. we have to respect the advice of our legal service – advice also echoed by the legal service of the council. as i said in my opening address on this point, the commission's proposal aims to take to the very limit what is legally acceptable, given the constraints of the treaty. we simply cannot push this any further. that said, i would ask you to consider that if we discount those amendments that go beyond the scope of article 152, we can accept, fully or partially, a majority of them. i am pleased to note that most of those amendments substantially improve the directive. article 152 still allows us to take all necessary precautions to enforce the central requirement of the european group on ethics, namely in the protection of the health of the recipient. i now turn to the detail of the amendments before us today. on the scope of the proposal i can accept some clarifications, but the wording has to ensure legal clarity. a series of amendments aimed to limit the use of certain types of cells, such as cells derived from cloning or abortion. i share many of your concerns with regard to these issues. however, with this proposal we seek neither to mandate nor to prohibit the use of specific types of cells because the eu does not have the competence to do so. it is neither legally possible, nor appropriate, for the community to act in an area where it is best left to the member states. i wish to emphasise that decisions on the use of any specific type of cells and tissues – whatever the type – are a matter for our member states. if, however, any particular use of such cells is authorised in a member state, then the directive kicks in, to require the application of all provisions necessary to protect public health. as regards the exclusion of organs from the proposal, i reiterate that the commission does not intend to drop the subject of organs from the agenda. i attach the utmost importance to taking forward a legislative proposal based on sound science, and will follow it closely. we are presently engaged in the acquisition of the information and the scientific advice to enable us to bring forward legislation along these lines. this will take some time. i appeal to members of the house, particularly to such distinguished members as mr blokland and mr ó neachtain, to think twice before holding this piece of legislation to ransom and perhaps even taking the step of voting against this report and legislation because the commission cannot move at a speed that people believe is more appropriate. as representatives of our various institutions, we both respect the other's institution. no-one respects the rights of this institution more than i do myself. but i seek the same respect for my institution, which includes the right of initiative. it is one of the fundamental requirements of the community method that we all enjoy and support. one of the justifications for the retention of this right of initiative is that the commission brings forward a proposal when and if it is ready – but in this instance, when it is ready. i have said i will, but i cannot do it now. i cannot give a promise that i will have a legislative proposal before this house before this summer. if, with that information, you feel it necessary to vote against this legislation, so be it. but i would ask you not to do so. incidentally, the issue of organ trafficking is being addressed by a new initiative of the greek presidency under title 4 of the eu treaty. this initiative, which i support wholeheartedly, aims to make organ trafficking a criminal offence in all member states. in addition, we hope that a conference on organ transplantation, organised by the italian presidency in venice this september, will help us to determine the way forward in this area. in the meantime, the commission is compiling information on the current situation with regard to organ transplantation in the member states and applicant countries. once again, i appeal to members to look to their own responsibility and not to hold this particular piece of legislation to ransom because of the views they have about the speed of bringing forward this piece of legislation. returning to ethical issues, i have made clear that because of the legal position that has been underlined repeatedly by the legal services of the council and the commission, i cannot agree with a large number of the amendments on the table today. these amendments concern, in particular, voluntary unpaid donation, the principle of not-for-profit procurement and the requirements for donor consent. the question of voluntary unpaid donation was discussed at length during the codecision procedure on the blood directive. in the light of this experience, and also in view of the results of the debate in the council health group so far, i believe that it would save a lot of crucial time if the council and parliament did not seek to re-open this debate, but instead stayed with the blood solution, as a number of speakers have already said. on donor consent, i pointed out that the proposal states that the use of human tissues and cells should take place under conditions protecting the rights and health of all parties, and that the consent of donors and recipients should be given, following the international convention on human rights and biomedicine. with these basic principles in our proposal, we adhere to international standards. it is then for the member states to introduce detailed rules. i do not recommend going any further than that. provisions on consent vary across the member states. for example, if the donor is deceased, some presume consent whereas others do not. on the other hand, consent issues are well regulated in all member states and applicant countries, so the added value of binding provisions at eu-level is, in my view, very doubtful. in conclusion, i am very pleased to be able to accept, at least in principle, the majority of the technical amendments on the table today. a full listing of the commission's position on each of the amendments is being made available to parliament. i trust that this will be included in the minutes of this session. this dossier is one of the greek presidency's priorities as regards the health sector, which we hope can achieve a common position in the council, following parliament's opinion. through this proposal the community can establish significant new standards for the health of our citizens. i thank you all, once again, for your efforts on this dossier. i trust that you all share my desire to see this through to a satisfactory conclusion. protecting and improving public health is, after all, at the very centre of our citizens' concerns and expectations.

(es) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner, i would like to congratulate the rapporteur because, in my view, sweeteners are not an easy subject. i think the commission's proposal is in line 350 mg/l, in accordance with the opinion of the scientific committee for food. however, the commission changed its mind on the maximum dose and, after initially proposing 350 mg/l, has now supported - the next item is the report (a5-0138/2003) by mr glante, on behalf of the committee on industry, foreign trade, research and energy, on the promotion of cogeneration based on useful heat demand in the internal energy market.
the commission (es) mr president, the proposal for a directive on the promotion of cogeneration is, as the rapporteur, mr glante, has pointed out, a frankly complex matter. the debate in the committee on industry, foreign trade, research and energy has also revealed the diversity of positions, as have the meetings, hearings and seminars held in the past few months in this parliament, which demonstrate the interest that this initiative has aroused in various sectors of society. i would like to congratulate the rapporteur on being able to combine and agree with the various members concerned a solution which, in the end, means that we are talking about only eleven amendments. the creation of a european framework for cogeneration is a major challenge, ladies and gentlemen. i am pleased to say that i think the proposal for a directive on the promotion of cogeneration, which we are discussing, is up to the task and is also a response at a time when we are talking about the integration of the european energy market and, in particular, the electricity market. as the rapporteur has pointed out, cogeneration can be an efficient way of producing heat and electricity together in a single process, and its correct and appropriate use increases the security of supply, brings undeniable energy savings and the consequent reduction of greenhouse gas emissions. but we know that it faces problems in the energy market, because its advantages are not reflected in the same way in this sector. no legal instrument solves this problem and the directive creates the necessary framework to ensure a stable environment for initiatives to promote cogeneration. in this context, it is up to the member states to make a greater effort to promote this process and increase production through concrete measures in the form of economic support programmes. they can also facilitate new investment, ensure a level playing field and remove administrative and other obstacles, but all within an integrated european market. under our proposal, member states are obliged, through the analysis of the potential for high-efficiency cogeneration, to estimate the expected demand for heat in their territory, which can be adequately exploited by means of cogeneration techniques. it is the first step, which should facilitate future initiatives and follow-up in this field. moreover, as a result of the future directive, power and cogeneration producers will be able to apply for a guarantee of origin which shows that the electricity sold to the grid actually comes from high-efficiency cogeneration, from cogeneration which generates overall energy savings. this element is an instrument to increase the level of knowledge and transparency of the market and the proposal also insists that cogeneration power producers should not be discriminated against in connection with the conditions for connection to the electricity grid or in connection with the purchase or sale of electricity. in addition, the states will have the right to give priority to electricity from cogeneration. the sector - as you know - has repeatedly expressed the need for these measures to be in place if this type of production is to be developed properly. the definitions of cogeneration, and in particular of high-efficiency cogeneration, may seem very technical, but the adoption of a common methodology is an important step, which provides the sector with undeniable legal certainty as regards efficiency requirements. it provides a tool for states to develop support programmes that can promote cogeneration while avoiding distortions in the internal energy market and even distortions in competition more generally. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i have explained to you the commission's objective in relation to this proposal and i look forward to the debate that will take place now. i hope, together with the rapporteur, that we will be able, during this parliamentary term, to adopt this text at second reading, which i believe is extremely important in order to complete all the actions we are taking to strengthen energy efficiency and energy saving and to promote renewable energies, as we have been doing over the years.
the commission has also proposed that the council adopt a directive on the protection of the environment in the event of a fire. (es) mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, this is a directive which has involved complicated, long and heated debates, particularly in the committee on industry, foreign trade, research and energy. we have tried to stress that cogeneration is not an end in itself but a measure of energy efficiency and that this proposal, which continues the commission's strategy of increasing energy efficiency in the european union, was welcomed but at the same time presented a number of problems, as originally put forward by its rapporteur, mr glante. we have then seen how, through close dialogue and debate between several members of the committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy, we have put forward a balanced proposal which is really important from the point of view of energy savings. as i said earlier, demand-side cogeneration will therefore make it possible to optimise greenhouse gas emissions and to balance the operation of the electricity system. however, this whole building could have collapsed if it had been used to create an unnecessary demand for heat. a too simplistic approach - as i believe was proposed at the outset - would have led us to encourage the construction of cogeneration plants without there being any real demand for heat. and that is precisely the opposite of what we thought this proposal was aiming at. i would like to congratulate mr glante and all those who have taken part in the various meetings on this subject, because the subject was not easy to understand. among them, my colleague, mr vidal-quadras, who has worked hard on this directive. we went over numbers, formulas, variables, sub-indices and finally, i think we've been able to bring our views together. the compromise amendments are a good step towards reaching a final agreement and it is important that the existence of different technologies has been recognised throughout the european union. it is true that the more heat a plant produces, the greater the overall efficiency of the cogeneration process. but to reduce the whole directive to this statement was simplistic and unrealistic. a plant for the sole production of heat with an efficiency of 80% is absolutely inefficient - i might even say obsolete - and yet a power plant with an efficiency of 50% can become very efficient. and why all this? well, for the simple reason that electricity is a more elaborate form of energy that is obtained from heat. once it becomes clear that the overall efficiency of the plant is not an adequate or absolute parameter for determining the goodness of cogeneration, what is left? we are left with - as i think mr vidal-quadras will also point out - savings in primary energy and, consequently, savings in gas emissions. this is the most appropriate parameter for measuring the benefits of cogeneration compared to separate production of heat and electricity. we must not forget one very important nuance: cogeneration has developed in the different member states according to cultural patterns. in the countries of central and northern europe, heat is predominantly used for municipal purposes and it is clear that the needs for heating and hot water are enormous for a large part of the year; in other latitudes, cogeneration has been developed where the proportion of heat is lower for obvious reasons, so that electricity predominates for industrial purposes. the remainder is traded on the network. mr glante was able to see that this proposal needed a thorough analysis before reaching definitive conclusions. however, as rapporteur for the committee on the environment, public health and consumer protection, i have to say that this was not the case in this committee and that the opinion adopted in the committee, in the light of what is proposed today, after the debates and the meetings that have taken place, lacks realism and rigor. the complexity of this issue was evident from the outset and i, as rapporteur, supported by my group, called for a more flexible timetable. i have asked for this proposal to be seriously discussed and for more time to be given to discuss our different views with the committee on industry, foreign trade, research and energy. this request was refused and the motion was voted on in haste with the result i am now telling you. i, mr president, and my colleagues, believe that we must all try to avoid situations like this. it is not possible to draw up an opinion as was done in this case with the opinion of the committee on the environment on cogeneration, which i am afraid is not an isolated case but is rather a relatively frequent occurrence in parliament. finally, i believe that a rigorous, proportionate and necessary proposal has been reached. and in that sense i congratulate the rapporteur and my colleagues in the committee on industry again for their excellent work and, above all, for not settling for a first proposal and for fighting and struggling to reach agreements on a proposal that satisfies everyone. i'm not sure i can do that.
(es) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, there is no doubt that the promotion of electricity production by the method of cogeneration is a goal worth sharing, and for a number of reasons. we are therefore going to support the commission's initiative, which deserves our full respect and for which we congratulate the commissioner. production by the cogeneration method allows, firstly, energy savings and thus achieves an environmental protection objective, as it reduces co2 production. there are other reasons why this method is worth supporting. firstly, by producing heat and electricity in a combined way, it is possible to reduce costs and even, if you wish, to offer users an alternative supply, which in some cases means a certain form of introducing competition, especially in those markets - as in the electricity market in my country - where there is a strong oligopolistic component. the support for the promotion of cogeneration was endorsed by this parliament in its resolution of 25 september last and we will therefore be supporting this initiative in a consistent manner. but the problem is that the concept of cogeneration conceals very different realities, which correspond, on the one hand, to the countries of the north and, on the other, to the countries of the south. it was therefore very difficult to encompass such different realities in a single proposal. in the northern countries, cogeneration is mainly used for heating, whereas in the southern countries it is a system that is used in certain industrial sectors requiring intensive heat production and also makes electricity cheaper. examples of this are the paper and ceramic industries. it follows from this that the cogeneration plants used in some countries are radically different from those used in others. while in plants dedicated to heating steam turbines are used, and only it is necessary to generate heat during the cold months of the year, in those intended for the production of cogeneration for industrial purposes the heat needed is of higher intensity, and is used throughout the year. this implies differences in size and systems, and it has been difficult to encompass all of this in a single directive. i think that the efforts made by the rapporteur to include and accommodate such different realities in the text of the directive have been more than remarkable and for that i of course sincerely congratulate him. i would like to say that, in general, we will support the text of the report with the amendments that are put to us.
(es) mr president, the drafting of this directive and of the report by parliament on this piece of legislation has indeed been very laborious, but i would not say that there has been a confrontation, but a gradual and patient convergence towards rigor and service to the general european interest, through the sharing of arguments and points of view. the three main points we have achieved, mr president, through this long discussion, have been, firstly, to put primary energy saving at the centre of the directive as an essential parameter of the definition; secondly, to calculate the percentage of energy saving in relation to electricity produced and not in relation to the total of heat plus electricity, in order to put the emphasis where the energy saving occurs; and, finally, we have clearly distinguished between two situations: that of installations which work permanently by simultaneously producing heat and electricity and that of installations which, for reasons of their operation and the purposes they pursue, produce electricity and heat simultaneously only part of the year, and the other part of the year work exclusively in a condensing mode. these three points, mr president, were essential to achieving the purpose of this directive, which was to define cogeneration in a good way, which will then enable us to define a good system for stimulating this form of energy production, which will translate into what we all want: primary energy savings, reduction of co2 emissions and improvement of the union's independence from external energy sources. unfortunately, this discussion, in which we all participated with great enthusiasm, dedication and goodwill, was not enough for the whole house - for example, mr turmes - but we cannot expect everyone to understand everything at once. i am sure that mr turmes, who is a man of great knowledge in this field, will continue to reflect on this and that what is not clear to him today will soon be clear to him. i am prepared to continue explaining the same things to him and his collaborators, as i have done so far - although after your intervention i see that without success - because it is always a pleasure to talk to him, in political and human terms. mr glante, allow me to make a remark very specifically to you, to whom i warmly thank for your receptivity and your goodwill throughout the work we have done together: when a sculpture is finished and is almost perfect, there are always final strokes of chisel that achieve absolute perfection. i would draw your attention to amendments nos 75 and 81, which correspond to the agreement reached after the committee meeting and which are essential for our group: amendment no 75, which abolishes the 80% threshold, which is no longer relevant, and amendment no 81, which clearly distinguishes between the two types of installation. commissioner, general de gaulle used to say that politics is action in the service of a strong, clear and simple idea. if that is so, then you, commissioner, have an energy policy for the union in mind and, as you continue to develop it, this parliament will support it, because it fulfils the objectives we all seek: improving our competitiveness, guaranteeing the well-being of all europeans and better economic growth.
commission. - mr president, i would like to thank all the rapporteurs for their comments and to say that i agree with all of them. what we are doing is to propose, over the years, greater energy efficiency, better energy saving and use, and all this in the service of sustainable development, which means not only ensuring competitiveness and quality of service for users, but also respecting the environment. but i think all honourable members will agree that what we cannot do, under the guise of 'cogeneration', is to allow a system to be created which ultimately consumes more energy than would be consumed separately in the whole process and also benefits from subsidies which are ultimately paid for by the users, the taxpayer - there are various possibilities - or simply the customers of the network, causing not only poor energy use, higher energy consumption but also distortions of competition and a lack of competitiveness of the whole system which i do not think benefits anyone. the aim is to support real cogeneration and to prevent subterfuge by those who under the pretext of carrying out a cogeneration activity carry out another type of activity. i would like to thank the rapporteur. several honourable members have referred to the complex and difficult discussions. i understand that there are a number of aspects which involve considerable technical complexity and i therefore want to reiterate my thanks for the effort and quality of the work done, even if the commission cannot accept some of the elements raised. of the remaining 85 amendments, the vast majority can be accepted in whole or in part or by means of a reworking. however, there are 28 that we reject outright. i will provide you with a full copy, mr president, so that there is no doubt the commission's position on the amendments let me refer to some of the points that have been raised and explain the commission's position. for example, we cannot accept amendments which change the terminology of the commission throughout the text and which, in my view, can be misleading. i am referring to the amendments replacing the term 'useful heat' with 'useable heat energy' and to the deletion of the term 'high efficiency' associated with certain types of cogeneration where specific quantifiable savings are achieved. cogeneration must be based on a real and justified demand for energy and we must insist on high efficiency as a guarantee of energy savings. i hope that you will understand the position of the commission. i agree with the rationale of some of the amendments which seek to set national and european union targets for the development of cogeneration, but i cannot support their content, because insisting on the objectives of cogeneration will lead us into a situation of total conflict with the council. the commission's proposal is to be submitted to the council for approval. moreover, this target was not indicative for each member state but was an overall target for all 15 member states. in this sense, in order to arrive at targets for each member state, we would have to carry out an analysis, as we did in the case of 'green energy', where a country-by-country assessment was made of the renewable energy potential available to the various countries for electricity production. we have not sufficiently assessed this situation. there are also very important developments in consumption in some countries at the moment which do not allow us to set these individual targets in a truly realistic way; we can do this as a voluntary act, but it would not be a realistic element. you know that when i make a commitment and set a target, i want it to be realistic and therefore ambitious, but achievable and linked to the potential and capabilities of each member state. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the use of the term 'competition' in the definition of the term 'competition'. these amendments cannot be accepted, because we must ensure that producers of cogeneration energy have equal access to the electricity grid, without any discrimination to their detriment, but we must ensure the distribution and transmission of production wherever necessary and under conditions for the exchange of electricity which are equitable. we could not accept an amendment which would require us to submit a proposal for a directive on the promotion of energy from cogeneration after a certain number of years. although this is a complex subject, i think we have had enough time to be able to develop these aspects in this work. i understand that the rapporteur wishes to establish an exact and detailed definition of electricity from generation in annex ii. however, the commission cannot accept amendments nos 70 and 75, which introduce a method of detailed calculation of the legislative text, because we are not convinced that the industry can unanimously accept this method and, even if it could, i do not think it would be appropriate to include it in the directive, as it would make it an excessively rigid directive. i understand and support the intentions expressed on the need for specific measures for micro-generation, although some amendments cannot be accepted - i am thinking of amendments nos 38 and 41 - but i would also like to express my agreement with the european parliament on the need to seek from the outset the maximum harmonisation of calculation principles and primary energy savings. i would like to thank the honourable members once again for the work done and to acknowledge the complexity of the matter, but i would stress that this is one of the elements which can enable us to significantly increase energy efficiency and therefore energy saving, which is one of our priority objectives from the point of view of energy policy and security of supply.

- the report (a5-0129/2003) by mr nicholson, on behalf of the committee on regional policy, transport and tourism, on the proposal for a regulation of the european parliament and of the council on insurance requirements for air carriers and aircraft operators.
commission. - (es) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i should like to say very briefly that the community rules in force simply require airlines to be insured, but they do not set any criteria, conditions or amounts which the granting authorities in the member states of the union have to respect. it was therefore necessary to clarify this situation, especially after the events of 11 september 2001. as the rapporteur has rightly said, it is a question of restoring confidence and making it easier for even small companies to have adequate insurance cover. the commission's objective is therefore to ensure that all aircraft flying to europe are insured at all times against various risks, including those of war or terrorism. i would like to thank the rapporteur, mr nicholson, for his constructive work, which has brought a more balanced approach, particularly to third party insurance issues. the commission has a strong interest in the rapid adoption of this proposal and will continue to monitor the aviation insurance market to ensure that the current situation excludes any risk of insufficient cover. but i would say to the honourable member that, as regards the impact report, the reality is that before preparing this proposal, the commission gathered various information on the question of insurance conditions applicable in the various states of the union through the european civil aviation conference and from third countries, including also everything relating to insurance associated with leasing, aircraft rental contracts, the commission has been following very actively the development of the insurance market, both at european and international level. first at european level, in order to finally put an end to the special conditions which allowed the public sector to cover certain types of risks, but also through the international civil aviation organisation, which is where we believe that these types of issues should be tackled in a fundamental way. the proposal which the honourable members are discussing today is also the result of various discussions in a special group set up specifically to discuss insurance problems after the tragic events of september. the insurance and airline industries were represented in this special group. finally, i would like to say that, following the introduction of special conditions which have been in place for some time after 11 september 2001 (until we understood that the market had recovered sufficient capacity to cover all risks at reasonable prices), the commission has been monitoring the support measures and the rates applied in the various member states, which has enabled us to know first-hand and directly the reality of air insurance in the various member states. so, in that sense, ladies and gentlemen, mr president, mr nicholson, we understood that there was no need for further impact studies, because we had more than enough information to develop this proposal.

- question no 26 by mr casaca (h-0254/03): subject: storm on 11 and 12 april in the azores on 11 and 12 april, the autonomous region of the azores was hit by an extremely violent storm which caused extensive damage to housing and public infrastructure on all the islands of the archipelago, but which was particularly severe for agriculture. as the author has experienced firsthand, widespread and profound damage has been inflicted on all greenhouse production, especially pineapples in são miguel. fruit and vegetable production - especially bananas, oranges and passion fruit - has suffered extensive damage and the wine sector is almost totally ruined. given the high frequency of this type of phenomenon in the autonomous region of the azores, the regional structural funds programme, prodesa, already provides for specific actions in the event of a disaster. there are, however, two questions which remain open and for which the author would like to have an answer from the european commission. the first is whether the commission will take account of the effect of this storm in the decisions to be taken on the regional allocation of the programming and performance reserves of the community support framework. the second question is whether, as in the case of the measures taken for farmers in central europe affected by the bad weather last summer, the commission intends to provide the farmers concerned with specific measures to reduce as far as possible the negative impact on their yields.
the commission (es) mr president, first of all i would like to say that i am sorry for the storm that has hit the azores. unfortunately, there have been various weather disasters in various parts of the european union in recent times, but i would point out that the regional operational programme of the structural funds provides, in some of its measures, for aid which can make good the damage caused by the inclement weather to which the honourable member refers. i would point out that the problems suffered on 11 and 12 april in the azores - mentioned by the honourable member - do not, in principle, give rise to the allocation of additional amounts from the effective reserve. as the honourable member knows, the commission is an instrument designed to stimulate the effectiveness of operational programmes. its allocation shall be based on indicators defined by the member state, in consultation with the commission, which reflect the effectiveness, management and financial execution of the programmes and allow the results to be measured in relation to the objectives defined by the programme. in other words, they are designed to encourage the various european regions, the various countries of the european union, to manage the structural funds at their disposal in the best possible way. on the other hand, the allocation of the programming reserve proposed by the member state when programming the community support framework may take account of the extraordinary needs of the agricultural sector in the azores. there would be room for reallocation of funds. portugal can therefore propose that the climatic conditions to which the honourable member refers be taken into account, but i repeat, by means of the programming reserve. as regards the possibilities of aid to farmers, certain measures may be adopted, at the request of the member state concerned, within the framework of the common agricultural policy, although, as the honourable member is aware, the commission has not received, to date, any communication or request for intervention from the member state or the regional authorities in connection with the events in the azores. if the commission is consulted on this, it will of course study, in the context of the legislation in force, the measures that can be taken to deal with the consequences of these climatic events.

- question no 27, by mrs gutiérrez-cortines (h-0289/03): the commission has not yet decided whether to grant aid to the victims of the floods in the canary islands. subject: oil spills in gibraltar for years, ship refuelling, loading and unloading operations in the vicinity of gibraltar have been causing oil spills at sea, with serious consequences for the environment and the economy of the neighbouring spanish territory, where economic activity is mainly based on the fishing and tourism sectors. this is just one example of many of the highly polluting substances that are being released. these discharges, which are harmful to the landscape for citizens, also have serious economic consequences and cause incalculable damage to the environment by making it impossible for a long time to carry out any normal activity in the polluted area. in the face of this type of disaster, and in the light of the commission communication to the european parliament and the council on enhancing maritime safety following the sinking of the oil tanker prestige (com/2002/0681 final), when will the commission present a study on the appropriateness of revising existing legislation and existing mechanisms for environmental protection in order to minimise the risk of accidents and the damage that this entails? second part
the commission (es) as the honourable members and mrs gutiérrez-cortines are aware, the commission adopted on 13 december a communication on the reinforcement of maritime security following the sinking of the oil tanker prestige, which reminds the member states of the need to apply in advance and accelerate the implementation of the erika i and erika ii legislative packages, and proposes new measures. these new measures were given a boost at the last council of ministers in march, when the commission, without waiting any longer, implemented some of the provisions proposed in its communication. the european maritime safety agency has therefore been set up: its executive director was appointed on 29 january and its activities are already beginning in brussels, with a provisional headquarters, while the final location is being decided. the commission has also started to set up the community vessel traffic monitoring system, safeseanet, and has asked member states to define in advance national plans for receiving vessels in distress in ports or shelter zones. the various countries of the union must designate these areas of refuge before this summer. two coordination meetings have already been held in this connection and i would like to remind you that the commission, in addition to addressing all the neighbouring countries of the mediterranean basin, but also russia and norway, has already held talks (not only has it written to all these countries) to highlight the importance of maritime safety and the control of oil tankers by the port authorities, but also, in particular with russia, norway, algeria and morocco, we have discussed these matters in bilateral meetings with the relevant ministers and, in the specific case of russia and norway, we are looking at the possibility of establishing a system of control of maritime traffic in the baltic and north sea area, which will make it possible to increase safety and avoid any kind of problems. it should be added that on 20 december the college of commissioners adopted a regulation prohibiting the transport of heavy fuel by single-hull oil tankers to and from ports in the european union and accelerating the replacement of single-hull vessels by double-hull vessels. this proposal has also been agreed by consensus in the council and examined at first reading by the committee on regional policy, transport and tourism of the european parliament and should therefore enter into force as from next june, if the council's agreements are maintained. finally, i would point out that the commission sent the european parliament and the council on 5 march a proposal for a directive on pollution from ships and the introduction of penalties, including criminal penalties, for pollution offences. this proposal concerns illegal, accidental or voluntary discharges - because there are also voluntary discharges: the cleaning of bottoms and bilges, to which the honourable member refers - by establishing responsibilities throughout the chain from shipowners, charterers, classification societies, etc., which will make it possible to close the gaps in community law on deliberate or accidental pollution by ships and which will oblige the union states to adopt the relevant legislation. finally, the fipol fund, which we have seen in the case of the erika, but also in the case of the prestige, is clearly insufficient in its present size, and it must be increased to a maximum liability ceiling of eur 1 billion, in accordance with the commission's proposals, in accordance with an agreement of the council of ministers, which has agreed that if this fund is not increased within the international maritime organisation, at least in the european region, a decision will be taken within the european union to establish a supplementary fund to enable these levels of compensation to be reached. on 16th of this month a diplomatic conference is to be held in the framework of the international maritime organisation, and i hope that our approach will be accepted, namely that the european union simply protects itself at a level equivalent to that of a country such as the united states.

the commission (es) i agree with the honourable member that this is a process. if, for example, we are talking about cleaning up sewers, we can demand that there be no discharges into the sea because we have adopted - and this parliament supported us in this proposal - a directive which imposes an obligation on all the member states of the union to establish, in all ports of a certain level in the union, the facilities necessary to be able to clean up the seabed and sewers in ports, without having to resort to cleaning them up at sea, which has been the usual practice over the years and which is the cause of more than 90% of the pollution by hydrocarbons that occurs year after year. the pollution of the seabed is not caused by major catastrophes, like erika, prestige, amoko cadiz or the aegean sea. these have a brutal local impact, as we have seen, but also, year after year, tons and tons are deliberately dumped into the high seas, nine to ten times more than the major catastrophes. as regards gibraltar, i would like to say to the honourable member that the directive and regulation adopted, as regards the requirements for double-hull vessels, heavy oil transport, fleet rejuvenation and so on, are very clear: they apply to all ports, berths or anchorages in the european union. gibraltar is in the european union and gibraltar, like any other place - like algeciras - to mention the port opposite - is affected. of course the commissioner for the environment fully shares the measures we have proposed, although we are setting a specific rate for the oil and oil pollution sector. a specific type which has to do with the fact that the fipol fund provides specific and differentiated cover and insurance for oil pollution - which other types of potential polluters lack - and furthermore, in the field of criminal sanctions, we also understand that oil pollution and cleaning of sewers has a component which calls for a specific type of sanctions or which, at least, may require that at best other types of environmental crimes are not raised as such a crime, with criminal sanction in some countries. but in this case, where there is clearly a voluntary nature and very serious effects on the surrounding populations and the marine environment, it is logical to demand that this type of action, which is absolutely unacceptable, be criminalised.
the commission (es) we are talking about proposing that the member states of the union, and this is what i have put to the council and parliament, should make marine pollution by dumping, including by cleaning up the bottom, a criminal offence, with penalties of deprivation of liberty, when it occurs - as the honourable member says - deliberately on the high seas. we're talking about this being a felony within 200 miles of the exclusive economic zone. this is complemented, as i said earlier, by increased control of maritime traffic. i think that - and we are going to launch some studies in this direction - we are at the moment carrying out a control of maritime traffic of a certain type of vessels, namely oil tankers, and also in certain areas. the point, in my view, is to go a step further, to control all types of vessels that are in circulation, except for the low-water traffic - as we call it in spanish - that is, near the coast, three, four or five miles; that, from a certain distance from the coast, all traffic must be controlled. this will mean greater safety on a sea which is increasingly frequented by shipping and recreational activities, but also on a sea which is increasingly polluted and which must be protected more consistently. what is done in the air with airplanes could clearly also be developed, with the appropriate differences and modifications, in the sea area and that is what we are working on, starting - i repeat - with the control of the traffic of all oil tankers entering european union waters and of all traffic in certain areas of the european union.
- question no 28 by mr lage (h-0222/03): subject: appointment of a portuguese official to the post of director-general for press and communication during a parliamentary debate on 26 march in connection with a motion of censure, the portuguese prime minister interpreted the appointment of a portuguese to the post of director-general of the commission as a diplomatic victory for his government and criticised the inability, in his view, of the previous socialist government to do so. subsequently, the commission's representation in portugal publicly stated that appointments to senior posts in the commission were based on criteria of merit and competence, as well as on the principles of equal opportunities and geographical balance. the choice of a portuguese for the post in question is undoubtedly motivated by the favourable assessment of his skills. nevertheless, the prime minister's statements may raise some doubts. can the commission state whether the appointment of a portuguese person as director-general for press and communication is due solely to the fact that the person selected was considered competent in the light of the required criteria or whether it is the result of diplomatic pressure from the portuguese government?

commission. – the commission considers that angola has made substantial progress towards consolidation of the peace process since the signing of the peace agreement in april 2002 and that a return to furthermore, the presence of landmines continues to be a major threat. in fact, when people started moving after the peace agreement had been signed, we saw an unfortunate increase in the number of accidents due to landmines – a terrible consequence. the commission is continuing to assist the government and society in general to address these challenges. as regards the situation in cabinda, may i refer to the answer to the question from the member, written question e-640/03 on this subject. the commission is following the developments in the province closely, and there have been indications of some positive developments in the conflict recently. the overall humanitarian situation, while still serious, continues to stabilise. emergency pockets and areas exist throughout the interior of the country, particularly in areas where mines and damaged infrastructure still limit access. the commission considers the successful demobilisation and reintegration of ex-unita soldiers to be crucial for national reconciliation. there have been problems, but given the difficult circumstances, the demobilisation process can be qualified as successful, although reintegration has not yet been fully achieved. in march this year i visited angola and also one of the biggest camps of ex-unita soldiers, and had a thorough exchange of views with them concerning their prospects in this situation. everything seemed relatively well organised. the commission is in contact with the political parties, although a regular dialogue really is not up and running yet. it is intended to strengthen the effort to create such a dialogue. as regards churches and civil society there is an ongoing dialogue as well as co-operation on a number of specific projects. concerning the donors’ conference, which will take place in brussels, there is still no confirmation of date, modalities and agenda. the success of the conference is strongly linked to the establishment of a credible government plan for rehabilitation and reconstruction of the country, including a poverty reduction strategy, as well as to an improvement of the relationship between the government of angola and the imf. the commission has repeatedly offered to assist in the preparation and organisation of the conference. transparency of public accounts and revenues from national resources, oil and diamonds, could improve definitely with the new economic team in place since the december cabinet reshuffle, although concrete results are not yet visible. the diagnosis of the oil sector, which the government is currently undertaking with kpmg should be an important element and the commission awaits its publication with great interest. i raised these issues very directly with the government during the visit i just mentioned. the commission and other donors are working together to encourage the government to increase transparency. the next presidential and legislative elections will be a crucial test for the government’s commitment to democratic practices. the commission will follow developments very closely and has offered to assist in creating conditions for free and fair elections. the priorities for the european community’s co-operation with angola are spelt out in the recently signed country strategy paper. in the short to medium term, priority is given to funding the measures necessary to support the peace process and national reconciliation, including creating the conditions for free and fair elections. in the medium to longer term, the commission will gradually increase the focus of its support, concentrating aid on health, education and food security as the three main focal areas. angola has also been included as a focus country under the european initiative for democracy and human rights (eidhr).
commission. – firstly, i agree with the view expressed that this broad, open dialogue, which can consolidate pluralism, is important at this stage. fortunately, owing to the structure of the peace agreement and the way in which the two opposing movements are in general able to talk and do things, we are now at a point at which peace is irreversible. however, we should not rest on our laurels. the demobilisation and the reintegration of ex-combatants is a huge problem. the offers we and others can make have to be suited to the individual, and this is not an easy thing to do. many of them should go back to agricultural activities and this is the key to doing what needs to be done concerning the majority of these people. i see the focus on health education and food security in our programme in angola as something which will be useful for precisely this endeavour.
commission. – it is true that the increase in known reserves of oil in angola points to a very interesting future for the next years and the question of licensing and who gets what gain from the large potential of oil production in angola needs to be followed up very carefully. the commission supports the uk initiative. others are involved in this too, but the uk has been the leading player here, in regard to declaring what you pay and creating more transparency about revenue in industries such as oil. it is absolutely necessary to discuss this with angola. i have raised this matter myself in very clear terms. i agree that the elections are the big test. that is where we also have to invest in terms of capacity-building and strengthening the system.

commission. – we cannot launch anything in today's world without making a new acronym. this is the fti – which, by the way, is also supported by the ifis – but i am a member of acronyms anonymous and so are many other people. i think i will talk about 'education for all' and the 'fast track initiative'. the objectives set in dakar and the millennium development goals in this field of education are the basis of our policy in developing countries. overall, the community has allocated an estimated eur 1.3 billion to education in developing countries for the next 5 years. this is the global figure. it is also providing substantial financing to acp countries under the 9th edf in the form of general budget support – eur 1.66 billion – part of which will benefit the education sector. it is difficult to say exactly how much, and with what sort of direct focus, but one part of this is clearly relevant. in this context we devote full attention to the fast track initiative as a means to accelerate progress towards education for all. so far only 10 countries have an approved proposal for the fast track initiative, including 7 acp countries. unfortunately these 7 acp countries have not chosen education as a priority sector in their cooperation with the community. the commission is therefore looking into the possibility of using old, dormant funds to support the fast track initiative in these 7 countries. the initiative has been prioritised as one of a number of possible so-called 'fast disbursement' mechanisms for the use of dormant amounts of old european development fund money. this process is now being discussed with the acp partner countries. in addition to the 10 countries that have an approved proposal for the fast track initiative, all other developing countries that meet the eligibility criteria for this, such as a full poverty reduction strategy paper and a credible sector plan, can expect further support to implement their plans. where possible, the commission will participate even through existing mechanisms or by recommitting dormant funds. this is now an ongoing effort. as far as the analytical fast track is concerned, its exact role is still being defined. a specific working group has been set up to further develop this concept. the timetable is also part of the issue. we recognise that further efforts are required this year and next year to ensure that the implementation of european development fund resources is managed in the most efficient manner possible. to this end, seminars were organised in february and march 2003, bringing together the different players in the project management cycle within the process. delegations, dg-development and aidco. during the seminars, in order to free up idle resources, a substantial effort went into identifying dormant commitments lying under previous edfs. targets were agreed with all delegations for decommitments to be achieved by the end of this year. decommitments imply an administrative procedure that also involves the headquarter. the same goes for recommitting the money, which will take place in the annual reviews. partner countries of course have the final say on decisions to use these dormant funds for the fast-track initiative. this is not the only use of the money that we try to free up and accelerate the use of, but the fast-track initiative is clearly identified as one of the priorities.
commission. – i would maintain that the budget support which the commission and parliament discussed in great detail a couple of years ago is an extremely important tool where a partner country has reached a reasonable level of quality in its sector policy for education. we have a basis that is good enough to inject money through budgetary support relating to the more detailed work carried out by member states or other donors working very directly at a technical level in that country. on this issue of money, we are doing important things. in addition, in having this initiative organised as broadly and energetically as it is, we are inspiring – not to say pushing – african and other countries to lift education higher up the ladder of priorities. our water initiative has the same effect, and we offer real assistance to those governments that face up to this. it is quite helpful but, again, successful coordination and approaching the problems via sector programmes is exactly what this initiative can also accelerate.
