council mr president, ladies and gentlemen, today we have the opportunity to inform you of the current state of the presidency's negotiations with the united states of america on the two agreements, one on extradition and one on mutual judicial cooperation. these negotiations have now reached their final stage. the text of the draft agreements was sent to the european parliament two weeks ago. the presidency hopes to obtain approval for their signature at the jha council on 6 june. this will enable the presidency to sign the agreements at the european union-united states summit scheduled for 25 june in washington. the fact that we are in a position today to be so optimistic about the outcome of these negotiations is largely due to the considerable efforts of previous presidencies. after a first negotiating meeting under the spanish presidency, extensive negotiations were conducted by the danish presidency with the assistance of the commission and certainly with the support of the council secretariat. at its meeting on 28 february 2003, the council agreed that the presidency had conducted the negotiations satisfactorily, with a positive outcome, and that the negotiation of the agreements should be suspended in order to allow the member states the necessary time to examine the essential aspects of the text. some member states are still in the process of consulting their national parliaments. the council therefore decided at its meeting last week to facilitate the completion of the information. the presidency has, i recall, informed the european parliament on several occasions of the state of play of the negotiations with the united states of america, and we had the opportunity to inform the libe committee on 20 march. if the council of 5 june gives the presidency the power to sign the agreements on behalf of the european union, some of the member states will have to follow their own constitutional procedures, which implies approval or ratification by national parliaments. article 24 of the treaty on european union explicitly allows member states to declare that they must follow constitutional procedures before being bound by an agreement. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. the european union will be bound only after the exchange of the legislative acts of ratification with the united states of america, which will then take place only after the council has taken a second decision authorising the presidency to exchange the legislative acts of ratification with the united states of america. between the signing of the agreements and the exchange of the instruments of ratification, the presidency will inform the european parliament of the text of the agreement, although the treaty on european union does not require this. it is logical that such briefing will take place at this stage, given that constitutional procedures have traditionally provided that governments will seek the consent or advice of national parliaments on the final text of the agreement. it is obvious that a text becomes final only when it is signed by the parties. the presidency believes that this agreement has added value to the existing bilateral extradition and mutual legal assistance agreements between the member states of the european union and the united states of america. i should like to stress that if we do not reach an agreement, we will have to live with the existing bilateral agreements which the member states have concluded. in any event, the agreements between the european union and the united states of america will not supersede bilateral agreements between member states and the united states of america. the agreements we are informing you of today are based on articles 24 and 38 of the treaty on european union. they will coexist with the bilateral agreements. they will complement and in some cases replace provisions in bilateral agreements. it is also important to understand that member states will be able to continue to invoke the grounds for refusal of extradition or judicial cooperation contained in bilateral extradition and mutual judicial cooperation agreements. if a bilateral mutual judicial cooperation or extradition agreement between a member state and the united states of america provides for a ground for refusal, that member state will be able to continue to invoke it after the entry into force of the agreements between the european union and the united states of america. in addition, the draft extradition agreement contains a provision which, to my knowledge, has no precedent in international extradition law. it recognises that the requested state may refer to its constitutional principles, which need not be contained in the text of the constitution itself but may have been enshrined in a text at a level equal to that of the constitution, for historical or other legally binding reasons which impede the fulfilment of its obligation to extradite a person. in such cases, of course, the requesting state and the requested state should consult each other in order to resolve the issue. this is particularly important with the explicit reference in the preamble to the principle of a fair trial conducted by an impartial tribunal established in accordance with the law. this provision actually allows member states to refuse extradition of a person in the case of specialised courts if they do not have this right under the bilateral extradition agreement with the united states of america. the member states which in future conclude new agreements with the united states of america should clearly respect these agreements of the european union, since they will form part of the acquis of the european union. these future bilateral agreements should therefore be compatible with the agreements of the european union and the united states of america. the negotiations were successful in the view of the presidency. we have succeeded in making a positive contribution to the current level of cooperation, in increasing efficiency and, above all, in agreeing on additional safeguards. it is of the utmost importance to understand that the agreements add safeguards to existing bilateral agreements and that without the conclusion of these agreements the present legal protection will be reduced compared to if the agreements are concluded. the draft extradition agreement between the european union and the united states of america contains a provision prohibiting extradition in the event of the imposition or execution of the death penalty. this provision goes beyond the level of protection provided by the bilateral extradition agreements, since it creates a general condition for the outcome described and does not depend on the non-execution of the death penalty on the assurances given by the government of the united states of america. unlike what has been the case up to now in almost all bilateral extradition agreements, the non-execution of the death penalty by the government of the united states of america is not dependent on assurances given by the government of the united states of america on an ad hoc basis, but may be made conditional by the member state to which the united states requests the extradition of a person. the european union member states may also make it a condition that the united states of america shall not impose the death penalty. the united states of america will then be bound by this condition, unless this is impossible for procedural reasons. such a case is where the death penalty has already been imposed before the person is surrendered or where the criminal prosecution of the offence for which the person is accused automatically entails the possibility for the competent court of the united states of america to impose the death penalty, as is the case in very few states of the united states of america. member states wishing to continue their bilateral practice will, however, be able to do so if they do not apply this provision and/or if they make a declaration at bilateral level jointly with the united states. some of the other issues where the draft agreements bring added value are related to the issue of: in the case of sensitive information, the draft agreement shall allow consultation to be requested in order to determine the extent to which the information contained in a request can be protected by the requested state. with regard to concurrent applications, the agreement deals with the issue of the simultaneous submission of an extradition request by the united states of america and by another state or where that other state is a member state of the european arrest warrant. in this context i would like to refer to the question of the international criminal court, since the presidency is aware of the particular sensitivities and concerns of parliament in this regard. at the start of the negotiations it was agreed by both negotiating parties that the agreement would have no impact on the respective positions of the member states and the united states of america with regard to extradition requests originating from the international criminal court. the european union and the united states of america have agreed at the negotiating level to develop this in writing in an explanatory note, which reads as follows: article 10 is not intended to affect the obligations of states parties to the rome statute of the international criminal court. the question of simultaneous extradition requests by the international criminal court and extradition requests by the united states of america is therefore regulated and will continue to be regulated in such a way that it falls within the exclusive competence of the member states, and the council will not be able to make any statement on it. in the field of mutual legal assistance, some of the main achievements of the negotiations with the united states of america are to be found in the following areas: the draft agreement improves cooperation in the field of investigations into possible financial elements of serious crime, including organised crime, terrorism and financial crime. member states that are not currently bound by a mutual judicial cooperation agreement with the united states of america may invoke the public policy, security, national sovereignty or other interests of the requested state to refuse the transmission of information in certain cases. the agreement contains extensive provisions on data protection and the provision of evidence and information. the draft agreement contains provisions to facilitate the use of joint research teams and the possibility of teleconferencing between member states and the united states. these provisions facilitate the member states in making use of these possibilities but do not oblige them to do so. the draft agreement allows the use of modern means of telecommunication, fax or e-mail for the exchange of mutual assistance requests and responses with an explicit acknowledgement of receipt. mutual judicial cooperation, to the extent not already provided for by bilateral agreements, is offered for use by the administrative authorities of both the united states of america and the member states when investigating criminal conduct with a view to prosecution or reporting such conduct to the investigating or prosecuting authorities. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank you once again for the opportunity to inform parliament of the progress of the negotiations between the european union and the united states of america on extradition and mutual judicial cooperation agreements.

council the cotonou agreement is based on three main pillars: political dialogue, economic and trade cooperation and development aid. this partnership shall focus on the objective of reducing and eventually eradicating poverty, consistent with the objectives of sustainable development and the gradual integration of the acp countries into the world economy. acp-ec cooperation is based on a transitional agreements long before its full entry into force in april 2003. with the entry into force of the cotonou agreement, the funds of the 9th edf are now available. the programming of these resources, i.e. the preparation of the country-specific support strategy, based on the specific medium-term objectives and development strategies of the country, and the establishment of an indicative council the council acknowledges that the overall situation with regard to the doha negotiations on development issues is far from satisfactory, mainly because deadlines were not respected in certain areas, such as the details of access to medicines and the details in the field of agriculture. the drug impasse is due to the refusal of the united states to agree on a solution that was acceptable to almost all other countries. the situation is more complicated in agriculture, and the repeated efforts of the chairman of the wto committee on agriculture, mr harbinson, have been rejected by all the parties, but for opposite and divergent reasons. the council is of course willing to consider any new text which mr harbinson or anyone else may put forward. however, despite these difficulties, it is essential at the present time to maintain the momentum of the wto negotiations and to make substantial progress in the run-up to the cancun conference. first, in the current volatile international political climate it is even more important to make substantive progress on trade issues. in addition, the latest multilateral meetings in geneva have shown that there is an increased awareness among wto members that the preparatory process should move forward in the coming months so as not to create an excessive workload for the cancun conference. finally, the council does not share the pessimistic views expressed by some commentators on the cancun conference. the problems to be solved before cancun are numerous but this is not the first time we have experienced time pressure in trade negotiations. if all the relevant actors make a serious effort and show real political will, progress can be made on all outstanding issues in the coming months. positive links between issues should therefore be sought in order to restore the momentum of the process, since all parties know that there is no agreement until full agreement is reached. as regards agriculture, the council, at its meeting on 8 april 2003, confirmed its support for the community's proposal for the agricultural details and encouraged the commission to continue its efforts to reach an agreement on this basis, as it considered it to be the most realistic means of completing the negotiations in accordance with the timetable set out in the doha ministerial declaration.
council i would like to refer to the concept of rational expectations and rational behaviour and say that, obviously, whatever outcomes are reached in the negotiations taking place within the european union, they will not be reached with the prospect that they cannot be secured and cannot be compatible with those that will be decided at world level.

council the issue of nuclear safety is of general concern to the council, which fully supports the achievement of a high level of nuclear safety throughout the european union. however, the responsibility and responsibility for nuclear safety lies with the member states concerned, and the council is therefore not in a position to comment on safety and other aspects concerning specific reactors in specific member states. as the honourable member will be aware, any reactor should normally operate only for as long as it meets the high level of nuclear safety requirements. the existing community legislation on the safety of nuclear installations is based mainly on chapter 3 of title ii of the euratom treaty. directive 96/29/euratom laying down the basic safety rules for the protection of the health of workers and the general public against the dangers arising from ionising radiation lays down the basic radiation protection obligations to be complied with. the council also takes note of the recent proposal for a directive by the commission laying down the basic obligations and general principles relating to the safety of nuclear installations, which it intends to examine carefully.

- the next item is the report (a5-0141/2003) by mr kreissl-dörfler, on behalf of the committee on agriculture and rural development, on the proposal for a council directive on the control of foot-and-mouth disease (com (2002) 736 - c5-0029/2003 - 2002/0299 (cns)).
commission. – following my presentation of the commission’s proposal on community measures for the control of fmd to the committee on agriculture and rural development, i was very pleased to learn that mr kreissl-dörfler had been appointed rapporteur for this dossier. this prudent appointment ensured that the highly-valued expertise on fmd acquired by the temporary committee has been directly incorporated into your assessment of the proposed fmd directive. at this stage, i should like to pay tribute to the officials in my own office – i do not normally do this – and point to the quick response of those, one of whom is here this evening, who, on that fateful night in february 2001, when informed by the competent authorities in the uk of this outbreak, at 9.30 p.m., were in a position to make sure that the competent authorities of all other member states were aware of the outbreak by 10.30 p.m. their quick reaction contributed considerably to the containment of this disease. this is true in circumstances where we deal with communicable diseases, whether animal or human diseases. a fast response is of critical importance. containment saves the situation considerably. not surprisingly, the commission’s fmd proposal has prompted vigorous debate amongst all interested parties. the proposal has been subject to in-depth analysis in the technical expert working groups chaired by the greek presidency in the council. the overall opinion emerging from various discussions has been positive. the commission has received wide support for the general policy laid down in this proposal, not least because it is a carefully considered, pragmatic reform, rather than a revolution. the commission notes with satisfaction the general support of this house for the increased emphasis on emergency vaccination. this has also attracted the broad support of member states. i note, however, that some members would have liked us to go even further in this regard, but to do so would have compromised the fundamental elements of choice and flexibility that we are aiming to promote. we agree that disease preparedness must be enhanced and that contingency plans should be based on a worst-case scenario. in addition, and perhaps more importantly, contingency plans must be regularly reviewed and subject to critical analysis through carefully prepared and realistic exercises. in the report of the committee on agriculture, 48 amendments are proposed. the commission can, in fact, agree with 47 out of the 48 amendments tabled. the commission cannot agree to amendment no 32 which, although in line with the report of the scientific committee of 1999, is against the current rules of the oie. i would however add that the commission’s proposal provides for rapid adaptation, should the oie recommendations be modified. on the additional amendments tabled for this plenary session, the commission can accept amendments nos 51, 52 and 53 in part. in the international framework, the commission is committed to addressing, at every suitable opportunity, the issue of regionalisation policy and to contribute to adaptation of the oie animal health code to reflect scientific and technological progress. to proceed unilaterally would block international trade of eu animals and their products. in this regard we hope to make progress within the next week at the general session of the oie. before concluding let me address one issue of particular concern – that of veterinary funding. the proposal before us today does not address community rules on the veterinary funds because the principles of our control policy have not changed. furthermore, a study on a possible future animal health insurance scheme is well advanced but not yet completed. finally, i would like to address some of the questions raised by a number of members such as mrs corbey, who asked who is responsible for fmd vaccination. that responsibility rests with the member states. however, as a matter of prudence, the member states are advised to inform and get clearance from the commission before embarking on this for a number of reasons, not least funding for compensation and also to ensure that there is an agreement with other member states in the event of cross-border trade. she asked me how we could ensure that supermarkets sell meat from vaccinated animals. it is true to say that there is no law requiring the labelling of meat from vaccinated animals, but there is a requirement in respect of the stamping of carcasses of fresh meat but not in respect of other products. this is an issue that needs to be addressed but i cannot see how this can be dealt with by regulation. it is a matter for the free market. regarding mr mulder's question regarding insurance, this is being undertaken. work has been done and a report is anticipated. mr whitehead asked me about research on vaccines. i can assure him that work has been undertaken under the dg research programme. there will be a report on that issue in due course. i thank members for the speed with which they have delivered their opinion, thus paving the way for these new provisions on the control of fmd to come into force as soon as possible.
commission. – i am happy to be able to tell mr mulder that quite an amount of work has been undertaken in relation to this research at the moment. public tenders have gone out. i understand some of them have been finalised quite recently and i expect the others to be finalised imminently.

- the next item is the report (a5-0066/2003) by mrs ferrer, on behalf of the committee on development and cooperation, on capacity building in developing countries (2002/2157 ((ini)).
the rapporteur. (es) mr president, commissioner, i regret that we have to debate this report tonight, in this late session, when it was originally scheduled for thursday, which could have given more prominence to this debate on development cooperation. but unfortunately, the facts are what they are. the experience of the last few decades in the field of development cooperation and the lack of substantial results in this area have highlighted the need for a change in approach to development policies, to improve the effectiveness of aid, to reduce the gap between rich and poor countries and thus to achieve the sustainable development objectives we have set ourselves. it is true that there are many and very diverse factors which prevent the poorest countries from being able to take the development train and win the battle to eradicate poverty: the issue of external debt, first of all, the great scourge which weighs on the developing countries, the fratricidal wars which plague so many poor countries, the aids pandemic, corruption at all levels of public life, but also the recourse to foreign models and the fact that development objectives have been defined in the past without the participation of the beneficiaries of aid. it is therefore not surprising that the idea of capacity building as an indispensable factor in improving the outcomes of development policies has been gaining ground, particularly since the rio declaration of 1992, which recognises that a country's ability to pursue sustainable development is largely determined by the capacity of its people and institutions. the committee on development and cooperation, which fully shares this principle, therefore held a public hearing on capacity building a few months ago and subsequently agreed to a report on this subject, for which i was the rapporteur. the report was adopted unanimously, as the committee unanimously agreed that capacity building is a fundamental and key element of development cooperation, indispensable to ensure the effectiveness of aid. to understand better the scope of the proposals contained in the report, i think it is necessary to point out that capacity building is, for me, first and foremost a new way of understanding and, above all, of implementing development cooperation policy, which requires a comprehensive and long-term strategy, designed for the various actors in the various sectors of society and which must be geared to improving the skills and conditions that must be provided for a country to be able to improve its levels of economic and social growth. all this in support of national efforts that each country can carry out on its own, based on the design that each country has made according to its specific needs and interests, in line with what is being done, precisely, with the country strategy papers. the european union and its member states - and not only them, but all international donors - must therefore rethink their methods of cooperation and change the focus of their development policy so that capacity building, as a participatory process based on ownership, is the foundation of this policy, with the aim of enabling individuals and civil society organisations to develop the potential and capacities that will enable them to achieve the development objectives that they themselves must also be able to define. to give them the means - in a word - to take on the role of protagonists of their own development which is their right. in other words, to help them improve their institutional capacity, to help them achieve the level of training needed to open the door to development. the commission will also support the efforts of the member states to develop and strengthen their trade policies and to strengthen their economic and social cohesion. a development cooperation policy that is oriented in this direction is the most appropriate instrument for advancing on the path towards poverty eradication and the achievement of sustainable and equitable development for all. the commission's communication on development aid is therefore a necessary - i would say, a necessary - instrument for the development aid policy of the european union and its member states and for the various formulations of the motion for a resolution which we are going to put to the vote. because only through these policies, only by responding to the measures needed to increase capacity, will it be possible to end the injustice of the 20% of the world's population having 80% of the world's wealth, while the 80% are deprived of the right to live in accordance with the inalienable dignity of every person. (applause) i would like to thank
(es) mr president, capacity building in developing countries is one of the new concepts shaping contemporary cooperation policy, based on the appropriation of development processes by the recipient societies. it consists of an endogenous process, by which a society increases its social capital, through the attitude of individuals, organizations and institutions, to exercise their functions and set and achieve their objectives in all areas. it is therefore a very broad concept, which has been well captured in the report we are debating today, and for which i would like to congratulate mrs ferrer. but while capacity building in developing countries must permeate all aspects of development, it must focus on essential capacities, which, in the view of the socialist group, are the organisation of civil society and the strengthening of democratic institutions on the one hand, and individual empowerment through education on the other. all this, of course, is based on a minimum level of development that guarantees the survival of the population, which implies compliance with minimum standards of basic health. civil society organisation refers to the structuring of citizenship and their participation in social and decision-making processes. all this is done within the framework of an endogenous dynamic and, therefore, external aid, and we ask the commission to do so, must be devoted to strengthening grassroots organisations, associations of citizens and farmers, local ngos and traditional social institutions, rather than direct aid to the budgets of the beneficiary countries. the commissioner has acknowledged this evening that this is a timely and necessary report and that it reflects well the contributions of the capacities that must be given for development. the strengthening of democratic institutions is one of the outstanding issues of cooperation in general and of community cooperation in particular. democracy goes beyond the periodic holding of elections, it requires the setting up of fluid mechanisms for citizen participation and dialogue with institutions, as well as the democratization of these, on the basis of the concepts of good governance and transparency, good governance and the fight against corruption. individual training, through education, is the training system par excellence. the socialist group considers education to be a sine qua non for poverty reduction and development, and we have made this clear in the community budget. in this own-initiative report, parliament calls on the commission to join the major donor organisations in including capacity building as a cross-cutting element of its cooperation policy. i would like to congratulate mrs ferrer and all the groups who have contributed, with our amendments, to the fact that this report contains guidelines for updating and improving the community's development cooperation policy.

the rapporteur. (es) mr president, i would like to begin by focusing my speech on what we are discussing. we are discussing economic guidelines here which, in my view, present three important novelties: firstly, they are economic guidelines for three years, not just for one year; secondly, they are to be discussed together with the employment guidelines; and thirdly, they are being discussed at a time of recession. we woke up this morning to the news that the union's most powerful economy has entered recession and so these are not ordinary economic guidelines. in view of this situation, i was asked in the committee on economic and monetary affairs to draw up a report in time for the commission and the council to consider it and to try to reach the widest possible agreement. and we did it. all the groups have left their pens in the discussion, but we have all been able to reach an agreement. i would like to emphasize the good work of the speakers: othmar karas of my group, robert goebbels of the socialist group in the european parliament and charles-alfred gasòliba i böhm of the group of the european liberal, democratic and reformist party. and i would simply say to the commission that parliament, when it has been asked to respond, has always responded well. as they say in the song of my cid, "what a good vassal if there was a good lord!" i would like to ask you to take note of this and to involve this parliament in the discussion of these economic guidelines. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. the main points of my report are as follows: firstly, we ask for clarification as to whether the current coordination mechanisms are sufficient or whether something more is needed. we know that the treaty says that national policies, supply policies, short-term policies are policies of common interest and that they must be coordinated. every time the commissioner comes to us he tells us that the delay in implementing the lisbon strategy - and we have been three years behind - is due to a lack of implementation, to a lack of diligence on the part of the member states. we do not want to stop at complaints, but we are asking what needs to be done to correct these shortcomings in implementation, and we propose two things: that the commission immediately lists the rigidities that are hindering the implementation of the internal market and structural reforms, its priorities, the actions to be taken and the timetable for achieving the lisbon objectives by 2010. we also ask the commission to tell us what it can do to correct this lack of diligence if the member states' lack of diligence is the cause of the delay. there was a spanish constitution that said that spaniards had to be just and benevolent, but there was no article that said how that precept was going to be applied, and we had three civil wars in the 19th century. we want that coordination to ensure that economic policies all go in the same direction. that's what coordination is for. secondly, i would stress my absolute faith in the maintenance of large budgetary balances. just because things are bad doesn't mean that things that are good need to be fixed. and what has gone well in this period is the monetary policy geared to price stability and managed by an independent bank and a stability pact that has maintained a certain discipline - just a certain discipline - in the member states. as discipline - i repeat - is only relative and there are states which have fallen off the scale, i continue to reaffirm my belief that the objective must be budgetary balance, that countries which have been wasteful will have to reduce their structural deficit by half a point of gdp, as the commission believes. thirdly, convergence programmes must be assessed in a new way, as the commission itself has stressed. the commission, in addition to checking that the member states are strictly complying with the 3% ceiling, must take account of their starting position. what is their debt situation, what are they going to do with the resources they get, and what are their obligations to the future? because it is not the same situation for a country that has no debt, whose expenditure is earmarked for public finances - particularly those that reinforce the lisbon strategy and which do not have major obligations in the future - as for another that does just the opposite. we ask the commission to ensure that, in times of prosperity - in biblical terms, in times of 'fat cows' - the member states are able to make a cushion, a budgetary reserve to meet the bad times, and we also stress that where tax reductions are possible - and we are committed to a reduction in taxes which increase labour costs, in order to promote employment - those countries which cannot afford to do so should seek complementary measures - by reducing public expenditure or increasing incomes on the other hand - simply because it cannot be said that we want to maintain budgetary balance and reduce taxes at the same time. as we say in english, you can't blow and suck at the same time. in the field of wage policy, we are committed to maintaining wages at the level of the cpi, real wages at the level of productivity, to increasing the mobility of workers, and we ask the commission to speed up the removal of the fiscal obstacles to the transfer of employment pensions, to complete the issue of pensions, which has just been approved, with the appropriate fiscal policy. we are calling for a social dialogue and we are calling - i repeat - for a tax incentive for employment, for a reduction in the burdens which make it difficult for people to be employed, especially those on the lowest wages. in investment policy, we know - and it is repeated - that the cause of our lag with the united states is our lack of investment and especially our lag in technological investment. we also know that we are more or less on par with the public in terms of investment and that the private sector is making the least effort. that is why we are asking for a benchmarking exercise to find out what are the needs, the shortcomings, the deficiencies of those companies, particularly small and medium-sized ones - those employing less than nine workers - to access these new technologies, because only by knowing where we are going can we apply our resources efficiently. it is simply a matter of knowing what is happening and we want the commission to inform us in good time because, as a spanish poet says, 'there is no favourable wind for those who do not know where they are going'. we simply ask in this report to be told what the shortcomings, the deficiencies, of small and mediumsized enterprises are so that we know what to do. in conclusion, i would like to thank all the groups, the speakers, for their efforts, and the commission, and i would like to reiterate the goodwill of this parliament and its capacity and willingness to help us out of the difficult situation in which we find ourselves.
(es) mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, the report by mr garcía-margallo y marfil, supported by the liberal group, rightly stresses the need to provide a more appropriate framework to ensure the achievement of the objectives set out in the respective stability pacts and in the main broad economic policy guidelines, the implementation of which underpins the soundness and credibility of the union's economy and its single currency. these days we are experiencing the social unrest caused by the inevitable proposals for the reform of pension systems, which is necessary precisely to ensure the continuity of these, as well as the benefits derived from them, which define the welfare state that characterizes the european union, which, of the large economies, is undoubtedly the one that offers and guarantees greater social benefits and greater social balance. to preserve this balance, the european union must take even more decisive action against the repeated calls for action in recent times. not long ago, when we were preparing the spring council in brussels under the present greek presidency, we reiterated, firstly, the failure to achieve the objectives set in lisbon and the need for what is fundamental, namely to tackle some structural reforms, which have not yet been carried out and which are mentioned in the report by mr garcía-margallo and mr ivory. i would like to stress this point because there are some key issues, such as the liberalization of sectors, the current structure of which still hinders the possibilities of the economy and its development at the level of the european union; commission. - mr president, this owninitiative report by mrs mann on regional free trade areas deals with two central issues in the union's trade policy. the first is the question of trade policy as a strategic tool for external relations, particularly in the field of development policy. the second concerns the relationship between the multilateral approach and the bilateral approach. in general, i should like to thank mrs mann for her excellent work and the spirit of cooperation with which she has conducted it, which has enabled us, for some time now, to exchange ideas and information which, i believe, has led both parliament and the commission to make progress in our reflections. as mrs mann has just said, our approach remains based on the amsterdam conclusions of june 1997. the union's trade policy operates at two complementary levels: first, the multilateral level, that of the world trade organisation, and then the bilateral level, which is increasingly regional. these two levels are justified, firstly, by the fact that unilateralism is not an option for the european union, and we have known this for a long time. secondly, because, since multilateralism is our priority, regionalism, or our bilateral agreements, are complementary to this multilateral option, the second level being in some way subordinate to the first. in this sense, regionalism is not a substitute for multilateralism, but a complement to a fundamental option, namely the world trade organisation. we believe that globalised markets require common rules and global institutions to regulate them. this multilateral approach, which was the union's approach a decade ago, is even more so today. we want to frame globalisation, we want to reduce a number of its destabilising effects. the approach to a multilateral trading system is the priority, as reflected in the agenda adopted in doha. in this respect, i believe there is a very broad consensus between the position expressed by mrs mann and that of the commission. so it is the multilateral approach that is our number one priority at the moment, and that is why we have postponed any decision to launch new negotiations on free trade areas until the cycle we started in doha is completed. in addition to this time constraint, we consider that any new initiative in this area should be duly justified and meet a number of conditions. firstly, compatibility with the wto, and mrs mann recalled the rules on this. secondly, a bilateral agreement must be a plus in relation to the wto, and when i say that i am thinking of the wto as the end value of the negotiating cycle launched in doha. thirdly, we must not allow any new initiative to distract us from our multilateral priority. but would we still be neglecting free trade areas? no, i'm not going. the union has been a major user of these regional negotiations. we are pursuing a number of them very actively, with mercosur, with the gulf cooperation council, and we have recently concluded agreements with chile and egypt, for example. these agreements, whether the most recent or those we are negotiating, reveal features which are somewhat new compared to the conventional concepts of the free trade area. we've kind of switched generations. the liberalisation of trade in goods and services is now increasingly accompanied by the adoption of rules which we establish bilaterally and which go beyond multilateral rules. the second feature of this transformation is that the union is increasingly seeking to develop relations between regions. examples: mercosur and the gulf cooperation council, but also the andean countries, central america, south-east asia - i will come back to this in a moment - or even the regional negotiations which are about to start in africa. we now believe that this regional approach, involving several of our partners, is likely to produce more economically attractive results, since regional integration on the part of our partners in some way increases the market potential and makes regulatory efforts more cost-effective. this is what mrs mann was calling deep integration at the time, and this is the kind of initiative we are launching, including with south east asia, and the very recent eu-asean transregional initiative, launched just over a month ago in luang prabang, laos. we intend to launch an action programme focused on the major regulatory priorities on both sides. this is also the path we have taken in our relations with canada and the one underlying our approach in andean and latin america. to sum up the commission's position on this point, i would say that if the prodi commission has not launched new free trade area initiatives, it is not out of passivity, it is deliberate. this is of course due to the priority given to doha, but also to the conviction that free trade areas in the traditional sense are no longer really the appropriate instrument for opening up trade in the 21st century and that we now need to change this type of format. this is also what guides us in our relations with the developing countries, which mrs mann talks about at length in her report. we share the view that while trade openness has its advantages, it can only be achieved under a number of conditions. first, market access is necessary for developing countries, but it is clearly not enough to turn the whole thing into growth and jobs. a key element is the support for business capacity building. this is what we are doing at multilateral level. this is also what we are doing at the stage of preparing the negotiations for regional economic partnership agreements with our acp partners. so are we in complete agreement? not exactly. and since we must find some differences between us, i will mention two before concluding. the first concerns the idea put forward by mrs mann of opening negotiations with singapore with a view to the creation of a free trade area. we are not, at this stage, convinced of the ripple effect that can be expected from such an initiative for the region. so for the reasons i have just mentioned, we still prefer, mrs mann, a common approach with the asean countries. another reservation relates to the idea you put forward in your report that the union should commit itself to making up for the budgetary losses that would be associated with the reduction of customs duties in developing countries. these tariff losses are not yet proven, especially if the volume of trade increases as we would like both in the south-south and north-south directions. we are not closed to this idea, but it seems to us, at this stage of the available data, premature. these are the two small reservations i wish to make on behalf of the commission. however, it is clear that the elements of convergence with your report are very much in our favour. i can also testify that it is an asset for the commission to see its strategy and its positions supported by the european parliament in international negotiations. for all these reasons, i see in this report the confirmation of the quality of our working relationship and i thank mrs mann once again for her excellent report.
the rapporteur for the opinion should. {es) mr president, first of all i would also like to congratulate mrs mann on her report. it is true and well known that trade relations are a factor in economic growth, but it is also true that not all countries have been able to integrate into the world trade system and take advantage of the opportunities it offers to improve their development, which has increased the inequalities between rich and poor countries. this reality implies the need to manage globalisation through multilateral rules drawn up from the perspective of policy to make global trade relations a force for good for all, contributing to the goal of poverty eradication and sustainable and equitable development. it is therefore important that the european union develops a trade strategy which puts the specific needs of the least developed countries at the centre of trade negotiations, in order to make possible the gradual integration of these countries into the multilateral trading system. the right of access - even if it is not reciprocal - of the poorest countries to the markets of the developed countries is far from sufficient to guarantee a real development of trade flows if, at the same time, as you yourself reminded us, mr commissioner, their capacity for industrial and agricultural development, for respect for the rules in force in the importing countries and for knowledge of the marketing circuits, as well as their administrative capacities and financial institutions, are not strengthened. it is precisely because of this concern that the committee on development and cooperation fully supports the inclusion of the development dimension in the doha agenda and welcomes the impetus that the european union, and in particular you, commissioner lamy, have been able to give in this respect so that this development dimension can flourish. but at the same time it considers it essential to ensure coherence between multilateralism and regionalism, between the rules laid down by the world trade organisation on the liberalization of regional trade and the development of free trade areas, including the proliferation of agreements between countries and regions with very different levels of development, because it believes that only in this way, with this coherence, will it be possible to make trade relations a genuine factor of development for all peoples and finally eradicate poverty.

the rapporteur. {es) mr president, in the debate we had in this parliament on 14 may, i said what we thought was good and what we thought was bad about the agreement we are discussing today. the recommendation i am presenting today, on behalf of the commission i chair, is very clear on all this. firstly, these agreements must be the instruments for extending the protection of fundamental rights in the sense that europe has developed on the basis of our constitutions and the case law of the luxembourg and strasbourg courts. the european union cannot negotiate on the basis of standards which are inferior to those which it must itself respect. this seems obvious to us and we cannot accept extradition or criminal legal aid when there is a risk of the death penalty or of a process which is not fair, as would be the case in military courts. secondly, these agreements can serve as a laboratory for improving the methods and even the legislation of both parties. this should be the case, for example, in data protection which should apply on both sides of the atlantic. thirdly, an international agreement is meaningless without a condition of reciprocity between the two parties. we therefore demand that the situation of european citizens detained at guantanamo bay be brought to an end once and for all. although my group does not wish to make the signing of the agreements conditional on this question, it does wish to express its strong support for an immediate end to this situation. fourthly, these agreements must also be an opportunity to strengthen our internal legislation, making it more effective. for this reason, the rules that already exist between member states, such as the european arrest warrant, should take precedence and these agreements should not be in competition with other relevant treaties, such as the international criminal court. fifthly, agreements of such importance as those signed with the united states must be monitored at both council and commission level and at parliamentary level. a joint committee of members of the united states congress and the european parliament. in the interests of both parties, it must be set up as soon as possible. finally, i would like to refer to the most delicate point, namely the procedure which the council announced to us during the last debate in the house. we have not found a positive response to our request for a formal consultation between the decisions on signing and ratifying the agreements. these are the first international agreements of the european union to be based on both the second and third pillars, and regular consultation of parliament is therefore necessary for a number of reasons. on the one hand, because this consultation must be the rule for the adoption of acts belonging to the third pillar, including those acts which have the nature of international agreements. secondly, because parliamentary scrutiny of such agreements is the rule in all the member states and must therefore be regarded as a common principle which the european union must draw on, in accordance with article 6 of the treaty. for all these reasons, we consider that consultation of parliament is the only procedure which would fully respect the principles of democracy and the rule of law as set out in article 6 (1) of the treaty on european union. mr president, how can we explain to the european citizens at the time when we are drawing up the new european constitution that agreements which directly affect their fundamental rights can come into force without the control of the european parliament? we believe that a decision by the council to consult the european parliament on the occasion of ratification of agreements based on articles 24 to 38 would be perfectly in line with the treaty and would be an appropriate option from the point of view of institutional policy, as the commission has already suggested. for all these reasons, mr president, we hope that the general affairs council will change its attitude and, in its own interest and in the union's, avoid creating a serious democratic deficit by changing its current position.
commission. mr president, i wish to begin by thanking parliament, in particular mr hernández mollar, the chairman of the committee on citizens' freedoms and rights, justice and home affairs, for this report on such an important and sensitive issue. i welcome the fact that the draft agreements have been declassified and that the opportunity has been given to the european parliament to examine them in parallel with the examination by national parliaments in the member states. one must recognise that these agreements under articles 24 and 38 are negotiated by the council. the commission is not the negotiator of these agreements in the external arena. therefore, in this debate the commission participates as it is associated to the negotiating process, but the council of ministers has the final word. we would like to recognise the efforts made by the belgian, spanish, danish and now the greek presidencies to launch these agreements following the decision taken by the european council after the events of 11 september 2001. on the basis of this authorisation, and the directives for negotiations that were adopted by the justice and home affairs council, the commission welcomes the fact that this consultation procedure should be concluded in time to allow for signature by the european union and the united states of america during the summit at the end of this month. pursuant to the authorisation given by the council to the presidency to negotiate the agreements with the united states in april last year, the commission assisted in the negotiations from the beginning, so it is particularly well-placed to appreciate the real difficulties experienced therein. we understood that the commission's role was to help to reach a positive result. like parliament, in its draft recommendation, the commission is of the opinion that stronger solutions would have been preferable on a number of points covered by these agreements. i had the opportunity to have a constructive discussion on a number of the concerns raised by parliament in the committee on citizens' freedoms and rights, justice and home affairs, together with the greek minister of justice. the greek minister also discussed a number of these concerns in the debate that took place in plenary last month on the eu-us agreements. let me stress that the united states side did not get satisfaction on a number of points of major importance to them and which were strongly opposed by the union, such as the extradition of european union nationals and the limitations of the political offence exception to extradition. we now need to make an overall assessment of the result of the negotiations. one of the criteria for this assessment is the added value of a union agreement compared with the situation that currently exists on the basis of bilateral agreements between member states and the united states of america. this assessment has to be made taking due account of the fact that this is, as the president mentioned, the very first union agreement in the field of justice and home affairs, and it will be a historical precedent. in addition to the incontestable advantages that the agreements on extradition and mutual legal assistance with the united states will bring in terms of concrete judicial cooperation in criminal matters and the fight against organised crime and terrorism, i would focus on the following, trying to address some of the major concerns raised by this parliament. regarding protection against the death penalty, the draft extradition agreement compares with the strongest anti-death penalty clauses that can be found in existing bilateral treaties, whether an agreement with a member state or one with a candidate country. this means that as far as all the other bilateral agreements are concerned, this anti-death penalty provision is stronger in the current european union agreement than in the vast majority of others. in addition it allows the invoking of all grounds for refusal available pursuant to a bilateral extradition treaty between a member state and the united states, and will open the possibility of consultation in the event that constitutional principles or final judicial decisions binding upon a requested state may impede the fulfilment of an extradition. this provision, combined with specific references in the recitals to individual rights, fair trial and an impartial tribunal, offers significant guarantees. i would insist that member states be bound by the european convention on human rights and its protocols. nothing in these draft agreements should lead to decreased compliance with these international obligations. it is also my deep conviction that the european convention will conclude positively on the inclusion of the charter of fundamental rights in the future constitution, thus giving it a legally binding and constitutional status. as regards article 10 of the draft extradition agreement, and in particular the situation of an extradition request that conflicts with a european arrest warrant, a member state confronted with such a situation of conflicting requests shall take into account a number of criteria in order to take a decision that widely corresponds to the lists of such competing requests already provided by the framework decision creating the european arrest warrant. the designation of the competent authority is left to the requested member state. this can be a judicial authority unless the existing bilateral treaty between the member state in question and the united states foresees an executive authority. in addition, the final wording of the agreement drafted very recently at the last negotiation session has improved in the sense that it better underlines the fact that the framework decision on the european arrest warrant could be amended in the global context of further european union integration. this might in turn lead to the adaptation of the agreement with the united states in line with the natural evolution of the legislation on the european arrest warrant. finally, regarding data protection provisions, the relevant provision in the draft mutual legal assistance agreement with the united states is modelled on the two most recent european texts: the european union's convention on mutual legal assistance in criminal matters of 2000 and the council of europe's convention on cybercrime.

commission. mr president, in this debate the commission acted like an amicus curiae because it was not the negotiator, it assisted the successive council presidencies in their negotiations. therefore, i will just try to clarify some of the points raised and give the commission's opinion on those points. i shall begin with article 13. i shall try to make myself clear. the us-eu agreement is a bilateral agreement that regulates the relationship between the european union and the united states of america. it does not regulate the relationship between the member states of the european union among themselves or the obligations that member states have under other international legal instruments. all the member states have subscribed to the european convention on human rights and to the specific protocol that forbids the death penalty. this means that, acting in accordance with their international obligations under the european convention on human rights, member states will refuse extradition where the death penalty is concerned. that does not derive from an obligation between the european union and the united states of america. it derives directly from the obligation of the member states to be in line with the european convention on human rights, with the protocol and, i hope, with the charter of fundamental rights of the european union that will have constitutional status and be legally binding after its inclusion in the new constitutional treaty. when it comes to the international criminal court, i would draw your attention to the fact that article 10 of the agreement does not apply to the international criminal court because that court is not a state and article 10 only regulates the criteria to be used when there is simultaneously, in regard to a same person, a conflicting request by a third state – like the united states of america – and by a european union member state. it does not deal with requests from the international criminal court. therefore, nothing prevents the member states from deciding what they want to do as far as a request from the international criminal court is concerned, irrespective of any bilateral agreement with the united states of america. when it comes to the european arrest warrant as such, i can even agree with parliament. however, unfortunately, the council did not adopt the commission's proposal on the primacy of the european arrest warrant. therein lies the problem. we are not talking today about a fully comprehensive primacy of the european arrest warrant over any other request for extradition. it does not exist. the framework decision on the european arrest warrant already recognises that when there is a demand under a european arrest warrant and a simultaneous demand for extradition by a third country, there are a number of criteria that will have to be taken into consideration in order to decide which demand has primacy. so we are not changing the legal system of the european union. the commission regrets that this primacy was not recognised in the past when the council adopted the european arrest warrant. however, today this primacy does not exist and therefore cannot be affected by the terms of a bilateral agreement with the united states. what we were careful to say was that the possibility of recognising in the future the primacy of the european arrest warrant could not be undermined or limited by this kind of bilateral agreement. there is a specific provision on the revision of this kind of bilateral agreement with the united states in case we decide to recognise the primacy of the european arrest warrant in the future. i hope that sooner or later we will do that. finally, on the matter of special courts. it must be said that the key issue for me – and i have always said this to parliament – is not the nature of the court, it is not the question of special courts as such – even some member states have special courts in the european union. the question is one of due and fair process and guarantees, so that extradition is only granted where there are guarantees that the requesting member state will follow a due and fair process. there are two recitals in the agreements that address this issue. the first one concerns due regard for the rights of individuals and the rule of law; the second one concerns the guarantees and the respective legal systems which provide for the right to a fair trial of an extradited person. above all, there is article 16a on non-derogation, which in paragraph 1 maintains all grounds for refusal relating to a matter not governed by this agreement available under a bilateral extradition treaty in force and which in paragraph 2 calls for consultation where the constitutional principles of the requested state may pose impediments to the fulfilment of its obligation to extradite. in my interpretation, everything that might be considered as a demand for extradition to a court where the rule of due process is not respected can give leverage to the application of this article 16a on non-derogation. finally, i sincerely hope that in the future constitution we will have specific provisions not only on consultation of parliament concerning these kinds of agreements, which will become more frequent in the future, but also concerning the competence of the european court of justice to guarantee the full compliance of these agreements with the future constitution of the european union.

longterm residents, the commission completes its legislative work with a view to laying the foundations for a common policy on legal immigration, since we have decided not to submit a proposal intended to cover all persons who are not covered by the previous proposals. i am glad that parliament has responded to the commission by adopting this report so quickly. this proposal concerns migration for the purpose of training of third-country nationals. this is a special type of immigration, in that it is temporary and limited in principle to the duration of the training, and it is part of a context of mutual enrichment, both of the countries of origin and of the host countries, not to mention, of course, the migrant himself who directly benefits from it. this proposal is part of the immigration policy but must also be seen in the context of community action in the field of education. our aim is clearly to encourage migration for training purposes, in particular by welcoming as many students from third countries as possible to higher education. the proposal for a directive is designed in this spirit. the conditions of admission provided for in it have been made as objective as possible in order to ensure a quick and easy processing of applications, while they are drafted in a clear and rigorous manner so that member states can fight against any attempts at abuse. i think it is also an innovative proposal in the context of the growing internationalisation of education, particularly as regards the recognition of the right of students to move to another member state to continue their studies after being admitted by a first member state of the european union. the proposal also covers the vocational training sector, regulating the conditions for the reception of unpaid trainees, for example those who come to follow training in an enterprise. the proposal for a directive on the admission of workers covering paid traineeships is complementary in this respect. following contacts with non-governmental organizations, provisions for secondary school pupils and volunteers coming to the european community have been integrated into our proposal. the aim is to facilitate exchange programmes for secondary school pupils. the community has the greatest interest in encouraging the discovery of culture by students who will then be tempted to return to the community as higher education students. a provision was also added to the proposal to regulate the admission of volunteers, avoiding them from filling a legal void. the commission has obviously not lost sight of public security considerations. the proposal contains a public order and security clause which will give member states the necessary leeway to take precautions, in particular against the terrorist threat.

(es) mr president, i would like to thank the committee on agriculture and rural development for the overwhelming support it has received for my report on rice and for the amendments to it which have enjoyed a great deal of consensus in our committee. commissioner, the open markets that are least protected are also the most vulnerable. climate change, prolonged droughts, and the significant pressures on wetlands, on those protected areas that are exercised by the urban sector or the administrations themselves, are putting these traditional areas of cultivation, a haven of biodiversity, at risk. the largest and most important bird habitats in europe are located in these traditional rice-growing areas and it is our responsibility to preserve them at all costs. in the context of the mid-term review of the common agricultural policy, the commission has proposed reform of the common organization of the market in rice, taking into account the imbalances caused by the sharp increase in imports and domestic production, which, together with restrictions on export refunds, are generating large surpluses which will tend to worsen from 2006 onwards by the progressive reduction in tariffs resulting from the implementation of the everything but arms programme. the commission itself acknowledges that it is impossible to estimate the full impact of this initiative, but nevertheless assures that the stocks in intervention will be unsustainable because of exports from third countries. the whole philosophy behind the reform of the common agricultural policy proposed by the commission is to abolish intervention without taking into account the specific nature of this type of crop in europe, and that in a globalised, liberalised world, small regional economies linked to crops such as rice are more endangered than ever. the common organization of the market in rice needs to be reformed to adapt it to the new conditions of market competitiveness, but ensuring a decent income for producers and in a way compatible with fair trade for the benefit of the least developed countries, preserving the crop with an important role for the european union in the social, environmental and landscape fields. all this has been ignored by the commission in its proposal, both in terms of market management and in terms of the specific rice payment and decoupled aid. without intervention, without protection at the frontiers and without the guarantee of quality and food safety that we demand of our products, the sector will disappear. with its proposal the commission is shifting the whole responsibility for finding solutions to hunger in the third world onto farmers, and that is not fair. a crop that requires special agro-climatic conditions, which causes it to be concentrated in certain areas as a monoculture, which has as its only alternatives desiccation, salinization or abandonment. the committee on agriculture and rural development supports in its report the commission's decision to reduce the intervention price for rice to bring it into line with world prices. however, we have rejected the proposal to create a private storage system whenever the price of rice falls below the effective support price. a new concept is therefore emerging: the effective support price, which is used to calculate the tariffs under the maximum price system and transfers it to the market management system. it is not, therefore, a form of support for the producer, as is the case with the intervention price, but a virtual system used to trigger another imprecise and undefined measure: private storage; a private storage proposal which will not work, as it has not done in other sectors, and which will worsen the financial situation of the farmer, already weakened, as he will have to bear at his expense a larger capital stock and high costs of maintaining and preserving the product. as for the special measure of 120 euros, the proposed safety net, to let prices stabilize around those 120 euros is to let the rice farmers go bankrupt. public intervention should therefore be maintained as a regulatory mechanism with an institutional price guaranteeing competitiveness and self-sufficiency. as far as border protection is concerned, the exchange arrangements were in line with the unfortunate marrakesh agreements in this sector, as a system of maximum import prices is envisaged. the entry price of husked loose rice would thus not exceed 180 or 188%, depending on whether it was indian or japanese, of the intervention price. this system does not take account of the processing costs of the husks and, moreover, leads to the importation of the best quality and most expensive rice on the community market at a lower rate of duty. the commission has asked the 15 for a mandate to negotiate in the world trade organisation the replacement of the current system of variable import duties by fixed duties, although there seems to be council mr president, ladies and gentlemen, when the greek government took over the presidency of the council on 1 january 2003, the reform of the common agricultural policy was at a crucial juncture. the negotiation of the closure of this dossier was one of the main objectives of the greek presidency, in cooperation of course with the european commission and the european parliament. our council discussed the commission's proposals at its meetings in february, march and april, on the basis of presidency questionnaires focusing on the specific issues of reform. the presidency drew positive conclusions from this process and decided to give a boost to the negotiations by setting up a high-level group. the role of this group was mainly to prepare the crucial council of ministers meeting in june. the momentum for agreement was reinforced at the council of 26 and 27 may, where commissioner fischler and i met with each minister to identify the main problems and possible solutions for a genuine compromise. the commissioner and i have both noted with satisfaction that we have the support of the majority of ministers for our timetable. the majority of the members are convinced that if differentiation, modulation. most member states have reservations about the amount of the eur 5 000 exemption from the obligation to gradually reduce aid, while some others want to provide for an intermediate scale to allow a more gradual application of the gradual reduction to the largest and most competitive holdings. the commission has also proposed that the member states should be able to take part in the negotiations on the new agreement on the common organization of the market in wine. it should not be forgotten that the regulation also aims to save resources which will be used to finance future reforms of the common market organizations. in other words, since the resources for agriculture are specific, any increase in the deficit or any other similar arrangement should not member states. the problem is that the project is seen as involving excessive administrative and financial costs, disproportionate to the purpose pursued. the commission's proposal for a directive on commission's proposals need to be improved so that the council can adopt them as part of an overall package. finally, the reform of the common agricultural policy must include specific measures for young farmers, who are the future of european agriculture, and specific arrangements for the less favoured remote and problem areas of the european union which are currently threatened with abandonment. i would now like to refer to the budgetary aspects of the proposals for the reform of the common agricultural policy. the council's discussions focused on the expected budgetary impact of that diversification and degressivity measures are necessary to ensure compliance with the budgetary constraints set by the brussels summit in october 2002. as the presidency, we will seek to ensure problem with the commission proposal is decoupling. if it were to be applied, farming would cease on the least productive farms and in less productive areas. in the face of lower market prices and aid unrelated to production, farms with lower gross margins would decide not to bear the costs of production. in areas with lower yields, along with agricultural activity, the economic activities linked to it would disappear, creating unprecedented problems in the economic, social, environmental and land-use planning spheres. rural development aid, with all its limitations, cannot be expected to remedy these shortcomings. in my opinion, decoupling is ethically unacceptable. it would be a mere remuneration for the ownership of the land, so that, in addition to the reduction of agricultural activity, it would lead to a speculative process in the land market. moreover, the granting of aid based on the average aid received over the last three years would perpetuate existing imbalances between farms, sectors and regions. a cap based on decoupling would be counterproductive to cohesion because it would limit the receipt of aid to the historical base, encourage inactivity in areas with natural difficulties and concentrate it in areas with more intensive agriculture. in the most disadvantaged areas, problems of depopulation and reduced economic activity would be created. in farms, sectors and regions needs to be rebalanced. society needs a living agriculture, with an adequate number of farmers and farms capable of ensuring balanced land management, with a varied economic activity and safe products for the consumer. but unfortunately for us, the commission's proposals are going in the diametrically opposite direction.

strengthened more than was intended. i would like to return briefly to the question of decoupling, because many people have raised the question of partial decoupling: i think it is problematic to believe that decoupling can be introduced gradually over a long period of time or that only a certain percentage of each measure can be decoupling. these mixed forms of partial decoupling ultimately result in the disadvantages of the existing system being combined with the denial of the advantages of the new system. so you have to be very, very careful here. the main disadvantages of the current system are that farmers are not free to make their own decisions on their farms. the disadvantages are that farmers have to deal with a higher and more complex level of bureaucracy, and what is being denied them is, above all, the freedom to do business. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. the main reason for this is that when you compare the market forecasts which we have based on agenda 2000 with the market forecasts now published by the same institutions, such as fabri, these institutions have had to drastically reduce their very positive expectations at the time. for example, wheat by 14 percent, barley by 10 percent, corn by 16 percent, butter by 37 percent, and skimmed-milk powder by over 30 percent. but why can we accept a 5% reduction in the intervention price? it is only because we were much more cautious then than these forecasts would have suggested that we can now take a more moderate approach. but to do nothing would mean that we would have further market imbalances, and that would mean nothing more than price pressure. finally, on the question of mediterranean products, i should like to make it quite clear that next week, when the council is called upon to take a decision, we will continue to call for the council of agriculture ministers to make a declaration of its own accord, together with the commission, to ensure that mediterranean products are treated equally and are assessed in the same way when new steps are taken.
