- question no 25 by mr beysen (h-0315/03):is the commission aware that there are ongoing threats to the legal parallel trade in medicines in the european union, which saves member state governments and european patients millions of euros every year? has the commission considered using article 82 as a legal basis to ensure that pharmaceutical manufacturers comply with the rules of the single market?
the commission the honourable member's question is not only of undeniable interest but also of great relevance. the question is certainly interesting because the obstacles to parallel trade in pharmaceutical products have long been a source of concern for the commission, which has already investigated numerous practices in this field in the past and continues to do so. in the field of competition in particular, a number of cases are currently being examined, at the request of both pharmaceutical laboratories and complainants. the question is also, as i said, of great importance. the commission has, as is well known, two legal instruments at its disposal for taking action: articles 81 and 82. as regards article 81, mr advocate general tizzano of the court of justice recently presented his opinion in the bayer case, concerning parallel trade in a product of that company. i do not wish to go into the details of this case and of the advocate general's opinion, which concern a very specific legal technical matter. however, the findings are not in favour of the arguments put forward by the commission in this case. the court's ruling will be delivered in a few months' time, without prejudice, in any event, to other commission decisions on issues other than those dealt with in the bayer case, such as the decision adopted by the commission on 8 may 2001 concerning the double pricing system applied by glaxo. as regards article 82, this is precisely the direction the commission is currently taking. this raises a number of new issues, particularly as regards the definition of markets or abusive practices. the court of justice received a reference for a preliminary ruling from the hellenic competition commission, the greek competition authority, in february. the purpose of this reference for a preliminary ruling is to establish to what extent the refusal by a pharmaceutical undertaking in a dominant position to supply a wholesaler with the aim of disrupting parallel trade may constitute an abuse prohibited by article 82 of the ec treaty. the commission will, as always, be required to give its opinion to the court in the coming weeks. the the commission. mr president, several years ago, in 1989, the commission issued a recommendation to the member states on the introduction of the european citizen card for those over 60. the commission's recommendation at the time concerned the possibility for older people to have access to all the facilities granted by member states' decisions to their own older citizens, from museums and cultural activities to free subsidised transport. the technical barriers to the introduction of this card have, of course, proved to be extremely significant. three feasibility studies have been carried out to date, which have documented the systems in place and the constraints and obstacles that exist in many member states. the final report of the last study was submitted to a contact group of member states' representatives on policies concerning older people and to the group for the association of older people's organisations. no member state and no pan-european organisation of older people supported the idea of the card or the proposals contained in the report in this group to which the final study was submitted. the commission therefore does not consider it possible to introduce an old people's card in the european union.

(es) madam president, first of all i would like to thank mrs fraisse, the rapporteur, for all her efforts. ladies and gentlemen, times have changed a lot. in 1912, when the legendary pierre de coubertin was asked about the possibility of organizing a women's olympic games, he replied: "that is impractical, uninteresting, unsightly and incorrect. the design of an olympic games must respond to the following formula: periodic and solemn exaltation of athletics, loyalty as a medium, art as a framework and female applause as a reward". a hundred years ago, that's not much. women were not in the olympics, and now, however, we are over 40%. and if we consider that there are continents where participation is very, very low, i think we have really made a lot of progress. however, i, who have devoted 20 years of my life to sport as an amateur and then as a professional, think that there are two fronts on which there is still a lot to be done and a long way to go. the first front is the media. in spain, sports newspapers, which are the most widely read newspapers in our country - even more than national newspapers - do not devote even 4% of their content to women's sport, with the aggravating factor that often the content referring to women's sport is news of the "pink" or "heart" type, as we call it in spain, or about the postures or clothing of our athletes. this is not just a problem in spain, in france the newspaper l'équipe devotes a maximum of 5% of its news to women's sport. this is a problem which affects the whole of the european union. the second front is that of sports bodies. in the world of politics, we often complain that the participation of women is too low; however, i have to say that the participation of women in the world of politics is light years above the participation of women in sports bodies. in view of the dramatic situation, the international olympic committee decided in 1996 that by the end of 2000 10% of all positions in all decision-making structures should be reserved for women, including international federations and bodies belonging to the olympic movement, with the aim of increasing this quota to 20% by 2005. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. ladies and gentlemen, at the closing of the first world conference on women and sport in lausanne in october 1996, juan antonio samaranch said that the 21st century would have to be the new era for women in sport. we must all do everything in our power to make the statement of juan antonio samaranch a reality.
(es) mr president, commissioner, in the year 2000 more than 216 000 women in the european union developed breast cancer and more than 79 000 died from it. breast cancer is the most common cause of death in women aged 35 to 55. cancer rates differ significantly from one country to another within the european union, being higher in the nordic countries and lower in the southern countries, such as greece or spain; lithuania and latvia also have low rates. in all countries, the rate is increasing every year; economic, environmental and even cultural factors have a great influence on these figures; breast cancer affects women of higher social class to a greater extent. the european guidelines for early cancer detection, which is the most effective measure for achieving a good outcome and a high survival rate, are only recommendations without any legally binding nature. the national states draw up their prevention and treatment plans, with great differences from one to another. in some member states, programmes are regional and there are still member states where early detection programmes do not reach all women at risk. this timely and well-done report aims to draw attention throughout the european union to this problem, which affects women in particular. the commission's work on this has been a success. every woman has the right to access high-quality early detection, treatment and follow-up of breast cancer, and the differences that currently exist between member states, which result in survival rates with differences of up to 16%, should be eliminated. the most effective measure to date for curing cancer remains early detection. the community programme 'europe against cancer' has proved to be very effective, exemplary and exemplary and we should therefore follow this path in the future. early detection, with programmes established to screen women regularly from the age of 50, should be established in all member states and also in the candidate states. the cooperation and awareness of women is of enormous importance, as self-examination is a very useful aid, not to mention that mammography is the most effective technique for detecting cancer at an early stage. the fight against breast cancer should be a priority of health policy and member states should develop effective health policies and strategies for better early detection, diagnosis and treatment. the report is very complete, detailed and accurate, and i also congratulate mrs jöns on her attitude of collaboration, accepting suggestions and amendments which have enriched the text.
(es) mr president, first of all, and as we have done with all the speakers, i would like to congratulate mrs jöns on her efforts, on her work, on her excellent report. breast cancer, mr president, is the most common cancer in the european union. and mrs jöns' report contains very important data and a number of clues which the member states should take into account. both the public health programme 2000-2008 and the sixth framework programme for research are really very suitable spaces to continue this task of reducing the effects of breast cancer. genetic research and therapy will also help us. we must also congratulate and thank the work of the national and international networks for the fight against cancer, without which it would probably be impossible to make progress in this task. but we must agree on a number of things, such as the ages at which early detection programmes need to be started. maybe we're starting late and we need to standardize that therapy. it is also important to harmonise data collection and to bring the realities and treatments closer together. the disparities in the impact of breast cancer between the countries of the european union and between them and the candidate countries are enormous. it's very important that we all work together to homogenize this situation. probably the most important is health education, prevention, early detection, self-examination, and of course, mammograms. rapid treatment is essential; there are many women who have little means at their disposal to work in this direction, to know how they should self-explore and at what point in their lives they need to start treatment. i therefore believe that it is essential that mrs jöns' work should continue along this line, because we will all benefit from it.

president of the european parliament delegation to the convention. (es) mr president, thank you very much for your words and my congratulations on having convened this plenary session a few days after the closing session of the convention and a few days before the thessaloniki european council. this parliament will be the first to debate the draft constitution. and let me recall with emotion how, in 1997, it was this parliament, in a report on which dimitris tsasos and i were rapporteurs, which approved the replacement of the intergovernmental method by what we then called the community method for the reform of the treaties. this community method, which is set out in the resolution of 19 november 1997, is the convention. the european parliament's bet has therefore been a successful one, because i want to say with all solemnity that in 16 months of work by the convention we have done much more than in 10 years of intergovernmental conferences. first of all, mr president, we have a constitution. i remember that this parliament was also a pioneer in calling for the constitutionalisation of the union in the report drawn up by olivier duhamel. a constitutionalisation that will bring more efficiency, that will produce a union of results. many of our demands are in the text: the pillars are gone, the union has legal personality, we are going to strengthen the community method, we have guaranteed the commission's monopoly of initiative, the legislative procedure in which the council and parliament are on an equal footing is going to be the normal procedure. we have also managed to move from unanimity to qualified majority voting in many areas, and this parliament will be intervening in 70 of them, whereas it is now intervening in 34. we also have, mr president, a great simplification of methods: we have been left with five decisionmaking procedures and have managed to use language far removed from the community jargon. but we have also democratized the union, and this from the very first article of the constitution, when it speaks of the union's dual legitimacy, something which this parliament has always defended as a union of states and citizens. when i entered this parliament - in 1992 - it was a consultative assembly. after the constitution, this parliament will be a parliament worthy of the name. and this democratizing effect also affects national parliaments. i would like to pay tribute to president napolitano for his report, as head of the committee on constitutional affairs, because we have created the way to involve national parliaments in the community procedure through the early warning system. i would also like to say to all those who have always seen a rivalry between national parliaments and the european parliament that in this convention our main allies have been the national parliaments. and i want to pay tribute to them for that. i also believe, mr president, that we have done something enormously important, something that we have fought for in this parliament, such as the incorporation of the charter of fundamental rights into the constitution. we asked for this before nice and we did not get it, but the charter of fundamental rights is now going to become the identity document of europeans. and we have not only strengthened the representative institutions, but also the participatory ones. we have precisely recognized in the constitution the role of associations and non-governmental organizations, and we have incorporated the popular initiative as an instrument of semi-direct democracy. mr president, when mr giscard d'estaing was asked last week who had won, he said that in this constitution the european parliament had won. i think the citizen has won. i believe that we are witnessing a triumph of the european citizens who will have a union capable of producing better results, a more transparent union and, above all, a more efficient union. and let me say that as chairman of this delegation i have been very honoured to carry out this task. i am very honoured because the 32 members of the delegation - we have not distinguished between full members and alternates - have done an exceptional job of defending parliament's positions and of providing technical and political support at all times to myself, klaus hänsch and andrew duff. and let me tell you something, mr president: you go to thessaloniki. i think that the political message from this parliament is a very clear political message. you said this constitution was a radical breakthrough. i believe that this is the most important step forward in the european union since the treaties of rome, and i am therefore convinced that the intergovernmental conference will not improve it. i therefore believe that we must defend to the end a text which we have tabled without options, as this european parliament wanted. and at the end of your process, mr president, i think what we have to do is put it to a referendum. some governments, such as spain, have asked for it to be endorsed on the same day as the european parliament elections; i believe that would be the culmination of that democratizing element contained in the european constitution. thank you all so much for your help. without your help, without the help of everyone, this would have been impossible. annan, who contacted me not many days ago to ask whether the european union would be willing to commit itself to an operation of this nature. the operation is not easy, the operation is complex and the un secretary-general, the european union was able to launch a complex operation for the first european union military peacekeeping operation to be carried out autonomously in africa. i like to say an important role. operation artemis, i insist, is going to be a difficult operation. you know that a few days ago we started to deploy the force, there are now 400 soldiers in the area. the operation commission. - madam president, as we all know, the textile and clothing sector plays a major role in international trade: 350 billion euro in trade flows in 2002, i.e. more than 5% of total world exports. it is a vital sector for developing countries. it accounts for 50% of world textile exports and 70% of world clothing exports. for many of them, it is the main source of export and industrial employment. for us europeans, it is also a key sector for the future, thanks to the investment, the upgrading and the global leadership we have created in a sector such as fashion. europe is now the world's leading exporter of textiles and the second largest exporter of clothing. the textile and clothing industry employs 2 million people in our present europe and 2.5 million in enlarged europe and generates 200 billion euro in turnover. aware of the sensitivity of the textile and clothing sector in many countries, the european commission organised an international conference on 5 and 6 may, which brought together participants from more than 80 countries. we discussed the challenges facing the sector in the coming years, particularly in view of the final end of quotas on 1 january 2005, the date which coincides with the scheduled conclusion of the negotiations currently under way at the world trade organisation. this conference led us to four major findings. first, developing countries, especially those most dependent on textile and clothing exports, are very vulnerable. this is particularly the case in the least developed countries, fragile or poorly diversified economies. the same applies to countries with which we have preferential agreements, such as the southern and eastern mediterranean countries, certain acp countries and other small exporters. most of these countries depend heavily on the textile and clothing sector for export earnings, which can account for almost all of their exports and a large share of their employment. secondly, the conditions for access to the textile and clothing market are very different worldwide. for example, while europe has an average of 9% customs duties, many countries have customs duties of 30% or more, and they still have significant non-tariff barriers. if we limit liberalisation to the abolition of quotas in 2005, we risk facing an unbalanced world market, where competition would be focused on the markets of the industrialised countries, our own, which are experiencing low growth. the third observation is the importance of the euro-mediterranean area. it is the natural competitive space for european industry. i'll get back to you. we have plans in this regard. fourth observation: increased competition risks increasing pressure on natural and human resources and poses serious problems in terms of sustainable development, but also in terms of fair competition conditions, for example in terms of fundamental social rights. what are the elements of the response, which of course must be put forward not by us, or by the americans, or by the indians, or by the chinese, but in favour of negotiations with all the parties concerned, in accordance with the rules of the world trade organisation? the first element of the answer is development. in order to mitigate the effects of the abolition of quotas on the poorer and weaker countries, we need to think about how to concentrate the preferential access we give to developing countries, including through the generalised system of preferences, on probably the most vulnerable countries. i am thinking of the ldcs, the least developed countries. i am thinking of the acp countries. i'm thinking about the small savings. we must also consider measures to facilitate the use of these preferences by the countries concerned - i am thinking, for example, of the rules of origin - while, of course, ensuring that these countries are the ones who actually benefit from the preferences we give. secondly, we must, in the context of the doha round, achieve fair and comparable conditions of access to markets at world level. we cannot simply limit the opening of markets to the elimination of quotas in 2005. as i said, this would create imbalances in terms of access; however, our current proposal in the multilateral negotiations is based on fairness arguments. we call on all other wto members to bring their tariffs down to a common level, the lowest possible, and of course to eliminate non-tariff barriers. all countries, except, in our view, the least developed countries, are called upon to contribute to this exercise, including of course those whose textile and clothing exports are very competitive. i would like to reassure european industry and the countries which enjoy preferential access to the union's markets. we do not intend to further reduce our already low customs duties without gaining in return greater access to external markets. we also believe that there should be progressivity and transitional periods for the application of common customs duties, so as to allow those who have problems to make the necessary adjustments. the third element is the euro-mediterranean area. it is in the process of integration and should soon benefit from the expected effects of the pan-euro-mediterranean cumulation of rules of origin which we should be producing very soon. the new protocol on rules of origin is expected to be presented to trade ministers at the euromed conference in palermo on 7 july. this system of diagonal cumulation of origin is intended to enable economic operators in the euromed area as a whole to expand their supply possibilities by allowing producers in this area, which is somewhat unified in this respect, to use intermediate products from the whole area without hindrance. we expect this to have a positive effect on trade, in particular by contributing to the development of intra-regional trade. our aim is to be able to apply this cumulation effectively in all the countries of the area by the end of 2004. finally, the promotion of sustainable development: we must give priority to incentive mechanisms and to respect for multilateral standards. we must continue to examine how public action can ensure that liberalisation does not come at the expense of working conditions or the environment, and that failure to respect social or environmental standards is not used as a competitive advantage. for example, consideration could be given to increasing the margin of tariff preference under the gsp for countries that apply these international standards, or to encouraging private programmes to promote sustainable development, or to exploring the possibilities of increasing consumer information on products to offer those consumers who wish to choose fair trade. as you can see, and this is my conclusion, the european commission is very aware of the challenges facing the textile and clothing sector in terms of sustainable development, the fight against poverty, industrial and social policy and regional balances within the union. it is one of the areas where the issues of equitable distribution of the benefits of trade and globalisation are most acutely raised and one where we have the opportunity to develop policies at both trade and industrial level that address all these legitimate concerns. we have launched a study within the european commission to identify the most exposed product categories, the effects of liberalisation on production, its effects on employment in the enlarged union and its impact in the regions most dependent on textile production. the social partners, in the framework of a sectoral social committee, are following these developments very closely with us. we are also in discussions with the economic and social partners to identify what further measures could be taken to promote the competitiveness of the sector. finally, my colleague, erkki liikanen, and i intend to submit to the college of commissioners, next autumn, and then to the parliament and the council, a communication on industrial and trade policy in the textile and clothing sector after 2005, in order to provide - as is our mission - all interested parties with a clear, predictable and coherent framework so that they can plan their strategies, investments and activities. we must all work together to give the attention we owe to the whole textile and clothing sector.

commission. mr president, i am pleased to see that parliament endorses the approach proposed by the commission. it is true, as is highlighted in the report, that the commission has conceived an ambitious plan, but this is warranted by the importance and complexity of mediterranean fisheries. the community must do its utmost to deliver sustainable fisheries in the mediterranean. many fishermen's associations, public opinion and the european parliament too have repeatedly requested a more stringent, reliable and strategic common fisheries policy in the mediterranean. the plan will respond to this challenge and, if properly implemented and supported by our member states, it will allow us to achieve the main goal of reconciling fisheries with conservation of exploited resources and the environment within a framework of economic and social sustainability. we are worried about the state of resources and sustainability of fisheries in the area. both the general fisheries commission for the mediterranean and the scientific, technical and economic committee of the commission have underlined the poor state of some of the species in the area. there are clear signals that the fisheries are not properly exploiting the production potential of the resources. in addition, the poor economic performance of several important mediterranean fleets means that the current exploitation pattern needs to be revised. the commission will make use of all the management tools available on the basis of scientific advice. even though effort management, together with improved control of fishing capacity, is likely to be the most appropriate tool for mediterranean fisheries, it is undeniable that improving technical measures is also necessary. the commission has already started work on a proposal to improve the technical measures to achieve better protection of juveniles, of habitats and, in general terms, of biodiversity. we have already convened two meetings on 19 may and 16-17 june 2003 to discuss this measure with the fishing industry. improved dialogue with the industry will allow the commission to adopt quite soon a proposal on technical measures that takes into consideration the expertise of the sector. immediately after the adoption of the technical measures package, the commission will start to address the fishing effort issue and i hope that a formal proposal could be put forward early in 2004. however, we are well aware that all our efforts could be wasted if we do not establish cooperative management with the other mediterranean countries. there are many international waters with open access. in addition, the trawlable shelf extends well beyond territorial waters. this means that the community must work together with mediterranean third countries to establish harmonised measures and to freeze or reduce the fishing capacity operation in certain shared areas. we are well advanced in the organisation of a ministerial conference in venice scheduled for 25-26 november 2003. that should hopefully deliver a further boost to multilateral cooperation in fisheries. however, as the biggest fisheries player in the area, we have a responsibility to lead the process and to promote responsible fisheries, first of all, on our own side. establishing so-called fishing protection zones is, in the commission's view, a necessary move to improve control and fairness in international waters, as well as to create an international framework to deliver responsible fisheries and to ensure conservation of straddling and transnational stocks. this should enhance multilateral cooperation without prejudice to the historical rights of our fishermen and the legitimate aspirations of the other bordering countries.

- the next item is the debate on the report (b5-0098/2003). we will be discussing a number of questions to the commission. question no 30, which was to be asked first, will be formulated later to coincide with mr lamy's answers. part one
- question no 31 by mr lage (h-0393/03): subject: reform of the common fisheries policy and the principle of stability in the debate and vote in the european parliament on the reform of the common fisheries policy, the principle of relative stability in the management of fisheries resources was approved by a large majority. the principle of stability has the dual advantage of helping to improve the management and conservation of resources - one of the key objectives of the reform - and of avoiding undesirable conflicts that jeopardise the development of harmonious relations between peoples and communities that live off fishing. the last example is now being seen, for example, along the portuguese coast, where the european authorities are increasingly the target of public concern and revolt. what steps and initiatives does the commission intend to take to ensure that this principle is accepted and thus to reassure fishermen and public opinion?
the commission is not prepared to accept the amendments tabled by the committee on budgets. in his question mr lage referred to access to portuguese continental waters, which plays a role in the council in the context of the new regulation for western waters. the commission's task is to ensure that two principles are observed: firstly, the principle of relative stability, which is laid down in article 20 of the new framework regulation for the common fisheries policy. this principle of allocating fishing rights among the member states applies, of course, also to portugal and portuguese waters. in addition to this principle, there is a second principle of the common fisheries policy which is of fundamental importance, and that is the free access to waters beyond the 12 mile zone, as laid down in article 17 of the new framework regulation. it is clear that the commission must take the same approach to the question of access to portuguese continental waters as it does to all other waters in the community. beyond the 12-mile zone, the waters must be accessible to all member states. however, it is possible to restrict access on biological grounds, but these restrictions must not be discriminatory. it is therefore legally impossible to protect fish stocks by prohibiting access to the waters to fishermen from the neighbouring country. but there is a solution, and the right solution is relative stability together with tacs and quotas for economically important stocks and possibly additional technical measures.
the commission. i am aware of this reaction in some parts of portuguese society, but you will also understand that we have only the possibility of acting within the legal framework at our disposal. i have told you that there is a practical solution, especially if there is a corresponding willingness on the spanish and portuguese sides to agree on the quotas. in concrete terms, it is essentially a question of the sardine fishery. no quota has yet been fixed for the sardine fishery in this area of the sea. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. then we'd have a solution that i think everyone could live with.

- question no 33 by mr nogueira román (h-0356/03):subject: state of progress of the mercosur-eu association in the light of the new political situation in brazil and argentina - economic relations with these two countries in this context, what is the current state of economic relations between the union and these sister countries?
commission. - mr president, mr nogueira román's question has three points. the state of negotiations between the union and mercosur first; then the influence of the arrival of mr kirchner at the argentine presidency and, finally, the issues of economic cooperation between the union and mercosur to facilitate the integration of this region. let us first examine the state of the negotiation. as you know, we relaunched the process last year and since then negotiators from both sides have been working hard to move forward on the various plans. it is a complex negotiation that involves trade in goods, services and regulations. so we adopted a roadmap last year in rio and we are sticking to it. tariff proposals, which were of a fairly good quality, were exchanged. since march of this year, the climate has been serene. we also noted some progress in the areas of rules of origin, investment, public procurement, dispute settlement, trade facilitation, standardisation and technical regulation. all of this is rather auspicious. the march negotiations also provided the basis for an exchange of proposals on services, investment and public procurement. this was done at the end of may last year, although we were a little disappointed by the offers from our mercosur partners. as you can see, we are still actively conducting this negotiation. we have confidence in our partners' will to do so. a round of negotiations was concluded last week in asunción. we must continue to move forward, because much remains to be done, not least because our friends in mercosur are eagerly awaiting action from the union. we shall only take such steps, if necessary, in the context of a general balance which has not yet been fully achieved. optimism about the negotiation is therefore relative. it is probably premature at this stage for us to decide to launch the final phase of the negotiations - which is always an important moment - because there are many issues involved and it takes time. we are considering this, in particular because this negotiation - particularly in the agricultural field - cannot be distinguished, from the point of view of the european union's negotiating credit, from what is happening in the multilateral framework of the world trade organisation. we welcome the arrival of mr kirchner as president of argentina and the various statements by presidents lula and kirchner on the future of mercosur. both of them, of course, wanted to make known to mercosur, that is to say also to paraguay and uruguay, to latin america and, more broadly, to the whole world, their wish and their will to strengthen the mercosur integration process. we can only record these statements with satisfaction. the integration of latin america is one of the political priorities of the european union and that is why we felt from the outset that we should negotiate with mercosur as a bloc. we therefore want a 1+1 negotiation and not a 1+4 negotiation as is done in other fora such as the north-south american free trade area. i have always said, including publicly to our mercosur partners, that the european union's commercial ambition towards mercosur would be commensurate with mercosur's own ambition for political, economic and commercial integration. what are the means we are making available to mercosur in the context of our economic cooperation? first, there is what we are doing at regional level: we have a mercosur/european union regional strategy on the contribution to the implementation of the mercosur internal market, that is, for the period 2000-2006, just over one million euros. we are spending more than €10 million over the same period on the institutionalisation of mercosur and there is a third strand of assistance to civil society. our experience as europeans enables us to contribute to the implementation of the internal market, trade integration, the statistical system, the system of veterinary and phytosanitary standards, the harmonization of technical regulations, in short, to everything that requires cross-border instruments. we know these questions because we have been confronted with them - question no 35 by mrs kinnock (h-0392/03): what is the commission's response to the acp countries' concerns about the lack of agreement on the implementation of paragraph 6 of the declaration on trips and public health? since the declaration as a whole is an important step forward in the campaign for access to medicines, does the commission agree that any attempt to limit the agreement to a list of diseases would be harmful?
commission - first of all, i would like to reassure mrs kinnock that i am not tempted to deviate from any of the provisions, particularly in relation to the december compromise, in the preparation of which we ourselves took part. if i put on the table in january this proposal to consult the world health organization if necessary, it is because my diagnosis is that there is no agreement at the moment from the american side. the us pharmaceutical industry considers that the system as it is on the table still has a number of shortcomings and does not trust that the system will be done for the reason it was put on the table. the position is similar in the developing countries, which also lack confidence and believe that the pharmaceutical industry in general will use every opportunity to get the cover, as they believe it has done in recent years. so the diagnosis is clear. there is a text on the table with which we agree, which the americans do not because they do not trust the system. so we need to increase the level of trust in the system on both sides and that is what we are working towards. however, this must not be at the expense of the compromise on the table concerning the diseases concerned - a compromise which exists and which we do not want to touch - or at the expense of countries which could benefit from the provisions of the agreement insofar as they do not have pharmaceutical production capacity. so the perez motta compromise, as we say in technical jargon, is on the table. that's the one. it is simply necessary to increase the level of confidence in the system a little on both sides.

- question no 40 by mrs plooij-van gorsel (h-0402/03): the commission has not yet decided whether to grant aid to the victims of the floods in the netherlands. subject: principle of fair compensation the principle of 'fair compensation' is introduced by directive 2001/29/ec oj l 167, 22.6.2001, p. 10. in 2002, commissioner bolkestein confirmed that this was a new concept, different from the 'fair pay' principle (levies-system). in april 2003, however, the commissioner admitted that the directive did not require member states to abandon existing pay schemes. does the commission really believe that this principle of fair compensation is a new concept? does the commission consider that the existing systems based on fair pay are compatible with this directive? does the commission consider that the member states should amend their legislation by introducing an express reference to the principle of fair compensation? finally, does the commission consider that this principle of fair compensation introduces a harmonised basis which can put an end to the diversity of arguments put forward and, therefore, to the differences in amounts?
the commission mr president, i can confirm that the principle of 'fair compensation' as described in the directive is a new concept which is not the same as the right to receive fair compensation, referred to by the term 'copyright' in the context of private copying. as set out in the directive, the concept of fair compensation provides member states with a significant degree of flexibility or discretion in determining the form, modalities or level of fair compensation schemes. however, it follows from recitals 35 and 38 that member states which apply copyright fulfil the condition of fair compensation. the relevant legislation implementing the directive does not necessarily contain an explicit reference to the principle of fair compensation. the directive requires member states to provide for fair compensation for three of the reproduction rights exceptions listed in the directive. first, the private copying exception. this is the exception with the greatest relevance to copyright, as rights are usually levied in respect of the copying for private use of sound and audiovisual material. secondly, the exception for reprography or photocopying and thirdly, the exception for broadcasts in certain public institutions such as hospitals or prisons. it is likely that member states that have already provided for charging schemes in the past will continue to allow private copying in conjunction with charging schemes and will also apply them to certain digital products. it is true that the different systems continue to cause differences in application in terms of the media or equipment to which they apply and/or the amount claimed, including differences in application to digital media. this is because the ec legislator opposed a higher degree of harmonisation during the negotiations on the directive. as regards analogue copying for private use, the directive recognises that the existing differences may not have a significant impact on the development of the information society. as regards digital copying for private use, the directive stresses that due account should be taken of the differences between digital and analogue copying for private use and that in certain cases a distinction should be made between the two. at the same time, it should be stressed that the directive does not oblige member states to abolish copyright, nor does it take a position for or against copyright as compared to digital rights management systems, as they are called in english.
the commission i can well imagine the disappointment of mrs plooij, but as i have said before, the legislator, and therefore the european parliament, felt that far-reaching harmonization was not desirable. the legislative process has been completed and there is nothing to be done about it. but i can understand mrs plooij's disappointment. it would have been better to have applied a higher level of harmonization, but unfortunately this has not been the case.
commission. let us see how all this works in practice. as mrs thors and mrs plooij-van gorsel know, the directive has not been transposed in the legislation of all member states. the commission hopes that this will soon be the case. it may be that a more significant degree of harmonisation would have been better for the internal market. but as i said earlier in reply to mrs plooij-van gorsel, unfortunately that is not the case and we have the directive that was approved by council and parliament. so let us see how this works in practice and how quickly the whole system of digital right management is put in practice in europe. if mrs thors would then like to ask the commission for further investigations and analysis, the commission would be more than willing to oblige. the issue is important and essential aspects of the internal market are at stake.
- question no 41 by mrs mckenna (h-0362/03) subject: early warning notifications does the commission intend to publish an annual summary of 'alert notifications', 'information', 'additional alerts' and 'additional information' from 1992 to 2003, by foodstuff and by country of origin, specifying the brand, supermarket or company concerned? can it say how and in what timeframe it will publish this information? if it is not prepared to publish this information, could it explain how its position serves the public interest?
commission. in further response to mrs mckenna's question, firstly, i would not characterise our system of alert as being in any way vague. it is very targeted and the purpose of the exercise is, as i am sure she will appreciate, to transmit as fast as possible the relevant information to the competent authorities of all member states, so that they can make a rapid response and take rapid action in relation to the risk that has been identified in respect of any particular food or feed in question. what is important here is public health, rather than some kind of naming and shaming. i would like to emphasise that once the rapid alert has been made and responses have been taken, and if it is shown that it is a genuine problem from which consumers need to be protected, the member states in question, where there is a risk – and it is for them to determine this – will immediately inform their own consumers in their member state. that is their responsibility under the rapid alert system. in those circumstances it would be appropriate for them to then identify, for instance, trade names or companies which would assist consumers to make the appropriate response. however, bear in mind that the rapid alert system is designed to allow member states to react quickly and to remove, for instance, foods from the market. in addition to that, if it is necessary on further reflection and further analysis of the information that has come from the rapid alert – which is activated under article 50 - that an emergency procedure under article 53 is necessary, this would be something which could again be done at member state level or, indeed, could also be done by the commission. in those circumstances, the relevant information that would be made available would include the information that you referred to relating to trade names and companies, etc. i want to emphasise that the rapid alert is designed for a specific purpose, which is to transmit information as fast as possible, even in circumstances where all information may not be available. the important issue here is to identify the risk to the public to which the member states must respond. i believe, in those circumstances, we have struck the correct balance. in relation to the second part of your question concerning the figures for 2002, i do not have the specific figures to hand relating to the breakdown between farmed fish and wild fish, but i am sure this kind of information is available to my services. i will seek to ensure that it is made available by them and transmitted to you in the normal course.

- question no 44 by mrs izquierdo rojo (h-0378/03) subject: increase in bovine spongiform encephalopathy (bse) or mad cow disease in spain due to the 'irresponsible' attitude of the authorities in june 2000, the european union's scientific committee designated spain as a high-risk country, while the spanish minister of agriculture called this european report "irresponsible" (in 2000, the author of this question submitted several parliamentary questions in this regard). in addition, in recent months, a sharp increase in cases of bovine spongiform encephalopathy (bse) has been recorded in spain and the same trend is observed in 2003. does the court of justice not consider that the community's 1996 decision to prohibit animal meal for ruminants has not been complied with in spain?
commission. the scientific steering committee has classified spain as a gbr iii country, having confirmed cases at a lower level. the upper limit of this level is an incidence of 100 cases per million adult cattle over the past 12 months. the bse incidence in spain has been increasing since the beginning of 2002. the incidence is, however, still well below this upper limit of around 45 cases per million adult cattle over the past 12 months, and it is not increasing rapidly. therefore, the classification of spain by the scientific steering committee still remains valid. in the first quarter of this year, spain reported about 50% more bse cases than during the corresponding period last year. at the same time the number of cases decreased or was stable in all other member states, except portugal. compared with other member states, spain has a rather high rate of young animals born in 1997 and 1998. the feeding of ruminant proteins to ruminants is considered to be the main source of bse transmission to cattle. therefore, the commission imposed a community-wide prohibition of the use of mammalian proteins in ruminant feed in 1994. it is, however, evident that this ban was not fully enforced at that time, since most of the bse cases reported today were born after 1994. meat-and-bone meal continued to be allowed in feed for non-ruminants, and thereby ruminant feed was contaminated in feed mills and during storage and transport. another source of transmission was cross-feeding of feed intended for non-ruminants to cattle on mixed farms. shortcomings in the implementation of the feed ban were observed throughout the community. to put an end to the transmission of bse the feed ban was extended to the use of all animal proteins in feed for all farmed animals at the beginning of 2001. other measures to reduce the transmission of bse are improved rendering standards – which came into effect in early 1997 – and a ban on the use of so-called bse risk materials in food and feed, which became effective in october 2000. the current community legislation should, if rigorously implemented, be sufficient to prevent new animals from becoming infected. bse cases will, nevertheless, continue to appear in spain, as in other member states, for a number of years because of an incubation time of four to six years or even longer. that is why it is important to maintain current safeguards, in particular the removal of specified risk material.
(es) mr commissioner, by the way, in your reply, so technical, so diplomatic, with so much caution not to alarm, i have heard that you actually confirm that since 1996 there has been a breach of that prohibition of community legislation in spain. the increase in mad cow disease which has also occurred in spain in recent years - and your words also confirm this - is the consequence of the fact that the then spanish minister, mr arias cañete, who denied the risk in spain - and yet the scientific committee did declare it - did not comply with community rules, and that is the cause of this proliferation and increase in mad cow disease. mr commissioner, is not this confirmed breach of community rules by spain since 1996 regarding the ban on meat meal reprehensible? is that not reprehensible? your answer has to be yes. there is no social alarm, but it is the failure to comply with the regulations that is causing spain to be at the forefront of mad cow disease in recent years.
commission. in response to the supplementary question, let me say that the commission does not know the exact reason why the number of bse cases is still increasing in spain and not in other member states, with the exception of portugal, as i mentioned earlier. possible explanations, in addition to shortcomings in the implementation of the feed ban, are introduction of the removal of specified risk materials in spain only at the end of 2000 and a higher than average exposure to infected meat and bone meal in the 1996-1998 period. it should be stressed, however, that the commission's food and veterinary office has carried out missions in spain in order to verify the correct implementation of the community provisions with regard to the control and eradication of bse in 2001 and 2002. shortcomings are still being detected. spain has also informed the commission of a number of breaches of the feed ban detected in 2002. the number of breaches is very small and below the average in member states.

the rapporteur. i would like to begin by briefly referring to mrs klaß's report in support of the transaction amendment concerning the official list of ingredients to be included in annex iiia within two years. i do so because there are products such as casein, egg albumin or fish tail which have been used for centuries in the production of wine or beer and which are part of the oenological practices covered and allowed by regulations (ec) no 1493/1999 and 1622/2000 and, above all, because there is no scientific evidence that they behave as allergens in the final product. why do we have to put them under suspicion in the form of labeling? the council and the commission must be in line with parliament in this perception of the problem. and with that, i move on to my own report. first of all, i would like to thank the commission, the council and the shadow rapporteurs, mr lund and mrs paulsen, very sincerely for their excellent cooperation in reaching compromises which could lead to us adopting this proposal for a directive at first reading. my main concern in the preparation of this report has been that the food additives included in it not only represent a technological advance but also do not pose a health risk or mislead consumers. the compromise amendments which we tabled in plenary, together with the socialist group and the liberal group (amendments nos 19 to 32), are the result of this concern which we all share. annex ii to the framework directive 89/107/eec on additives specifies that 'all additives shall be under a state of continuous observation and evaluation'. however, in view of the concerns about the use of polysorbates, the judgment of the court of justice of 20 march 2003 on maximum doses of nitrites and nitrates and the statement of the scientific committee for food of 4 april 2003 on parahydroxybenzoic acid derivatives, two new paragraphs are introduced to article 2 through amendment no 21. to have the commission review the use of the additives e 432 to e 436 - polysorbates - e 251 and e 252 and e 249 to e 250 - nitrates and nitrites - and to have the conditions of use for parabenzenes revised from e 214 to e 219 by 1 july 2004. as regards biphenyl, orthophenyl phenol and orthophenyl phenol sodium, which are now considered as plant protection products, the commission intends to include them in future pesticide legislation by deleting them from directive 95/2/ec. we agree with that and all we want is that there should not be a legal vacuum, as is reflected in amendment no 21 and amendment no 4 to the report which was adopted in the committee on the environment. we are also concerned that additives may be introduced into food through an additive in flavourings which should not be labelled. we therefore table amendment no 22 to limit its use to the minimum necessary to ensure the quality and safety of flavouring when it has no technological function in food. otherwise, these flavouring additives shall be labelled. in conclusion, i would like to stress that it is very important that we make consumers aware that thanks to the legislation on additives and the work of the scientific committee on food they can enjoy adequate food safety and food products suited to their needs. today, cities are getting bigger and bigger, industry needs new additives, and this makes life easier for us when it comes to consuming cooked or pre-cooked products. i would like to thank the council, the commission and the shadow rapporteurs who have helped to reach important agreements.
commission. i thank ms corbey for her work as rapporteur on this subject. i know she has done a very serious job and looked at this in depth. in 1999 a total amount of 63.5 million tonnes of packaging waste was generated in the european union. this corresponds to around 17% of municipal solid waste and 3% of the total waste generation by weight. the packaging and packaging waste directive has made the collection and recycling of packaging waste a normal activity in all eu member states, increasingly so also in the accession countries. in this way the directive has helped to reduce environmental impacts and to strengthen the internal market for packaging and packaging waste. this revision builds on this success. i am very pleased that the european parliament has, since the first reading, given clear support for our proposal to more than double the minimum recycling targets and to further increase the recovery target. it seems that there is now widespread agreement on the levels of the targets. the key remaining question is whether the implementation deadline will be 2008, as in the common position, or whether an earlier date should be set. in my view deadlines should be both realistic and ambitious. it will also be important to give greece, ireland and portugal – member states already granted later target dates under current legislation – a reasonable time to adapt to the new targets. this also applies to the accession states. i intend to propose deadlines for these countries before the end of this year. i am also pleased that parliament largely agrees that other aspects – in particular, prevention and re-use – should be further studied before new decisions are taken. however, the need for further analysis also applies to the new obligation referred to in the first part of amendment no 7. this new obligation to minimise the environmental impact of packaging risks duplicating the existing essential requirements and facing the same problems in regard to enforcement. i fully understand the concerns of parliament regarding exports for recycling. i agree that we should make sure that recycling in non-eu countries should only count for our targets if it is done properly. however, controls and paperwork should be focused on where they are really needed. i do not see any reason why this should apply to materials such as metals, paper and glass. these materials are part of a functioning, internal, international market. i doubt that we need written proof of the recycling of each exported batch. it would also seem strange to me to apply stricter controls on exports of packaging waste than the provisions on waste electrical and electronic equipment, which we decided just a few months ago. there seems to be a great deal of concern in parliament – as we just heard from the rapporteur – about the effect of the packaging directive on ceramics packaging. let me be clear that nothing in the directive obliges member states to set up recycling systems for this type of packaging. excluding ceramics from the scope of the packaging directive raises the question of why we should exclude ceramics and not other, similar packaging types. it also gives member states the freedom to take any measure on ceramics packaging, as long as it is within the framework of the treaty. therefore i believe it is better to ask the technical committee to solve any possible implementation problems, rather than excluding ceramics from the scope of the directive. i know that flower pots, self-adhesive labels and related issues are important for the industries concerned. therefore they merit a proper discussion. conciliation is, in my view, not the right framework for such a discussion. this is a job for detailed work by the experts in the technical committee. of the 32 amendments the commission can accept 20 amendments in full, in part, or in principle. a list of the amendments concerned has been handed over separatelycommission's position on parliament's amendments: see annex..

does he feel, as some leaders do, that the world is safer now and that the risk of terrorist attacks is less? question no 3 by mr nogueira román, replaced by mr ortuondo larrea (h-0355/03) subject: states of the union and the terrorist attack in morocco which killed 41 people what is the council's view of the terrorist attacks in casablanca which killed 41 people, including several union citizens, and injured a large number of others? given that these attacks occurred after the war in iraq by the united states and its allies, does the council attach particular significance to the fact that a large number of people were killed or injured in an establishment linked to a member state? what policy measures does it intend to take to prevent or limit the risks posed by such terrorist acts?
i suggest. i will answer both questions together, first of all by saying that the european union, as is obvious, once again strongly condemns the barbaric terrorist attacks in casablanca and elsewhere in the world. those attacks in casablanca have brutally confirmed that terrorism is a growing threat to democracy, peace, international security, from which no country can consider itself free or safe. the fight against terrorism requires the utmost determination and the strongest will to cooperate and take concerted action from the international community. the european union will continue - and i believe this is a top priority of the italian presidency - to do its part to prevent and eradicate this threat. the union has adopted a comprehensive approach to the fight against terrorism, which encompasses all eu policies, is based on an action plan whose implementation is proceeding as planned and a regularly updated roadmap. as you know, an updated presidency report on the activities in the fight against terrorism was presented to the council at its june 2003 part-session. internally, the union operates through political, economic and judicial instruments; at the same time, the union shall ensure that the fight against terrorism is incorporated into all aspects of its external policy. in the meetings of political dialogue with all third countries - and of course morocco - this issue is regularly on the agenda. the european union, at the same time, continues to promote dialogue and exchanges between cultures, religions and civilizations. substantial work is being done, in particular, in the context of the barcelona process for the creation of a euro-mediterranean foundation for dialogue between cultures and civilizations, a measure which can help to eradicate the causes of all forms of extremist violence which can lead to terrorism.
(es) mr president, mr minister, speaking on the subject of suicide bombings, i am reminded of a recent book by the french sociologist and thinker emmanuel todd entitled 'after the empire'. in it he points out how societies, as their education improves, evolve towards democracy as a political system that guarantees freedoms and justice, and, in this development, the west appears as the great driver of democracy, progress and development of peoples, as well as leader and arbiter of conflicts. however, if the west does not act with justice and equity in international relations by putting its own interests first, it is creating a new form of anti-democratic autarchy which will eventually confront it with the rest of the world and cause its unsustainable decline. in the light of mr todd's reflections, i would like to ask him whether he does not believe that with unjust impositions and exploitation, with preventive wars based on false evidence of weapons of mass destruction and risks to world security - as is the case in iraq - what has been generated by the invading rulers, instead of peace and freedom, has been new despair and new hatreds that see no other way out than bombings and terrorist self-immolation to achieve a fairer world for those who suffer exploitation and aggression.
i suggest. i believe that terrorism can never be justified - i say never - when women, children, innocent people are killed, when civilian life is affected. that said, it is clear that the structural causes of terrorism must be addressed, and those causes can also be found in despair, poverty, the difficulty of dialogue between cultures. that is why i believe that the overall european strategy must be, on the one hand, a relentless fight against all forms of terrorism and, on the other, a profound dialogue between civilisations and cultures. it is a question of addressing the structural reasons which can lead - but, i repeat, never justify - to acts of terrorism.

- question no 4 by mrs ludford (h-0354/03): subject: profiling of persons suspected of having committed terrorist acts following the recommendation adopted at the justice and home affairs council in brussels in november 2002 on the preparation of terrorist profiles, a pilot project appears to be planned. the first report (march 2003) of the community network of independent fundamental rights experts indicated that such profiles posed a major risk of discrimination and could only be accepted when the relationship between the characteristics of the persons concerned and the risk of terrorism was demonstrated in a fair and statistically relevant way - a demonstration which has not yet been made. what safeguards are the council/member states implementing to ensure that the pilot project does not risk discrimination or undermining democratic freedoms?

i suggest. i think i can confirm to the honourable member that it is and will be the duty of the council to take account of what has emerged from today's debate. i shall certainly inform the council secretariat so that it can take account of this intention and where this pilot project should be prepared in the future, which - i repeat - i do not know.

the commission (es) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, first of all i would like to thank the rapporteur, mr bradbourn, for the work he has done and also for the speech by mr dover, the rapporteur's deputy, in this presentation to the house. ladies and gentlemen, i would like to thank parliament in general for its constructive attitude, which has enabled us, thanks to an informal tripartite meeting last november, to reach an agreement which will enable us to launch the marco polo programme with an allocation of 75 million euro over four years. a project to facilitate the development of intermodality within the european union. intermodality is absolutely key if we are to make our transport systems effective and efficient. intermodality is about moving beyond the unimodal view of transport and considering all the different systems and modes to optimise the resources and possibilities we have in the european union to achieve efficient transport. the first of these projects is the motorway of the sea, which is already under way under agreements between italy, france and spain in the western mediterranean, and other projects of this kind in the atlantic area, together with other projects on the combination of river and rail transport and, ultimately, of course, also maritime and road transport. i would like to thank you again for the work done, i think it is a good text, we have achieved a reasonable and balanced result and what is needed now is to promote, with this and all the other measures, a competitive and efficient transport in the service of economic efficiency and the development of growth.
(es) mr president, commissioner, we are today discussing the marco polo programme, with a view to reducing road congestion and contributing to an efficient and sustainable transport system. we shall vote in favour of the text proposed by the committee on regional policy, transport and tourism, but we cannot say that we are fully satisfied with it. firstly, because the financial allocation we are asking for has been cut by the council of ministers from 115 to 75 million euro, a cut which, we believe, will prevent the objective of transferring to other alternative modes the total annual increase in international road freight transport, which is expected to grow by 50% by the year 2010, from being achieved. to do this, according to the white paper on transport, rail and shipping would have to absorb an extra 39% more tonnes/kilometre of goods than at present, which, added to its own trend increase, which is already 29%, would mean a 68% total increase in its traffic capacity, which i do not think can be financed with the cut in the budget. if, as the commission points out, 500 tonnes could be transferred with one euro of subsidy, then with the 75 million euros that the council accepts, 37.5 billion tonnes/kilometre could be transferred, instead of the 52.250 million tonnes per year that road transport is expected to increase. in other words, the objectives of the marco polo programme could not be achieved. we are also not satisfied that the possibility of financing measures to reduce and prevent the transport of goods by road itself, without necessarily involving transfer to other modes, has not been included. we believe that it is possible to act in the phases prior to the loading operation of the lorries, for example by encouraging a more compact form of packaging of the goods so that they take up less space and require fewer lorries. and finally - although this may be the subject of another proposal - we believe that it is also necessary to reflect on the current model of production and distribution of goods. if we really incorporate, without exception, all the external costs of transport, perhaps we will come to the conclusion that we should retouch our theory of economies of scale in production and the benefits of concentration of production.
we have tried to find a compromise. i think there are two ways of doing politics. the inflexible one, which makes dialogue difficult, and the flexible one, in which we give in and try to build a positive policy. we propose to accept a combination of passive and active measures (which could have been included in another directive anyway!) in the event of replacing the eec-wide tests, provided that these passive measures do not constitute more than 25% of the tests. alternative measures to the actual hse tests (effectively tested for more than 20 years) would not differ by more than 25% from them. we concede that the hse tests may be subject to a new feasibility study (as may alternative measures presented by industry). the condition is the complete independence of this study. finally, we wanted to clarify that alternative measures should, in any event, maintain the same level of protection as the echa tests, so that they protect all the body parts included in these tests. i consider these concessions to be a major effort on the part of my political group and i hope they will be accepted by my colleagues and improve the protection of pedestrians.

(es) madam president, mr commissioner, mr president of the european central bank, ladies and gentlemen, i think that the report of the committee on economic and monetary affairs, which i have the honour to represent, could not have come at a more opportune time. this report is based on the european commission's report on the first four years of the euro and, as has been said, on another report on the use of euro banknotes and coins. the euro has consolidated itself in a very short time, but it has shown its strength and stability. we should congratulate the european central bank and its president, mr duisenberg, on their successful management and express our appreciation and our best wishes for the future in this last appearance in the plenary, wishing him to enjoy them in the company of his grandchildren, who have only known the euro as a single currency. the consolidation of the euro, its growing acceptance and appreciation against the dollar inevitably lead to consideration of the role of the euro in its international projection, which is the main focus of the report. at the thessaloniki european council, the president of the european commission, romano prodi, said that it was absolutely necessary to build up the external representation of the euro. the report seeks to respond to this need, as expressed by president prodi, and proposes that there should be a single representative of the euro in the international financial institutions, mainly, and that there should also be a display of this representation of the euro at international level. the report does not go any further, because we believe that there must be a broad consensus and, of course, the appropriate formulas must be analysed and adopted in accordance with this principle in the appropriate institutional forums. but there is a suggestion, made by mrs peijs herself shortly before she was appointed as a minister in the new dutch government, that the figure already adopted and proposed by the european convention should be used for the european minister for foreign affairs. the same could be said of a minister for european economic and monetary affairs who represents the euro at international level in this way, as proposed by ecofin and accepted, of course, by the commission, and who is "mr euro" or "ms euro" and holds the post of vice-president or vice-president of the european commission. i would like to stress that this is a suggestion, it is a figure which has already been adopted and proposed in the convention, it seems to have been accepted at political level, including by the european council itself, and it is therefore a parallel which we consider to be valid. in a recent article in the financial times, martin wolf said that the eurozone will soon surpass the dollar zone, and he bases this on the credibility and the strength of the economy and the economies that are integrated into the eurozone. obviously, this solidity and credibility are based on the observance of the stability and growth pacts, which are absolutely necessary to monitor and implement. we refer to this aspect - observance and need for observance of the stability and growth pacts - as an element and guarantee of the soundness, credibility and stability of the euro, and we naturally analyse the use of the euro at international level in various fields and, in particular, in the international financial markets, its use by the new neighbours, including russia and the baltic countries. we also mentioned the need for greater stability in the supply of raw materials, which are very important because of their dependence on the european economy. we believe that energy supplies should be made in euros. we are also referring to the growing number of central banks worldwide that are increasing their reserves expressed in euro. in conclusion, ladies and gentlemen, i would just like to remind you that in the report we also analysed some suggestions, proposing a study that the european central bank and the central banks of the euro area should carry out on the use of banknotes and coins in some of the areas already mentioned by mrs randzio-plath.
the commission (es) madam president, i would like to thank mr gasòliba i böhm for his presentation and for his interesting report, whose viewpoint i share, and i welcome the creation of the euro as a great success. i should like to focus my remarks on two fundamental points in his report: firstly, on economic policies, and secondly, on institutional problems, to which he has devoted a little more attention. as regards economic policies, the new broad economic policy guidelines were adopted in thessaloniki, and we hope that the ecofin council will formally adopt them at its next meeting, and the guidelines maintain the tone that had been set by the commission, including some of the comments of this parliament contained in the report that mr garcía-margallo y marfil presented at the time. the project, in general, confirms the main line we are all working on: sound macroeconomic policies, which are essential to increase demand, growth and employment and to increase growth potential, based on lisbon. that means the need to move forward with policies of modernization, of structural change, and, at the moment, our great challenge is the implementation, the implementation of those policies. and here i believe that parliament has a fundamental role to play in this aspect of the implementation of policies, through its dialogue with the citizens and its dialogue with the national parliaments. as regards economic governance, i would like to make two comments. firstly, the eurogroup has played and continues to play a key role. in our view, the recognition of its role in the constitution should be seen as positive, while maintaining its informal character. the commission regrets, however, that the idea of creating an ecofin council for the eurozone has not been retained. we believe that there are a number of formal decisions which must be taken publicly by the euro area countries and that, however, the existence of the eurogroup is not sufficient to solve these problems. we are pleased that some progress has been made in the decisions to be taken by the euro area countries, including in the framework of the current ecofin, but some of the commission's requests have not been met and we believe that this will not help the system to function better. decisions such as those on the excessive deficit procedure, multilateral surveillance in the euro area and i hope we can make progress. i want to make one last comment on the aspect of the external representation. the thessaloniki european council, as mr gasòliba i böhm has just said, stressed the interdependence. the effective and consistent representation of the euro area in this respect is essential. however, it must be acknowledged that, apart from raising the problem, little progress has been made in terms of external representation. in recent years, the main progress has been better coordination of strategic positions at international meetings, which has allowed us, in many cases, to make joint proposals, but not a common approach. we must move further in this direction. i take note of your suggestion, which is not far from any other that the commission has put forward in the convention. however, we must be aware of the technical, legal and institutional difficulties involved and, in the face of these, i believe that a high degree of political sensitivity is essential in order to be able to define clearly what we want to achieve in the future. in this respect, the commission will continue to work with the convention, trying to clarify certain points in the corrections to the final texts, in the part still under discussion, and in any case, at the intergovernmental conference, the commission will try to put forward a more ambitious, even innovative, vision that will
