(es) mr president, commissioner, unfortunately once again, forest fires have ravaged the mediterranean forests with a special virulence this summer, because of the climatic conditions we have suffered. beyond the loss of human life, which we must mourn, beyond the dantean images that the fires have left behind and the economic losses they have caused, the scale of the disaster that year after year is looming over the forests of southern europe and the consequences that this entails for the european union as a whole highlight the need for a community policy for the protection of forests against fires with its own financial resources, which takes into account the specific nature of mediterranean forests and which includes preventive measures as an integral part of forest management, as this parliament had already called for at the time. it should not be forgotten that mediterranean forests and northern forests have a completely different development and are therefore governed by completely different laws. the limiting factors for growth, like soils, are water in mediterranean forests and light in boreal forests. in the mediterranean, where there is no lack of light, the top trees, the shrubs and the grasses close to the ground compete for water, and as a limiting factor, there comes a time when every drop of water that falls must be distributed at ground level. the water table then falls, the roots don't reach that level and die, and then the aerial part, the mass, becomes dense and finally - unfortunately - the fire comes in a recurring way that forces us to start again. this differentiated development requires differentiated forest management and that in mediterranean forests, management and prevention form an inseparable whole, the only way to avoid, each summer, these waves of fires more or less serious depending on weather conditions. the mediterranean forests are part of the common heritage of all europeans, and therefore the fight against forest fires is not the responsibility of the member states or the regional governments which have competence in this field alone, although it is clear that a correct application of the principle of subsidiarity is essential to improve the effectiveness of the measures to be taken. the community's environmental responsibilities and the commitment made by the european union in kyoto require a greater budgetary allocation and a greater involvement of the european union in firefighting. mr president, i would like to begin by congratulating mr koukiadis on his excellent report, which is a valuable working document on the sensitive relationship between criminal sanctions and community law. the report also has the merit of being the first institutional document to take a comprehensive look at this problem, which is certainly not new. the commission's services have also been working hard to identify the issue in various working papers for almost all of the proposals mentioned in mr koukiadis' report, particularly in the areas of protection of financial interests, environmental protection through criminal law, racism and xenophobia, which have never been dealt with so systematically outside the academic world. the second reason why i am pleased on behalf of the commission is that i read this report and see a great deal of convergence of views with the position taken by the commission. like mr koukiadis, the commission considers that the community does not have general jurisdiction in criminal matters as the treaties currently stand. on the other hand, the commission considers that, within the framework of the powers of attribution which it has for the purposes of the objectives set out in article 2 of the ec treaty, the community has the power to impose sanctions, including criminal sanctions, at national level, where this is necessary to achieve a community objective. this approach is based, as mr koukiadis has pointed out, on the case-law of the court of justice, according to which article 10 of the treaty - i quote - 'requires the member states to take all appropriate measures to ensure the scope and effectiveness of community law'. however, as the treaties currently stand, the harmonisation of the criminal laws of the member states can only be covered by the provisions of title 6 of the treaty on european union. the commission, supported by the parliament, defends this position before the court of justice in the action for annulment of the framework decision on the protection of the environment through criminal law. finally, i believe that mr koukiadis' report, and in particular its conclusions, have the immense merit of perfectly illustrating the way in which the interplay between the subjects of the first community pillar and the means of action considered to fall within the third pillar is a source of permanent difficulties. moreover, this situation entails risks of blocking the decision-making process which, even when overcome by artificial cuts between acts with the same purpose, often make the union's action largely incomprehensible to citizens. it is also important that the european parliament and the court of justice be given the same role as in the first pillar, so that the concern for efficiency is combined with the improvement of democratic and judicial controls. the commission therefore welcomes the proposal for the communityisation of title 6 of the treaty on european union, as advocated by the convention. the commission will do all it can to ensure that this major breakthrough survives the intergovernmental conference which will begin next month. i know that parliament is in full agreement with the commission on this.

the commission. the proposal we are discussing, mr president, ladies and gentlemen, proposes the introduction of a european quality mark for seafarers from third countries who hold certificates of competency issued outside the community and who are serving on board community vessels. the purpose of this proposal is to ensure that in all cases foreign crews working on ships flying the flag of the member states of the union are trained and certified in accordance with international requirements. the proposal is particularly important in the light of the maritime disasters of the erika and prestige. the human factor is a very important aspect of safety at sea, but it also preserves the marine environment. the commission has also proposed that the community should be able to provide a financial contribution to the community's fishing fleet in the form of a financial contribution from the community. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial interests are protected. firstly, the proposal establishes a european harmonised system for the recognition at community level of maritime education and certification systems of third countries, which fully complies with the requirements of the stcw convention, i.e. the international convention on the training, certification and penal code of the seafarers' profession. the second point concerns the provision of an effective procedure for direct action on changes in the training and certification system of third countries. regular monitoring and, where appropriate, the withdrawal of recognition are two key elements of the text. the proposal provides in particular for the regular reassessment of all recognised countries every five years. thirdly, the key element of the proposal is the newly created european maritime safety agency, which will offer its expertise and professionalism to assist the commission in these vital tasks. this new legislation will improve the quality and efficiency of the system for the recognition of seafarers' certificates through a single community system. the ministers for transport reached unanimous political agreement on this proposal in march. the council's examination of the proposal has enabled us to introduce certain amendments which improve on our original proposal. for example, the recognition of a third country remains valid unless there is evidence of non-compliance by that third country, in which case the recognition is withdrawn. the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the european union's fishing fleet is able to compete with the other fleets in the world.
the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the social partners are able to take part in the negotiations. i would like to make it clear that i am speaking on behalf of my colleague mr pérez álvarez, who has not yet been able to attend this part-session. as the rapporteur has rightly pointed out, there have been a number of events at sea, a number of disasters, which have given rise to reflections, from the point of view of safety and health at work or the environment, on the aspects of a productive activity, which also makes a very important contribution to the realization of the right of every worker to exercise his activity in conditions which respect his health, his safety and his dignity, as enshrined in article 31 of the charter of fundamental rights of the european union. the training of personnel in maritime professions is a key element in the level of safety in maritime transport and in the prevention of accidents. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council and parliament on the subject of the protection of the environment, and i would like to thank the rapporteur for his excellent report. it is true that the training required in the european union can be ignored or ignored by using the recruitment of seamen from third countries to join european union ships, given the lack of maritime professionals from the union who lack the required training. the committee on employment and social affairs will be considering four aspects in its opinion: the possibility of maintaining a selective approach to the recognition of certificates of qualification; the rapporteur. {es) madam president, greenland, an autonomous region of denmark, was part of the community from 1973 to 1984, when 52% of greenlanders voted in a referendum to leave. since then our relations have been governed by the greenland treaty, which grants the island the same status as 19 other overseas countries and territories, allowing the free export of greenland fishery products to the community in return for a fisheries agreement with satisfactory possibilities, initially for ten years and extended over time. the fourth protocol, concluded in 2002, provides for an interim review which we are now dealing with, justified by its long duration and high financial amount. the commission's communication goes beyond mere fisheries matters, because relations with greenland go beyond this area. the committee on fisheries therefore believes that parliament should take the initiative and draw up a general report covering political relations, development aid to greenland and fisheries relations, placing all this within the policy of the arctic dimension. (mr president, may i draw the attention of the president to the fact that i do not see the minutes of my speech on the screen as they are running. i'd like to see it, to know how much time i have left. ) in addition to referring to the relations between greenland and the union, the commission's communication reviews the current state of the agreement and, since any amendment must be approved by the local government of greenland, proposes a thorough review of the agreement, but after 2006 - when it is concluded - and is now limited to a simple adaptation. even if we limit ourselves to an adaptation, in view of the criticisms of this parliament and the court of auditors itself, we think we should try to bring it more closely into line with the principles of governance, transparency and the optimal use of community financial resources without waiting for that date in 2006. the conclusions of my colleague mrs langenhagen two years ago on the fourth protocol are still perfectly valid for this mid-term review phase. clear the fisheries agreement of non-fisheries elements, inform the european parliament about the use of fishing rights, promote the creation of joint ventures. in addition to encouraging the setting up of joint ventures, the committee on fisheries now calls for the promotion of temporary associations of companies, which are more flexible structures and are better adapted - in this case - to the realities of both the european - community - and greenland fisheries sectors. the committee on fisheries also calls for a balanced sharing of the cost of the agreement, as is done in the southern agreements between the shipowners and the community budget. i note, however, commissioner, that the commission does not propose this question even for the adaptation it is currently undertaking, and i think that the justification offered to us - we are referring to the small size of the greenland administration - is not very credible or very justifiable. the annual financial contribution paid by the european union to greenland under this agreement is very high. the agreement is worth eur 42.82 million per year, making it the most expensive of all, after the mauritania agreement. not only expensive, but very expensive, if we take into account that at least 14 million euros have nothing to do with the payment for fishing opportunities or the development of the fisheries sector. the fishing opportunities corresponding to the remaining eur 28 million are very poorly implemented. other non-quota fleets - i.e. those other than those of germany, denmark, the united kingdom and france - are not allowed to take advantage of the paid and unfished fishing opportunities, which is allowed in other southern agreements. we welcome, mr fischler, the fact that in the agreement reached between the commission and the greenlandic government in june this taboo has been broken and other fleets can enter, albeit timidly, to fish for certain species and for experimental fishing activities. nor is there any encouragement for the creation of joint ventures or temporary associations of undertakings, which would be very beneficial for greenland, whose economy is stagnating, and for the community itself. the previous agreement provided for eur 6 million for this purpose. fifthly, the agreement allocates quotas for species which are practically non-existent in greenland waters, such as cod and norway lobster, which are not caught but which are nevertheless paid for by the community. we also welcome the fact that in june negotiators agreed on quotas adjusted to reality, in this case increasing the fishing opportunities for flounder, prawns and snow crab and that negotiators have thus tried to eliminate the so-called paper fish. sixthly, the community's financial contribution has been increasing in each protocol, while fishing opportunities have been decreasing. in this respect the agreement is untenable and - as mrs langenhagen said at the time - the protocol is an incoherent protocol. in conclusion, while it is commendable that the commission should rethink the current model with greenland and take appropriate steps - such as those i have just mentioned - in june in the agreement reached with the greenlanders, we believe that the commission should be more ambitious and should try to introduce substantial changes now. if we want this fisheries agreement to stop violating sacrosanct principles of the community's financial regulations, such as transparency and the proper use of financial resources, we cannot confine ourselves to a mere make-up review. the european union's support for greenland is fully justified, but not in the form of a fisheries agreement, as i indicated to the greenlandic minister for fisheries, whom i met here in strasbourg last july. greenland is a key element in the development of the european union's arctic dimension and, in this sense, we should consider financing the non-fisheries part of this relationship under heading 4 of the financial perspective or through the european development fund. in any event, parliament will, with this report from the committee on fisheries, set out its position so that the commission and the council can take it into account, if possible now, and if not, in the run-up to the negotiation of a new agreement in 2006.

commission. in its conclusions, the general affairs and external relations council at its october meeting last year agreed that the russian proposal to open discussions on the conditions for the eventual establishment of a visa-free regime would be considered as a long-term issue and that further discussions should take place within the structures of the partnership and cooperation agreement. on the same issue, the european union-russia summit in st petersburg in may 2003, which i attended, agreed to examine the conditions for visa-free travel between the european union and russia. the commission, in close consultation with member states, is considering how best to launch these discussions with russia in the framework of the eu-russia partnership and cooperation agreement. some media outlets appear to have misinterpreted comments made by the head of the commission's delegation in moscow on this matter. i can clarify that he rightly said that the european union is prepared to discuss with russia the conditions for visa-free travel as a long-term issue, and that this question is linked to a number of related matters which also need to be addressed, such as the need for more effective border management, cooperation in the fight against organised crime and illegal immigration. the conclusion of a readmission agreement with russia will be an important confidence-building measure in this context. that is a point which i have put to my russian colleagues and interlocutors on a number of occasions.

commission. as you know, last year in seville the european council strongly affirmed the need to develop a strategy on the management of external borders. the council adopted a comprehensive plan comprising, among other measures, joint operations to be carried out by the member states. in june 2003 the european council of thessaloniki confirmed this priority and carried out a first assessment of the results achieved so far, while setting new priorities. these joint operations are unprecedented and represent a first effort of cooperation in tackling the smuggling of illegal migrants. the ulysses joint operation, for example, has been organised and led by spain, but other member states have also participated. this is a first attempt to pool the efforts of the member states in addressing the tragic situation of migration flows by sea and in attempting to put and end to, or at least diminish, the risk of the kinds of tragic accidents that regularly occur on our seas as a result of the criminal actions of smugglers and traffickers. the commission did not take part in planning or managing the various off-shore operations, but – via the argo programme – we co-financed these external border management operations to the tune of eur 670 000. the commission will receive a final report on the results and the impact of the activities undertaken in accordance with the relevant procedures of the argo programme before the end of the year. in the light of the objectives of the argo programme, the commission will then be able to evaluate the impact of such an operation for the management of common external borders. at thessaloniki the greek presidency presented a report on the implementation of programmes, ad hoc centres, pilot projects and joint operations. a chapter of this report is devoted to the ulysses operation. i suggest that mr medina ortega takes a look at this report, where there is a comprehensive description of the operation's content.

commission. i share the view of the honourable member that migratory flows are very flexible, and when the pressure increases in one place, there will be lower pressure somewhere else. that is why the commission has proposed the creation of a stable operational framework to deal with the control of maritime borders. we asked for a feasibility study to be carried out. i shall present this next week to the informal justice and home affairs council in rome. our proposal is to create three permanent control centres for our southern maritime border. meanwhile, we need to learn from both successful and less successful joint operations, in order to incorporate this knowledge in the project that we are going to present to the council.

commission. it is difficult for me to reply immediately to the question as to whether the problems will be such that some kind of protection for each and every athens citizen will be required. i doubt that is the case and i hope they will be able to organise these construction works in such a way that the citizens of athens will continue to be able to live, work and breathe there. our directives and the different limits and levels that are set do not take into account whether there is a special event, but it takes into account and measures those factors that affect human health. we will continue to ensure that greece measures, monitors and reports these things to us. that is why i announced that we are willing to look into the type of monitoring, reporting and measuring that is necessary in greece in order to fulfil the requirements in our directives. we will continue to do so. you have given us reason to ask whether there will be special problems connected to the construction works which would require athens to take special measures. i cannot answer your question today. however, i will be willing to return and give you a more detailed answer later on.
- question no 54 by mr vatanen (h-0470/03) subject: designation of sites by the natura 2000 network article 4 and annex iii (stage 1) of the habitats directive 92/43/eec oj l 206, 22.7.1992, p. 7 describe the procedure governing the first stage of the selection (at national level) of the natura 2000 sites. in accordance with paragraph 20 of the judgment of the court of justice of the european communities in case c-371/98, this national step has legal effects for landowners, governments and the commission linked to the conservation objectives of each site, namely the identification of the habitat types and species (including birds) to be protected, as referred to in particular in article 6 (3) of the habitats directive. it is essential that the commission ensures the scrupulous transposition of the provisions relating to this first stage into national legislation, in accordance with the guidelines established by the court of justice, and that it ensures that these provisions are not deliberately misinterpreted by the national authorities when drawing up the national lists. what does the commission intend to do to help finnish landowners, for example, who claim that the national authorities and courts have approved the drawing up of national lists and the selection of sites in a way that is contrary to the provisions in force?
commission. the commission has, on several occasions, looked into the correct transposition of the habitats directive and the birds directive into finnish legislation. at present the commission is of the opinion that the articles referring to the procedure of establishing the natura 2000 network have been correctly transposed. as the natura 2000 network has caused a considerable amount of controversy in finland, the commission has looked into the national procedure for site selection and has in past years notified finland of some shortcomings, both in the number of sites to be protected and the quality of the data. finland has endeavoured to address these shortcomings. the present quality of the data is acceptable to the commission. the complaints from finland seem to contain some misinterpretations of the evaluation principles. the commission bases its evaluations on the latest submitted data, not on the oldest information. the commission is aware that some landowners in finland have been dissatisfied with the natura 2000 proposals. the commission has been informed that all landowners have had the possibility to see the proposals and to lodge complaints against them before finland officially submitted the proposals to the commission. the finnish courts have examined the complaints on a case-by-case basis, considering each time the validity of the data. the majority of the complaints have been rejected by the courts. the directive does not establish any requirements for consultation at the national level and thus, in respect of the principle of subsidiarity, it has been for individual member states to exercise their responsibilities, taking account of national laws and procedures. the commission's concerns are therefore limited to respect the scientific selection criteria as set out in the directive. although the commission can understand that in these cases the dissatisfaction might persist, it cannot conclude that the finnish authorities have arbitrarily misinterpreted the rules or proceeded in a way that has been contradictory to those rules.
commission. the honourable member has raised a very valid question. how do we communicate natura 2000 and the creation of this important network, when the original motives have been lost in the debate in the years that followed the introduction of this directive? i hope that we will also be better able to assist member states in giving good examples of how to communicate the directive, but i am not convinced that we will ever be able to solve this problem of the finnish government and authorities having to introduce a consultation process with, for example, finnish landowners. we will never be able to solve that from brussels, but hopefully we can do better in giving good examples of how this consultation process can be implemented and carried out in different countries. it is important that we also make clear where the responsibility lies with the commission and where there is a case for subsidiarity and we will thus have to rely on a member state – in this case the finnish government and authorities – to also organise work on this. from a formal point of view, we have not found any wrongdoings in the finnish having, for example, arbitrarily carried out this work. we cannot find any such formal mispractice at all.

the commission. mr president, i would like to thank mrs lynne and the committee on employment and social affairs in particular for the preparation of this report. the report confirms that the issue of disability is a political, social and economic issue. it is a matter which concerns all the policies of the european union. in the context of the european year of persons with disabilities, this report sends a clear message to the european union and to the member states, making parliament's commitment known in the clearest possible way. the first point i would like to make is the future un convention which is expected to be a very important, historic document. your report will be useful and will play an important role for the commission's services in the discussions with the member states and the un on this future convention. it is very much in line with the commission's proposals and communication. we share the same principles and the same goals. i would like to focus in particular on the central political core on which we agree, namely an approach based on the issue of human rights, social and political rights. it is worth noting that the un convention is yet another recognition of the fact that it is not the disability of the individual that needs to be corrected, but the inhibitory environment that needs to be adapted in order to ensure full participation and equal opportunities. the emphasis is shifting from the medical model to the so-called social model, to building a policy based on fundamental human rights on the one hand and social rights and equal opportunities on the other. in issuing this communication, the commission has made clear its intention to promote this rights-based approach at european level and to build on the european experience it has gained so far in combating discrimination. the commission also insists on the social inclusion of disabled people approach, placing disability as one of the key elements in the elaboration of national action plans for social indicators and the fight against poverty. the commission had requested negotiating directives because part of the convention deals with the issue of 'non-discrimination', which has become a competence of the european union since the treaty of amsterdam. the discussions with the council are still ongoing, while the commission is working closely with the presidency on the preparations for the convention. mrs lynne referred to the particular issue of developing countries, but also to the policy on development cooperation which has so far been limited to the drawing up of an explanatory note on disability and development. this note, addressed to the delegations and services of the european union, was drawn up in close cooperation with the non-governmental organisations representing disabled people. this document, which was distributed to the european union delegations in developing countries, has had a positive reaction both at the level of governments and civil society organisations, and it is important that for the first time we have an approach to this issue of disability in relation to development policy and development aid. while it is difficult at first to call for disability to be mainstreamed in development aid policies, it is a clear statement that disabilities must be included and addressed in the policies of each state in all areas. the commission has already made a number of proposals in this area. as mrs lynne has already said, since 2000 the european union has had a general directive on non-discrimination in employment, which also covers disabled people. the directive, which was a real step forward for europe and was accepted by all the member states, has not proceeded as we would have expected. most countries have not yet submitted a draft transposition of the directive, although the deadline is december 2003. despite repeated efforts in the discussions in the employment councils, my letter to all the ministers, the mobilisation of european and national organisations, it seems that in the member states there are considerable difficulties, political and economic in nature. i would also ask parliament to play an important role in putting pressure on the member states to adopt this directive in principle. but i think that the situation as it stands today makes it clear that it is premature at this time to push for a new directive which would extend the scope of policy beyond employment and across all policy areas. i think it would create a difficult situation in the council, but it would also make it perhaps even more difficult to implement the first directive, which is facing the difficulties i have mentioned. at the same time, however, the commission has proposed that member states consider and respond themselves to the question of whether community legislation should be used to combat discrimination on grounds of disability in areas other than employment in a report on the implementation of the equal treatment directive. the commission's proposal for a directive on the protection of the health of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos at work is a very good one, and i would like to thank the rapporteur for the work he has done on this subject. in conclusion, the commission is committed to actively participating with the member states in the negotiations for the un convention. participation in these negotiations will continue beyond the end of the european year of disabled persons as part of the continuation of this year, because our aim is to present at the end of 2003, at the end of the year of disabled persons, a european action plan which will be the result of all the processes carried out in all the member states during that year, so that we have commitments from the member states in terms of legislation, financial budget, policies and programmes.

at least - intention to move towards a return to economic and civil liberties. all this certainly makes the daily life of the cuban people difficult. we reiterate our strong encouragement, our strong incentive for there to be a sign of economic reopening and of the presence of a private economic sector in cuba. in the light of the above, the presidency once again hopes for a change of attitude. the common position, which has been expressed in recent months, remains valid: the union shall continue to support the efforts of the united nations and the international criminal court to establish a constructive and continuous engagement as the basis of the union's policy towards cuba. in order to promote more effective implementation of the objectives of this common european position, the council considers that political dialogue, including intensive critical dialogue, should be pursued in order to help achieve tangible results, especially in the political sphere, and thus in the sphere of political freedoms, the economy and civil rights. the council would therefore be prepared to encourage the strengthening of development cooperation by the european union towards cuba in those areas which can facilitate the transition, the path towards a pluralist democracy and respect for human rights, and in those areas which can improve the quality of life of the cuban people and thus also sustainable economic growth. the presidency believes that this funding should be provided only if it provides a real and immediate benefit to the cuban people or a major contribution to the process of opening up cuba to a system of economic reform. it is therefore clear - and i will conclude by answering some of the questions raised by president brok - that the measures taken by cuba, which europe has considered to be violations of fundamental civil and political rights, have affected the union's relations with that country. as already indicated by the european commission, the latter has decided to postpone its assessment, necessary for any consideration of cuba's request to accede to the cotonou agreement. the withdrawal of cuba's request for the second time on 17 may was not surprising. however, the council is not obliged to comment on that decision: i'll just say we weren't surprised. the measures announced by the initiative of 5 june and the council conclusions of june and july are intended to express clearly the european union's support for the peaceful and democratic cuban opposition and to demonstrate to the cuban authorities that trade relations cannot continue normally unless there are concrete signs from that government. we are concerned about political freedoms and also about the closure - albeit timid and limited - of the door to greater private initiative in the economic sector. the eu heads of mission will continue to monitor the situation of political prisoners and their conditions of detention in havana. the political dialogue with cuba, which was resumed in 2001, should certainly be continued, albeit with the conditions and limits i have indicated. the political dialogue also includes, of course, the human rights situation. we regret the refusal of the cuban authorities to engage in political dialogue, as expressed in recent public statements, and the decision, which has been made public, to withdraw funding from the european countries and the commission. this semester the presidency will be looking, in the light of parliament's views, at ways of enhancing the practical effectiveness of political dialogue, which is sincere, constructive and, when necessary, of course, critical. commission have established a human rights working group in havana to follow human rights issues in cuba, including the matter of political prisoners. the commission is regularly informed of detention conditions through this working group and through bilateral contacts with family members of those imprisoned, as well as with local human rights groups. the european union has repeatedly called for an immediate release of all political prisoners and has appealed to the cuban authorities that, in the meantime, the prisoners do not suffer unduly and are not exposed to inhumane treatment. repression in cuba has received a prompt, firm and sustained reaction from the union. last july it re-evaluated the common position on cuba, six months ahead of schedule. this re-evaluation reaffirmed that constructive engagement remains the basis of eu policy towards cuba. the eu intends to continue its dialogue with havana to promote political, economic and civil rights reforms and is willing to provide aid whenever possible via non-governmental organisations in order to promote democratisation and improve living standards for ordinary cubans. i believe that the common position is the best policy instrument we now have for cuba. it is a coherent policy document and should, therefore, be maintained in its present form. based on it, political dialogue with the government and the opposition needs to be strengthened, as well as the promotion of human rights, pluralist democracy and an open economic system. the commission regrets the decision of the cuban government to withdraw its application for accession to the cotonou agreement. cuba is the only caribbean, and practically the only developing, country in the world with which the commission has not been able to sign a cooperation agreement. membership of the cotonou agreement would have provided the right framework to develop a structured dialogue with the cuban authorities and to improve the delivery of aid to that country. the commission is positive about the operation of our new delegation in havana. our presence in cuba is more important today than ever. the main tasks of the delegation are not only to assist with the implementation of aid programmes and projects, but also to promote a political dialogue with the cuban authorities and civil society, to monitor human rights issues and to protect the interests of the member states in terms of trade and investments. as a result of the events that have taken place recently, the commission delegation in havana will have to focus its attention in the future more on monitoring the human rights situation in cuba, on trying to promote a political dialogue and on looking after the trade interests of the eu member states. this is a heavy and difficult agenda to pursue, but it is essential if we wish to promote political and economic changes in cuba. the latest evaluation of the common position encourages the strengthening of eu development cooperation in cuba in areas that promote the transition to pluralist democracy and respect for human rights, that improve the living standards of the population of cuba and promote sustainable economic growth. the common position states that funding should only be channelled through governmental institutions if it directly benefits the population or if it promotes a meaningful contribution towards economic reform and a more open economy in cuba. commission projects have been undertaken in this context. according to a recent statement from havana, it seems that in future the cuban government will only accept aid from the commission and the eu member states that is channelled through un agencies, ngos, foundations, solidarity movements, autonomous regions and local governments. furthermore, the cuban government will apparently refuse to negotiate directly with the member states and the commission on development cooperation themes, programmes and projects and will only agree to deal with ngos on such issues. however, as the commission has worked mainly with ngos and independent technical assistance teams in the past anyway – and with good results – there is no reason to believe that the same cannot continue in the future. the only thing we need to ensure is that the visibility of community operations is maintained and also that monitoring of such operations by eu bodies can continue. finally, i was informed that the european initiative for democracy and human rights is not currently funding projects in cuba.

facilitated by the fact that it is not faced with a text with several options but, on the contrary, with a single text, widely shared by the members of the convention and already approved by the a high, noble compromise between different instances, sensibilities and interests; i would like to make a few brief comments on the commission's proposal. the incorporation of the charter of fundamental rights into the constitutional text; the commission's proposal is to be submitted to the council for adoption. the clearest division of powers between the union and the member states, with full respect for national identities and internal organisations of the states, the dual principle referred to by president giscard; the introduction of mechanisms for effective respect for the principle of subsidiarity and for the ever-wider involvement of national parliaments in the life of the union. the convention has established that there are four institutions: the council, the european parliament, the commission, but also the national parliaments, which represent the will of our public opinion. and then again: the standardisation of legal and financial instruments and acts, introducing for the first time a true hierarchy of rules; the creation of the minister for european foreign affairs perhaps the most innovative institutional figure to emerge from the convention's work following the union of the functions hitherto exercised by the high representative and the commissioner for foreign affairs and, equally important in the future, the possibility of a merger conclude on the institutional balance achieved by the convention: the commission's proposal is a delicate balance, one that has been sought from the outset because it was clear to the whole convention that one institution could not be strengthened at the expense of another. e a balance based on a division of powers between the european council, which assumes a political role, with the task of defining the general political guidelines and priorities of the union; the commission, representing the member states, which retains its central role as guardian of the treaties and guarantor of the community's interests; the european parliament, which becomes a full co-legislator. i would like to stress here that one of the most important innovations is the election of the commission by the european parliament, which thus sees its powers of legislative and budgetary codecision strengthened, the distinction between compulsory and non-compulsory expenditure disappearing and acquiring the right to propose a future revision of the constitution, if necessary, using the convention method. this innovation, like the others, is part of an institutional package which, as president giscard d'estaing said, can certainly be improved, but which it would be very dangerous to try to change in depth, at the risk of upsetting the balance of a complex system based on the dual legitimacy of i suggest. as president giscard d'estaing and president fini have said, the convention has indeed constituted and built a pillar in the process of european integration, and the italian presidency regards this result as a point of reference for the work of the intergovernmental conference. the presidency intends to draw inspiration from three guiding principles in guiding the work of the conference, which will open in rome on 4 october. firstly, the presidency considers it necessary to respect the timetable laid down by the thessaloniki european council: the commission has also proposed that the council should adopt a timetable for the implementation of the budget, which requires that a positive result be achieved in time for the european parliament elections scheduled for june next year. this approach has given rise to a central objective of the italian presidency: the european parliament has been asked to take part in the conference at a rapid pace with a view to reaching a global and comprehensive agreement on the constitutional text as early as december. this will enable the future constitutional treaty - a constitution for europe, as president giscard d'estaing called it - to be signed between 1 may 2004, the date of accession of the ten new member states, and the elections for the renewal of our parliament, scheduled for june. the extension of the constitutional negotiations beyond these dates would raise two serious problems of legitimacy and democratic transparency: on the one hand, the assets of the convention would be progressively dispersed; on the other hand, european citizens would be asked to vote in elections to the european parliament without knowing the constitutional outlines of the future union. the second objective of the presidency is to safeguard the structure and implementation of the text drawn up by the convention. we believe that it is appropriate to respect, as i have already said, what we must clearly say is the constituent heritage, accumulated in sixteen months of work by a democratic body in which governments, national parliaments and the institutions of the european union were represented. we also consider it inappropriate to reopen debates which have already been held at length. the political value of the success achieved should not be lost or diluted in the work of the conference: the commission will have to work to improve and complete those parts of the treaty on which there is still no full agreement, parts of the treaty - i repeat this for the sake of clarity - which do not touch on the institutional pillars defined by the convention. the italian presidency will therefore oppose any challenge to the overall balance of the project and its basic elements. the interests of europe and its citizens must, in the view of the presidency, prevail over the defence of particular interests which tend to this or that substantial amendment of the treaty. in this context, the opinions to be presented by this parliament and the european commission will be an element to be taken fully into account during the conference. the third and final point which will be a guideline for action during the work of the conference is: the need to find consensual solutions on certain issues which are still controversial, with the principle of unanimity which has been invoked, will not in any case lead the presidency to negotiate a compromise 'downwards', that is to say, one which produces backlogs in relation to the convention's proposals. president of the commission. mr president of the parliament, mr president of the council, mr giscard d'estaing, ladies and gentlemen, i should like to begin by expressing my sincere thanks to all the members of the convention and to you in particular, mr president giscard, for the dedication and intelligence you have shown during the long months of intensive work that have characterized the phase of the constituent process. the successful experience of the convention has changed the course of the democratic life of the european union for the long term: a great job and an unexpected result. the draft drawn up by the convention is therefore the basis - i would say the best basis - for the final drafting of the convention. and that is a good thing, because this is a text which, above all, has great symbolic value: it is the first time that the foundations of the union have been debated in an open democratic forum, representative of the peoples and states of europe. secondly, the draft constitution resolutely addressed the issues of institutional balance and the complex nature of the union. the debate was intense and thorough and made it possible to deal coherently with all the problems which had been put to us: how to build a new and more effective coexistence between the two souls of european construction, the community and the intergovernmental; how to establish the balance between the political representation of the states and that of the citizens, with the consequent role of parliament and the council; how to organise the representation of the general interests of the union and the legitimate interests of the individual member states. thirdly, the convention has laid the foundations for the necessary work of updating the union's policies. the intergovernmental conference is now beginning to finalize and formalize the work of the convention. i see two extreme positions emerging at this stage, which i think it is important to discuss openly: on the one hand, there are those who believe that the draft should not be touched because it is the only compromise possible. on the other hand, some would like to be able to question everything because the states are, in the end, the ultimate depositaries of sovereignty and they have the final say. while both positions are understandable, i think they are both objectionable: as the commission has always said - ever since we, after nice, invoked the convention method with parliament - the intergovernmental conference should have been short, focused and conclusive. this does not mean, however, that it must be a mere notarial act, because that would deprive it of its proper political responsibility. this conference is certainly not like any other that has preceded it, as it will have to work on the basis of the excellent work of the convention; however, it retains its primary function, which is to enable the heads of state or government to exercise their political responsibility and to submit the final text for approval by the institutions and, as president giscard said, by the citizens of their member states. it is therefore a new phase of political approval which does not require a long intergovernmental conference, but which will require a period of appropriate maturation. there are, in fact, aspects of the draft constitutions which clearly show that the compromise reached is incomplete and that the result achieved at this point cannot constitute a final point of arrival, as we had originally hoped. it is therefore appropriate that the states, the ultimate holders of sovereignty, should discuss this further to see if they can do better. it is our task and duty as the commission to point out these points. the current draft constitution still contains more than 50 unanimous decisions, some in key areas of the union's life. they also agree that one of the shortcomings of the present situation is the absence of a real instrument for coordinating the budgetary policies of the member states. i wonder, however, how such coordination will be achieved if the present veto power is maintained, and the same consideration applies to indirect taxation and business. (applause) there is also the central problem of the future balance of power between the commission, the council and parliament. the draft constitution proposes a composition of the commission which, in my opinion and that of the college for which i am now responsible, will make the task of the institution representing the general interest of the union less effective and less credible. the proposed solution discriminates between commissioners by creating a second category which is unnecessarily halved, and no people in the union deserve to be represented by a second-class commissioner. (applause) this would break the unity of the college, whereas the link with the member states has been the driving force behind the commission's work for the last 50 years. it is therefore necessary to take an additional step - which is in no way incompatible with the short duration and the rapid conclusion of the intergovernmental conference - and to allocate a commissioner for each member state who has the full range of his functions. at the same time, the current text of the draft constitution leaves open the choice of fundamental issues, such as the functioning of the councils and responsibilities in the field of external relations. the task of the conference is to make the action of the institutions more transparent and effective and to avoid duplication and hybrids which may generate future conflicts. this is more a matter of qualification than of innovation. finally, the convention has not had time to update the current formulations of community policies, some of which date back to the 1950s and are partly or wholly outdated. it is obvious that it will be difficult to resolve all the remaining open issues; however, our task is to reflect with caution and wisdom, detached from the political contingencies of the moment, on the points where it is still possible to make the necessary corrections now to make the constitutional structure even more suitable for the challenges ahead. the commission has already made a number of proposals. is there no such will or are there considerations of realism which suggest that we should not deal with these problems now and leave the text as it is? if that is the case, the commission is of course prepared to take note of it, calmly and realistically, aware that in any case very important steps have been taken. this has been the case with every amendment to the treaties: the european parliament has been a great help to the people of europe in the past, and it is a great help to the people of europe today. but then we must know that, as has happened in other cases, we must be prepared to face other crises and, consequently, to negotiate new changes and new adaptations. and this is perhaps the story of european integration: the commission's proposal is to be adopted by the council at the end of the year. it is our history and we know it well, although there are times when we need to walk with a quicker pace; and today we are, of course, in this situation. in any case, to draw on our experience and if we really want to write a constitution that will last, we must provide mechanisms that allow us to decide tomorrow what is not possible to decide today. i therefore - and this is the conclusion, but also the final point of my brief speech - must raise the question of the most realistic procedures for amending the constitution, which will enable us to act quickly and effectively when, under the pressure of a crisis - and we will inevitably have a crisis - the plan we are outlining today should prove to be insufficient. the worst-case scenario would be to find ourselves with inadequate constitutional provisions, the amendment of which would be made impossible by the mechanism of a unanimous review by 25 or more member states. this applies to unanimity, which is still in force in many areas today, and it is even more so for the updating of policies which we are not in a position to tackle today. a constitution that is stuck and rigid, incapable of ensuring that future crises are resolved, would be a denial of the history of european integration. we must avoid this at all costs if we are to carry out responsibly the historic task we have set ourselves. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, in our action we must keep clear the direction in which the union must continue to move: the european parliament has a duty to ensure that the european union is able to play a full part in the development of the union. to do so, we must equip the union with the operational tools to achieve these objectives. the union must speak to the world with one voice, strong, authoritative and peaceful. it must be able to assert, internally and externally, the force of law which imposes duties but also protects individuals, preserving their freedom to act in an orderly and creative civilization. the union must also have the means to demonstrate solidarity. it is expressed through support for the most vulnerable in an inclusive society. it is expressed in joint action to provide relief in the event of natural disasters; it is based on the duty to defend each other, in the conviction that the defence of each of our member states is the strongest affirmation of membership of a single family. ladies and gentlemen, we have now entered a new phase. we must conclude the good work of the convention by acting with wisdom, perseverance and courage. we must, of course, conclude quickly, but above all we must conclude well. the commission will continue to play its part in contributing to this objective. - question no 1 by mr nogueira román, substituted by mr ortuondo larrea (h-0433/03): subject: tragic deaths of immigrants drowned on the atlantic and mediterranean coasts of the southern part of the european union in recent days, 70 african immigrants have drowned, this time off the coast of sicily. the same tragic events are systematically repeated off the atlantic and mediterranean coasts of the south of the union, in particular the canary islands and andalusia, and weigh on the conscience of europeans. thousands of immigrants, including many pregnant women and children, have already died in recent years. what other political measures, apart from repression, does the union intend to take to prevent these disasters?
i suggest. i am sorry to inform you, mr president, that i cannot accept your request because of the schedule of my plane. all questions will be answered in writing, so that we can honour our commitment. as regards question no h-0433/03, the council regrets that the tragic events mentioned by the honourable member have occurred. the union's strategy on immigration is aimed not only at developing and implementing measures to combat, prevent and control illegal immigration but also at strengthening relations with third countries of origin and transit of immigrants, in particular with a view to establishing a full partnership with those countries. it should therefore be recalled that the european council meeting in seville on 21 and 22 june 2002 noted in its conclusions that it is of paramount importance for the european union and its member states that migration flows be managed in accordance with the law, in cooperation with the countries of origin and transit of those flows. it also noted that the phenomenon of illegal immigration, which requires a greater effort on the part of the european union, requires the use of appropriate instruments in the framework of the union's external relations. he therefore said that an integrated, comprehensive and balanced approach was needed to tackle the root causes of illegal immigration, which must remain the union's constant long-term objective. it also recalled that the intensification of economic cooperation, the development of trade, development aid and conflict prevention were all instruments to promote the economic prosperity of the countries concerned and thus reduce the root causes of migration. in line with the seville european council, the thessaloniki european council of 19 and 20 june this year noted in its conclusions that the european union's dialogue and action with third countries in the field of immigration must be part of a general and comprehensive, integrated and balanced approach. it should also be noted that in december 2002 the commission presented the communication entitled 'integrating immigration issues in the european union's relations with third countries', in which it stressed in particular the link between immigration and development. this link and synergy is also recognised and emphasised by the council in its conclusions on the communication, adopted on 19 april this year. in particular, the council states that an effective and coherent development policy is an essential part of an effective migration policy and recognises that migration, if properly managed, can be a positive factor for growth and development both for the european union and for the countries concerned, whereas illegal migration has a negative impact on individuals and on countries of origin, transit and destination. the council therefore notes that, in order to establish an effective migration policy, a genuine partnership with third countries must be developed with a view to improving the joint management of migration flows. the commission's working document of july this year on enhanced cooperation with countries of origin for the management of migration flows should also be mentioned. the document, which is intended to implement the conclusions adopted by the council on 19 november 2002, examines the situation of cooperation with various third countries and makes proposals to deepen and improve it. the implementation of the conclusions of the seville european council and the thessaloniki european council, based in particular on the guidelines emerging from the commission's communications, is the subject of in-depth examination by the council's bodies.

- question no 2 by mr medina ortega (h-0439/03):could the council take stock of the ulysses project concerning the control of illegal immigration in the western mediterranean and the atlantic?
i suggest. as noted in the reply to question h-0086/03 by the honourable member, a final report on the implementation of programmes, ad hoc centres, pilot projects and joint operations was submitted to the justice and home affairs council meeting of 5 and 6 june 2003 for transmission to the thessaloniki european council. the european council took note of the results of the various operations described in the report. as regards the ulisse project, the council was informed that it was to be implemented in two stages: the first in the mediterranean, which took place between 25 january and february this year, and the second, which was due to take place at the beginning of april this year, was temporarily suspended as a result of the conflict in iraq. the second phase was carried out between 27 may and 2 june this year and involved the surveillance and control of the territorial waters around the canary islands in the atlantic ocean. several member states participated in both phases of the operation: italy, france, the united kingdom, portugal and spain have actively participated in the first phase of the project; greece, norway, the netherlands, germany and poland, as well as europol, participated as observers. the second phase saw the active participation of the united kingdom, france and spain. the added value of the ulisse project was that different equipment and human resources from the member states were pooled and deployed jointly in different operational tasks and that information was exchanged using advanced technologies. it was reported that, in total, 454 illegal migrants were stopped and 15 vessels were intercepted as a result of the coordinated efforts of naval, air and ground units.

- question no 5 by mrs kauppi (h-0437/03): subject: continuation of the e-voting initiative for interactive democracy on the internet under the italian presidency during its presidency, the greek government successfully promoted the development of interactive democracy on the internet through the e-voting initiative. the initiative gave 170 000 citizens of the european union the opportunity to express their views on how the european union should evolve in the future. in this respect, it was particularly positive that the greek presidency was incorporating information obtained from citizens into its daily work. their opinions and proposals were incorporated directly and in real time into meetings, negotiations and decisions at community level. it would be a pity if the e-voting initiative was not continued in some form during the italian presidency. will italy continue with the e-voting initiative? will the italian government, during its presidency, adopt any other programmes or measures to promote the use of new technologies, in particular to increase the participation of citizens in political life? how does the italian government intend to ensure that european citizens feel that the european union is working with their views in mind and that it is putting into practice certain aspects that are considered important, especially by ordinary europeans?
i suggest. the presidency recognises the importance of dialogue with citizens on european integration. this was particularly important during the greek presidency, since it was also the time of the final stage of the convention's work, which culminated in the presentation to the thessaloniki european council of the draft treaty establishing a european constitution. the e-vote initiative of the greek presidency, as well as other instruments of the community institutions, such as the 'futurum' website and the convention website, have effectively contributed to making the voice of citizens heard on the future of europe. the thessaloniki european council in june 2003 asked the italian presidency to initiate the procedure provided for in article 48 of the treaty in order to convene the intergovernmental conference in october 2003 to approve the constitutional treaty. during this conference, the presidency will endeavour to inform the public in an appropriate manner of the progress of the proceedings. the italian presidency's website will be one of the tools for information on the igc and all the work of the current six-month period. i would therefore like to emphasize that the italian presidency attaches great importance to the participation of young people in european integration. in the context of the implementation of the commission's white paper 'a new impetus for european youth', which is intended to follow up the council resolution on the framework for european cooperation in the youth field, the presidency intends to support the awareness-raising process aimed at increasing the participation of young people in policies and decisions affecting them. it is also intended that appropriate strategies be developed subsequently to take account of these aspects, based on the analysis of the results of the consultation on the participation and information of young citizens of the european union.
i suggest. i think that is an interesting proposal to think about and to study. as president fini and president frattini have also said today, we are very keen to ensure that the process of drawing up a new constitution for the european union involves not only the members of parliament and all the institutions but also the citizens of europe as much as possible. so your comment, mr president, will certainly be taken into account. i shall be responsible for examining how the proposal in question can possibly be adopted.
- question no 6 by mr papayannakis (h-0443/03) subject: detention in iraq amnesty international, in a recent communication, expressed its deep concern at the conditions of detention of hundreds of iraqis (in abu ghraib prison and in specially equipped detention facilities at baghdad airport) arrested in iraq by the occupation forces. in particular, the complaints of this humanitarian organisation concern the inability of detainees to receive legal assistance and to communicate with their families, as well as the lack of drinking water and sanitation services. at the same time, according to amnesty international, there is strong suspicion that many of the prisoners have been subjected to very harsh, inhuman and humiliating treatment during their detention. what is the council's view of the legal status and responsibility of the occupying forces in iraq? how, in his view, can the fundamental rights of citizens in the occupied part of the country be safeguarded?

- question no 7 by mrs izquierdo rojo (h-0446/03): the commission has not yet decided whether to grant aid to the victims of the floods in the canary islands. subject: euro-mediterranean dialogue and the status of women the presidency conclusions of the thessaloniki european council (19 and 20 june 2003), in paragraph 66, 'relations with the arab world', state that 'the european union will strengthen its partnership with the arab world and promote closer political dialogue, pluralism and democratic reform', and in paragraph 68, that civil society in the countries of the region, including women, should play an important role in promoting democratic values, social awareness, education and development. nevertheless, the status of women in some countries in the southern and eastern mediterranean still constitutes a serious violation of human rights. the modernisation of these societies requires the participation of women in the process of democratization. heads of state who try to limit modernisation to the economic and technological sectors, leaving intact the foundations of these obsolete and patriarchal societies, are failing. women are now the main drivers of modernity: when women modernise, the whole of society modernises. in this connection, what concrete measures does the italian presidency intend to take to promote women in the mediterranean basin?
i suggest. the barcelona declaration of november 1995 recognised the decisive role of women in development and the need for their active participation in economic and social life and in job creation. similarly, the meda ii regulation referred to the need to recognise and strengthen the economic and social role of women and the importance of education and job creation for women. an innovative aspect of the barcelona process is the dimension of regional cooperation with regional programmes open to all. the promotion of opportunities for women in this context was underlined by the euro-mediterranean conference of foreign ministers held in brussels in november 2001 and by the valencia and crete ministerial meetings held in april 2002 and may 2002 respectively, which welcomed efforts in the euro-mediterranean context to promote equal opportunities for men and women. this led to the development of the euromed regional programme on the role of women in economic life, with a budget of eur 5 million for 2004, to promote women's opportunities by promoting capacity building and information. the programme aims to develop action plans at national level, focusing on women's access to and participation in the labour market, supporting reforms in the legislative framework and policy-making for active training and labour market. it encourages the promotion of women in business by creating networks dedicated to women in the professions and commerce and by facilitating women's access to financial instruments. the definition of the priority areas of cooperation for which action is envisaged will be completed during the italian presidency and calls for proposals for this specific programme will be published by the commission's europeaid cooperation office in the second half of 2003.
(es) mr president-in-office of the council, you have not really been very explicit, because you only tell me that in the second half of 2003 proposals will be presented, but you do not give me any details. i am very grateful for your reply and would like to know whether you do not think it desirable to include women's issues progressively in the political dialogue.
i suggest. this is certainly a subject of great interest and we have the necessary sensitivity to make progress in this direction. in political dialogue too there can be - and it is right that there should be - a greater interest in women's issues. we will therefore take this comment of yours very seriously, mr izquierdo, and we will also make a commitment to try to make the best progress possible to achieve the best results.

- the agenda calls for the following reports, drawn up on behalf of the committee on development and cooperation, to be discussed jointly:- a5-0273/2003 by mr lannoye, on the commission communication on water management in developing countries: eu development cooperation policy and priorities (com (2002) 132 - c5-0335/2002 - 2002/2179 (cos)) - a5-0277/2003 by mrs morgantini, on the commission communication to the council and the european parliament on trade and development: 'how to help developing countries to benefit from trade' (com (2002) 513 - 2002/2282 (ini)).
(es) mr president, i would like to congratulate the commission on its swift response to the challenges raised in johannesburg on the subject of water and water scarcity, and also mr lannoye, to whom i now turn. however, it seems to me that the report that the commission has produced on water falls short and perhaps avoids some of the most important structural issues and basic conceptual problems that we are going to have and that we have with water. firstly, i understand that the debate goes far beyond privatisation or liberalisation. europe is used to offering general solutions, to giving directives to everyone in the european union. and i think we have to be clear that sustainable development is a tailor-made suit, that the problems are not the same in one place as in another and therefore we have to proclaim from the beginning flexible and open policies that allow a thousand different solutions, hundreds and thousands of small projects, appropriate to the site and the place. we must introduce this philosophy into the criteria for investment, aid, and other things, because without local efforts and the adaptation of programmes to local projects, we will not achieve anything. i therefore advocate that concept of flexibility, adaptability and many small projects, regardless of whether there are big problems. however, speaking of the framework concept, there is another subject i would like to mention. if water is a universal commodity, as necessary and indispensable as air or land, it is also limited and, ladies and gentlemen, it is a transportable commodity, unlike land. it therefore requires protection and regulation not only by the states but also internationally. it's a commodity that should be shared. and just as the great rivers are shared and enjoyed by people of different languages, religions or nationalities, it is a transboundary good and therefore requires international agreements and conventions for the sake of justice and sustainability. as a universal good, europe must propose an international agreement, a convention module that will make it possible to regulate rivers by their water catchment areas, as the water directive says, avoiding the slavery of interventions by one country which, as in the case of the tigris and euphrates, leaves other nations in precarious conditions. europe must also make decisions and talk about the fact that water, being a universal good, cannot belong only to those who live at the headwaters of the river basins or to the people who want to appropriate it along its course; we must discuss the possibility of making transfers without prejudice, to solve problems of desertification or water stress; to solve the problem of development of the people located at the mouths of the rivers or along their course. i believe that there are very important legal issues that europe should promote and also introduce the concept of flexibility, sustainability and tailor-made clothing.
commission. the contribution by mr khanbhai corresponds to mrs sanders-ten holte's remarks about the wish of parliament to be involved in anything relating to the water initiative and the water fund. this is not difficult to understand. the money we are talking about is part of the edf. we are working to set the budget for the edf. the commission and parliament are in full agreement on this, also for very principled reasons. we want a special facility or fund in order to have a more flexible instrument, more ability to work across the board. there is no reason for the worry expressed in the report by mr lannoye about the 0.3% management of the fund. this is not an attempt to create one solution. it is more like a facility. it does not matter if we use the word 'fund'. the main idea is to be able to accelerate actions as necessary and to be a catalyst for the various partnerships that it is possible to create and promote. we are not talking about a conventional method of funding projects, but something that could accelerate things. we hope that this debate and the welcome support from parliament will make it possible for member states to accept what we have proposed. to be direct, this is about eliminating the risk of losing eur 1 billion of the eur 13.5 billion reserved in the 9th european development fund which is up for evaluation next year. that money was made conditional some years ago, under the cotonou agreement and the 9th edf, on the performance in the first part of the period. this is a totally political judgement. this is why we came up with the idea of reserving this money for the water initiative, in order to make sure that we all agree on this high-priority dossier and reserve the money for it so as to more or less lift this eur 1 billion out of the general discussion. that is what we are trying to do. i hope that support from parliament on this will muster enthusiasm among member states. regarding the trade aspect of the discussion, i agree with mr belder about the very difficult situation in terms of coffee. it is ironic that we urged developing countries to diversify and pointed out that coffee was a good cash crop. the result is that now, vietnam and many other developing countries are quite successfully moving into coffee production, consequently dumping it on the market, and damaging the market to such an extent that we have a crisis that is very difficult to deal with. there is no easy answer to that. the reality of the market is here to stay.
