- the next item is the report (a5-0217/2003) by mr bowis, on behalf of the committee on development and cooperation, on the communication from the commission on 'health and the fight against poverty in developing countries' (com (2002) 129 - c5-0334/2002 - 2002/2178 (cos)).
commission. mr president, i would like to start by thanking mr bowis for his good work. while we give support to health directly in many countries, the commission is increasingly investing in budget support strategies where the linkages to improved health outcomes are ensured. in this context the follow-up through key input and outcome indicators is crucial and this is a high-priority area of work. this relates to a long discussion with parliament and the committee on development and cooperation about the percentages allocated to different sectors. the commission is prioritising support for improved health and education outcomes. to reflect this, it is not enough simply to calculate funds for health and education where they appear as focal sectors. all support to related social sectors, such as investment in water and sanitation, and budget support linked to improved health and education outcomes, has to be taken into account. doing this brings us to something that adds up to more than 40% of the programming for the 9th edf. it is a matter of the credibility of the link between budget support and outcomes in these sectors, but this is the best way we can do this. we are relying on other donors or partner governments to do more of the substantial work. we are providing a lot of money, but this is also what complementarity is about, what donor coordination is about and what ownership is about. i am in no way apologetic about these percentages and i will never get tired of arguing like i do here whenever, like tonight, i hear figures – which i feel are wrong – regarding how much we do in these sectors. the interreg contribution through budget support is real and it has the advantage that it also makes it possible for us to fund, and for support to be received for, the ongoing recurring costs. it does not do much to help to build a nurses' training centre if the teaching there cannot be sustained. that is one of the advantages of budget support. this is in no way an excuse, but it is a real, hard-core explanation. the specific challenges as regards hiv/aids, malaria and tuberculosis have been meaningful, leading to our contribution to the global fund. our engagements at country level mean that we now know better what to do than we did some years ago. attempts at solving the hiv/aids problem are made more difficult as it involves having to cope with the ideological battle of reproductive health and sexual rights. i do not want to start a discussion tonight on these issues, but it is an added problem on top of all the other existing problems. as regards financing i am pleased that it was possible to get the united states to accept what everyone else agreed to in december last year in the wto on trips and the use of generic medicines. the point i want to make here is that it is very nice to see that our decision last year to untangle the procurement of medicine for these diseases adds to the reality and impact of what was agreed in the wto last weekend. if we still tied procurement to european producers, the wto agreement that third world countries should be able to buy generic medicine would not have carried much real importance. so it is the combination of this deal in the wto and our untying of procurement there that really is dynamic. i do not want to prolong the discussion ahead. i will end by repeating my appreciation of the input provided by mr bowis.
the commission has also proposed that the council should adopt a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos. {es) mr president, the people with the least resources are the ones who have the worst health. disease and poverty are two sides of the same coin and any strategy to combat poverty must take this interrelation into account. the lack of health drastically reduces the development opportunities of the peoples and groups who suffer from it. in developing countries, 28,000 children under five die every day from diseases that could be prevented with the medicines that are currently available. diarrheal diseases alone kill over one and a half million children a year and one in every thirteen african women may die during pregnancy and childbirth, leaving the care of the rest of their offspring to the immediate risk of death. aids is not only killing more than two million people in africa, but it is also destroying the development of their societies by taking away thousands of young people and mothers who are abandoning their children. women are the poorest and sickest in developing countries. they are also much more exposed to the risks of disease, which is always linked to poverty, precisely because of their reproductive function. we have therefore wanted to stress the importance of information, but also of access to reproductive health services, which would help to prevent the spread of aids, diseases resulting from continued pregnancies, childbirth and clandestine abortions. incorporating women's perspectives in the fight against poverty and disease is key for the most disadvantaged societies because they are the ones responsible for the care of children and because they are an essential driver for the well-being of individuals, families, local communities and nations. we believe that this report, whose rapporteur, mr bowis, has been so in favour of incorporating the gender perspective into the report, will improve the commission's communication and perhaps the still weak position of women in the development policy of the european union, which, i believe, must continue to strive to fulfil its commitments.

- the next item is the report (a5-0249/2003) by mr howitt, on behalf of the committee on development and cooperation, on the communication from the commission to the council, the european parliament and the economic and social committee on the participation of non-state actors in community development policy (com (2002) 598 - 2002/2283 (ini)).
(es) mr president, the socialist group has really welcomed the commission's initiative to define and strengthen the role of non-state actors, both european and host countries, in community development policy. i would like to congratulate mr howitt because his report was unanimously approved by the committee on development and cooperation. in addition, he did important work with a questionnaire to find out where the participation of ngos stood. it is a fact that ngos have had a decisive influence on the current configuration of a more open international society and on the democratization of a system of international relations which until very recently was restricted to states and intergovernmental organizations. in our view, the active participation of ngos in the implementation of community development policy is the main added value of european cooperation, since it gives it an effectiveness that development policies, which are carried out only from the intergovernmental sphere, do not have. this is not a one-way street, although there is no doubt that development processes need to be participatory if they are to be effective and sustainable. in only a minority of cases are ngos and civil society organisations in the recipient countries involved in the design and implementation of the development actions for which they are the beneficiaries. as the howitt report points out, we will hold the commission to account for the involvement of non-state actors in the preparation of strategy papers by region and country. it should be noted that the programmes and projects designed in this way are mainly financed by the edf, to which, unfortunately, non-state actors do not have direct access. the other funding line, decentralised cooperation line b7-6002, has very limited funds - - the next item is the report (a5-0209/2003) by mr martínez martínez, on behalf of the committee on development and cooperation, on the 2001 annual report from the commission to the council and the european parliament on ec development policy and the implementation of external aid (com (2002) 490 - c5-0607/2002 - 2002/2246 (ini)).
the rapporteur. the report is a report which should have been dealt with at the last part-session of parliament - before the summer - when it was ready for consideration, which had been produced, for the substance, in our committee on development and cooperation and, for the opinion, in the committee on foreign affairs, human rights, common security and defence policy and in the committee on women's rights and equal opportunities. the commission's proposal for a regulation on the protection of the environment is based on the principle of the protection of the environment and the protection of the environment. our report is the evaluation of a document prepared by the commission which analyses the european union's development policy and the implementation of external aid in 2001. it must be said at the outset that this is a very useful compendium of data and comments which are not available in any other form for easy consultation. the document gives a reasonably clear account of how the commission spent the funds available in 2001, both in the field of development cooperation and in humanitarian aid. this accountability is particularly relevant, especially when one considers the fact that the european union is the main donor of resources in both fields. the report makes a number of critical points, all of them in the best possible spirit and with the hope that in future years the shortcomings and deficiencies which have been identified will be remedied. all this, moreover, bearing in mind that 2001 was still a transitional period during which the outline of what european policy should be in the fields of interest to us here and the best mechanisms for implementing such policy were finalised. perhaps the most positive thing in parliament's view is to see that the commission's report unquestionably reflects the same policy objectives that our house has repeatedly recommended: the achievement of the millennium development goals, with particular emphasis on the eradication of poverty. however, it is less clear to what extent our actions - significant, objectively - are helping to bring us closer to these objectives. moreover, it is clear that the complexity of the procedures - often excessively bureaucratic - means that in certain regions and in the year under review the commission was unable to spend a very considerable part of the resources at its disposal. another question that remains is the pursuit of the greatest effectiveness of our action by selecting the most suitable partners with whom this action is carried out. the involvement of non-governmental organizations in our countries is often decisive in the success of our interventions. in other cases, the cooperation we are able to provide to the united nations and its specialized agencies on development and humanitarian issues is very important. the commission's delegations in the countries receiving our aid are more likely to be unable to carry out their work directly, no doubt because of the scandalous limitations on staff in these delegations. one of the criticisms that was most heard in our debates was that the report under review was a mixture of genuine development and humanitarian aid and aid to the candidate countries in 2001, preparing them for enlargement, and even action in the balkan region, which covered a considerable part of the available budgets. in the conclusions of our resolution there are a couple of them which i would like to highlight: the first is parliament's demand - repeated once again - that the european development fund (edf) be made part of the regular budgets of the european union in such a way that it is transparent and under parliamentary control; the second is, in fact, a congratulatory message to the commission - and more specifically to those responsible for our action, both in development cooperation and in humanitarian aid. we sincerely believe that, despite the criticisms, there is considerable progress in what is being done in these areas, but above all we see that there is genuine concern to be held to account, to raise problems and to seek the participation of many - including parliament, of course - to make things better every day. one of the recommendations we emphasize in our resolution is that the commission's 2001 report - with the attractive presentation in which it has been published - should be widely disseminated within the countries benefiting from our solidarity policies and also in our own states, reaching administrations - including local administrations, often very interested in cooperation and humanitarian aid policies - and, in particular, ngos, which are indispensable and splendid partners in this work of the european union. i thank you, mr president, and i thank all the colleagues who have helped me to draw up this report. i would also like to thank the commission officials who have been very helpful in clarifying matters and answering questions. finally, i would like to thank the officials of the committee on development and cooperation of the european parliament and those of my group in the european socialist party who have cooperated generously and very effectively with me throughout the whole of the preparation of our report.
commission. mr president, despite the improvements cited, the 2001 report is still by no means a perfect one. we are learning year by year. we started with a very difficult background. i have stated a number of times – some thought it was a bad joke – that the main reason why we are so bad as regards informing the public about what we do in development cooperation is that we do not know what we are doing. the truth is that statistically speaking, we are very far behind in our reporting and the whole mechanics of the system. we did not have an annual report that presented, across the board, a picture of what the commission was doing in this area. this was a very big problem a few years ago. so, getting started was very important. i am pleased to inform you that the 2002 report is just about to be published. in fact we sent it today to parliament and the council. even though preparations for it had to be launched at the end of last year, it takes into account many of the recommendations made by your rapporteur, such as more analysis on the effectiveness of aid follow-up to monterrey and johannesburg, more statistical information permitting a comparison among the regions, and an executive summary. so, as you will see from the new report, we really are trying to improve it. i should like to stress that production of this kind of report is a complex process. first of all, it addresses many different audiences. on the one hand, it is an important management tool for our own institutions. on the other, it is a public information instrument. following this dual purpose, there are conflicting demands. we have to fulfil our obligations on a number of regulations, resolutions and so on concerning reporting. for that reason we had to include a lot of detail. at the same time, it should be easy to read, without too much technical jargon. all in all we are happy that we have done it although we are not yet totally happy with the quality of it. the great help we get from parliament and the feedback from this good report by mr martínez martínez is, from our point of view, one way of continuing to improve the standard.

- the agenda calls for the report (a5-0271/2003) by mr michl ebner, on behalf of the committee on culture, youth, education, the media and sport, containing recommendations to the commission on the european regional and minority languages - minority languages in the european union in the context of enlargement and cultural diversity [2003/2057 ((ini)) ].
commission - mr president, first of all, let me thank the rapporteur very warmly and sincerely for his commitment, because it is a commitment to languages and therefore to human beings and our citizens. it aims to create a multilingual and multicultural europe, whose diversity we champion, because we are convinced that this is the real wealth of europe. the rapporteur, the commissioner and you want the same thing. the instruments for achieving this are yet to be determined. i come now to the two legislative proposals contained in the report. the first concerns an agency for linguistic diversity. i think that such an agency would be useful. however, it is necessary to think before embarking on this enterprise; the commission has already taken a number of initiatives in this area. it would make it possible to know precisely all the existing instruments, including those for regional and minority languages. my services have started an evaluation of all activities concerning regional and minority languages, which should lead to a report early next year and will be a first step in this direction. as you are aware, ladies and gentlemen, a feasibility study on the creation of an observatory for cultural cooperation, the ruffolo report, is already under way. i think it would be useful to learn from this before embarking on a new exercise. i would like to emphasise the importance we attach to the activities of the council of europe in the field of languages. i agree with you that there must be coordination of efforts between the commission and the council of europe. before moving further towards the creation of an agency, an exchange of views on how to achieve greater coordination would be necessary. the second point concerns the adoption of a multiannual programme. i must say to you, mr president, that this is a problem because the commission cannot accept this recommendation. it is not a question of substance, because you know very well that we are on the same page on substance. i have already had many opportunities to speak to you about this. i argued that in the present circumstances, the best way to promote regional and minority languages is an integrated approach. i am convinced of this, because a separate programme would mean for me the continuation of the segregation of regional and minority languages. but now the time has come for the opposite, namely openness. support for these languages must be ensured by using the possibilities offered by existing programmes. moreover, the european year - you will agree with me - was an experiment in the integration of regional and minority languages. the implementation report shows that regional and minority languages have been given a prominent place. after careful consideration, the commission undertook to present an action plan, which the rapporteur has quoted and which i have brought with me. you should have received it. if you don't, i have some copies, come and get them. does the president want one? president roca, your copy is waiting for you! this action plan is based on the conclusions of the helsinki conference on regional and minority languages, organised under the auspices of president ahtisaari in october 2002. mr president of the committee on culture, youth, education, the media and sport, i will present to you in more detail, if you wish, this action plan adopted on 24 july and inform you of its implementation. this plan provides for the integrated approach i was talking about, because we need to focus on funding opportunities within existing programmes and make sure that these opportunities are better known and better used. the commission therefore published a call for proposals on 31 july, thanks to the budget voted by parliament, and the submission of projects is planned for the end of this month. let me also say that we should take advantage of the discussions on the new generations of programmes, because if we really want to take concerted action in favour of languages, new programmes should have a very important multilingual component. before i close, i would like to mention very briefly a few points made in the report. as regards the definition, i think we agree: we use the council of europe's definition, which is included in the european charter for regional or minority languages. secondly, as regards the european bureau for lesser spoken languages and the mercator network, i know that many of you in this house are very interested in these instruments and wish that they could continue their work. i can tell you that the proposal for a decision establishing an action programme for the promotion of bodies active at european level in the field of culture is currently being negotiated. the office and the mercator network are to receive eur 5.4 million for the period 2004-08. so any concern about this can be dismissed. finally, mr president, the annex to the draft resolution lists 20 points relating to various requests. i would point out that the majority of these requests go far beyond what could be done under the two legislative initiatives proposed by parliament itself. i would not like to go into detail, but just to remind you that many concrete initiatives to promote regional and minority languages are included in the action plan i have mentioned and that a lot of funding already exists. - the next item is the report (a5-0164/2003) by mr fernández martín, on behalf of the committee on development and cooperation, on the communication from the commission to the council and the european parliament on the special framework for assistance to traditional acp suppliers of bananas (council regulation no 856/1999) - commission biennial report (com (2002) 763 - 2003/2091 (ini)).
the rapporteur. the commission's communication complies with the provisions of the council regulation on the special aid scheme for traditional suppliers of bananas in the acp states, the objectives of which are to improve competitiveness and to support the diversification of their agricultural production. i would like to point out that this aid was substantial, amounting to some 44 million euro - in both 2001 and 2002 - and that the commission is reporting on the results of this management during these years, among which i am particularly pleased to note, firstly, the increased effort to diversify production and, secondly, that this diversification is being sought through the encouragement of agricultural and rural development projects. in both cases, either by fulfilling or by expressing the wishes which both the commission and this parliament had set as their objectives when adopting this programme. i should point out, however, that some problems have been identified - which the commission is certainly aware of - but for which some corrective measures must be taken without further delay. firstly, in some cases there have been repeated delays in accessing and using the funds, which are not due to anyone's express wishes. but these delays have created major difficulties for producers in the producing countries, some of which are among the 40 poorest countries in the world. some of these producers have expressed to us their doubts and, in some cases, their dissatisfaction - particularly producers from west african countries - with the commission's methods of assessing the competitiveness of producers, which is the basis on which the commission bases its criteria for the allocation of aid. this method of assessment takes into account the average cost of production, insurance and transportation freight as given by eurostat. but these figures do not correspond to a single definition, which leads to errors which are, in some cases, not insignificant. in some cases these are very serious errors to the detriment of some of these countries. i am concerned, mr commissioner, about the reduction in the volume of this aid in the 2003 budget, especially as we approach the changeover from the current model to a single tariff system which can have very negative effects not only on the production of traditional acp countries but also on the european banana-producing regions themselves, if we have not been able to take the necessary measures at the time of the transition from the current system to the single tariff. i would like to conclude by expressing two specific requests which are very much appreciated by this parliament and, i hope, also by the commission: greater efforts to avoid any delay in payment of aid from now on, and an evaluation of the methods of cultivation and production in order to avoid financing projects which have negative effects, not only on the environment but, above all, on the health of the people working in the banana sector in the producing countries, giving priority to the use of biodegradable substances in the banana cultivation process.
commission. let me start by say something about the evolution of payments. i agree that this has been quite a problem in the start-up phase, but i can also inform you that the amount invoiced in 2002 was nearly eur 41.5 million. this represents nearly seven times more than the amounts invoice in 1999 and more than three times the amount invoiced in 2001. although we cannot draw clear conclusions yet for the current year, the overall trend is quite positive and a similar disbursements of some eur 40 million is expected for this year, taken as a whole. we are now at a level of activity that corresponds reasonably well to expectations. all this is quite complex, there are so many different interests deserving protection, many historical, social and political factors in everything that relates to bananas. the commission is well aware of the difficulties in combining the principle of equitable market access with consideration for the structural problems faced by small vulnerable economies. the special framework of assistance stems from those concerns and addresses them in a tangible manner. also it should be noted that this was not something imposed on our partners in this area but reflects thorough negotiations. after the undeniable difficulties of the start-up phase, substantial progress can now be observed in the implementation of the scheme: i have just given these figures. now we have reached a satisfactory rate in terms of payment. in response to the repeated suggestions by the commission, several acp banana suppliers are changing their strategies and seeking more financial support to fund diversification where the banana industry is no longer sustainable. it is expected that this process will continue, with the least competitive banana suppliers using the available funds exclusively for diversification and social compensation. as far as the possible increase in imports following enlargement, which is an important discussion, is concerned, it was agreed at the copenhagen summit that appropriate arrangements would be made in order to ensure a sufficient supply of bananas to eu consumers in conformity with wto rules. any increase in the banana quotas, agreement including those relating to ensuring the continuing outlet for acp bananas on the european market and we are of course committed to do anything we can to respect this.
(es) mr president, on behalf of the socialist group i would like to thank mr fernández for the report he has drawn up - it is not a legislative report, but an evaluative one - and i also thank commissioner nielson for his statements. as the rapporteur has pointed out, we are in the final stages of a banana protection regime - which ends on 31 december 2005 - and the european union has tried to maintain a privileged position of twelve small countries, as mr fernández has said. some of them are among the poorest, such as somalia, jamaica or the island of dominica, and they need our help. the date of 31 december 2005 is very close, there is a guarantee and a tariff preference set out in the cotonou agreement, which will have to be maintained. but, of course, these banana producers are going to have a hard time as that date approaches. in other words, there is a very great risk that the community market will be flooded with bananas handled by multinational companies, and above all there is another danger, which the rapporteur has also mentioned: that, as a result of enlargement, this will be used to grant even greater preferences to these multinational companies, opening up our markets in a way that will be detrimental both to community producers and to producers in the traditional acp countries. i think commissioner nielson is aware of these difficulties at the moment, he has pointed out that the figure has remained roughly the same for the last few years - around 40 million euros - and i do not know to what extent this figure will be able to adapt to the needs that will necessarily arise from the transformation of the banana regime, from a protection regime to an opening regime, subject only to the tariff limitation. i therefore reiterate our support for mr fernández's report and hope that the commission will continue to protect this small group of low-income countries.
the rapporteur. mr president, at the present time the world is more interdependent than ever. problems are becoming common: poverty, hunger, war, immigration, communicable diseases, ecological disasters and so on. efforts to solve them must be coordinated and shared by all. in this context, the question of development aid is more important than ever. and it is now that the commission's communication to the council and parliament which we are discussing today comes about, in my view, in a very timely manner. the report i am presenting today on behalf of the committee on development and cooperation is the result of the work and contributions of both the political groups and my colleagues, whom i particularly thank and value. the european union and its member states are, as we know, the main donors of official development aid, but the classic mechanisms of the european cooperation model have not allowed the desired objectives to be achieved successfully. we have difficulties in ensuring the monitoring and in making a correct evaluation of the results, mainly because of the dispersion of the programmes and projects carried out, both by the national cooperation agencies and by certain practices which link in one way or another the receipt of aid with the acquisition of goods and services obtained thanks to this aid in the donor countries. according to the world bank figures - which were made known here in this house during the speech by the bank's president, mr wolfensohn - the untying of aid would result in a reduction of up to 25% in transaction costs. we therefore welcome the commission's initiative, which can help to give life to the debate on this issue, which is currently taking place both between the member states and within the multilateral bodies, where, incidentally, an agreement that commits everyone, especially the main donors, is still a long way off. i firmly believe that this debate should be based on the idea that the priority of aid should be in the interest of the recipient countries, something which is almost obvious to everyone, but which is not currently being done, and this is the case of some european countries which are very much involved in cooperation as donors of official aid, whose returns from the implementation of that aid far exceed - sometimes by far - their own contribution to those programmes. i think that is something we all know and that is a clear demonstration of a certain cynicism on the part of the donor countries, that is to say, on the part of our own countries. this is what makes it necessary for us to make an effort to try to correct this situation. of course, things happen that way not because of a deliberate, perverse desire to do them wrong, but for many reasons - which it is not the time to analyze now. the important thing is that we should promote the application of these ideas on the basis of experience, taking into account some considerations such as those mentioned in paragraph 4 of our report, in order to ensure that our objectives are met and to avoid some undesirable effects. i am referring, for example, to the need for the commission to take account of the need for equal treatment in both horizontal budgetary and geographical or regional aspects in order to introduce and guarantee open and transparent tendering which does not always take place. tendering for all member states and candidate countries, for all developing countries and for all developed countries, on condition of reciprocity by the third country and with the agreement of the beneficiary country. i would like to end by specifically mentioning a request widely voiced by developing countries and ngos. i refer to the priority to be given to the award of contracts to local suppliers and service providers, both in the beneficiary country and in neighbouring regional countries, provided that they demonstrate adequate capacity for the complete and not frustratingly incomplete execution of projects, for many obvious reasons which are almost obvious to mention, but which are summed up in the desirable contribution to the development of the local markets of these countries.
(es) mr president, aid conditional on the purchase of goods or services from the donor country has been repeatedly denounced as immoral and ineffective, first by the countries receiving aid and by the most committed ngos and then by the general body, including many intergovernmental bodies, dealing with development issues. as far back as 1996, the oecd development assistance committee, in its strategy paper shaping the 21st century: the contribution of development cooperation, pointed out that the practice of conditionality in development aid was incompatible with the new philosophy that should guide development aid. this philosophy has since been concretized and expressed in a series of important declarations and resolutions - i will quote the recommendation made by the committee on development assistance, adopted in may 2001, calling for the untying of this aid in the case of the least developed countries. more importantly, in the monterrey consensus in march 2002, the international community at the world conference on financing for development committed to supporting initiatives to end conditional aid. in its november 2002 communication entitled 'unlinking aid for efficiency', the commission responds precisely to this commitment, reached in monterrey, and goes even further than the oecd development assistance committee resolution, since it extends the need to unlink aid to all developing countries and not just to the least developed countries and all aid sectors, including food aid. all these recommendations, which continue to advance under militant pressure from civil society and ngos, have not, however, made much of an impact in a number of countries that continue to maintain blatant or disguised linking practices. unfortunately, this is also the case for several member states of the european union, which means that there is a marked disconnect between the policy supported by parliament and the commission and the policy pursued by some of the community partners, for example spain under the government of josé maría aznar. it is not surprising that the report presented by mr fernández martín, a member of my country's popular party, initially showed a number of reservations about the progressive and disengagementist approach to development cooperation policy advocated by the commission. however, it must be said in favour of the rapporteur that he showed understanding and flexibility in accepting the amendments which were put to him in his first proposal, so that the text with which he concludes his work has been substantially improved. we are therefore reaching a draft resolution adopted by parliament's committee on development and cooperation, which we will vote with reasonable satisfaction on, since it is in favour of the total untying of development aid, both from the european union and from each and every one of its member states.
mr president, i wish to inform the house about the situation regarding the number of subscriptions to the magazine focus on europe, published by the european parliament. the last issue appeared in may 2003. it was published in the 11 working languages of the european parliament and, for the first time, there was a special edition in the catalan language as well. i thought it would be interesting to find out how many catalan-speaking citizens have requested a subscription for this magazine in its catalan version. according to information obtained from an office of the european parliament last week, 31 000 have taken out a subscription to the catalan version. if we compare this figure with the subscriptions taken out in other languages – for instance, 63 000 in french and 51 000 in italian – and analyse the ratio between the subscriptions and the number of speakers of a given language, the conclusion is that there is a very high ratio in the case of catalan speakers. this is a clear demonstration that it was a positive decision to publish the focus on europe magazine also in the catalan language.

- doc. a5-0238/2003 by mrs mccarthy, on behalf of the committee on legal affairs and the internal market, on the proposal for a european parliament and council directive on the patentability of computer-implemented inventions (com (2002) 92 - c5-0082/2002 - 2002/0047 (cod))
(es) mr president, the socialist group does not believe that the amendments adopted by the committee on legal affairs and internal market reflect the current situation regarding the patentability of computer-applied inventions. it is important to start from the fact that this is not a proposal for a directive on the patenting of computer programs. the system for these, as the rapporteur for the committee on culture, youth, education, the media and sport, mr rocard, has pointed out, is already regulated by a community directive. this is the area of intellectual creation, which has rules which are very different from those governing industrial protection. industrial protection, as mr rocard has pointed out, concerns the application of industrial uses, and there are already quite well-established rules. what has happened here is that there has been a very dangerous drift on the part of the american jurisprudence, which has allowed the patenting of purely intellectual creations which do not have, as such, industrial applications. the attempt to establish a monopoly on computer programs through patents has caused justifiable indignation among all those who are currently using the open network in europe, and who would be impaired in their ability to act. it would set back the european advance towards the creation of an information society as formulated in the lisbon declaration. the socialist group therefore believes that the proposal for a directive must be substantially amended, setting out very clear limitations, so as not to distort the nature of the industrial patent. we cannot find ourselves in a situation like that in the united states, where there are certain companies which can now virtually prevent any work on computer programming. it is true, as mr bolkestein has pointed out, that the european patent office has been led, in part, by this dangerous drift, as has, for example, the japanese case law. and that is precisely why a community directive is needed. we believe that the field of intellectual property in the field of computers must be maintained and that a community directive is needed which regulates only industrial applications, not computer programs, and which regulates it in such a clear way as to prevent falling into that drift, so that the case law of the european patent office does not drag the countries of the european union down the path of patentability of computer inventions as such.
(es) mr president, this is a political chamber and i think that as a political chamber the first thing we should be thinking about, but the commission should also be thinking about, is why this proposal has caused so much fuss, has caused so much opposition. it is not right to disqualify anyone who disagrees with it and tell them that there has been aggressive lobbying. because at least those who have contacted me have been university professors of computer science, patent and industrial property experts and also representatives of small businesses and, instead of aggressiveness, what i have seen is concern; concern about progress and the danger with which the possibilities of invention were faced. the advocates of this initiative tell us that the only thing it seeks is to unify the practice of the national patent offices in a field in which there have been contradictory decisions recently. and that is true; what is not true, or at least what is not certain, and let us at least admit this intellectual doubt, commissioner, is that this proposal for a directive is going to solve the problems which it is said to want to solve. because that is very easy, the practice of the european patent office, breaking what was a traditional line of european law, has slipped into a practice very similar to that of american law. all honourable members know, all experts know, that in european law the characteristic required for an invention to be patentable is that it be of an industrial nature, which means that not only the method must be industrial but also the result of the product must be industrial, whereas in american law it is sufficient that it has a useful application. that has allowed for certain innovations and certain software patents. let us insist on that point. it is not logical to say that the report by the committee on legal affairs and the internal market and the commission's proposal solve these problems, because they are solved by the amendments adopted by the committee on culture, youth, education, the media and sport and the committee on industry, foreign trade, research and energy.
(es) mr president, first of all i would like to congratulate the rapporteur, mrs mccarthy, and the rapporteur of our group, mr wuermeling, on the effort they have made to reach consensus and, in mr wuermeling's case, to explain this complicated proposal in our group. the protection by patents of inventions implemented by computers is not a new problem and it should be clear, as other members have said in this house, that the aim here is not to establish a rule allowing computer software to be patented, but to extend the classical doctrine of patents to inventions implemented by computers. we want to apply what already exists for patents to computer-implemented inventions. it is clear that we must expressly exclude, as some amendments do, the patentability of an invention simply because it uses a computer. as regards the scope of the directive, i would like to focus on a very specific aspect: interoperability. interoperability or communication between programmes should be excluded from the scope of this directive. in a few years' time, this aspect should be reviewed. the exclusive use which the law allows patent holders requires the holder to explain his invention in a way that is understandable to a middle expert in the subject. i think that we should emphasize this aspect here too and require the applicant for a patent to explain sufficiently the subject matter of that patent, although perhaps not until the publication of the source code, as mr harbour has said. that would be excessive. as i said, it is particularly important in this area to require applicants to describe their invention. finally, many have criticised this proposal and said that it may harm the small and medium-sized enterprise sector. however, what we are doing is applying the traditional patent law to small and mediumsized enterprises, knowing that patents have benefited growth and have made it possible for all types of enterprises - including small ones - to carry out research and to invest in new developments. we are competing today in a globalised market, where the united states and japan are developing many patents and inventions. we cannot be left behind and we must regulate, also in europe, the possibility of registering inventions implemented by computer as patents.

relationship between pension systems and the labour market, and i shall explain how the commission, through a series of initiatives, is responding to the report's calls. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. it is clear that on the one hand it is important and necessary to change the age limit, for reasons of sustainability, on the other hand this cannot be done alone and without accompanying it with employment policies which will help the elderly worker to stay in the labour market, because today, because of the culture that exists in the labour market, the reality that has existed for many years, it is very difficult for elderly unemployed people over 55 to find work easily. in this context, both the european employment strategy and the european social fund have an important role to play. the second important point is that the commission, following the mandate of the european council, continues to apply the method of coordination. in 2005 we will be moving to a new report on the monitoring of systems, while the social protection committee will be examining the contribution of social systems to the extension of working life. finally, we are continuously monitoring the indicators we committed ourselves to in barcelona and have agreed on the need to increase the effective retirement age by five years by 2010. i do not repeat what mr andersson said about the gender dimension. the gender dimension is of paramount importance in pension systems, and particularly in the private sector. i would remind you, ladies and gentlemen, that in the private sector there is no equal treatment between men and women, and the gender criterion is taken into account in the calculation of pensions. two other points: the enlargement issue, where we are in constant contact with the new member states so that they can join, and the issue of mobility. the report goes into great detail on how to overcome the obstacles to the european labour market and mobility, a subject on which we have tabled a ten-year action plan.
(es) mr president, few things concern european citizens more than the health of their pensions, few things in their family and social life give them such continuous attention throughout their lives, perhaps because pensions for millions and millions of europeans are the only important asset they accumulate and the only security they have against the risks of biological life or economic life. this excellent report by mr andersson is the culmination of a working legislature of the european parliament in which we have brought our agenda into line with the citizens' agenda. this is an important legislative term because the european parliament, following also excellent communications and excellent initiatives by the commission, has for the first time put the issue of pensions on the community agenda. we are very pleased that at the end of this parliamentary term there has been progress in a philosophy which has radically broadened the appreciation of this phenomenon. it is no longer just a concern driven by financial reasoning or the balance of public finances. we now have a doctrine, a strategy, which we have enriched and supplemented with the objectives and needs of the european citizens. we are therefore pleased that this report and the commission's communication have analysed the strategies of the member states, taking financial viability into account, of course! perhaps this is another way of showing that we are responsible politicians. there are basically two categories of politicians: there are irresponsible politicians, who only think about the next election, and there are responsible politicians who are the ones who think about the next generation. the andersson report is thinking about the next generations, but it is also thinking about adequacy so that social security, pensions, can meet the objectives and fight poverty. it also considers modernisation and the categories of workers, especially women, who are at such risk in the new social and labour market arrangements. what does the commission say about the situation in our member states? we see that there is a will, but we also see that there is sometimes a delay and a lot of caution; i would say that there is also fear of reform in the member states, perhaps because the population is afraid that reform is a sweet way of talking about cuts in their social rights. it is therefore very important that we help to overcome these fears of the people by introducing reforms which are not just about cuts, but which are reforms which tend to meet their present and future needs in a safer, fairer and more equitable framework. tomorrow the socialist group will support the andersson report, it will support the work of the commission because we believe that the changes which are proposed are not changes based on frivolity, they are not changes based on conjuncturalism, but they are changes which are required by our social commitment to this generation of workers, to these citizens and also to those who will live in europe in the next generation.
(es) mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to add my congratulations to the rapporteur. i should like to begin by saying that retirement, while still a technical, legal and economic actuarial issue, has become a subject of the greatest media interest and has acquired the nature of a central issue of politics in general and of social policy in particular. back in 1950, sixty years marked the threshold of old age; sixty-five years meant retirement from active work life, and not making a will at seventy was certainly reckless. from this we can conclude that today's society, which has crossed the end of the 20th century and entered the 21st, has many very old people, who until recently were described as "old", and these elderly people have a strong social image, are current, are vitally active and have a well-founded life expectancy. in this context, a long-term perspective is needed in the field of pensions and, although the policy and management of pensions is the primary responsibility of the member states, in accordance with the principle of subsidiarity, the european contribution seems necessary, both in the exchange of practical improvements and in the strengthening of consensus, and in the common regulation of certain aspects necessary to ensure the possibility of transferring pension rights of all kinds and their viability. pension systems through public income-linked schemes (pillar one), private occupational schemes (pillar two) and individual retirement pension funds (pillar three) should offer europeans opportunities to maintain their standard of living after retirement. a system which prevents or hinders the free movement of persons and the fear of the european citizen of his or her ageing or physical or mental deterioration should therefore be excluded. the third pillar is to be seen as a means of eliminating fear and business and ensuring the viability of the pension system, which must respond to changes in society and the forms of production organization: the greater presence of women, an older working population and atypical recruitment methods.

the commission (es) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, first of all i would like to thank and congratulate mr cashman on his comprehensive report on the subject of transparency, which is the subject of our debate today, and to which our three institutions have made a firm and determined commitment. i would like to thank you for the opportunity to clarify, on behalf of the commission, some of the essential points raised by mr cashman. firstly, i share mr cashman's view that, while acknowledging the progress made, which is considerable and very important - our recently presented annual report gives a fairly complete picture - the situation can and must still be improved. the case law is also helping us in the interpretation of regulation (ec) no 1049/2001 and this will allow us to improve the application of this important instrument of transparency and, therefore, democracy. on this point, i have to mention, for example, the judgments of the luxembourg court of justice concerning the non-disclosure of legal opinions, which confirm our practice on this subject, recognising the need for the institutions to preserve the independence of such opinions, that is, to have a certain margin of reflection. we are therefore making progress and this report points out that, in order to achieve the objective of maximum transparency, it would be desirable to have a single register of documents instead of the existing ones. however, if it is a question of making it easier for citizens to search for and identify documents, the decisive factor is not the choice of one or more registers, but a single entry point to a unified portal, which clearly indicates which documents are grouped under each register, as mr cashman has very well said. in any case, we must study these technical solutions, which will allow us in the future to move towards a better integration of these instruments. i would also like to highlight the important progress made in terms of the number of documents which are directly accessible, such as commission agendas, minutes of our meetings, etc. and we certainly hope that this trend will continue and be reinforced when, for example, the register of documents relating to comitology is opened to the public by the end of the year. in addition, we have put our practice on access to documents relating to infringement proceedings in order, which is another of mr cashman's criticisms, so that when a proceeding is closed, there is in principle a presumption that we can disclose those documents. it should not be forgotten here that regulation (ec) no 1049/2001 allows for the protection of what still needs to be protected, namely the investigations carried out under those procedures. thus, the presumption of non-disclosure, which i mentioned earlier, is balanced when a proceeding is ongoing, not concluded. finally, ladies and gentlemen, i would point out that the commission has never refused documents without giving a proper justification for its decision, relying precisely on regulation (ec) no 1049/2001. the unspecified replies in our annual report refer simply to cases where the refusal to disclose documents was based on several, not just one, of the exceptions provided for in that regulation, without any further precision being possible. this is 12% of the information denials, i.e. 38% of the 30% of denials. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i cannot but thank mr cashman for his recommendations for further progress in this area of transparency, which are extremely useful to us in all the institutions, and which will be taken into due consideration. we will look at possible progress towards greater integration of the instruments for archiving and document identification; we will look at a common methodology, to which mr cashman also referred, for the preparation of the annual reports, in order to facilitate comparisons. their suggestions for the evaluation report, which is to be submitted by the commission in early 2004, will be duly considered. all this was discussed yesterday by the three institutions in a meeting which was frankly productive and fruitful. there are difficulties and we have doubts about the possibility, mentioned in mr cashman's report, of drawing up a directive to harmonize national legislation in this field, in the absence of an appropriate legal basis for taking that step. i also know that mr cashman sees these doubts and shares our reservations, because he said so at the meeting yesterday. in view of all this, i sincerely believe that the balance sheet for one year of application of regulation (ec) no 1049/2001, as the rapporteur has pointed out, is highly positive. this is not an excuse, of course, but on the contrary a stimulus to continue to improve the initiatives and measures taken. but when we do it right, we should say it, even if it's not perfect. it is also worth stressing the fact that this important instrument of transparency, which grants a clear and unequivocal right to the citizens of the union, has been used mainly, as far as the commission is concerned, by legal professionals, in particular, and law firms, something that cannot be forgotten. and from this fact, it cannot be avoided that, in general, citizens are more interested in obtaining good, clear, accurate and timely information on the activities of our institutions, through the usual means, rather than in concrete documents, although it is also true that, for example, universities and non-governmental organizations have made extensive use of these possibilities. in this area, which is so closely linked to transparency, our efforts to achieve a permanent improvement in the information provided by the institutions on their activities must be constant. i thank mrs maij-weggen, who is leaving this parliament, for the excellent work she has done over all this time, working for transparency and improving the quality of information for our citizens, for a better exercise of democracy.

the commission mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the commission fully recognises the role that the selfemployed can play in making the european union's economy more competitive, thus contributing to the achievement of the objectives set by the lisbon european council itself. the commission has no doubt that undisputed professional competence and the ability to build client relationships based on mutual trust are essential components of success for freelancers; this ensures a high level of customer satisfaction in europe. it is in this spirit that the commission has taken several initiatives to ensure, as has been said, the full protection of the general interest and, in particular, a high level of independence and professional ethics in this area: see also the recent wouters judgment of 19 february 2002 and the protection of customers' rights. in march 2003 we launched an evaluation exercise to provide a comprehensive picture of the regulation of the professions and its effects in all eu countries. this exercise takes two aspects into account: first, precisely because the liberal professions have a decisive impact on the competitiveness of other sectors, it is important to examine the economic consequences that regulation can have on production and efficiency, on the price level and on employment: secondly, as the questions suggest, it is essential to take account of the non-economic aspects and to examine carefully the reasons for the different regulations. if it turns out that some of these regulations go beyond what is objectively justified in order to guarantee high quality services on the one hand and the protection of consumers' interests on the other, the commission - but i am sure the professionals themselves - will have to do everything possible to ensure that these regulations are reviewed. the contribution of the independent professionals and consumers to this evaluation exercise is being analysed. on 28 october 2003, ms lehne, a hearing of the interested parties will take place, the hearing to which you refer, and we hope to gather a broad range of views from all sources. of course, if honourable members of the european parliament would like to participate, they would be more than welcome: i am sure that the debates will be of high quality, will allow a better understanding of the workings of the professions, and their views, if they wish to participate, will undoubtedly enrich the debate. finally, mr president, i would like to remind you that on 7 march 2002, on a proposal from my colleague, commissioner bolkestein, the commission adopted a proposal for a directive on the recognition of professional qualifications, the main purpose of which, in the light of the objective set in lisbon, is to consolidate 15 existing directives in this field and to increase the mobility of skills. the proposal is currently before this parliament in first reading. without calling into question the question of professional qualifications, which remain the primary responsibility of the member states, the proposal aims to make it easier for self-employed professionals with qualifications in one member state to provide services to customers in any other member state. at the same time, the commission is exploring, in a broader context and in line with the strategy for the internal market in financial services, a coherent way of overcoming the obstacles which still hamper the provision of crossborder services, with the exception of those linked to the simple recognition of professional qualifications. it is clear that if the commission were to submit a new proposal in this area which also covered crossborder services provided by freelancers, it would take due account of the general interest objectives at stake, and in particular of the particular importance of independence and ethics for these professions. in conclusion, while reaffirming its commitment to respecting the restrictive regulation and self-regulation that apply to the professions and that can be justified by reasons of general interest, the commission believes that it has a duty to increase its efforts to create a level playing field for qualified professionals, with the aim of increasing cross-border mobility and healthy competition, in the interests of both the professions themselves and consumers. i take up your expression, mr lehne: we are all aware that supermarket rules are neither necessary nor sufficient. we are dealing with a very specific sector which, however, we think could benefit from (es) mr president, the speakers who have preceded me have stressed the special features of the professions and the need for differentiated regulation. however, as commissioner monti has pointed out, this differentiated regulation must be done in a free market, where customers normally have the choice of their professionals and can also expect certain standards of behaviour. the danger that we should avoid is that professional organizations for the professions will remain a kind of medieval institution, very difficult to join, and that, above all, professional organizations of this kind will prevent the free movement of persons within the european union. in other words, both objectives, namely free access for clients or users to the liberal professions in any country of the union, with the right to have a general regime, and the right of access for professionals from one country to another in the european union, must be guaranteed. and within this framework, the specific regulations for the professions should be directed, first of all, at ensuring the discipline of the professions themselves. in many cases, this is not so. and it would be a bit gratuitous for the commission to assume that the functioning of the professions is guaranteed by the professional organizations, and then we find that in many cases the ethical standards of the professions in question are not really regulated within that profession. and we know many examples in all the liberal professions. i therefore think that the commissioner has made a very balanced analysis and i must also congratulate him on his initiative to hold a hearing with the participation of people from different sectors, who i hope will not only be members of the professions themselves but also representatives of other sectors - industrial sectors, users, consumers - in order to take all aspects into account. in short, i believe that new regulations, somewhat specialised regulations, will be needed for the professions, but such regulations should not be contrary to the general rules of the european union. as commissioner monti has said, this is not a supermarket - you cannot go to a supermarket to buy the services of a doctor - but, within the market situation, customers also have the right to benefit from the possibility, for example, of competition in a sector where there is more supply of professionals than demand for professionals. the supply and demand mechanism can even act as a selection element, in the sense that clients will normally go to those professionals who offer them the best conditions, including remuneration conditions. but if regulations are too restrictive, if the conditions for access by customers are too strict, the customer will find himself effectively imprisoned by the existence of these organizations and the prices they set, and will not even have the possibility of appealing against them. i therefore think that the commissioner has put the problem very well: we must find a balance so that the special requirements of these professions - for which we all want very high ethical standards, which the first ones who should be concerned about maintaining are probably the liberal professionals themselves through their organizations - do not result in detriment to the customer, to the consumer, to the user. the latter must have the right of access to legal rules and to judicial and administrative bodies in order to ensure that services enjoy the maximum protection and that, within the limits of the requirements mentioned by mr gargani and mr lehne, free competition can be guaranteed, both within each of the countries of the union and across the union's borders.

(es) mr president, the committee on legal affairs has been dealing with this issue since the beginning of 2002. we were responding to communications from the commission in which it raised the problem of the shortcomings of community legislation. i remember speaking to a spanish national legislator - a very experienced one, by the way - who told me that there was no one who understood the community directives. we work so hard on them, so many people are involved in their preparation: the council, the commission, the european parliament and so many others, that in the end we get a text which can be defined as a 'camel', that is to say, the horse drawn up by a committee. and this is the real situation. while the regulation is admittedly a little more precise, the directive is a real disaster. the commission was naturally concerned to improve this situation, a concern which is shared by both the council and parliament. in particular, at a time when parliament is going to increase its legislative powers, it makes no sense for us to continue with this procedure of drawing up legal rules. but at the same time, in the legal affairs committee itself, we realised that in order to make the commission's proposals go ahead, it would be necessary to provide a proper constitutional framework for this issue. we raised this in the first questions of the report, and then the committee on constitutional affairs, which had decided to draw up a series of reports after discussing the matter with the committee on legal affairs, realised the importance of the subject for parliament's institutional role and, with very good judgment, welcomed the report. at the same time, we insist on our conviction - and that of the committee on constitutional affairs - that an interinstitutional agreement between the three institutions is necessary so that the respective institutions are not deprived of their powers. i believe that the result of this exercise - in which two separate committees of parliament, the legal affairs committee and the constitutional affairs committee, have dealt with the subject - has been positive. i think that the interinstitutional agreement reached is a good agreement and i would like to congratulate my colleague, mrs frassoni, on the work of the committee on constitutional affairs, which she has done, and also on the good work done by president gargani and by a number of members of that interinstitutional working group - mr swoboda and mr clegg - and, from the point of view of the committee on legal affairs, we welcome the result. this report, for which i am the rapporteur, was adopted by the committee on legal affairs before the interinstitutional agreement was reached. we therefore put forward a number of recommendations to the interinstitutional group. as the agreement has already been reached - and i believe that our objectives have largely been achieved - i think it would be most appropriate to return the report to the committee on legal affairs to be re-worked from the point of view of our committee, taking into account the achievements included in the interinstitutional agreement and, from there, to move forward. i would certainly stress - and i agree with mrs frassoni - the importance we must attach to the problems of self-regulation and co-regulation. because civil society is talked about with too much cheerfulness and when civil society is talked about here in the european parliament and in the european union, representatives of a few organisations are invited, which someone says are representative. but in reality, in democratic regimes, civil society expresses itself through the electoral process. the electoral process protocols the expression of civil society, and the result of that electoral process is the legislative bodies, which are the ones that have to adapt the general rules. the problems with self-regulation and co-regulation are that they are a step backwards; they are a return to the middle ages, when particular sectors issued rules that were binding on everyone. in modern societies these rules have to come from society as a whole, through elected bodies, elected in perfectly protocolled and guaranteed processes, which in this case are the european parliament, the council itself - insofar as the council is made up of governments elected by and accountable to their national parliaments - and also the commission itself, insofar as it is elected by the council and by the european parliament. i therefore have the impression that the interinstitutional agreement has set some limits, but we in this parliament must continue to insist on improving the technical quality of community legislation and on not throwing the baby out with the bath water and not giving up the progress made in our europe with the development of the liberal and democratic state, which allows decisions to be taken by legislative bodies elected by the popular will.
- the next item is the report (a5-0294/2003) by mr bodrato, on behalf of the committee on industry, foreign trade, research and energy, on the european space policy - green paper (com (2003) 17 - c5-0209/2003 - 2003/2092 (ini)).
the rapporteur. - (it) mr president, the green paper presented by commissioner busquin, which was warmly welcomed by parliament, once again underlined the strategic importance of space policy for the independence, security and economic growth of a europe which wants to remain at the forefront of scientific research and technological innovation. in recent months, a milestone has been reached with the constitutional convention, which has given space policy a specific role, thus providing a legal basis for community programmes and consolidating the strategy launched with the extraordinary success of the galileo programme. however, we must not ignore the fact that the commission has also responded specifically to the unprecedented crisis in the space sector, particularly in launchers, which has undermined the activity of many industries and exacerbated distortions in the world market. space is essential to the concentration of skills, research and technology that characterises the development of the knowledge-based economy. it is a resource that should not be wasted, and the commission and the council of the european space agency have shown that they are fully aware of this. the parliament's report stresses the role of esa and the national agencies and expresses satisfaction with the framework agreement which the european community and esa have supported and which parliament has insisted on. this framework agreement confirms esa's unique role in the organisation of technological and industrial research and development. this role should be specified in a european space programme redefining the commission's responsibilities in the face of public demand and new initiatives requiring political representativeness and specific institutional competence. giving europe a leading role on the international stage by involving all the eu countries is not incompatible with the conviction that international cooperation is necessary: cooperation with the united states, first - i am thinking here of the international space station - but also with other countries, including russia, japan and china itself. but we must be aware that the quality of international agreements - especially those concerning space - depends on the quality of scientific, industrial and financial support. europe's objectives must be based on public resources, as is the case around the world, and on more active development of common policies in areas such as agriculture, telecommunications, the environment and transport. we must give impetus to private initiatives, as with galileo, but we must also recognise that the objective of doubling the space budget over ten years will only partially help to close the gap with the united states. space science has played a pioneering role. however, the quality of human resources and basic research requires greater attention. the future of european space policy depends on this increased attention. we therefore believe that the next research framework programme should devote more funds to the space sector, guaranteeing a quota in this area for small and medium-sized enterprises, which are becoming an indispensable support for new innovative enterprises. my last point concerns the idea of the convention to create an armaments agency open to all member states, according to the method of structured cooperation. this idea could help to exploit the industrial and technological asset. it is not a question here - and it is worth pointing out - of militarizing space, but rather of recognising that there are dual activities, both military and civilian, and a european security strategy which cannot be abandoned because of unilateral american temptations. for the avoidance of doubt, the report refers to the un resolution on preventing an arms race in outer space and to the convention itself, which proposes to promote peace and contribute to security and sustainable development on earth. we are now looking forward to the white paper, after having discussed the green paper. our expectations are based on the positive views we have expressed so far and we believe they are the expectations of the scientific world as well as of the european industrial world.

(es) mr president, when we voted here, about a year ago, on the first reading of this parliament's report and obtained a sufficient majority to support the theses i defended, i felt strongly supported by the whole of this parliament. these theses included the need for political firmness on the part of this parliament in the face of the proposal for the forest focus regulation, which was presented by the commission to replace the two old pollution regulations: the fight against pollution in europe and the fight against fires in europe. in the commission's proposal, these two objectives - 'pollution' and 'fires' - were joined by the study of biodiversity, climate change and carbon sequestration. the commission said that all this had to be done with less money - €51 million - and that the issue of firefighting, in its prevention, would be transferred to the rural development regulation. in this way, parliament abandoned codecision for the sake of a simple opinion, without being able to control whether or not these programmes were to be implemented, since they were left to the discretion of the member states and were now included in a regulation whose control by parliament was reduced to an opinion. so this parliament could not politically accept that proposal, nor could it accept it when the council's common position was sent and discussed and a small effort was made, of half a million euros, to go from 13 to 13.5 million per year, which was a minimal effort when it came to assessing our forests, because it is not enough to say that we believe in them, but our support must be translated budgetarily into a greater increase, into a greater effort, since it is the only regulation we have for our forests. we have held numerous meetings, both with the council and with the commission, to reach an agreement and to see that it is translated into a major commitment, which will be reached, god willing, tomorrow in this parliament. a proposal from the council has been received and accepted by coreper, which already considered the primary and priority needs which parliament had outlined at its first reading. article 1 covers firefighting and fire prevention on an equal footing with the other objectives of the foras focus regulation. article 13 sets the budgetary increase, not at the rate we would have liked, but at the rate that has been possible to reach this agreement between all the member states - up to eur 61 million until 2006 - and article 18 calls on the member states to present an evaluation of the regulation before the end of 2005 and on the commission to present new proposals from 2006 onwards. with this agreement, reached by most of the political groups in this house, i hope that we can conclude this regulation at second reading tomorrow and give a political impetus to the construction of europe. it was very difficult for the countries of the european union, especially those that have been burning this summer - europe on all four sides, but mainly the countries of the south - to understand that prevention was not covered by this regulation. we are pleased that it has been introduced on equal terms and i would like to thank the commission, commissioner blin and commissioner blin for their efforts to achieve this agreement; i would also like to thank the council for its tenacious efforts to achieve this agreement and all the alternative rapporteurs from all the political groups for the progress we have made so that this agreement, at second reading, is possible and we have solved what was presented to us as a serious problem: the fight against fires.
