regional policy, transport and tourism, and we in the commission are fully aware of this. i would like to reiterate to this parliament once again that we are involved in the background of these amendments, but that in the commission we have a commitment with parliament and with the council to present the proposal for opening up passenger transport to competition and we will do so before the end of the year. we have almost finished the texts - we are just now seeing the last of the internal discussions, because they are more complex than they might seem at first sight - and before the end of the year - in a month and a half - they will have the text on the table. it is true - as i heard you say, mr jarzembowski - that even if the commission were to put it forward, we would not be able to discuss it during this term. i am not sure that the first reading will be completed. i would like to say to the honourable members that the commission is going to submit this text and we hope that this parliament will start its work and that - whether this parliament or the next one - it will be able to complete it, because we fully share the view that it is important to introduce competition in passenger transport and that, moreover, when the transeuropean network is being established, we must stop thinking about national railway criteria and start thinking about european railway criteria. the geographical area of reference is europe, not any country, but the european network. the various companies already existing in the various countries of europe must therefore have access to this european network and, once they have access to it, they will be in competition with each other. it is the pure law of the internal logic of the steps we have taken. the moment we establish a european railway law, the different operators that already exist in europe enter into competition with each other. the moment the criterion is europe - and not a particular country - we automatically have competition. it is not an ideological problem, it is a purely factual problem, of the internal logic of the measures we take. it is an advantage to build europe. i have to say that i also believe that competition will serve to stimulate a modernisation of the spirit of the railway companies in all that they have to modernise, because i agree with all the honourable members that there is a key mr president, commissioner, the railway network, as well as all the communication infrastructure and media, are crucial elements in the structuring of the european union as a political entity without frontiers. they are as much in the way that they have been in the structuring of modern states for the past two centuries. they are a necessity for the progress and modernization of the economy, so that in this context the extension of the high-speed network is indeed a necessary measure to boost and relaunch productive activities. so contrary to what mr jarzembowski says in his report, which my group rejects, and in accordance with the sterckx reports on safety, ainardi on interoperability and savary on the european railway agency, which we will approve, the railway package is not simply a new instrument for private companies to get their business done as soon as possible, but rather an instrument in this process of political, economic and social construction of the union. for me, as a galician, and for the people who live in nations far from the geographical centre of europe, these decisions of the european parliament should naturally be a way of ensuring high-speed communication with the whole of europe. this is also the sense in which the infrastructure investment plan which the commission is preparing should be, especially taking into account that rail networks are the most respectful of nature and also the most favourable to social welfare.
(es) madam president, madam commissioner, first of all, i would like to join the general - i would say complete - consensus in congratulating our rapporteurs, who have done a splendid job and the proof is that, even at the last moment, they are pushing the council's positions forward, calling for more speed in different areas and attitudes more in line with what we need. but i would like to begin by saying that the vital importance of the issue that concerns us today can only be gauged and observed if we take into account four variables. the first is the serious situation of european transport at the moment and the forecasts that all the studies put on the table. we are therefore not making a graceful legislative process but a compulsory and urgent legislative process. secondly, the european variable, which the commissioner put on the table. it is impossible to rationalise european transport without taking the european variable into account. no state, however long-established it may be, can claim to solve its transport problems without taking account of this beautiful and, moreover, very important variable. we need the european variable: transport problems, as a whole, at european level. thirdly, we cannot do a watertight analysis. we also need to understand the situation of all modes of transport, since each of them has to contribute a part of the solution and the train is embedded in a critical situation among the rest of the modes of transport from which we want to remove it. finally, we are not interested in each mode of transport, but in the interoperability of all modes. as regards the railways, i hope that the encouragement you will receive from these reports and proposals will be fundamental and historic, because so far in europe the directives have worked, but the trains have not. we must say that today's mission is to save the railway and therefore any other perspective is wrong. the railway is sinking - vote in december on a budget based on a europe of fifteen, with a technical annex for the ten new member states. we will then vote next year on an additional budget for these ten new member states. another feature of this 2004 budget is that it is drawn up on the basis of activities. we have identified new gaps in this area which we hope to fill in the course of the year. for parliament, it is particularly important to be able to monitor the degree of implementation of programmes and to identify the types of technical evaluations available. overall, we voted in favour of an economic budget. appropriations will improve the situation. you said: 'is it appropriate to increase payment appropriations at this time?' compared with the level of increase in payment appropriations in recent years, guarantees than they can take advantage of. at the same time, a training programme for bank managers should be associated with this. the chapter on internal policies provides for another reduction on there to do its job, but we believe that the appropriations proposed by the commission need to be reduced, since there is still no legal basis for this. we hope that will be done this year. this year we also paid close attention to the agencies. these are constantly increasing and other creative projects are also underway. we want parliament to have more control over these agencies. parliamentary committees and parliament itself will be responsible for monitoring their work programme. we also want to pay more attention to the organisation chart of these agencies, as we do to that of the commission. this is a requirement that agencies can meet without too much difficulty. i hope that a solution can be found in this respect for the second reading. i would like to add a few remarks - question no 34 by mr grosch (h-0528/03) subject: introduction of the motorway tax in germany in its reply of 2 october 2003 (p-2694/03), the commission confirmed information concerning discrimination against undertakings from other member states in relation to germany. in the meantime, the federal republic of germany has postponed the introduction of tolls indefinitely. in the light of this information, i would ask the commission to indicate whether the working party will continue its work in its present composition (representatives of the commission, the german government, the transport sector, the company toll collect), so that, if a new date were to be set for the introduction of tolls, a detailed report could be drawn up on the difficulties of implementing such a system and opinions could be issued on the possible existence of a breach of the treaty. in the event that the working party is not allowed to continue its work, will the commission, in the light of the current state of knowledge on the matter, initiate a state failure procedure against the federal republic of germany in order to oblige the latter, or more precisely the operating company, to prove that the discrimination still existing at present has disappeared in all its forms?
commission - (es) mr president, i would like to point out that germany has informed the commission of its intention to introduce a toll system based on the distance travelled by commercial vehicles and proposing an average fixed amount of 12.6 cents per kilometre. on 6 march, germany informed the commission of its intention to introduce a toll reimbursement system - at least partial reimbursement or payment - on the basis of special charges, which would allow an average payment of up to 15 cents. the commission must assess whether the notified measure is compatible with the common market and complies with the community legislation in force. in view of the doubts raised by this measure, the commission decided on 23 july 2003 to initiate a formal investigation in accordance with the procedure referred to in article 88 (2) of the ec treaty, in order to give germany and the other interested parties an opportunity to submit their comments. on 27 august 2003, the text was published in the official journal of the european union and the commission's final decision is expected before the end of the year. the commission is of the opinion that the toll system could prove discriminatory if certain technical problems are not resolved before its introduction. the commission and the german government have therefore set up a working group to examine the technical problems raised by the introduction of the toll system, and this group is proving to be a success. i would also point out that the commission has asked the german government to ensure that the installation of tolls impedes the free movement of traffic in europe as little as possible and has stated that if problems arise once the tolls are in operation, the commission will take appropriate action. i would like to say, however, that in all cases the commission has acted to defend the treaties and that since the end of august and the beginning of september we have established channels of cooperation with the german government which are working more than satisfactorily.
the commission (es) i would like to say that there has been no discrimination yet, not least because the toll is not in operation. i would point out that it was the german authorities themselves who decided, in view of the non-compliance of the industries in the consortium with which they had agreed to build the equipment and put the system into operation, and given that faults were detected, to postpone the start of the toll. the german minister for transport, mr stolpe, has repeatedly assured me - and the facts prove him right - that this system will not be put into operation until it is operational in a normal, smooth and non-discriminatory manner. so that is what i am referring to.
the commission (es) mr rübig, there is now a regulation, called the eurovignette, which lays down the criteria according to which compensation for the use of certain infrastructures, tolls, can be established. the fact is that we believe that the directive is not sufficiently clear or complete and, for example, does not provide for the possibility of cross-financing alternative infrastructures, which seems to be a key element in our ability to have adequate infrastructure in the european union. we have therefore put forward a proposal on a legal basis, the legal basis for transport, which is adopted by a majority and does not require unanimity. it is true that the current eurovignette directive has a different legal basis, which is the tax legal basis; therefore, it is considered a tax, whereas in the proposal we are making now, what we are proposing is compensation, a payment for the costs incurred by the use of an infrastructure. and we can maintain that legal basis, which is transport, because we are talking about a payment for the use of an infrastructure, as long as the money collected for this concept does not add to the state's accounts, because if it goes to public accounts, to administrative budgets, whether of the state or of an autonomous community or a region, we would automatically be back on the fiscal legal basis and therefore require unanimity. i think it is essential, mr rübig, that we keep what is proposed in this proposal: linking these revenues to the use of infrastructure, to the maintenance of infrastructure and to the transport sector, and not linking these revenues to public revenue, to the revenue of administrations, because then - i repeat - we would have to go for another legal basis and we would have to approve it unanimously, and i do not know whether that would be the best way if we really want to get a change in the eurovignette directive.

commission. - community legislation on medicinal products strictly regulates the authorization and placing on the market of medicinal products and their classification. the same is true of their advertising. however, the supply of medicinal products to private individuals, i.e. the distribution to the public by a pharmacist, is not regulated at community level by pharmaceutical law. therefore, the sale of medicines to individuals via the internet is not covered by european pharmaceutical legislation. this sale is a matter of national measures, to be considered in the context of the 'general principles' of the treaty, i.e. articles 28 to 30 on the free movement of goods. the commission therefore does not have concrete data on the extent of legal e-commerce of medicines in the european union. nor does it have data on the total quantity of medicines that are supplied via the internet within and outside the european union, with or without an electronic prescription. this issue could also be examined in the light of the directive on consumer protection in respect of distance contracts. the latter provides that, in order to ensure a higher level of consumer protection, member states may adopt or maintain more stringent provisions, but these must be compatible with the treaty. such provisions shall include, where appropriate, a prohibition, on grounds of public interest, on the marketing on their territory, by means of distance contracts, of certain goods or services, in particular medicinal products, in compliance with the treaty. the question of the compatibility of the national measures with the treaty, i.e. articles 28 to 30, is currently the subject of the docmorris nv and jacques waterval case, which is pending before the court of justice. this includes assessing the proportionality and justification, for the protection of health and human life, of such national measures. the sale of medicines via the internet raises health protection and legal issues. improving information for patients is one of the key elements of the commission's latest communication 'strengthening the european pharmaceutical industry for the benefit of the patient'. the commission is committed to exploring the establishment of a realistic and practical framework for patient information on prescription medicines. in addition, the commission intends to set up a european health portal, which could address these issues. however, it should be noted that informing consumers about the dangers of online shopping and monitoring such activities is the primary responsibility of the member states. the commission can therefore only act in very limited areas.
commission. - i should first like to thank mr staes for his question on the addition of water and protein to poultrymeat. this question was discussed at the sitting of 1 july 2003, so today is the opportunity to inform the house of the current state of play. i would first like to say a few words about the history of this problem. you are aware that the british and irish authorities have uncovered fraudulent practices designed to artificially increase the weight of poultrymeat by adding water and protein to other ingredients. this process is used to retain a significant amount of water, up to 40% or even 50%. that is why i have asked my services to do everything in their power to improve this sad situation. in line with the proposal of the uk authorities, my services have been working on a commission directive requiring the addition of water to these products to be clearly indicated on the label. a preliminary draft was discussed with experts from the member states and interested parties. it asked that the name of the product itself be accompanied by the words 'with added water' and the percentage of water added. however, i remain convinced that labelling products containing added water is a secondary solution if the water has been added only to artificially create weight and thus to deceive the consumer. the practice of adding water to food in order to deceive the consumer is despicable. i have therefore reiterated my request to my services to examine whether the community legislation currently in force offers a possibility of prohibiting this practice. this work is currently in progress.
commission. i have to say to mr whitehead that i do not approve of the procedure whereby water is retained in a product for the purpose of bulking it out, increasing the weight, so that consumers are misled into believing they are buying more protein than they are actually buying. it is a clearly misleading practice designed to defraud the consumer. i do not, therefore, have any ambition to put in place an upper limit for the inclusion of water which, even at 20%, has the effect of misleading the consumer. on the question of whether this protein can be disguised or not, this is also part of the ongoing work. but what i am focusing on at the moment is the capacity of the commission to bring forward a proposal founded on any legal base that may currently exist. in other words, is there legislation in place at the moment that can be interpreted in such a way as to lead to the banning of this particular activity? that is the focus of my attention at the moment. these other issues, as you rightly point out, are of importance also, and we will address them in due course.
commission. - the community has a coherent and comprehensive tobacco control policy through legislation covering the content, packaging and labelling of tobacco products. even though it has been able to develop strong legislation in this area, it faces challenges every day, ranging from litigation to the incorrect implementation of the provisions of this legislation. the honourable member asks whether the cardboard boxes covering cigarette packs to hide the prevention message are contrary to the 'spirit of the directive'. this problem must be considered in the context of the implementation of the tobacco products directive. article 5 of that directive requires that tar, nicotine and carbon monoxide contents be printed on the pack of cigarettes and that each unit of cigarette packaging bears a general warning and supplementary health warnings covering at least 30% of the front surface and 40% of the rear surface in order to inform the consumer of the risks of tobacco consumption. one of the main objectives of the tobacco products directive is to warn consumers of the health effects of tobacco through clear and visible warnings. in this sense, the directive provides that these texts may not be concealed, obscured or separated in any way by other indications or images or by the opening of the package. if the cigarette pack and the carton are sold separately, it could be argued that this is not in direct contradiction with the provisions of the directive, which concerns the sale of tobacco and not the sale of the carton. whether the carton case is bought deliberately by the consumer is an individual decision of the consumer, who has undoubtedly noticed the texts and warnings and does not seem to like to see them. in this context, therefore, the directive has fulfilled its objective of informing consumers about the health effects of tobacco. however, if the carton is directly or indirectly promoted by the cigarette manufacturers themselves and, for example, distributed free of charge in tobacco shops, even if it is offered or sold separately there, this could affect the sale of tobacco as provided for in the directive and undermine its beneficial effect. as the honourable member suggests, this could be interpreted as contrary to the spirit of the directive. the commission is aware, for example, that in some cases these cartons are sold in government-approved tobacco shops and that advertising brochures are sent to these shops by the distribution companies that supply the tobacco. it is incumbent upon the member states to take all necessary measures to ensure the correct implementation of the directive. the commission urges the national authorities responsible for this implementation to be vigilant in this respect. the community has a powerful legal instrument which must be applied correctly. the commission will analyse all practical problems arising from the implementation of the directive and will present a report to parliament before the end of 2004.
commission. i fully agree with the implication of the question you ask and the last part of your question is directed to whether the tobacco industry itself is involved in this, or indeed the retail outlets themselves. as i indicated earlier, there seems to be some evidence that government-sponsored tobacco shops may be engaged in this exercise. the extent to which these products may be sold or given free of charge in conjunction with the sale of tobacco is an issue that must be addressed and resolved, particularly in the context of the implementation of the legislation which comes within the powers of the member states themselves. however, if there were two completely separate and distinct transactions, one the purchase of cigarettes and the other, in a different shop in another area, the purchase of a package such as this, where an individual is free to do as he wishes with his packet of cigarettes, it seems to me that in such cases, we are reaching the point where regulation becomes more difficult. but, as i said earlier, the fact remains that the purchaser of the cigarette package will have been aware, and it will have been brought to his notice, that this information is contained on the packet of cigarettes. the photographs you refer to may also be included, if the member state in question chooses to print them on the packet of cigarettes, though it is not compulsory to do so, and to that extent information is imparted to the consumer in the way intended by this legislation. so to that extent the legislation is not circumvented. but there are issues involved here. one is to ensure the proper implementation of the legislation and the other is to ensure that we do not intrude upon the freedom of the individual to do whatever he wishes with his own property, even in circumstances where we would not approve of it.
the commission has already adopted a proposal on the protection of animals during transport. the commission is aware that parliament and some member states have asked for transport to be limited to 8 hours or 500 kilometres. however, it should be very clear from the relevant scientific advice that the scientific committee has not recommended specific time limits for the transport of animals as a means of improving their welfare. the commission proposal takes full account of the opinion of the scientific committee and of a series of consultations with the parties concerned. the commission decided that the best way to make the outcome of this process effective was to propose travel and rest times which correspond to the rules applied in this field for drivers. therefore, one of my main objectives - the effective enforcement of stronger animal protection rules - could be applied in a much more direct way. the data provided by the tachograph would make it possible to verify compliance with the rules. i look forward to parliament's views on our proposal, as well as rapid progress in the council. speculation on a particular scenario would be inappropriate in view of the respective roles of our institutions as defined in the treaty.
commission. i am aware of the issues that you raise. there are, however, some factual errors in the point that you make. there is no derogation in place at the moment. the derogation that was in place was removed in 1995. it would therefore be incorrect to suggest that the current draft legislation under consideration does anything to change the situation from the status quo ante. having said that, this morning i discussed this very issue with your colleague, mr parish. i am aware that there is concern in the uk about the issue. i have expressed my views on that and i am sensitive to the points that have been made. those views will, i understand, achieve some publicity in the press in the uk tomorrow. i have asked my services to look at this particular point to try and achieve an outcome that you might like, while at the same time ensuring that the rules of the operation of the internal market are not damaged. so, the issue is under consideration.
commission. - i fully share the concerns of the honourable member on this important matter. alcohol is one of the main factors affecting health in the community. i can assure you that the commission will also focus on reducing the harmful effects of alcohol as part of the further development of the community strategy on public health. the community adopted two important documents on alcohol policy in june 2001, under the swedish presidency: the council conclusions of 5 june 2001 on a community strategy to reduce alcohol-related harm - mentioned by the honourable member - and the council recommendation on alcohol consumption among young people, in particular children and adolescents (2001/458/ec). the stockholm conference on alcohol and youth, held in february 2001, was a key step in the preparation of these documents. it should be noted that, in addition to being a crucial issue in health policy, alcohol is also a controversial and politically sensitive issue, both at community level and within the member states. any community strategy must therefore be carefully planned in collaboration with the member states. it must also be based on facts. we must therefore assess the different measures and the different situations prevailing in the member states. the adoption of the new public health programme has provided the commission with an effective instrument for developing this strategy. first, a report on alcohol will be produced by the end of 2004 as part of the health information strand of the new programme. this report will address the economic and social costs of alcohol and consider issues of alcohol promotion and protection of children and adolescents. secondly, we will create - i hope, as early as the beginning of next year - a network of specialised organisations to support the implementation of the council recommendation on alcohol consumption among young people and to work towards further developing the community strategy envisaged in the council conclusions referred to by the honourable member. the commission has recently set up a working group on alcohol and health, in which representatives of the member states discuss various aspects of alcohol policy in the community and, more specifically, how member states are implementing the council recommendation on alcohol and young people. the working party will also enable us to monitor the situation in the new member states. the commission should present a report on the implementation of the council recommendation on alcohol consumption among young people by the end of 2005. this document will consider the degree of actual effectiveness of the proposed measures and the need to review them or go further. the commission is also considering, with the who euroregion and the member states, the possibility of holding a conference on alcohol and health in 2005, following on from the stockholm conference in 2001. the results of this conference, together with the report on the implementation of the council recommendation, will enable us to define the strategy which will reflect the situation of the enlarged european union. the progress made at community level should not make us forget the crucial role of the member states in combating these phenomena. an integrated approach to alcohol-related problems requires concerted action by all relevant parties, including families, schools, employers, industry, advertisers and national regulatory bodies. effective compliance with existing national legislation on issues such as alcohol-driving or age limits could make a significant difference.

commission. the commission does not have any ambition to increase the consumption of alcohol in the european union or indeed in the member states, and nor do its policies seek to achieve that. as i have indicated to you, the measures that are being undertaken by my directorate-general and by others in the commission, seek to achieve a situation whereby there will be a reduction of binge drinking in particular, especially among young people. this phenomenon exists in a number of member states, not all member states. it is, however, an issue for the member states themselves. it is a national competence issue and it would be wrong to look to the policies of the european union either to encourage or discourage alcohol consumption. we can only act in the light of the competences that are available to us at european union level: this issue is the primary responsibility of each individual member state, and some member states have a bigger problem than others. those member states that have a bigger problem should ensure that they put in place policies at national level to try to resolve this situation.
commission - i thank the honourable member for raising this important issue and for giving me the opportunity to outline the commission's position on this matter. the honourable member's question refers to the report of the scientific committee on animal health and welfare on the impact of the production of duck and goose liver oil on the welfare of these animals. this report was adopted in december 1998 and deals with a wide range of issues: the origins and distribution of foie gras production, farming and feeding practices, the behaviour of ducks and geese, the consequences of feeding, in particular welfare indicators, the socio-economic aspects of improving the welfare of animals farmed in the foie gras sector and research. the scientists have not looked at the issue of foraging in isolation but in the context of all the factors involved in the production of foie gras. however, the scientific committee, recognising that feeding birds as it is currently practised was harmful to their welfare, made a number of recommendations. the main objective of these recommendations is to improve production methods in order to reduce avoidable suffering. the scientists therefore suggest that the objectives should be, in order of priority, to reduce mortality and morbidity rates, to reduce the degree of suffering and distress endured by all animals in the process and to enable animals to engage in normal behavioural activities. the report stresses that it is very important for the future development of foie gras production that alternative techniques are put in place that do not require the use of intensive feeding. my services have brought this report to the attention of the sector. since then, the industry has been studying and researching better production techniques, more respectful of animal welfare. i would also like to draw the attention of the honourable member to the two recommendations adopted under the european convention for the protection of animals kept for farming purposes. the measures are aimed specifically at protecting ducks and geese reared for the production of foie gras. i am pleased to say that the commission took an active part in the adoption of these recommendations. these texts deal with welfare considerations for ducks and geese on farms and, in particular, with the gradual abolition of small individual duck cages. the recommendations reflect the need to reduce the most intensive form of livestock farming, as recommended in the scientific committee report i have already mentioned. the community, all member states and most of the future member states have signed the convention and are therefore obliged to act on the recommendations made. in particular, the signatory parties will be required to report on the state of implementation of these specific recommendations to the council of europe after 1 january 2005. the commission will closely monitor the implementation of these recommendations, which have led to significant improvements in welfare.
commission. the clear advice that i have in relation to this issue is that the traditional methods of feeding ducks and geese for the production of foie gras are not contrary to animal welfare considerations. the real issue for concern, and the focus of attention of all the scientific evaluation on this issue, has been related to the intensive farming, intensive production and the intensive force-feeding of the birds in that way. the ban you mention is not on a welfare basis but rather on an ethical basis, which is a different issue. what we are considering here is the question of animal welfare and the treatment of animals and birds in these circumstances. i take note of what you have said. this is an issue that will be discussed at a future time.
- question no 45 by mr alavanos (h-0559/03): the commission has not yet decided whether to grant aid to the countries of the former soviet union. subject: repeal of a temporary decision concerning the transfer of personal data to the united states in a report to the commission, mr bolkestein and mr patten, members of the commission, stated that the united states had not provided them with sufficient guarantees concerning the protection of personal data of passengers of european airlines travelling to the united states, which is what the us authorities are asking for. nevertheless, a temporary decision (of 5 march 2003) allowing european airlines to pass on these to the authorities in question is still in force. when does the commission intend to repeal the temporary decision of 5 march 2003, as it constitutes a clear breach of community legislation on the protection of citizens' personal data?
commission - the commission would like to start by clarifying the misunderstanding which seems to be at the origin of this question. there is no decision or agreement at the moment. so there's nothing to be repealed. a us law requires airlines operating to and from the us to give access to passenger identity information. most airlines comply with this requirement, which is understandable given the negative consequences for airlines and their passengers of refusing to provide this data to the united states. the february joint statement was accompanied by the us commitment to work with the commission to reach an adequacy finding on the level of data protection guaranteed by the us. the honourable member is right: the commission considers that the us provisions do not provide adequate protection. this in itself does not justify the closure of the procedure. the commission intends instead to pursue this with vigour, in order to persuade the us to improve its provisions with a view to reaching this adequacy finding and the definition of an appropriate legal framework for the transfer of air passengers' personal data. as i stated before the competent parliamentary committee on 9 september 2003, the commission set itself a christmas 2003 deadline.
commission. in reply to the supplementary question, perhaps i may once again explain that the commission is in active negotiations with the government of the united states. i was in washington early last week, and during my stay i had discussions with mr tom ridge who is the secretary for the homeland security department, in other words the man in charge of seeing to it that the united states is a secure and safe country. the legislation of the united states requires all passengers going to the united states to have their personal data sent on before their arrival. quite apart from what the commission thinks, airlines and, where necessary, computerised reservation systems, supply that data. that is not strictly in compliance with european law and, therefore, the situation is not good. european law is laid down in the data protection directive which, incidentally, has not yet been transposed into the national legislations of a number of member states. anyway, it is a directive and should be policed by member states, not by the commission. once again, this is not a good situation. we need to decide whether there is adequate protection of the data in the united states, that is the so-called 'adequacy finding'. as i told the relevant parliamentary committee in the first half of september, i cannot as yet conclude that there is adequacy on the other side of the ocean. therefore the legally precarious situation continues to exist. once again that is not good. the honourable member said that there was a secret arrangement. there is nothing secret about anything at all. the situation is of doubtful legality, but the commission is in discussions with the american government to try and rectify. on my last visit to washington i managed to achieve some limited commission. - in reply to the question by mrs riis-jørgensen, i would point out that under article 28 of the treaty parallel importation of medicinal products is a lawful commercial practice within the internal market. it is also subject to derogations relating to the protection of human health and life and to the protection of industrial and commercial property, in accordance with article 30 of the treaty. the european court of justice has held that the derogation from the free movement of goods, justified by reasons of protection of industrial and commercial property, is admissible only for the purpose of preserving the rights which constitute the object of property itself. the specific object of a registered trade mark is, in particular, to guarantee to the proprietor the exclusive right to use that registered trade mark when a product is first marketed. consequently, national legislation protecting industrial and commercial property rights cannot justify a prohibition on importing a product which has already been lawfully marketed in another member state by the owner of that right or with his consent. in some cases, parallel importers are obliged to change the name of parallel imported medicinal products in order to obtain effective access to the market of the importing state, especially where the use of different registered trade marks by the owner contributes to the artificial partitioning of markets between member states. this market segmentation would persist if the importer could only sell the product on certain parts of its market. the court ruled that the change of packaging and name was not necessary if the parallel importer was only seeking a commercial advantage. according to the case-law of the court, a change of name is considered justified if it is objectively necessary. that need must always be assessed on the basis of factors such as those mentioned in the question - the conditions in force at the time of marketing of the parallel imported pharmaceutical product in the member state of destination. in each case, it is for the national courts to decide whether it is objectively necessary for the parallel importer to use the registered trade mark used in the member state of importation in order for the imported products to have effective access to the market. as regards the national measures referred to in the question, the commission will assess, in the light of the case law of the court, any more specific information which may be submitted to it.
commission. if mrs riis-jørgensen has more specific details concerning any particular case that has come to her attention, the commission would very much like to learn of it and will follow it up in the light of the case-law of the courts with the appropriate action. the commission will be grateful to mrs riis-jørgensen for bringing those circumstances to its notice.

- the next item is the report (a5-0334/2003) by mrs smet, on behalf of the committee on women's rights and equal opportunities, on the violation of women's rights and the european union's international relations (2002/2286 ((ini)).
commission. i would like to start by commending ms smet, a former colleague, indeed one of two former colleagues taking part in this debate. we were a very distinguished vintage. i would like to thank ms smet for her work as rapporteur on this report. her political commitment to the cause of women's rights is well known in both the commission and the council. this own-initiative report raises a wide range of issues. it is an extremely valuable contribution in placing women nearer the centre of the european union's foreign policy. the violation of women's rights in international affairs is an extremely serious issue. it is an issue to which the commission and the european union both attach considerable importance. this year alone, we have launched three major gender initiatives, under what we call the programme of action for the mainstreaming of gender equality and community development cooperation. first of all, we have set about the drafting of a concise manual setting out essential principles and guidelines for gender mainstreaming in development practice, and it is targeted at commission officials. secondly, we have issued a call for tender for the setting-up of a very large training programme for staff, both in our headquarters in brussels and in delegations, including also the staff of beneficiary countries. thirdly, we have launched a call for proposals to support non-governmental organisation projects. the commission has also been very active in contributing to eu efforts to promote the human rights of women in international fora, such as the un commission on human rights, the third committee of the united nations general assembly, and the office of democratic institutions and human rights of the osce. for example, we co-sponsored the resolution on the elimination of violence against women at the last commission on human rights. it was tabled, as the house will know, by canada, and we issued a strong statement on the human rights of women which highlighted, among other things, the growing problem of trafficking in human beings and the advantages of gender mainstreaming. however, what i would like to underline today is that it is our belief that women’s rights are an integral part of human rights as a whole. and for this reason, i would like to express the reservations of the commission over certain recommendations within the report. the item of principle concern to us is the call for the 'council and commission to include in future trade and development agreements, irrespective of and in addition to the essential elements clause, a specific clause providing for the imposition of sanctions and ultimately the suspension of the agreement in cases of serious and repeated violations of women’s rights'. as i am sure most members will agree, when considering issues such as equality, non-discrimination and violence, women’s rights are best addressed in the overall framework of human rights indeed, as quoted in the honourable member's report, the declaration from the 1993 vienna world conference on human rights clearly underlines that 'the human rights of women and the girl-child are an inalienable, integral and indivisible part of universal human rights.' moreover, it is important to realise that violence against women on a state level is an integral part of the human rights provisions dealing with torture and the death penalty, which are our priorities in terms of human rights. it is also worth noting that a separate clause on women’s rights would also imply the need to include various other human rights issues as individual clauses in subsequent trade and co-operation agreements; that is to say for example, a clause for the rights of the child, or a clause for the rights of indigenous peoples and minorities. the human rights clause is a dynamic instrument through which we can advance human rights in a positive manner. the measure of its success is not found in the frequency with which it results in punitive measures or suspension of agreements but rather in the structured exchanges on human rights which result in a more realistic way of realising the goals of the human rights clause. by separating women’s rights from the overall human rights agenda, parliament would not necessarily, whatever its admirable intentions, be serving the cause of human rights. indeed, such a separation would possibly result in a lessening in its leverage on the political agenda. let me give an example, a case in point. i would like to refer to the current negotiations with iran on a trade and co-operation agreement. central to the human rights dialogue with iran – and i think i can say that i played a prominent part in getting it started – is the issue of discrimination against women and iran’s non-ratification of the convention on the elimination of discrimination against women. it would seem that in certain cultural environments, it is advantageous for women’s rights to enter the agenda under the mantle of human rights. i do not make these points simply theoretically, simply as a result of intellectual or academic study. i was discussing these issues most recently in syria with a women's rights lawyer, as part of our discussions there to try to get an association agreement with syria. i have discussed these issues in iran with, for example, female members of the iranian parliament. so they are issues about which i can assure the house, even if i disagree with what is proposed, they are issues about which i feel pretty strongly. another important human rights instrument with regard to women’s rights is the european initiative for human rights and democratisation. the instrument is very active in involving local women’s organisations in third countries. and although gender equality is a horizontal issue under this european initiative, many specific gender projects have also been supported. for example, we are currently funding a project in egypt, jordan, lebanon west bank and gaza for legal aid and literacy, for counselling for women victims of violence and for awareness campaigns and research. i hope the house will take account of our arguments that it is not necessary to have a separate clause in trade and cooperation agreements, since this is an area and an issue fully addressed by our human rights agenda. i also hope that the house will not conclude from what i have said that we do not give as much priority to the issues very properly raised, for example, gender mutilation which i have not mentioned in this debate. i hope that the house will not think that we do not give the greatest possible priority to these issues. in my experience, as a long retired development minister, one of the crucial issues, perhaps the crucial issue, in sustainable development policy is gender mainstreaming and decent treatment of women. i first learnt that lesson 20 odd years ago in pakistan, and i have continued learning it ever since.

- the next item is the oral question (o-0066/2003 - b5-0281/2003) by mr gargani, mr rothley, mr lehne and mr manders, on behalf of the committee on legal affairs and the internal market, to the commission, on the german deposit system.
commission. mr president, the commission is fully aware of the above-mentioned issues. it has analysed the matter and i can inform parliament, as mr lehne has already mentioned, that this morning the commission decided to send a letter of formal notice to the german government because the commission considers that it has infringed article 28 of the treaty and article 7 of directive 94/62/ec. may i stress that the commission is not questioning the setting up of a deposit system as such, but rather the modalities under which this is occurring. the reasons for this are as follows: firstly, there are no nationwide return systems. at present the two systems deemed to be nationwide, lekkerland-tobaccoland and vfv, have a market share of no more than 12% of the beverages which are subject to the deposit. furthermore, they mostly cover small kiosks and canteens with a sales area of less than 200 square metres. under the relevant law, these smaller outlets have a legal obligation to take back empty bottles and cans of the 'same type, shape and size', but only of the same brands which they themselves sell. second, the so-called individual solutions – insellösungen in german – pose a continuous problem to intra-community trade. they are a direct result of the relevant german law under which the obligation for bigger retailers to take back empty packaging applies only to packaging of the same type, shape and size as that which they sell. today a number of individual solutions exist and they pose serious problems. this provision in german law induces major retail chains to force european producers to modify the packaging of their products and the european court of justice holds that, when eu producers are obliged to modify their packaging in order to market their products, that fact alone amounts to a barrier to intra-community trade. extra costs are incurred and the import of products becomes more burdensome. third, the systems are not all fully interoperable. indeed, on the one hand, for the growing number of individual solutions there is no legal obligation to take back packaging which belongs to any of the other collection systems, even if this differs only slightly from the one that they sell. furthermore, as far as the interoperability between vfv and lekkerland-tobaccoland is concerned, it appears that a number of technical issues have not yet been settled. for example, it is still not clear how a financial clearing of the deposits between several systems will work. fourth, delisting persists and one-way products that are not an individual solution are not to be found on the shelves of certain stores. we have firm evidence that several major retail chains in germany have delisted. importers from other european countries are particularly affected by this, as they sell their drinks almost exclusively in one-way packaging for reasons mainly related to long-distance deliveries. perhaps in the case of a number of existing individual solutions, some well-established importers do not necessarily suffer in their protected arrangements, but this does not compensate for the major losses incurred through the substantial decline in imports from other member states as a result of this fragmentation of the german market for these products. therefore the commission has now decided to issue a letter of formal notice in which it raises these and some other questions and it has asked the german government to reply to those questions and to provide a justification for the measures undertaken.

(es) mr president, first of all i would like to express my satisfaction and my thanks to all the colleagues who have worked with me to achieve the consensus reached in this report, a report which bears the significant title 'peace and dignity in the middle east'. unfortunately, we are far from peace, and humiliation - not dignity - is the order of the day in the tormented lands of israel and palestine. however, the report before us, in its letter and in its spirit, seeks to raise more and more voices, more and more consciences, here and there, in favour of this dual objective: dignity and peace, to which we can and must add stability for the region and prosperity for its peoples. it is true - as the report points out - that a climate of mutual trust between the parties has not been established and that, in recent times, the enemies of peace have erected many obstacles and pretexts in order to make the roadmap unviable, but it is our duty to continue to try to achieve it in the immediate, medium and long term. the report therefore calls on the governments of both parties and of all the countries of the middle east to implement a new educational policy based on the concept of education for peace and aimed at promoting tolerance and mutual understanding between different cultures and religions. however, and while we are at it, we must face the stark reality, and we do so by condemning the terrorist violence of palestinian sectors, as well as the excessive use of military force by israel against the palestinian people. unfortunately, this last mention is particularly timely these days, and i repeat, unfortunately. as the israeli newspaper haaretz writes today - and i quote verbatim - 'on monday, while sharon was delivering an empty speech, devoid of any realistic political vision, israeli helicopters bombed gaza, killing several terrorists and injuring many innocent palestinian civilians'; an odious practice which is not isolated and which, haaretz writes, 'the israeli army has stated that it will continue to do'. this, i say, leads the columnist - an obvious product of a democratic society such as israel's - to warn the israeli government and army that "they must not, with this policy, undermine the ethical standards that israel has adopted over the years. if that happens, a serious split will occur in israeli society, as public opinion will lose confidence in its political and military leaders". in the speech of monday, the israeli prime minister showed himself to the knesset as an ardent supporter of the roadmap. of course, with the 14 amendments submitted not to the quartet, but unofficially to the us administration. the prime minister, apparently alarmed by the response to the so-called geneva agreement, a peace initiative which has emerged from joint israeli-palestinian efforts, has stated that the road map is the only hope for progress towards peace with the palestinians. well, let's get to work. we will congratulate him if he makes genuine progress. but for the moment we would be satisfied if you would do what the report - in the exercise of consensus - asks you to do in paragraph 2: withdraw your army from the palestinian autonomous territories, stop targeted killings and freeze all settlement activity and the construction of the security wall. "you don't need to sleep to have nightmares", said a painting on the berlin wall. fourteen years after its destruction, another wall is causing nightmares in palestine. and while sharon, in his speech on monday, said he had ordered that wall to be accelerated, last night, at the un general assembly, 144 governments voted to ask israel to stop and reverse a project that the whole planet - except israel and the united states, which voted against - considers to be in contradiction with international law. the report addresses a number of hot topics. the european union is also calling on the palestinian authorities to take a realistic approach to the so-called right of return of refugees, so that a realistic solution can be found. however, as a european - i repeat and end - i naturally support the roadmap to the end, but the report recommends that, should it be blocked in the immediate future, and given the gravity of the consequences, which would cause greater suffering to israelis and palestinians, new options are envisaged, in particular the establishment of an international mandate under the authority of the quartet in palestine, which may even include an international force on the ground.

three examples: regional policy, which can be mobilised more systematically both to promote a culture of innovation and to facilitate the management of industrial change; employment policy, where the social dialogue, at horizontal and sectoral level, has a useful role to play in helping to deal with industrial policy issues; and research and development policy, where the implementation of the so-called ‘3% action plan’ has direct relevance from an industrial policy standpoint. with regard to industrial policy at the sectoral level, the commission is putting together a package of activities analysis of selected sectors. when necessary, specific initiatives aiming to improve the competitive situation of the sectors will be proposed. we are already working on a number of specific, sectoral commission. - mr president, the commission would first like to thank mrs figueiredo for her excellent report and for her support for the communication we have put on your table. following the reform of the common fisheries policy, member states and the commission must now do everything possible to ensure that the new rules in force are correctly applied. in order to achieve this common objective, i think we all agree on the need to intensify cooperation in the field of control. in this context, the commission communication sets out a strategy for cooperation and coordination between member states and at union level, covering both what can be done in the short and medium term. what we have designed as an action plan is to establish a coherent strategy to make the inspection and surveillance activities of the member states - since this is indeed their responsibility - more effective and we propose three main areas of action in particular. first, the definition of inspection priorities for the stocks most at risk. this approach will subsequently have to be extended to other activities, such as those involving fishing for highly migratory species in the mediterranean or landing vessels that may be engaged in illegal fishing. the second major area of action is the adoption of specific and transparent monitoring programmes which are adapted to the characteristics of each fishing activity concerned. our proposal is that all the national authorities concerned should be involved in the preparation of the programmes which will cover inspection and surveillance at sea and, of course, also the control of landings and marketing. third, strengthened cooperation to make control and enforcement of the rules more uniform and effective. experience shows that one-off or voluntary cooperation is insufficient, in particular as regards access to information, cooperation at operational level and the follow-up of all irregularities and infringements. we believe, as industry is demanding, that inspection procedures should be harmonised. voluntary cooperation is therefore no longer sufficient, and an organizational structure at community level is, in our view, now necessary: hence this feasibility study in which we propose to involve the member states and the interested parties - the foremost of which, of course, are the fishermen and their various communities, as mrs figueiredo has just said - the idea being a common inspection structure through a community fisheries control agency. this feasibility study would be carried out in the spirit of an agency responsible for the organisation and deployment of all means of inspection and surveillance in accordance with priorities to be established at community level. in conclusion, we have no problems with this dialogue on this communication and we would like to thank mrs figueiredo again for her comments and support.

i suggest. mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i am pleased to present to this house the state of progress of the process of constitutional reform of the european union. the italian presidency is convinced that only with the support of the european parliament will it be possible to solve the many problems we are facing and to reach a political agreement in december. for this reason, in accordance with a traditional italian position, we have fought to extend the european parliament's participation in the work of the intergovernmental conference to the greatest possible extent. the convention on the future of europe has been an innovative instrument in launching the current process of reforming the treaties. the draft treaty it drew up was not the result of a simple intergovernmental debate but was shaped by productive contributions and structured, global, public and transparent reflection on the future of europe, which, for the first time in the history of the european integration process, also involved the national parliaments and representatives of civil society. the political value of the success achieved must therefore not be dissipated or diluted by the work of the igc. the latter, on the other hand, has the task of improving and completing those parts of the treaty on which there is not yet full agreement. any other solution would be interpreted as an attempt to reduce the democratic and transparent method which was introduced by the work of the european convention. if that were the case, it would be a step backwards which our citizens would find it difficult to understand and justify. this approach is the basis for the central objective of the italian presidency: the european parliament has already adopted a resolution on the situation in the former yugoslavia. this will enable the future constitutional treaty - a constitution for europe, as president giscard d'estaing called it - to be signed between 1 may 2004, the date of accession of the 10 new member states, and the elections for the renewal of the european parliament. the extension of the constitutional negotiations beyond these dates would raise two serious problems of legitimacy and democratic transparency: on the one hand, the assets of the convention would be gradually dispersed; on the other hand, european citizens would vote for the elections to the european parliament in defiance of the constitutional guidelines of the future union. the need to find consensual solutions to the still controversial issues will not, under any circumstances, lead the italian presidency to negotiate a compromise to the downside which would result in a backlog in relation to the convention's proposals. our aim is to achieve a quality result that meets the expectations of european public opinion and is therefore capable of ensuring the effective and democratic functioning of the union over a long period of time. giving the european union a constitution is a challenge, not just for a few countries or for the italian presidency, which has the honour of leading the council at this stage, but a challenge for all of us. we owe it to our citizens: if we lose this challenge, then europe as a whole has lost. the union has lost its role as a factor of stability and prosperity on the world stage; we all lost. after the opening ceremony on 4 october, the work of the igc has been brought into focus. in this area, as was to be expected, institutional issues appear to be by far the most complex. the most important issues concern the composition of the commission, the procedures for electing and the powers of the president of the european council, the status of the foreign minister and the calculation of the qualified majority. these issues were discussed in depth at the igc meetings held in the first half of october. the ministerial meeting on 27 october broadened the range of analyses to include issues not addressed or only marginally addressed at previous meetings. the following subjects were discussed in particular: the chairmanship of council configurations; the extension of qualified majority voting; non-institutional matters, with particular reference to economic and financial provisions. the debate confirmed the existence of different positions among the member states and the substantially balanced nature of the proposals contained in the draft constitutional treaty approved by the convention. it has become clear that the reopening of discussion on specific aspects of the convention text leads to the repetition of opposing positions and not to the emergence of new forms of consensus. the following conclusions can be drawn from the proceedings of the session: the first is a tendency towards convergence of views on the future manner in which the presidency of the council formations will be exercised, although the subject will have to be reviewed in the context of an overall proposal on all the institutional aspects of the future enlarged union. the vast majority of states are opposed to the establishment of a council for legislative affairs: the italian presidency takes note of this opposition, but will try to do everything possible to ensure that the council for legislative affairs is kept within the treaty at least in a perspective perspective, that is, as a possible evolution of the council system. secondly, confirmation of the divergent positions on the subject of the scope of qualified majority voting: in the light of this situation, the presidency will reflect on the instruments for finding consensus solutions, particularly in sensitive and crucial areas such as taxation, own resources, judicial cooperation in criminal matters and police cooperation, while remaining firm that the draft convention remains the main basis for building a balanced and ambitious agreement. thirdly, the member states are clearly over-emphasizing other non-institutional issues, which are clearly incompatible with the igc calendar, which was defined in thessaloniki and confirmed by the heads of state and government in brussels. the presidency will examine this group of subjects on the basis of a selective approach, identifying those areas where an alternative consensus to the draft convention appears to be emerging and those requiring technical and drafting clarifications. it will then be for the member states to decide whether to insist on specific and minority points, bringing the matter to the attention of heads of state or government if necessary. based on the draft convention and the work of the foreign ministers, the presidency will formulate an overall proposal focusing on the institutional and defence package which will seek to take account of the needs of the acceding and candidate member states. the proposal will, however, be based on the draft convention and aim to achieve compromises which are at least as ambitious and noble. we are open to considering possible adaptations, but we are firmly against subversion and backwardness. the outcome of these negotiations will very likely determine the future of the european constitution. for this reason, and in view of the importance of the stakes, the approach to the constitutional negotiations will have to be characterised by a good margin of flexibility on the part of all the actors called upon to lay the foundations of the union of the 21st century. we must abandon particularism and break away from the logic of fair return, whereby for each individual concession a return equal to the cost incurred must be obtained. this is - or rather, would be - an approach which runs counter to the very concept of european integration and which, if systematically applied, would risk undermining the very foundations of the union itself. although fairness is an indispensable condition for any constitutional pact, no one can put a brake on the current evolution of the integration process. those who wish to do so will have to assume their responsibilities to history, to their european partners and, above all, to their own citizens. the adoption of the new constitution will be a success for all or a failure for the union: there can be no substantial conflict between national interest and european interest. commission. mr president, the commission proposal, as the house knows, aims at replacing the current asia and latin america regulation with a new, simple and modern legal framework, consistent with the principles underpinning the reform of external aid. this has already been done for other regions. it is now time for our partner countries in asia and latin america to benefit from the advantages of this reform. from the beginning, it has been clear that some misgivings were developing in parliament with regard to the premise and to the very nature of the new regulation. i have spent more time discussing those misgivings and this piece of legislation than any other for which i have been responsible since i have been a commissioner. i do not think i have had more meetings, more discussions in the commission or more conversations in parliament. i very much respect those of my interlocutors who have not agreed with me. the honourable gentleman mr salafranca knows a huge amount about the subject, but my sympathies and my intellect on this occasion are with some of those who spoke in the later stages of the debate, who also know a huge amount about development assistance: the honourable lady mrs kinnock, the honourable gentleman mr whitehead, and the honourable gentleman and my honourable friend, mr deva. let me just touch on some of the principal arguments. first, there has been a strong call in certain quarters of this house for two regulations instead of one. second, as the many amendments which have been tabled illustrate, there is also a strong wish for a more detailed regulation. i should like to respond to both these issues, and to reiterate the commission’s position on the form of the regulation. the commission attaches great importance to having a simple and a single regulation.why a simple regulation? so as to comply with the basic principles of the reform of external assistance, which requires flexibility in order to adapt cooperation to the specific needs of our partners by means of country strategy papers. that is the policy which parliament has enthusiastically endorsed. why a single regulation? so as to avoid the proliferation of legal instruments and the multiplication of procedures and committees; in short, to be more effective. also, to comply with the interinstitutional agreement on better lawmaking which calls for simplifying and reducing the volume of legislation. i have yet to hear a single argument as to why – the rules and the objectives being the same for both regions – two separate regulations would be better than one. as i have said on a number of occasions, i find it difficult to believe that if we were to follow the views of some in this parliament and support two regulations, there would be dancing in the streets in la paz or dancing in the streets even around the latin american embassies in brussels. references to other regions with their ‘own’ regulation – tacis and cards, for example – are, in my judgment, hardly convincing, since the objectives of these regulations are not those of development policy as set out in article 177 of the treaty and which apply equally to asia and latin america. nor do the differences between the two regions justify two regulations, as the similarity, and even uniformity, of the amendments proposed for each region tend to prove. but let us now turn to the substance of the amendments, and to the four most important issues on which, in my view, our further discussions should focus. first, there is the overall objective of poverty reduction and eradication. some of the amendments aim at stressing poverty alleviation and eradication as an overriding objective. i could not agree more. however, there must also be room for the broad support for overall community relations with asia and latin america, including support for capacity-building to help our partners in their fight against terrorism, illegal migration, trafficking in human beings and international crime. second, a subject which has been touched on in, for example, technical terms by my honourable friend, mr deva: the question of allocation of financial resources between latin america and asia the commission proposal seeks to respect, for the period 2000-2006, the broad 60/40 balance of appropriations for asia and latin america which has prevailed during the previous financial perspectives. this balance was slightly disrupted by events in afghanistan and international pledges made there by the european union. however, it must be borne in mind that asia still has by far the largest amount of poverty in the world - around 800 million people, or about two thirds of the world’s poor, live on less than one dollar a day. it is also important to bear in mind that assistance from the community budget per capita in asia amounts to eur 0.15, compared to eur 0.45 for latin america. on this basis, i would find shifting resources from asia to latin america hard to defend. of course, if the budgetary authority was to give us more money for external assistance for asia and latin america, i would be delighted to propose to parliament ways of spending it, but i do not think that christmas is going to come early this year. third, there is the question of a solidarity fund for latin america. supporting sectoral programmes linked to health, education and poverty alleviation in latin america’s poorest countries and regions could be achieved by means of the programming and implementation instruments which we have at our disposal. setting up a fund, seeking the participation of other financial institutions and agreeing on the rules governing the fund and its management would not only be wasteful but would also be a complicated and cumbersome process. the commission does not have the human resources for this task. fourth, and finally, is the question of sectoral targets and benchmarks. parliament proposes to introduce a number of sectoral targets in the regulation: 35% for social infrastructure and, within this figure, 20% for basic education and health; another 10% for the environment and up to 15% for civil society. all this adds up to nearly 60% of appropriations which would be 'pre-programmed'. as members of the committee on development and cooperation know, the current agreement on a benchmark of 35% for social infrastructure was reached two years ago after long discussions, in which i myself took part, between representatives of the commission and the development committee. i do not intend to re-open those discussions, and indeed it is the commission’s intention to remain absolutely faithful to that agreement. however, i would like to stress that it will not be in line with this agreement to add new conditions, in particular the 20% for basic education. furthermore, this contradicts the principle of country ownership and the very essence of the reform which entails that programming cannot be pre-defined by means of a regulation. the problem – at least that of the proposed 35% for social infrastructure – is rather theoretical, since in current country strategy papers for asia and latin america, 50% and 46% respectively have already been earmarked for social infrastructure. in conclusion, i should like to thank very warmly the rapporteur, mrs sanders-ten holte, for her very valiant efforts to bridge gaps. she has made a really wonderful effort, and there must have been times when she wished she had been reporting on a different regulation. i would like to invite parliament to support the commission proposals. informal discussions with the council – i just throw this in for information – have shown firm support for the commission proposal, and a great willingness to move ahead along those lines. above all, the interests of populations in need in asia and latin america should encourage us to do our utmost for the speedy adoption of a high-quality new legal framework for cooperation.
