commission. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, in 2002 the three european institutions worked together to put in place a new financial regulation, and this now provides a clear framework for the grants with which we support a large number of leading european organisations in the fields of culture, youth and education. now any funding decision must be justified on a legal basis. this obligation applies in particular to grants which, until now, were financed on the basis of headings which, because they were included in the budget nomenclature, were treated as administrative expenditure and which could be implemented without a legal basis. the amendment of the budget nomenclature introduced by the new financial regulation puts an end to this assimilation to administrative expenditure and therefore calls for legal bases for the grants concerned. and it is this new obligation that led the commission to present, last spring, seven proposals for new legal bases. these seven proposals, covering seven different areas, were accompanied by a communication from mrs schreyer highlighting the common context which justified their presentation, as well as the essential elements chosen to provide a similar response from one proposal to another to the common problems faced by these sectors of activity. mr president, today's vote concerns three of the seven legal bases for which rapid treatment was required, especially since these are texts adopted under codecision. i am grateful to mr rocard for having taken account of this urgency and for having ensured that the committee on culture, youth, education, the media and sport, which he chairs, could proceed swiftly with the examination of the commission's proposals. however, the shift from one budgetary approach to another may lead to severe financial difficulties, the consequences of which could be dramatic for the europe of culture, youth and education if the co-legislators do not reach an agreement as soon as possible. the proposals the commission has put to you are designed to ensure a smooth and smooth transition from the old system to the new one, and we have endeavoured to draw up texts which largely reflect the 2003 implementation arrangements, with a view to ensuring this essential continuity and not losing any of the advantages that taking account of the new financial regulation can bring us in terms of the sound management of public funds. in this context, the proposed legal bases must be seen as a technical adjustment and the temptation is great, however, to take this opportunity to provide them with innovations and improvements. but the best is the enemy of the good, especially if these additions compromise the whole in the council's eyes. and in this sense, the commission's proposals have been formulated soberly, with the essential aim of preserving the acquis, by giving it a legal structure in line with the new financial regulation. i would ask you not to stray too far from the commission's proposals and to give priority to all that will enable these legal bases to be adopted as soon as possible. in the case of the legal basis 'culture', the margin of manoeuvre is all the narrower as the council must act unanimously. such a margin of manoeuvre must be preserved not only in culture but also in youth and education, three areas which, it must be said, are essential to the development of europe. all the means of compromise must be explored if they can enable us to bring these procedures to a conclusion as quickly as possible. from 1 january 2004, in the absence of a legal basis, it will simply be impossible for us to provide financial support to all these bodies which contribute to the creative, cultural and intellectual vitality of europe. in other words, a first-reading agreement is essential if these bodies are to be paid in january 2004. in all three cases the commission's proposal followed the provisions of the financial regulation and it is on this same basis that i would like to clarify the commission's position on the amendments contained in the three reports. i congratulate mrs iivari, mrs prets and mrs pack on the considerable work they have done on this action, and they have fully grasped the decisiveness of it. we note that the duration of the programmes - five years for culture and education and three years for youth - has been assessed differently. we are happy to accept amendment no 16, culture, which proposes to reduce the proposed duration of the programme to three years, if this can bring the various institutions closer together to complete the procedures. we reject amendment no 8, on youth, and insist on 2006 as the deadline, because we would like to set up a new youth programme as early as 2007 which gives priority to the participation of european youth organisations. linked to the question of duration is the question of budget, in all three cases. amendment no 17, culture, reducing the budget would be acceptable if amendment no 16 reducing the duration of the programme is adopted. furthermore, if the duration is not changed, amendment no 11, youth, which proposes an increase in the budget, is acceptable to meet the challenges of enlargement. on the education side, we can accept in part or in spirit a group of amendments - 4, 6, 8, 9, 10, 11 - aimed at amending, in line with the changes in the 2004 budgetary process, the financial envelope and the maximum and minimum percentages of this envelope for each action of the programme. the guiding principle of the financial regulation is that the ultimate aim is to have calls for proposals open to all, the exception being the earmarking method, which is sometimes used at present to award grants. in order to facilitate the transition to the financial regulation, the commission has encouraged a mixed system of calls for proposals and budgetary earmarking for strand 2 of the cultural base. we therefore accept amendment no 18, but we must reject amendments nos 5, 15, 19, 20 and 23, which are too far removed from the situation we are trying to regularize. in this context, the criteria must be clear or more clearly defined. we therefore agree with amendment no 10, on youth, and disagree with amendment no 1, on culture, which stray too far from the financial regulation in its redefinition of bodies pursuing an aim of general european interest. and in this respect, we will not be able to accept amendment no 5 on education, which concerns the international federation of european houses (fime), and which wants to add it to the list of bodies covered by action 1, because, on the one hand, fime plays an intermediary role in the redistribution of grants, which excludes it from the scope of action described in the financial regulation, and, on the other hand, an audit of the grant activities carried out by the commission in recent years has been launched in view of the legacy of the past. however, i would point out that the commission has already put in place a phasing out of privileged collaboration activities with independent networks such as fime. in addition, fime and its affiliated european houses were invited to respond to calls for proposals launched by the commission either at central level or at national level, via the representations. each call for proposals shall be subject to a panel of experts, composed of external experts or commission officials, as appropriate, in order to ensure its objectivity and transparency. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the protection of the environment and the environmentally friendly use of energy. mr president, while adhering to these principles, the commission cannot accept these amendments which do not correspond to the provisions on relations between the institutions laid down in the comitology decision, or which interfere with the commission's executive powers. these are amendments nos 11, 21, 22, 13, 14, 15, 15, 22, 23 on culture and education. however, we agree with amendment no 17, youth, which proposes that parliament be informed of the annual implementation of our youth actions. the commission naturally imposes an obligation on those who have received a european grant to make adequate publicity of it. while we share parliament's view on this point, it seems more appropriate to include this obligation of publicity in the annex. that is why the commission accepts amendment no 12, culture, but cannot accept amendment no 3. the same situation would lead us to accept amendment no 20 on youth and reject amendment no 6, or to accept amendment no 12 on education and reject amendment no 2. the financial regulation makes it a rule to apply degressivity to operating grants renewed annually. this decline is not always well perceived and attempts have been made in various quarters to circumvent it. we cannot accept amendments nos 13 and 14, which seek to abolish degressivity. the only exception recognised by the financial regulation concerns cases where the beneficiaries have the characteristics of a european organisation of general interest within the meaning of that regulation. three youth amendments, 5, 18, 19 want to restrict the programme to youth organisations with such characteristics, which we accept. on the other hand, other amendments go much further in the opposite direction and we cannot accept either the youth amendment 24 or the culture amendment 24, both of which propose a considerable increase in the rate of decline. mr president, i shall quickly turn to the amendments with which the commission agrees and which are intended either to clarify or simplify the text or to strengthen it in line with the committee on budgets' rapporteur for the opinion. the commission has already made a number of proposals to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. there is no doubt that the committee on budgets has jurisdiction over the aspects of cofinancing and degressivity. however, the committee on culture voted against the amendment by the committee on budgets on these two points, on the grounds that it was contradictory to the other elements of the report. this is the crux of the matter, not only in relation to the three reports we are discussing today, but also in relation to the enhanced cooperation procedure in general. this procedure is intended to facilitate cooperation between the committees responsible and to strengthen the role of the committee responsible for delivering an opinion. but if there is not enough time to facilitate this cooperation from the outset and if, in addition, it is sufficient for the committee responsible for the subject-matter to table a single amendment contradicting the one tabled by the committee responsible for delivering an opinion, rule 162a is automatically annulled. and that is precisely what has happened in the committee on culture, with the opinion of the committee on budgets. that is to say, after article 162a, we automatically apply article 162, that is to say, we issue a normal and ordinary opinion. i am convinced that article 162a itself contains the trap, and that as it is currently worded it only serves to create unnecessary conflict between committees rather than to encourage cooperation between them. i therefore believe that it is essential that the committee on constitutional affairs should look into this article for the future, either for revision or for its complete elimination. i would like to return to the substance of the proposals and focus on two aspects: cofinancing and degressivity, which have raised the most problems. these are two fundamental aspects of the general system of granting grants because they allow the beneficiary to share responsibility for the proper implementation of the grant and also allow organizations not to depend solely and exclusively on the community grant to operate, thus favouring its implementation in the future. in addition, degressivity allows the money recovered through this route to be used in this case to subsidize new partnerships, especially those of the enlargement countries. the commission therefore proposes that all these grants be cofinanced and gradually reduced. however, i cannot help expressing my surprise at the fact that the commission has applied different percentages of both degressivity and co-financing to these three proposals, which are the responsibility of the same directorate-general. if article 109 of the financial regulation enshrines equal treatment as one of the principles for granting grants, there is no justification for associations which have the same objective but which operate in different fields to be treated differently. the amendment adopted by the committee on budgets sought to ensure that all associations receiving a grant under the seven programmes - depending on the different groups of associations identified - had the same rights and obligations in terms of co-financing and degressivity. in addition, in the case of co-financing, it was not a question of setting fixed percentages but of establishing minimum rates which would then enable the executive authority to apply the percentages in accordance with the actual needs or possibilities of each association. i would like to stress that this was not an attempt at harmonization but the application of the principle of equal treatment. the committee on culture, culture, education, information and sport has also taken the view that the commission's proposal is not a step-by-step approach, but that all associations eligible for a grant are of general european interest, in accordance with the derogation provided for in article 113 (2) of the financial regulation. in my view, this is too broad an interpretation and i cannot help but doubt that all these associations are really in the general european interest. the committee on culture seems to have interpreted the continuing degressivity of the committee on budgets as a kind of punishment for these associations when, in reality, it favours - together with co-financing and as i said before - their implementation for the future, because nowhere is it written that these subsidies are granted ad eternum. on the contrary, the day that, for one reason or another, that tap runs out, all the associations could be in serious trouble. finally, as i said in my speech on subsidies in the last part-session, the lack of time has had a relentless effect on the whole procedure. time has conditioned the commission itself in the presentation of its proposals and time has also conditioned the amended proposals which we are presenting to the house today. anyone who has studied them will have realized that there is more than one contradiction. i suppose we are all guilty and victims of this situation, but what concerns me most is to what extent the position of the european parliament will be strengthened after tomorrow's vote, because what we have, collectively, ahead of us is a difficult conciliation with the council, since it does not seem to be willing to give in on those points which it considers fundamental, such as pre-allocation, co-financing and degressivity, or the financial allocation of the programmes. - the next item is the report (a5-0279/2003) by mrs karamanou, on behalf of the committee on women's rights and equal opportunities, on women in the new information society (2003/2047 (ini)).
the rapporteur. - (el) mr president, madam commissioner, you are aware that the lack of access to new technologies and computer literacy are increasingly leading to new forms of social exclusion that directly threaten women. the evidence to date has revealed huge gender gaps in education and the labour market. the report i wrote on behalf of the committee on women's rights and equal opportunities first lists the reasons, such as social stereotypes and cultural prejudices, which restrict girls' choices and hinder their career development, as well as the more general negative consequences for the economy of a poor appreciation of human potential. we know that in the last decade, 3 million new jobs have been created, of which 1.6 million were filled by women. however, it should be noted that more than 60% of the new jobs created were in the high-tech sector, where women are underrepresented, particularly at the highest levels of technical expertise and decision-making. thus, in the current circumstances, economic development in the modern technology sector exacerbates structural weaknesses and widenes the gender gap. the division of labour continues to be gendered, with men predominating in new technologies and women in the lowest-paid, least-skilled and least secure jobs. not only are women significantly underrepresented in research and science, but they are underrepresented in some scientific fields and completely absent in others; they are significantly underrepresented at all levels of the scientific hierarchy and have fewer opportunities to receive research funding. of the 500 000 researchers working in industry in europe, only 50 000 are women. in the public sector, universities and research centres, the proportion varies from one quarter to one third, but in the most senior positions, it is less than 12%. the situation is even worse in industrial research, with the new technologies being the main target. better access for women to the research sector would certainly enrich scientific methods, themes and subjects. at the same time, in the media sector, women journalists are not represented or involved in administrative positions. no attention is paid to the problem of discrimination against women and images of women that have nothing to do with reality are often projected in the media. at the same time, the internet is still dominated by men and is primarily targeted at men, which gives rise to discrimination. surveys reveal differences in the way women and men use internet services. similarly, there are worrying data on the low proportion of women using the internet in the candidate countries. in order to increase the number of women in education and training in new technologies, my report proposes the integration of computers and the internet from the first years of primary education in order to encourage young girls to study in the right direction. studies show that early exposure to science and technology could change women's attitudes before the emergence of stereotyped attitudes affecting their behaviour. the lisbon strategy and the employment guidelines will have to be applied in a way that limits the segregation of the labour market according to sex, with a concentration of women in certain lower-skilled, lower-paid and low-advancement jobs. the commission and the member states must therefore commit themselves, making full use of the structural funds and, in particular, the social fund, to training in new technologies, with a special focus on women's access to or return to the labour market, always in the context of the lisbon objectives. at the same time, gender equality policies and programmes should be implemented that specifically address vocational training, lifelong learning, work-life balance and the equitable sharing of family responsibilities between men and women, which will facilitate women's participation in the information society. particular attention will need to be paid to multimedia content, to promote positive images of women, such as their surprising achievements at all levels of education. we call on the european commission and the member states to promote the full and equal participation of women in the media, including in the areas of administration, planning, management, education and screening. at the same time, policies should be adopted to improve working conditions in new sectors such as teleworking. particular attention should be paid to improving women's access to the internet and new technologies through the deployment of important technological infrastructure and equipment in rural and semi-urban areas, which are not sufficiently served, in particular in the poorest regions and in enlargement countries. all eu policies should promote a strategy to preserve the basic infrastructure, which will provide access, facilities and connectivity for every home, school, public building and library. to combat social exclusion, priority must be given to the most vulnerable categories of girls and women: migrant women, women with disabilities, single mothers, women farmers, etc. the commission also needs to gather additional statistics on structural differences in the information technology sector so that we can investigate the actual participation of women, their representation and labour market trends. the committee on women's rights and equal opportunities would like to point out that, until now, the gender dimension has been totally ignored in the new technology sector. we therefore call on the council and the commission to submit concrete proposals for a strategy and to contribute to the inclusion of horizontal policies for gender equality at the united nations world summit on the information society, to be held in geneva in december 2003. the digital economy offers women challenges and opportunities; the challenges that women face are different from those faced by men and are based on the different roles and places they occupy within the family and society. the integration of the gender dimension in the development of new technologies does not only raise the issue of access, quantitative participation and equitable representation of women. it also raises a deeper issue and provides an opportunity for a critical assessment of the culture of the information society, with its values, strategies and development objectives and the involvement of human resources. i hope that my report will contribute to the public debate on the kind of information society we want.
- the next item is the report (a5-0344/2003) by mrs roure, on behalf of the committee on civil liberties and human rights, on the initiative of the hellenic republic with a view to adopting a council regulation on the creation of a network of immigration liaison officers (9870/2003 - c5-0260/2003 - 2003/0817 (cns)).
the european council meeting in thessaloniki on 19 and 20 june concluded that it was necessary to speed up work towards the adoption, before the end of 2003, of a legal instrument to formally create a network of immigration liaison officers. the idea is that all these immigration liaison officers from the member states, posted in the same third country, work effectively together, in networks, to contribute to the progressive establishment of a coordinated and integrated management of the external borders. the regulation proposed by greece should provide a framework to formalise and strengthen this existing informal cooperation between liaison officers. ideally, we would have community immigration liaison officers with their own functions, trained and paid by the union, but unfortunately neither the competence nor the budget exists yet and some states are still too reluctant. the liaison officers are the external representatives of the member states and some do not welcome any loss of their national prerogatives. in the meantime, this new proposal for a regulation is, in my view, a step towards greater transparency. the tasks of liaison officers are essentially threefold: they are to contribute to the prevention of illegal immigration and the fight against smugglers, to assist in the return of illegal immigrants and to contribute to the management of legal immigration. the latter point, however, remains a mystery, since no article of the rules of procedure specifies the form this management might take, and yet it seems to me to be an essential point. so there is a gap to be filled. because, contrary to what some would have us believe, the foreigner is not dangerous, he is in danger. the person who leaves his country, his ties, to immigrate to the european union is a person who has important, often vital reasons for doing so. and any of us, in the same economic, social, psychological and emotional conditions would probably do the same. it seems to me therefore essential to disseminate information on legal immigration routes in the countries concerned. and for that, it seems necessary that we are clear, each other, about our immigration policy, which is not really the case at the moment. it also seems to me essential to warn people against the risk of falling into the hands of unscrupulous smugglers or of being caught up in a trafficking network. however, in order for these measures to be really effective, i would ask the member states to ensure that they do not organise a certain degree of secrecy themselves. to do this, i think they should act in two directions. first, the status of temporary workers. studies of undeclared work in agriculture in europe reveal that undeclared overtime, the development of illegal and sometimes even slave-like forms of recruitment of agricultural labour, are increasing in the member states. the large distribution chains often put pressure on producers, who then resort to unemployed and illegal workers, and it is unthinkable to accept contracts that place the worker in a zone of sub-rights. i would like to emphasize that very often the tightening of legislation reduces the number of legal immigrants and increases the number of illegal immigrants, which in any case does not prevent them from being adopted. on the other hand, it is essential to avoid assimilation between immigration and organised crime. illegal immigrants are not criminals. these are human beings who were not lucky enough to be born in the right place. the different roles of liaison officers, immigration liaison officers, airport liaison officers, document advisers, technical advisers and consular services, all of whom deal with immigration matters, should therefore be more clearly defined, and it seems appropriate to define the scope of the activities and tasks of liaison officers. the aim was to ensure that the training they should receive was harmonised, even if only partially. some of the liaison officers interviewed in a report drawn up by the danish presidency see this as a prerequisite for the emergence of a genuine network. this training could normally be provided in the form of seminars and workshops, which would have the undeniable advantage of allowing personal contacts to be established, which is the very essence of a network. in conclusion, i would like to stress that immigration should not be seen as a threat under any circumstances. under no circumstances should illegal immigrants be considered criminals. they are victims because they had the misfortune to be born into a land of suffering; victims because they are desperate and seeking compassion. if the european union is not able to understand this, then progress and the civilized world must despair.

- the next item is the report (a5-0361/2003) by mr hernández mollar, on behalf of the committee on civil liberties and human rights, on the proposal for a european parliament recommendation to the council on minimum standards for procedural guarantees for suspects and accused persons in criminal proceedings in the european union (2003/2179 (ini)).
the rapporteur. - (es) mr president, commissioners, ladies and gentlemen, i should like to begin by stressing the importance and significance of the recommendation we are debating today. today we are examining the first initiative, which took the form of a green paper, the purpose of which is to consider, together with other instruments, the future proposal for a framework decision which will regulate - as its title indicates - minimum standards for procedural guarantees for suspects and accused persons in criminal proceedings throughout the european union. judicial cooperation between the member states of the european union, both civil and criminal, has reached levels that were unimaginable a few years ago. these levels will peak when the european arrest warrant comes into force in early 2004, if things continue as they are and despite some difficulties that seem to persist in some member states. that is why, at the moment, as the building of an area of freedom, security and justice progresses and terrorism, organised crime and illegal immigration are increasingly a concern, there is better cooperation between police forces and judicial bodies in the member states, and it is becoming essential that we stop ignoring the necessary minimum standards for suspects and accused persons in criminal proceedings so that their right to a fair and impartial trial is guaranteed at all times. therefore, the aim of the recommendations we are discussing today is simply to achieve a certain degree of unification of procedural practices in the member states, on the basis of the rights established by the european convention on human rights, the case law of the strasbourg court and the charter of fundamental rights of the european union, but also in the context of the judicial and criminal convergence which is now a reality within the european union and which is based on mutual recognition, described by the tampere european council as the cornerstone of judicial cooperation at civil and criminal levels in the european union. it was at this same important european council that the groundwork was laid for us to be here today to discuss minimum standards of procedural safeguards for suspects and accused persons in criminal proceedings in the european union, as it stressed the need to work on those aspects of procedural law for which it is considered necessary to have common minimum standards in order to facilitate the application of the principle of mutual recognition, while respecting the fundamental legal principles of the member states. the green paper sets out the reasons why the proposals have been reduced to the five rights it mentions: legal aid, translation and interpretation, information on rights, protection of vulnerable suspects and accused persons and consular assistance. i wonder, commissioner, mr president, whether it would not have been useful to take account, in one way or another, of the types of crime affecting all or a majority of the member states - which, to a certain extent, would have completed the necessary unification of procedural practices. the admissibility and probative value of evidence, in absentia judgments and the rules on provisional release are left for later - and i would like to take this opportunity to ask the commissioner where the work is going - because these are issues which some groups have wanted to include in the recommendation, although that is not its purpose. i think that the approach adopted in the design of the green paper is reasonable, because it is still undeniable that the criminal justice system is the heart of the sovereignty of states and is therefore very inflexible when it comes to establishing important common procedures and systems. and even if the particularities of each european society and its own legal culture must be considered as the reasons for this resistance, criminal procedure is also a system that imposes limits on the state, which measures the quality of the state in terms of the rule of law and respect for the citizen, something that this house, as the ultimate expression of its will, must always defend. there is no doubt that this issue is therefore timely, which does not lead us to believe that the instruments adopted so far - such as the european arrest warrant - have undermined the fundamental rights and minimum standards applicable to our fellow citizens, but nevertheless makes it necessary to complete progress in this direction by a certain unification of procedural guarantees. apart from that, i must reject the two amendments tabled by the greens/efa group and the gue/ngl group, which seek to make the entry into force of the european arrest warrant conditional on the entry into force of the framework decision on procedural guarantees. i reject these amendments because the date for the entry into force of the european arrest warrant is january 2004 and because the european arrest warrant is itself based on mutual trust between the different legal systems of the member states, even though it is essential that the minimum standards imposed by the framework decision be implemented swiftly and as soon as possible. i simply wanted to highlight the most controversial point and the one which has given rise to the greatest differences between certain political groups. finally, i cannot pass up this opportunity to thank the political groups for the almost unanimous support which this report received in committee and which i hope will be repeated tomorrow.
the commission has already made a number of recommendations to the council, and i am sure that the council will be able to accept them. what we have today is the first initiative, in the form of a green paper, to reflect, together with other bodies, on the future proposal for a framework decision which will regulate - as its title says - the minimum standards of procedural guarantees for suspects and accused persons in criminal proceedings in the european union. the level of judicial cooperation between the member states of the european union, both in civil and criminal matters, is reaching levels that were unimaginable years ago. the european arrest warrant will come into force at the beginning of 2004, as planned, despite some difficulties which still seem to exist in some member states. that is why, at a time when the construction of a european area of freedom, security and justice is progressing and there is growing concern about terrorism, organised crime and illegal immigration, there is an increase in cooperation between the police and judicial authorities of the member states and it is essential to stop ignoring for a longer time the necessary guarantees which suspects and accused persons must enjoy in criminal proceedings so that their right to a fair and impartial trial is guaranteed at all times. the recommendations we are discussing today are therefore aimed at achieving a certain unification of procedural practices in the member states, on the basis of the rights enshrined in the european convention on human rights, the case law of the court of justice of strasbourg and the charter of fundamental rights of the union, and in the context of the legal and criminal convergence which is now being achieved in the european union, based on mutual recognition, described as the cornerstone of judicial cooperation in civil and criminal matters of the union by the tampere european council itself. it was at this important european council that the foundations were laid for the debate we are having here today on minimum procedural guarantees for suspects and accused persons in criminal proceedings within the union, as it stressed the need to work on those aspects of procedural law in respect of which it is considered necessary to have common minimum standards to facilitate the application of the principle of mutual recognition, while respecting the fundamental legal principles of the member states. the green paper explains why its proposals have been limited to the five rights set out in the green paper: legal assistance, translation and interpretation, communication of rights, protection of vulnerable suspects and accused persons and consular assistance. i wonder, mr commissioner, mr president, whether it would not have been useful to have also reflected on the types of crime which concern all or most of the member states, which would have supplemented the necessary unification of procedural practices. the conditions for obtaining and validating evidence, the sentences for contempt of court and the provision of provisional release pending trial - and i take this opportunity to ask the commissioner how the work is going - are matters which some groups have insisted on including in the recommendation, even though that is not its purpose. in my view, the approach adopted in the green paper is sound, because it remains an unshakable reality that criminal jurisdiction is the hard core of the sovereignty of states, and is therefore very unwieldy when it comes to establishing common substantive - the next item is the report (a5-0265/2003) by mrs honeyball, on behalf of the committee on economic and monetary affairs and industrial policy, on the communication from the commission on the taxation of passenger cars in the european union (com (2002) 431 - c5-0573/2002 - 2002/2260 (ini)).
commission. mr president, the operation of 15 different systems for the taxation of passenger cars within the european union has resulted in tax obstacles, distortions and inefficiencies which prevent both the european citizens and the car industry, and trade, from fully benefiting from the advantages of the single market. as a result, commission and parliament are receiving numerous queries and petitions each year on this one particular issue. on 9 september 2002 the commission presented a long-awaited communication on taxation of passenger cars, which received a warm welcome at the time from all parties concerned. the communication aimed, on the one hand, at providing options for action at community level which would remove tax obstacles on the movement of new and used passenger cars, which would not incur any revenue loss for the national budgets and would not increase a total burden for the citizens. on the other hand, it also provided some policy measures which would establish a more direct relationship between taxation levels and the polluting emissions of passenger cars, thus contributing to the community's environmental objectives under the kyoto protocol. the commission considered it necessary to launch this debate with the member states, the european parliament and with important stakeholders before launching any proposal on passenger cars. this pragmatic approach allowed for a more favourable position on behalf of the member states on a potential fresh proposal compared to the position they took in 1998 on the previous proposal which still remains on the table in the council. the commission hopes that the european parliament will provide strong support to the policy measures included in the communication and thus reinforce the commission's position during future discussions at the council. i am happy to see that strong support already appears in the opinions provided to the committee on economic and monetary affairs by both the committee on the environment, public health and consumer policy and the committee on regional policy, transport and tourism. i regret to note, however, that this support is not as strong in the final - mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, i congratulate the commission on its initiative and my colleague on her excellent report. it is true that today the tax on private cars in the union is, as we say in catalan, a real calaix de sastre, that is to say a couturier's drawer. the report rightly points out that the functioning of the internal market is affected by the diversity, heterogeneity and sometimes complexity of taxation systems. the commission and the report are therefore right to deal with this issue in order to improve conditions for competition. it seems very appropriate to consider taxing the use of vehicles rather than their acquisition. the commission is therefore right to propose the abolition of the registration fee and to introduce or increase taxes on traffic, fuel and the use of certain road infrastructure. it is a matter of giving priority to environmental criteria in order to achieve the kyoto objectives, as the report rightly reminds us. on the other hand, as regards diesel vehicles, i agree with my colleague that they should be given tax advantages. indeed, studies on this subject seem to conclude that the emissions of these engines are much lower than those of the others. the logical consequence of the polluter pays principle is to tax less those who pollute less. however, it must never be forgotten that from an environmental point of view and also because of geopolitical considerations, the ultimate objective must be the replacement of current fuels by non-polluting and non-conflict energy sources. to this end, all efforts to find new sources of energy, such as hydrogen, should be welcomed.
commission. mr president, political realism has led the commission to initiate consultation with the council, the european parliament and important stakeholders on passenger car taxation before drafting any legislative proposal on this issue. i understand that many members of parliament would have preferred a more ambitious report, especially as far as the measures to be taken against the fragmentation of the internal market are concerned. the commission will take the conclusion of this report seriously into account before taking any initiative in this area. the fact that a number of different approaches have been voiced in this room tonight provides an indication of how difficult it will be to reach a unanimous decision in council on such policy measures. with reference to the conclusions of the report, the commission would like to express its gratitude to the european parliament for the strong support it has given to policy measures, such as those necessary to abolish registration taxes (paragraph 16), to bring forward changes in order to introduce an environmentally-oriented tax system (paragraphs 12 and 13), and to use tax differentials as a tool to promote passenger cars producing less than 120 grammes per kilometre of carbon dioxide emissions (paragraph 7). additionally, the commission agrees in principle with a large number of paragraphs, such as 1, 4, 6, 10, 11, 14, 17, 18, 19 and 21. concerning paragraphs 2, 3 and 15, the commission does not share the view that existing barriers to free circulation of passenger cars within the internal market are due only to administrative practices or procedures. the commission considers that a clear reference to tax barriers, and particularly to double taxation caused by registration taxes, should be stated in these paragraphs, as is the case under the relevant part of the explanatory statement. with regard to paragraph 5, which refers to the annual circulation tax, the commission does not share the view that this tax does not affect the functioning of the internal market. diversified tax bases and important divergences in act levels can provide an incentive to citizens to register their car in a member state other than the one where they normally reside, which means this tax does affect the internal market. with regard to amendment 2, the commission does not support including safety of passenger cars among its objectives. the danger would be that the possible effect of fiscal incentives would be watered down. moreover, the problem of road accidents could be better addressed by other instruments such as speed cameras, fines, education, separate bicycle lanes and so on. i listened with great interest to the brief altercation between some british members of parliament, whilst thinking of minister dawn primarolo, who spent four years ironing out harmful tax measures. if one really were in favour of unlimited tax competition, why would one want to iron out so-called harmful tax measures? next time such members of parliament who have spoken on this matter meet minister primarolo, they might perhaps give her a piece of their mind and tell her that she has wasted four years of her time in trying to stamp out fiscal competition. that said, i should like once again to thank parliament and the rapporteur for their efforts and their supportive report.

which in the case of the agreement were in the form of recommendations by the international maritime organisation - compulsory in order to ensure the maximum level of protection envisaged and to avoid divergent interpretations from one member state to another. it establishes a single national contact point for the monitoring of the protection measures for ships and port facilities and provides for an inspection process, supervised by the commission, to verify the implementation of the national plans adopted under this regulation. the proposal adapts certain provisions agreed within the international maritime organisation for the benefit of national maritime traffic of states by extending the scope of imo safeguards to passenger ships on domestic voyages more than 20 nautical miles from the coast, extending the scope to other passenger ships and to cargo ships for domestic transport to a certain extent, and providing for adaptation procedures for ships on regular services. i would remind you once again that the international maritime organisation has insisted that these protective measures apply to maritime traffic from 1 july 2004. the main objective of this proposal for a regulation is to enable the member states to take the necessary measures within the time limit and thus to comply with the international commitment while ensuring that it is applied uniformly throughout the european union. given the imperative nature of this deadline, i can only support any action which makes it possible to adopt it as quickly as possible without distorting its content. i know that parliament and its rapporteur are fully aware of this and that they have been working all these months with the council to get the text adopted as quickly as possible - - the next item is the debate on the report (b5-0414/2003). we will be discussing a number of questions to the commission. part one
- question no 33 by mr purvis (h-0673/03):is the commission confident that the isps code (international ship and port facility security code) 2002 will be implemented in the eu in due time (1 july 2004) and that all non-eu jurisdictions, including those in countries granting a flag of convenience, will be able to enforce its provisions?
commission. – having had the opportunity to listen to the previous debate, i feel confident that the necessary changes will be manageable within this time. ultimately we will face the problem that it is one thing to have the right to deny access to our ports for ships that do not comply, but that, at the same time, the global spread of this whole idea will be a very strong disincentive for ships under other flags to continue to flout the standards. thus it is a highly meaningful and necessary thing to do.
- question no 34 by mrs flemming (h-0698/03): subject: liberalisation of the water sector as part of its internal market strategy up to 2006 and in line with the green paper on services of general interest, the commission is planning a wide-ranging liberalisation of public services. it seems that this liberalization will also affect the water sector. is the commission really intending to liberalise a sector of services of general interest as important as the water sector? how does the commission intend to justify such a radical infringement of sovereignty in the use of national water resources to the citizens concerned?
commission. – as announced in the internal market strategy: priorities 2003-2006, the commission is presently analysing whether there is scope for improving the efficiency and performance of the water sector. this analysis focuses in particular on how the current competition and internal market rules should be applied to this sector. the commission does not wish to rule any options out at this stage, including the possibility of further legislative measures. as part of its fact-finding, the commission has sent detailed questionnaires to current and future member states with a view to gathering information on the legal and administrative rules and requirements within which the water sector operates. the commission has also held informal discussions with regional and local authorities, business and citizens' organisations, and enterprises involved in the sector. the analysis is still ongoing, so it is too early to draw conclusions. once the analysis is complete, the commission will, of course, present its findings and set out its views on any possible additional steps to be taken, in full respect of treaty guarantees for services of general economic interest and of environmental provisions.
commission. – the line is that the options are open. we are analysing this at the moment and i think it is futile at this stage to speculate on conclusions.
- question no 35 by hedkvist petersen (h-0704/03):trafficking in human beingsit is difficult for thirdcountry nationals seeking protection to enter the european union. recently, there have been terrible disasters in which people seeking a safer existence have died at the union's borders. we must put an end to human trafficking and those who profit from the misery of others. an interesting proposal has been sent to the commission with the aim of reducing the market for smugglers and making the union more accessible to third country nationals. what is the commission's view of a system allowing refugees to apply for a special asylum visa at all eu member states' embassies and consulates around the world? second part
commission. – the commission has long shared the view that there was an urgent need to explore ways of offering rapid access to protection without refugees being at the mercy of illegal immigration or trafficking gangs. that is why we commissioned the study on the feasibility of processing asylum claims outside the european union against the background of the common european asylum system, published in december 2002. the study analysed the possibilities of the europe-wide use of protected entry procedures in regions of origin and examined how such procedures could allow a non-national to approach a potential host state outside its territory with an asylum claim and be granted a permit to enter that country. the commission has since noted, in its communications of march and june 2003, that protection capacities in the region of origin need to be consolidated and protection requests dealt with as closely as possible to needs. this might involve regulating access to the european union by establishing protective entry schemes and resettlement programmes. such measures could also facilitate more orderly arrival in the european union. the thessaloniki european council asked the commission to explore all parameters, in order to ensure the more orderly and managed entry of persons in need of international protection into the european union and to examine ways and means of enhancing protection capacity in the regions of origin. before june 2004 we shall be presenting a comprehensive report suggesting the measures to be taken. meanwhile, the current presidency hosted an experts' seminar in rome on 13 and 14 october which further explored the european council's mandate, focusing in particular on resettlement and protected entry procedures. the advantages and commission. – i share your view that it is quite clearly necessary to develop an asylum system that prevents those in need of international protection from being victimised by criminal gangs. one of the ways to address this objective is to enhance protection in the region, and to allow people to ask for asylum in the embassy of one of the member states. as the honourable member knows, some member states are already doing this. resettlement schemes are already ongoing in at least five member states. we are now studying experience gained in this area to identify the advantages and disadvantages involved in order to make a proposal to allow all member states to use the same scheme. i hope that in the june 2004 report i will be able to put forward concrete proposals in this respect.

- question no 46 by mrs mckenna (h-0648/03) subject: cancellation of the debt of low-income countries what steps does the commission intend to take to solve the problem of debt cancellation for low-income countries? in approving the cancellation of 100% of the debts of the poorest countries, the irish government recognised the need to help countries with a high prevalence of aids and advocated a better consideration of human development when assessing the amount of debt a country can pay. what is the commission's view of this debt policy? can the commission be expected to take formal steps towards adopting a european policy of debt cancellation for low-income countries, and when would this be possible?
commission. – i tried to explain this. the bilateral debt is relatively easy for the donors to manage; it is their own decision. the commission is not in a position to tell individual member states what to do. we have played a crucial role in the most difficult area, namely taking meaningful action on the multilateral debt, and in doing so we have gone far beyond our role as a creditor. what ireland is doing is fine. however, i have to say that in 1995, when i was the danish minister for development cooperation, we announced something similar for the least-developed poor countries. my hesitation about broadening the scope of debt cancellation to, for instance, middle-income countries, is based on the consideration that if we do that we will take money from the least-developed and poorest countries and give it to countries that are relatively much better off. that is not so easy to do in practice. what ireland is doing is commendable and it might inspire other countries to do something similar. however, the commission cannot tell member states to do that.

(es) mr president, commissioner, ladies and gentlemen, after many legislative initiatives, recommendations and studies, the european commission has promoted a thematic strategy for soil protection. the first point of reference - i think, basic - is that the soil is a limited resource, the basis of agriculture and production, of food and the support of the landscape. but perhaps because the horizon always seems to be infinite, society has a hard time believing and assimilating that this is a finite resource and therefore we have to protect it like any other resource. this document is not only about protecting the soil, but also about conserving the land and the landscape, and it is intended to guarantee the safety and health of citizens and to avoid all kinds of risks. i therefore congratulate the commission on its work. it is a well-made document, the starting point is coherent, it has taken many years of work and i know that work is still being done along the same lines. although the text does not have the status of a regulation - and i would like to emphasize this - it is a background document which will generate a number of actions, directives and recommendations and sets out the essential axes which affect the future of soil and landscape conservation. it is what we might call an invisible lever which the commission sometimes uses to shape thinking and attitudes towards problems. as a thematic strategy it aims to develop a scientific policy and to do much firmer, more consistent and coherent work than has been done so far. it's meant to detect cause and effect, impacts. we also recommend that the different character of each soil, its different typology, the diversity of soils be recognized and that measures, solutions and methods adapted to the site and the characteristics of the site be applied. as we have said many times, sustainable development is a tailor-made suit and all scientific work must be adapted to reality. this means that we are entering the realm of complexity and that the commission is accepting the difficult challenge of developing a soil policy which recognises the diversity of each site, each zone, each climate. what does parliament contribute? parliament stressed the need for reference catalogues and catalogues which could be approved, and gave the commission several mandates to provide, as soon as possible, a biography of the soils, typologies, structures and other variables in addition to uses, potential risks and historical, landscape or cultural values, highlighting risks of any kind. i urge the the napoletano report - and we shall be stressing the strategic importance of a stronger and more comprehensive relationship with our mediterranean partners and neighbours. in this context, the conference of euro-mediterranean foreign ministers in naples will bring to a conclusion an objective long sought by this parliament, namely the transformation of the euro-mediterranean forum into a real assembly. that means, in my view, a clear message in favour of strengthening that relationship in all areas and it must have a fundamental objective, which is to ensure the smooth functioning of euro-mediterranean cooperation, because this new assembly will make it possible to ensure the correct application of the european union's association agreements with each and every one of our mediterranean partners and that monitoring has been widely requested by the european parliament. given the broad content of each of these agreements, which includes clauses of a political nature, beyond the purely economic elements, the task of the assembly is, in practice, a political control of relations between the two shores. i think that we must now move forward in four areas. firstly, facilitating free trade, the closer we get to the establishment of a free trade area the more we will contribute to economic and social development by facilitating the emergence of positive synergies. secondly, the definitive setting up of a euro-mediterranean cultural foundation, and i hope that this conference will take concrete decisions in this area. thirdly, we must fight more firmly against the existence of trafficking mafias, which means more active involvement in the fight against illegal immigration. and finally, mr president, i think we cannot forget the countries that are not part of the barcelona process - libya and mauritania. it is precisely to this that parliament's delegation for relations with the maghreb will devote its priority efforts in the coming weeks and months. i would like to conclude, mr president, by saying that i believe there are reasons for welcoming this impetus, which will be institutionally reflected in naples, and for us to work on new initiatives.
(es) mr president, i think this debate should be seen in the context of the one we are going to have this afternoon on relations with the new neighbouring countries. i think we are at a key moment to relaunch those aspects which are lagging behind the barcelona agenda. and i'm especially interested in the cultural and human spheres. i think we have to make a real effort there. there is one area in which we could make this effort, if we are able to work on it in all its complexity: the movement of people and immigration. we should try to make immigration a factor that strengthens relations and stability between countries of origin and destination. we should create positive dynamics that could have an economic impact, introducing concepts such as 'mobility', which are more suited to the times than the rigid and bureaucratic rules with which we want to manage immigration. we should bring back the concept of co-development to our agenda. we can do a lot in this area, by creating european erasmus or by supporting local cooperation in so many areas. and from this global perspective, we could - yes - fight effectively against irregular immigration and its most odious part, which has given us the horrifying images of corpses arriving one after another on our shores. we could fight against illegal immigration, in the hands of human traffickers. a new agenda, based on the proposals of the commission and the greek and italian presidencies before thessaloniki, on immigration and the countries of origin of immigration, could strengthen the human and cultural pillar of the conference. but if the people living among us are to be a factor of stability and a factor in promoting our values, we must also work on integration policy.
(es) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i would like to emphasize an important aspect of the preparations for the naples meeting and i take this opportunity to congratulate the italian presidency on its special attention, which is also very logical, to the mediterranean dimension of european union policy. the aim is to strengthen and implement the euro-mediterranean investment and partnership fund, based on european investment bank credits, to facilitate private investment and private enterprise. as chairman of the mediterranean commission of the european league for economic cooperation, i have been analysing for years the economic causes of the mediterranean third countries' delay in eliminating imbalances with the european union. this is a key aspect, i.e. ensuring growth based on entrepreneurship, on exploiting the potential of these societies, is essential to eliminating existing imbalances. we believe that the fight against imbalances, against economic and social backwardness, lies in large part in economic development based on business and private initiative and i therefore propose that special attention be paid to this and that recommendation no 7 be followed.
(es) mr president, since the barcelona process until today, the whole mediterranean arc has been convulsed by a series of problems which have not only not been solved, but some of them have been worsening in a very alarming way. from the middle east conflict to the intractable situation in the sahara, from the total lack of control over immigration to the almost daily tragedies on our andalusian coasts and in the canary islands, to which human trafficking, drug trafficking and fanatical terrorism are added, which not only punishes some of our neighbouring countries but also uses all means to enter our european territory, these are some of the serious issues that should be of great concern to us in the run-up to the naples conference. we have common problems and we also have mutual responsibilities and each side must assume its own. immigration, for example, can only find a solution if, as called for at the euro-mediterranean forum in bari in june 2002, the countries of origin and those of reception share responsibility for regulating migration flows and for fighting organised mafias that promote illegal immigration. border control is a two-man job, not a one-man job. development cooperation? all that's needed and more. but the political and administrative structures in the mediterranean third countries must be responsive to transparent behaviour, to regimes where respect for human rights makes parliamentary and political dialogue easy and productive, such as the one that must be held in the new assembly, which we are talking about today, so that cooperation is effective, which unfortunately does not happen in some of them, and i avoid mentioning these countries, mr president.
mr president, i wanted to make the house aware of the problem i encountered yesterday. i had asked to be allowed to use the press conference room between 3.30 and 4.00 p.m. to present the case of the catalan independence fighters whose trial was due to take place in the morning before the european court of human rights on alleged acts of torture by the state....
(es) mr president, i would first of all like to congratulate mrs napoletano on her excellent work. europe has changed. the map of europe is being enlarged, and this means that we have new neighbours, and it is necessary to have a policy for this enlarged europe, whose composition coincides with that of the council of europe, and also a neighbourhood policy, and i shall refer specifically to the policy to be pursued in relation to the countries on the southern edge of the mediterranean. the report does not speak of the free movement of people in the mediterranean, but it is clear that with the countries of the southern mediterranean, from which we differ in demography and per capita income, we must establish cooperation relations based on crossborder cooperation systems, which can be summed up in four ideas: know your neighbour, understand him, trust him and, where there is trust, establish cooperation and work together.
(es) mr president, i agree with the commission's proposal and with mrs napoletano's report. as i understand it, it is a matter of recognising that enlargement is not, cannot be and will not be the union's only instrument for building europe and the euro-mediterranean region. that's the point. the enlargement will have a limit. twelve new countries are going to join; we have turkey as well; some more will join in the future. once that limit is reached, we cannot say that we lack the political, economic, security, cultural or human instruments to build europe. in other words, we are shaping a wider architecture which complements the instrument of enlargement and which also needs the deepening represented by the constitution we have in our hands at the moment. if we do not formulate these new neighbourhood policies, we will fall short and, after all, we are already collecting proposals which have been made by people who are very aware of the european situation and who have, of course, my support.

i suggest. on 16 and 17 october this year, the european council reviewed the state of play of the middle east peace process and discussed possible ways forward. it was reiterated that the european union is firmly committed to the clear objective of two states - israel and a viable and democratic palestinian state - living side by side in peace and security, within the framework of a comprehensive peace in the middle east, as set out in the road map. the european union also reiterates its determination to contribute to all aspects of the implementation of the roadmap and notes the importance and urgency of the establishment of a credible and effective monitoring mechanism by an external entity. the european council expressed its deep concern at the situation in the region and noted that, despite the support of the international community for a just and lasting solution, the parties concerned had made insufficient efforts to seize the opportunity for peace set out in the road map, as highlighted in the quartet's recent ministerial statement of 26 september. on the contrary, the growing violence is causing more and more suffering and death for both the israeli and palestinian peoples, and is endangering security in the region and beyond. the european council therefore called on both parties, israel and the palestinian authority, to honour the commitments made at the aqaba summit on 4 june this year. the european council called on all parties in the region to implement immediately policies conducive to dialogue and negotiations. the union's relations with those who act otherwise will inevitably suffer the consequences of such behaviour. the union shall take every opportunity to have the parties accept these positions. the eu-israel association council on 17 and 18 november provided the union with a good opportunity to send a clear political message to the israeli government. the union stressed in particular its concern at the layout of the so-called security wall and the continued expansion of settlements, and reiterated the need for israel, in its fight against terrorism, to avoid civilian casualties and destruction in order not to kratsa-tsagaropoulou, the council considers the geneva agreement to be a positive contribution to the discussion on solutions to the crisis in the middle east, in accordance with the union's position further support efforts to promote rapprochement, the creation of a climate of confidence and the search for a lasting peace. the modalities for reaching a final and comprehensive solution to the israeli-palestinian conflict are set out in the quartet roadmap.

- question no 7 by mr ortuondo larrea (h-0635/03) subject: state aid for the renewal of the fishing fleet article 9 (1) (b) of council regulation (ec) no 2369/2002 of 31 december 2002 amending regulation (ec) no 2792/1999 laying down the terms and conditions for community structural assistance in the fisheries sector provides that public aid for the renewal of fishing vessels may be granted only for vessels of less than 400 gross tonnage. similarly, article 1 (3) states that the measures adopted 'shall not lead to an increase in fishing effort'. however, there are certain types of fishing which, because of their specific conditions and those of the areas in which they operate (offshore vessels, freezer tuna vessels, etc.), could not be carried out with minimal profitability using vessels of less than 400 tonnes. however, there is a real interest in these fisheries in the renewal of old vessels without this leading to an increase in their current capacity. therefore, can the council indicate whether it would be possible to provide in its regulation (ec) no 2369/2002 for the granting of public aid up to the maximum amount corresponding to that fixed for 400-tonne vessels for the renewal of fishing vessels of a larger size and gauge, provided that this is in line with the other requirements of the regulation and that such renewal does not entail any increase in fishing effort?
i suggest. while thanking the honourable member for raising this question, the council would first of all like to point out that in the discussions of december 2002 particular attention was paid to the structural measures for the fleet which had to be adapted to take account of the new scope of the reform of the common fisheries policy. in this connection, the council was fully aware of the need to ensure consistency between the restructuring policy in the sector and other aspects of the common fisheries policy, in particular with regard to the objective of achieving a stable and lasting balance between fleet capacity and fishing opportunities in community waters and outside them. the decision on aid adopted in december 2002 therefore aims to concentrate community financial support on a number of actions which the council has identified as priorities in the new framework. as regards new vessel construction, regulation 2369/2002 provides that public aid in this sector will still be available until the end of 2004, but will now be granted to vessels of less than 400 gt. regardless of whether, in terms of economic efficiency, certain fishing activities can be carried out with vessels of less than 400 gt, it should be pointed out that the council regulation does not provide for the possibility of granting, for the types of vessels you mentioned, mr president, construction aid equal to that fixed for vessels of up to 400 gt. however, as regards investments in safety at sea, working conditions and product quality, regulation 2369/2002 provided for the granting of aid for equipment and modernisation after 2004 and without applying the limit of 400 gt. any measure similar to that suggested in the question would still require a proposal from the commission.
(es) mr president-in-office of the council, thank you for your reply. i am certainly in favour of respecting - how could i not - the fact that all possible fish species have a minimum stock which guarantees their survival and their continuity, and the first ones to be concerned about not depleting this resource, which is their livelihood, are precisely the fishermen themselves. that is why i asked whether, while respecting fishing effort and the maximum quantities of catches laid down, financial aid could also be authorised for the renewal of fishing vessels which, because of their specific nature, cannot be less than 400 gt. i am grateful for the information you have given me, but i do not know whether this covers the needs for the modernisation of the fleet of all types of fisheries. i would like to stress in this connection that we cannot regard seafarers as second-class workers. fleet renewal is vital not only for the survival of companies, not only for the environment, because it is less polluting, but also for the safety and working conditions of workers.

i suggest. in its statement of 21 october, the union welcomed the appointment of mr mesa gisbert as the new constitutional representative and underlined that it would continue to provide assistance and assistance to bolivia in order to strengthen democratic institutions, the rule of law and respect for human rights and to promote a more favourable climate for social progress and economic america, bolivia has received over eur 500 million since 1976. between 1996 and 2002, the european community's commitments totalled almost eur 200 million, while payments amounted to eur 183 million. these figures include financial, technical and economic cooperation, food security, humanitarian aid, cooperation with non-governmental organisations and human rights and other horizontal budget lines. the national strategy paper provides for a total allocation of eur 126 million for the period 2000-06 for financial, technical and economic cooperation with the european community. at the recent meeting of the advisory group, held in paris on 8 and 9 october, international donors made further commitments. however, at the present stage it is not possible to give a precise picture of the commitments in general and of the various forms they take, such as loans, grants, debt cancellations or swaps. on the other hand, the european union, like other donors, has also stressed the need to tackle the root causes of the crisis. the union believes that this requires further measures to ensure access to services for the poorest and most marginalised sections of the population, including the consolidation of land rights and greater political participation of indigenous peoples. the european union welcomes the commitment of the bolivian government to combat corruption and wishes to
