- the next item is the oral question (b5-0413/2003) by mr rocard, on behalf of the committee on culture, youth, education, the media and sport, on the current situation of european networks and info-points.
commission. i regret that parliament was not informed. this is not within my portfolio but i am told it was not intentional, and would not want it to lead to any deterioration in the essential cooperation between our institutions. we recognise the acuteness of feelings, especially since the work of the information system and centres is of clear importance not only to members of this house, but also to anyone committed to developing an understanding of the european union, what it does and what it stands for. the honourable member has made it clear that she, like many other members, has criticisms of the commission's decision to cancel from next year the operating grants hitherto provided to networks and info-points. i would therefore like to clarify exactly which information outlets we are dealing with, explain the nature, size and impact of the subsidies provided by the commission to them and update her and the house on the commission’s latest course of action in direct response to her question and the numerous questions and representations on this issue by members of this house and others. there are currently more than a thousand grassroots public information relays and networks overseen by the commission’s directorate general for press and communication. they are housed in what are known as 'host structures', which are generally national, regional or local authorities, ngos or universities. they include: 126 rural information and promotion carrefours; 140 info-points europe ipe in urban areas of the union; nearly 800 european documentation centres edc generally situated in large higher education establishments worldwide; and a network of around 500 experts in one or more areas of european union policy as conference or other forms of public speakers known as 'team europe'. all of these public information relays receive support services in kind from the commission. the main types of support are: free public documentation and publication: around 3 million copies a year and specialised assistance via a dedicated helpdesk at a cost of about eur 1.5 million a year; free training for relay staff totalling about 800 person-days a year; access to an interactive intranet; and an exchange programme for relay staff with over 3 000 person-days a year. these services are designed to help the relays provide their correspondents with quick and up-to-date responses to their questions on eu policies, programmes and funding opportunities. they are not in jeopardy. it has long been the commission’s intention not only to maintain such technical assistance but also to increase it. meanwhile, it is important to note, in order to avoid any misunderstanding, that only the 266 host structures of the first two of these relays and networks – the ipes and carrefours – have ever received operating grants from the commission since dg press started overseeing them in 2001. they generally amount to about eur 20 000 a year or eur 5.4 million in total. in the majority of cases, the money given to the host structures has been supplemented by larger contributions provided from domestic resources. as the house is aware, the financial regulation that came into force on 1 january 2003 no longer permits direct operating subsidies to be awarded to external bodies without either a call for proposals or the establishment of a legal basis for expenditure. i would also add that, in its 2002 activity report, the director-general of dg press felt compelled to enter a reservation about the management of the relays because it was not possible to guarantee, with the resources at its disposal, proper monitoring and control of a relatively high number of small grants. those misgivings were borne out by the recent findings of the commission’s internal audit service which recommended first, the development of different working methods and audit practices, second, the introduction of more appropriate management tools, and third, the improvement of the standard of agreements and the structure of the expenditure financed. the commission therefore confirms that the proposal adopted on 29 september 2003 to terminate grants with effect from 2004 complied fully with the financial regulation and its implementing provisions. it was therefore right, in legal terms and for practical purposes. the commission acknowledges, of course, that the decision provoked sharp reactions and protests from many national relay coordinators, several member states, and several members of this house. we understand the reasons but we also seek to abide by the letter and spirit of the law of the european union. further to the amendment to the 2004 draft budget tabled in this house, and placing in reserve the appropriations under three of the budget headings related to the activities of dg press, the commission was given the task of trying to reach an accommodation that, as far as possible, satisfied the demands for operational continuity sought by parliament, whilst also securing financial monitoring and control. the commission is aware of the particular political importance of the year ahead and, in response to the honourable member’s question, i would make the following points. first, at our meeting on 11 november 2003, the commission noted that we would have to take up the matter of host entities’ grants again, with a view to taking a final decision in the light of the outcome of the budget trialogue of 13 november. second, in order to retain the current system for 2004, there would need to be a commission decision providing for a waiver to the rule in the financial regulation that requires a call for proposals that is accompanied by adequate monitoring and control provisions tailored to the results of risk analysis and backed by a joint policy declaration by the three institutions. this solution would be justifiable for one year only, but may provide a kind of bridge that would ensure the continuity the honourable member seeks. that proposed solution was subsequently examined by the budgetary trialogue and will now be formally presented for approval at the conciliation committee meeting of 24 november 2003. in response to the honourable member’s third question, the commission has instructed dg press to formulate proposals that will ensure the proper availability of comprehensive information for citizens in the union of 25 member states. these proposals, to be set out in a communication that will hopefully be produced before christmas, will build on the july 2002 communication on information and communication strategy for the european union, and will follow four principles for relay management set out in that communication: a more homogenous brand; a more streamlined and decentralised set of information outlets and networks; closer partnership with member state authorities; and more interinstitutional cooperation. the relays act as a uniquely important bridge between the european union’s policy-making mechanism and the citizens to whom we are all accountable. the commission will therefore do its utmost to ensure that they continue to provide that facility at the dispersed centres throughout the union, which obviously is one of the features that gives them their greatest value.

- doc. b5-0490/2003 by mr cushnahan, mr van orden, mr mann, mr bradbourn and mr posselt, on behalf of the group of the european people's party, on sri lanka; - b5-0492/2003 by mr van den berg and mr carrilho, on behalf of the pse group, on the situation in sri lanka; - b5-0495/2003 by mr collins, on behalf of the uen group, on the threat to the peace process in sri lanka; - b5-0505/2003 by mr messner and mr lambert, on behalf of the green group, on the peace process in sri lanka;
commission. – i should like to thank mr cushnahan for raising this issue, together with other members of this house who clearly take a close and committed interest in sri lankan affairs. the commission has closely followed developments in sri lanka and is greatly concerned by the grave setback inflicted on the peace process by recent events, including the deployment of troops in the capital and the decision to bring the cabinet portfolios of defence, interior, and communications under the remit of the president. the council presidency and the commission have issued a joint statement with norway, the united states and japan expressing our common concern that recent developments in sri lanka may jeopardise the spirit of cohabitation between the president and the government, which has proved vital to efforts to sustain the momentum of the peace process. the presidency and the commission urged the two principal parties to continue to work together in support of a negotiated political solution to the longstanding conflict. commissioner patten has repeatedly contacted the sri lankan prime minister wickremesinghe by telephone encouraging him to find a way to return to constructive and functional co-habitation with president kumaratunga. the commission will continue its efforts motivated by the hope that the tension can be reduced. the commission is closely coordinating any action with norway, as facilitator of the peace process, and with other co-chair countries. naturally, the commission remains in daily contact with its delegation in colombo in order to keep abreast of all developments. commissioner patten will visit sri lanka on 25 and 26 november 2003 as planned. the visit will allow him to get a first-hand impression of the situation and discuss the significant issues with all relevant parties, and he will again be seeking to impress and reinforce the views of the commission and indeed this house which have already been transmitted to all parties in sri lanka. the commission is working in a coordinated manner with the council. we welcome a resolution by this parliament that encourages the sri lankan president and government to return to the co-habitation that had prevailed since the last general election in sri lanka. mrs de keyser talked of the hope for an incipient restoration of normal relations. this is a hope that we share and are seeking to reinforce.
- the joint discussion is over. the vote will take place this afternoon after the debate.
- b5-0491/2003 by mr van den berg and mr mcavan, on behalf of the pse group, on the situation in the indonesian province of aceh; - b5-0496/2003 by mrs sandbæk, on behalf of the edd group, on the situation in aceh; - b5-0497/2003 by mr andreasen, on behalf of the eldr group, on indonesia/atjeh (aceh); - b5-0501/2003 by mr bowis, mr tannock and mr posselt, on behalf of the group of the european people's party, on the situation in the indonesian province of aceh; - b5-0507/2003 by mr wuori, mr maes and mr mckenna, on behalf of the green group in the european parliament, on the situation in the indonesian province of aceh; - b5-0508/2003 by mr di lello finuoli, on behalf of the gue/ngl group, on indonesia and aceh;
commission. mr president, i would like to express the commission's gratitude to mrs mcavan for raising this issue and indeed to the other members of the house, who clearly have a close and continuing interest in and knowledge of aceh. the situation in the province is obviously a matter of concern for the commission, and in a recent statement the european union presidency and the commission, as co-chairs of the tokyo conference on peace and reconstruction in aceh, voiced their concern about the extension of the state of military emergency in the province. we also expressed the hope that it will end as soon as possible. the commission is seeking to encourage the government of indonesia to suspend martial law as soon as possible, and in the meantime has impressed upon it the need to carry out its activities with the minimum possible impact on the well-being of the people of aceh. in pursuing such a process we always include references to humanitarian aid, the restoration of civil institutions and respect for the law. the commission is also pressing for improvement in the transparency of the situation in aceh and continues to call, as honourable members have, for access to aceh for international agencies and relevant non-governmental humanitarian organisations. while the commission reiterates its commitment to the territorial integrity of indonesia, it is also firmly convinced that the conflict in aceh can only be ended by political means. despite the difficulties of obtaining reliable and verifiable information, our delegation in jakarta is closely monitoring developments in the province in coordination with member state missions to indonesia. it regrets that a recently planned mission to aceh by political councils from several embassies was cancelled at the last moment by the indonesian authorities. the commission will monitor the situation very closely and continue its efforts to impress upon the indonesian authorities that they should return to the negotiating table as soon as possible and, in the meantime, allow independent humanitarian aid providers to operate in aceh without hindrance. the cause of decency and humanity is well served by the interest demonstrated by this house, especially in the way in which honourable members were able to illustrate their concern and arguments by reference to the reality of the wretchedness inflicted on the people of aceh.

the truth is that in the united states, following a proposal from congress, the federal reserve is obliged to take inflation, employment and economic activity into account. we have to take these elements seriously, and this is the time to raise these issues. and it is time to make sure that the stability and growth pact can have a future, so i think, mr president, that we have a responsibility to respect the treaties and to have ecofin do it as we do the rest. - the agenda calls for the joint debate on the reports:- a5-0402/2003 by mr van den berg, following on behalf of the committee on constitutional affairs, on european governance (com ((2002) 704 - com ((2002) 705 - com ((2002) 713 - c5-0200/2003 - 2003/2085 ((ini)));- a5-0401/2003 by mr maccormick, following on behalf of the committee on constitutional affairs, on the commission communication entitled 'a framework for tripartite contracts and agreements between the community, the states and regional and local authorities' (com ((2002) 709 - c5-0202/2003 - 2003/2088 ((ini)).
the commission is not prepared to accept the amendments tabled by the committee on budgets. the commission welcomes the two reports by mr van den berg and sir neal maccormick. the commission welcomes parliament's support for initiatives aimed at better regulation, such as the introduction of compatibility checks, minimum requirements for stakeholder consultation, guidelines for the collection and use of expertise and the simplification of community legislation. next week the commission will present its annual report entitled 'better regulation 2003', which will provide for the first time an overview of all the work being done to improve the eu's regulatory environment. with the same aim in mind, the parliament, the council and the commission recently concluded an interinstitutional agreement on better law-making for 2003. this is a major step in the right direction and ensures that the competences of all institutions are fully respected in our future work for better regulation. but i would like to focus today on the two key issues raised by mr van den berg, namely the consultation of the stakeholders and the council, to which the experts are to contribute. what are the principles and minimum requirements for stakeholder consultation? the first is to provide a coherent and transparent framework for consulting these groups. the commission fully shares the view of the european parliament that consultation should not be a substitute for parliamentary democracy and stresses that the aim of the minimum requirements for consultation is to give the people concerned a voice, but not a voting voice. that means it's a hearing, not a decision. the decision must continue to be taken by the representatives of the peoples of europe. nor will the institutional role of the two consultative bodies, the esc and the cor, be affected by these measures. the general principles and minimum requirements for consultation formulated by the commission could also serve as a basis for a further interinstitutional agreement. the commission also shares the parliament's view that consultation should not slow down the legislative process and notes that the minimum eight-week consultation period for open public consultations represents a reasonable balance between the needs of efficient decision-making and the necessary input from external parties. in order to make consultation more transparent, the commission has published a formal and structured list of consultative bodies. this information can be found in the database of the consultative bodies. the development of guidelines for the acquisition and use of expertise is another important measure taken by the commission to improve the preparation of initiatives. as we stressed in the white paper, there is a need to improve the standards of european governance for the collection and use of expertise. the guidelines for the commission services that consult and use the expert advisory board are precisely aimed at ensuring that the high standards and best practices are an integral part of the working culture of all commission services. the commission should not only improve the quality of its action by careful preparation, but also make this process more transparent. for this reason, the commission will adopt a new standard explanatory statement for all its proposals next week, which will require that the grounds and facts be explained accordingly. this decision also includes expertise and stakeholder consultation. the commission has already made a number of proposals to this effect. the approach taken in the report is in line with the commission proposal and is both ambitious and reasonable. the commission's proposal is ambitious because it aims to enhance the role of regional and local authorities and to give them more responsibility for implementing community legislation and measures, something that is now increasingly clearly required. the aim is to bring the regions of the union closer together. the conclusion of tripartite agreements or conventions can be an interesting development in the implementation of certain community policies. the commission has also proposed that the council should adopt a decision on the proposal for a directive on the protection of workers from the risks related to exposure to asbestos at work. the commission was guided by the same idea when it adopted the communication on trilateral agreements and arrangements in december last year, in accordance with the white paper on european governance. we have also proposed that a trial phase be carried out first. this phase has already begun. in the field of the environment, a similar initiative aimed at concluding a tripartite agreement has been launched in three european cities. tripartite agreements could also be agreed in the near future within the framework of the measures implementing the sustainability pacts for the future initiative. in regional policy, the commission is convinced of the need for greater decentralisation. the use of tripartite agreements between the commission, the member state and the region could possibly become part of a new system for implementing the structural funds. it would also place greater responsibility on the regions and regional development actors. but we must exercise a certain caution. firstly, as the rapporteur has asked, we must take stock of the pilot phase and evaluate the results. secondly, we must consider what legal, political or institutional obstacles we might encounter in certain cases when we resort to such agreements. in particular, i would like to distinguish two phases in regional policy: the phase of defining the development strategy, in which it is desirable to involve local authorities more closely than the state - if this is compatible with the constitutional system of the member state concerned - and then the implementation phase. the commission's proposal for a regulation on the application of the rules on the use of budgetary resources and the obligations of the commission as guardian of the treaties is a matter for consideration. it is also necessary to examine the extent to which the commission is likely to have to assume additional administrative and control tasks. finally, i would like to assure the rapporteur that, in accordance with the rapporteur's wishes, the commission intends to involve parliament in the implementation and evaluation of future trilateral agreements.
the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the community's financial interests are protected. the commission is not prepared to accept the amendments tabled by the committee on budgets. i would like to begin by thanking you, mrs miguélez ramos, for your excellent report and for your support for our proposal. the commission has proposed to make some changes to the system of aid for the conversion of vessels and fishermen who were able to use the fisheries agreement with morocco until 1999. we propose the following amendments: the commission has also proposed that compensation be paid to fishermen who have lost their jobs because the vessel on which they were working has changed its fishing activity, for example by joining a joint venture. this will widen the circle of beneficiaries. we therefore need to extend the deadlines by one year so that all new beneficiaries can apply for aid and the authorities in spain and portugal have enough time to take a decision. i am also prepared to accept amendments nos 2 and 3. however, i cannot accept the amendment tabled by mr varela suanzes-carpegna because it calls for an amendment to article 12 of the fisheries structure regulation with regard to socioeconomic measures. we cannot change this regulation at the moment.

(es) mr president, the fisheries agreement between the community and morocco expired on 30 november 1999, which condemned 4,300 fishermen and 400 vessels to standstill. the aid to the persons concerned, under regulation (ec) no 2792/1999, charged to the fifg, then came into force. this aid was extended until 31 december 2001, but then a policy of conversion of the fleet was necessary, much of which could not be relocated to other fisheries. we have therefore adopted a measure, regulation (ec) no 2561/2001, based on national plans, for the socioeconomic diversification of these areas affected by the shutdown. in areas particularly affected, such as morrazo, barbate, algeciras and lanzarote, fishing activity was drastically reduced or simply disappeared, with effects on many other sectors linked to this activity and on local production as a whole. as you know, the solidarity fund has been used to finance these actions, totalling 197 million euro. the regulation also provided for derogations and exceptions to the rules defining the terms and conditions for structural assistance in the fisheries sector. however, the exceptional nature of the measure meant that the council approved a limited period for it, which was not sufficient to accommodate many of those affected. the rigidities contained in the regulation have also contributed to this and are now being removed by this amendment, which was proposed by the european parliament. that is why i am so glad that mr fischler says that the commission will accept these amendments and the amendments i propose in my report, because both mr fischler and we, the european parliament, want the fishermen concerned to be treated equally, so that they can benefit from aid for their conversion, regardless of the fate of the vessel on which they worked, because the linking of the fisherman to the fate of the vessel has been one of the great difficulties. in some cases, vessels could be relocated to other fisheries, catching less than they were fishing in the moroccan fishery and thus losing profitability. these ships had to reduce their crews. however, the regulation did not cover these fishermen because it tied the fate of the vessel to that of the fishermen, which prevented them from receiving the global premium for their conversion. for this reason, and in order to ensure that this rule - as the commission and the european parliament wish - can in practice cover as many people as possible, it is necessary to abolish the provisions whereby individual global premiums can only be granted to a vessel or to fishermen who were working on a vessel whose fishing activities have ceased definitively. and the amendment we are now discussing, as the commissioner has said, also means extending by 12 months the deadline for eligibility of expenditure, which will now be 31 december 2004, and the deadline for submitting the request for payment of the balance to the commission, which will now be 30 june 2005. this is what we were asked to do in the committee on fisheries by representatives of those affected by the closure of the fishery, such as the loitamar cooperative on the morrazo peninsula (galicia), which is made up of almost 60 moroccan workers who have been converted but who have not yet been able to fully implement their business project. now, with this extra time, they can do so, and all the members of the cooperative can - as required by the regulation - start working to be able to receive these individual grants. the andalusian government also asked us to do so, since it is one of the regions, along with galicia, the canary islands and the algarve, which has suffered most profoundly from the non-renewal of the fisheries agreement with morocco. i have to say to the honourable members that this amendment, as i put it, has no financial impact whatsoever, but that the financial resources allocated can be properly implemented, thus fulfilling the objective intended by the legislator when he adopted the regulation we are now reviewing. - the next item is the report (a5-0362/2003) by mr cashman, on behalf of the committee on civil liberties and human rights, on the adoption of measures concerning the repatriation of the remains of deceased persons (2003/2032 (ini))
commission. mr president, may i first of all thank mr cashman for his detailed and precise report on this very sensitive and important issue. this report sets out very clearly the problems regarding the repatriation of mortal remains that exist within the union today. i know how strongly many members feel about this issue. many members of this house have personally intervened to assist families of constituents who have faced these difficulties when trying to repatriate the mortal remains of their loved ones. i therefore appreciate the particular importance that must be attached to this issue. the commission agrees with mr cashman that these problems will multiply as eu citizens increasingly use their rights to work and reside in other member states. although the commission fully recognises the importance of this issue and the urgent need to deal with it, i must admit that it has been somewhat hesitant, as the report has clearly pointed out, in determining precisely what to do about this. the commission has signalled, in response to a number of questions by members of parliament, that it does not believe, at this stage, that specific harmonisation is required. i wish to stress today, however, that this does not imply that we cannot move to resolve these problems. in the coming weeks, i shall be asking my colleagues to adopt a directive on services in the internal market, and i believe that directive will help resolve a number of the problems raised by mr cashman's report insofar as they reflect restrictions on the exercise and provision of cross-border funeral services. in particular, it will simplify administrative procedures and abolish authorisation requirements that are not consistent with the principle of proportionality. i also hope to be able to deal with the specific problem related to zinc coffins insofar as a coffin is obviously an essential element of the funeral director's services. there will remain problems caused by different national requirements such as those on death certificates and autopsies. on those issues the commission doubts that it is legally possible to apply the principle of the free movement of people to contest restrictions on the transfer of mortal remains. it also believes that harmonisation on these issues would be likely to be contested on the grounds of subsidiarity. i wish to thank mr cashman once again for this report and i should like to reassure this house that the commission will seek to resolve as many of the problems raised in it as possible, but i cannot guarantee that we shall solve all the problems, given the uncertain legal situation regarding the free movement of people. in resolving the restrictions to the provision of funeral services the commission will do its utmost to make member states aware of the very important problems raised in this report regarding differing provisions on autopsies and death certificates. in particular, we shall indicate that national legislation in this field should respect fundamental rights, and in particular the dignity of people.

- the next item is the report (a5-0410/2003) by mrs randzio-plath, on behalf of the committee on economic and monetary affairs and industrial policy, on the proposal for a council directive amending directive 77/388/eec as regards reduced rates of value added tax (com (2003) 397 - c5-0359/2003 - 2003/0169 (cns)).
commission. mr president, i should first like to say something about annex k, on which a number of speakers have voiced their opinion. this council had established these rules, including those in the directive for evaluation - about annex k. the council - and not the commission - also established that the experiment should run for three years. in fact, it lasted four years, since the commission wanted more time to analyse the results. i want to stress that the council stipulated what the rules should be. the commission has not made a proposal to continue annex k. it does so because it is not effective. the reports that the commission has received from most member states - including the netherlands and france, where opinions differ - indicate that there is no noticeable positive effect on employment. the reason is quite simple: in too few cases is the decrease in taxation passed on to the consumer. in fact, i quote my wife, who said that she had never witnessed a reduction in hairdressers' prices. i do not know whether mrs lulling agrees with this, or whether she has witnessed a decrease in hairdressers' prices. my wife has not, and the reason is that the hairdressers pocket the decrease in taxation and, therefore, annex k amounts to a subsidy for hairdressers. i have nothing against hairdressers, but why should we subsidise them? it has no positive effect on employment, and if you want to stimulate employment, it is better to reduce the social on-costs of labour for the same amount of money. one will create 52% more employment by reducing the on-costs of labour rather than reducing vat. the commission sees no reason why it should make a proposal, and that is exactly why unanimity in the council does not work. it only works if there is a proposal, and then it is overturned. in this case, there will be no proposal and, therefore, unanimity in the council cannot overturn what is not there. the same situation happened previously in the case of the tax-free shops at airports. there was no proposal and, therefore, there was nothing to overturn. mrs van den burg said that i do not respect the rules of the european union. i should like to know which rule i do not respect. i am scrupulous in respecting all the rules of the european union. it is the council which established this entire experiment and set a three-year period. the commission made it four years. it is the council, and not the commission, which said this was in order to increase employment. the whole idea therefore originates from the council. it is an experiment, and experiments are supposed to be discontinued if they do not work. this is why they are experiments. therefore, why should the commission propose an extension of annex k if it has not worked? i fail to see, mrs van den burg, where this commissioner is not obeying or following the rules. on the wider issue of reduced rates, the standard rate is the normal rate. it is around 20% in most countries. that is the standard rate. all derogations must be construed strictly and, where the internal market and distortions of the markets are concerned, one should be extremely strict. mrs randzio-plath mentioned children's shoes, which are zero-rated in the united kingdom and ireland. but if you look at the figures, it is clear that there again there are no noticeable benefits to the consumer. the differences between the prices in the united kingdom and the prices on the continent are the same whether the high rate or the low rate is applied. that proves that it is the manufacturer or the trader that is subsidised, but certainly not the end-consumer. as regards cds, they are by their very nature easily transportable and, therefore, if the rates differ, there is a clear inevitability of a distortion of the internal market. at the moment, no member state applies the reduced rates to cds and, therefore, if we did, it would again be a step backward. that is why i now return to annex k. i have said to the council of ministers that the commission would not press charges or start infringement proceedings against those member states that would continue to apply annex k as if it were still in force - which it will not be. but i recognise that member states may need a certain time to organise their affairs and that is why i said for the first six months of next year i will not start any infringement proceedings. but annex k will no longer exist.
commission. mr president, in reply to the last remark by mrs randzio-plath for which i thank her i would like to say that the basis for the commission’s decisions is the reports that are produced by member states; these reports have not been drafted by the commission. according to the rules that were established four years ago, we rely on these reports. i do not see why mrs randzio-plath needs any further evidence. i can send her the reports if she likes, but they are the basis of the commission’s decisions. i am not responsible for the way in which member states draft their reports - that is their business. i use them as they come in. the commission has looked at them and has seen that there is insufficient evidence.

- the next item is the report (a5-0467/2003) by mr schmidt, on behalf of the committee on economic and monetary affairs, on the proposal for a council directive amending directive 77/388/eec as regards the value added tax system applicable to postal services (com (2003) 234 - c5-0227/2003 - 2003/0091 (cns)).
the commission has already taken a number of measures to ensure that the vat system is not affected by the introduction of the single currency. it represented a considerable step towards the effective abolition of restrictions on the movement of persons, goods, services and capital and towards the integration of national economies. for the first time, the community had a harmonised tax base and a harmonised list of exempt goods and services. in 1977, the community legislature introduced the postal services. this exemption dates from a time when, in most member states, the post office was a government agency, which held a monopoly on postal services. at that time, the post office was clearly a public postal service and the exemption of its services did not distort competition since no competition was possible. this is no longer the case today. in most member states, the post office is no longer a government agency but a commercial enterprise under commercial law. in some cases, its shares are traded on the stock exchange. some member states already apply vat to the postal service or to some or all of the services provided by the universal service provider, recognising the problems caused by an outdated exemption. some of these companies, like other postal operators from third countries, are now expanding their operations to other member states in order to reap the benefits of the internal market. consumers now demand services that only companies with a presence in several european markets can provide. however, under the current rules, a company providing exempt postal services in member state a is obliged to apply vat in member state b, as it is not recognised as a public postal service in that country. the postal market is now largely liberalised. although, as is often the case, postal liberalisation proceeds at a different pace in each member state, in all of them - largely due to the approval of directive 97/67/ec - operators other than the former monopolies can and do provide services. since several operators provide postal services and are not treated in the same way under vat legislation, competition is inevitably distorted. vat exemption is not a pure blessing. in particular, it leads to an inability to deduct the vat paid in advance, which in turn discourages investment. at a time when there is competition in the postal market and the communications revolution has created new channels which, to some extent, compete with the postal service, reduced investment rates expose public operators to risks. as is often the case with european tax legislation, the vat directive is lagging behind all these changes and now needs to be urgently amended as it no longer reflects the needs and the factual situation in the community. in accordance with article 93 of the treaty, provisions concerning vat are to be adopted to the extent that harmonisation is necessary to ensure the establishment and functioning of the internal market. in submitting its proposal, the commission is fulfilling its obligations under the treaty. it did so after extensive consultation with universal postal services and other postal operators, as well as with representatives of postal customers. it took account of their views, in particular those of private customers and charitable institutions, by proposing that a reduced rate be applied to services such as the sending of letters, small parcels and direct mail, which are the things these customers need most. the combined effect of the savings made by postal operators from the right of deduction which the proposal would grant them and the application of a reduced rate to a wide range of postal services is designed to limit or even to neutralise any increase in postal rates. the commission has defended the concept of universal service at the heart of directive 97/67/ec and considers that every citizen of the union has the right to a wide range of affordable and good quality postal services. universal postal service providers will not be able to provide such a service if they are discouraged from investing and modernising and, as a result, will no longer be able to compete with other operators in the market segments that are already open to competition. to be competitive in such markets, they need to be present throughout europe and have tools such as parcel tracking, which private operators and third countries already offer to european customers. the current vat exemption makes the required investment more costly. universal postal operators in europe recognise these challenges and therefore most of them support the objectives of this proposal. in conclusion, i would ask members to support the commission's proposal.

- question no 9 by mrs izquierdo rojo (h-0744/03): the commission has not yet decided whether to grant aid to the united kingdom. subject: migration policies and temporary migration migration policies should aim at preparing for current and future migration responsibly and effectively by channelling it and establishing an effective european framework. in fact, all member states are currently working to improve the management of migration flows by showing their willingness to work with the countries of origin of immigrants. in its communication on immigration, integration and employment (com (2003) 0336/final), the commission proposes ideas to this end, including the use of the opportunities offered by the wto general agreement on trade in services, which aims to provide temporary mobility mechanisms for persons arriving in the european union for the purpose of providing a service. this would fulfill the hopes of many developing countries. the commission also suggests that temporary migration be included in the european employment strategy and in community action programmes. in addition, very satisfactory experiences have been made with periodic temporary migrations, most of which are related to agricultural work. for example, temporary migration is managed through the issuing of temporary residence permits and job offers for seasonal workers from third countries. in the light of the above, does the council not consider that the migration policies of the european union should take into account and include, through positive measures, issues related to temporary and seasonal employment?

i suggest. i believe that, albeit briefly, the answer already contains everything that can be useful to answer the further questions that the honourable member has put to me. i would like to reiterate, however, that i am clear about the commitment to continue the debate on the temporary migrant worker, just as i am clear about the need for the council, the commission and the competent bodies to ensure that, from a regulatory point of view, all the rights that are enshrined and respected within the union are equally respected in relation to these issues. the debate on active labour policies, particularly in relation to women, is part of the work being done, and i have no reason to believe that there is no interest in this issue.

in all types of negotiations between the community and third countries: any cooperation or association agreement or any other type of agreement, whether recently concluded or still under negotiation, i suggest. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i very much welcome the opportunity to take part in this debate on the status of members of this parliament. mr president, in its letter to you on 21 november the presidency stressed the council's readiness to have a dialogue with parliament on this subject. this statement was in addition to a similar offer made by the greek presidency with minister papandreou on 20 june. that is why today's discussion is important. it provides us with an opportunity to move forward and to explore the possibility of finally reaching an agreement after 25 years. mr president, the council fully respects parliament's primary role in defining the status of its members. in accordance with the procedure laid down in the treaty, it is for parliament to lay down the conditions and general conditions for the performance of the duties of its members, after obtaining the opinion of the commission and the approval of the council, which shall act unanimously in taxation matters. it is therefore clear that the european parliament cannot adopt the statute without the council's consent and the council cannot approve the statute without parliament's presentation of acceptable proposals. i think it's good to remember that. mr president, i am aware that many of you are anxious to know the council's position on the statute in general and, more particularly, on certain proposals which have come from various quarters in recent weeks. when parliament submitted its draft statute last june, it was immediately clear that there were substantial differences between the positions of parliament and the council, which was therefore unable to give its consent. you will recall that earlier in march the greek president of the council, mr papandreou, explained to a delegation of members of parliament which aspects of the statute were acceptable or unacceptable to the council. unfortunately, the proposal made by parliament in june deviated substantially from the council's positions, and this made it impossible for us to give our consent. let me remind you again of the council's position on the most important points. first, the council unanimously considers that the statute cannot alter primary law: the first is that the commission is not in a position to take a decision on the matter. the presidency welcomed the recent measures taken by the bureau of the european parliament on the reimbursement of expenditure. the council considers that this reimbursement must be in accordance with the principle of expenditure actually incurred. on taxation of allowances paid to members of the european parliament this aspect, on which unanimity of the council is required for it to give its assent the provisions concerning the community tax to be applied to the allowances of members should not affect the power of the member states to make such allowances subject to national taxation provisions, provided that double taxation is avoided. as regards the retirement age, although the council has always shown a clear preference for 65 years, in a constructive spirit of compromise we would be prepared to accept a limit of 63 years. as regards the thorny issue of the allowance, the council is not opposed to the idea of setting its level by taking as a reference a certain percentage of the allowance received by a judge of the court of justice. this would solve the problem of its annual indexation. i would now like to draw your attention to the fact that all the positions i have just set out are the result of long and detailed discussions which took place in the council well before parliament adopted its statute on 3 june. as regards some of the initiatives which have recently emerged in parliament, the italian presidency has been able to record a first positive reception in the council by all the delegations. i therefore believe that if these initiatives are supported by this parliament, we will be closer than ever to an agreement on a long-dragged issue. as i said at the beginning of my speech, dialogue is the only way to resolve our differences and the council is ready to take up the matter. for its part, the italian presidency has always been ready to find a solution and i know that the next irish presidency fully shares this approach. vice-president of the commission. (es) mr president, i am a privileged witness, as willy rothley's fellow member for the last ten years, to his determination to get this dossier through. i want to congratulate him and express my appreciation, because he really deserves it. i would also like to point out that both the president-in-office of the council and the vice-president of the commission, as well as my colleague mr lehne, have pointed out that respect for primary law includes a very important principle, that of the unity of community tax legislation. in our proposal there is a modification of the exceptional tax status, contained in the so-called 'belgian compromise', which only makes sense in so far as it is a delegation, a kind of opting out with regard to general law, but which cannot be interpreted as a general power for the states to tax amounts paid by the community institutions. the proposal which the various political groups in the european parliament are now putting forward could in fact be a step forward towards the establishment of a unitary statute for the european union. i think that now is not the time to invoke the principle of subsidiarity, but quite the opposite: we are building a european union which must be based on common institutions which have a common functioning, and this is what explains the proposal for a european parliamentary statute and a statute for european political parties. it is not a question of granting any privileges, but of establishing a situation of equality between all members of the european parliament. i hope we can pass the text without any of the amendments which have been tabled to it.

i suggest. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, i should like to make a few comments on the prevention, management and resolution of conflicts in africa, a subject which has been the main focus of the italian presidency's six-month term in relation to the african continent. the most urgent task today is to stabilize the continent, that is to prevent or eliminate armed conflicts where they exist. the european union is unanimous in its conviction that development can only be promoted by creating general conditions of peace and security. without them, poverty eradication, the promotion of human rights, good work and the protection of the environment are chimeras or ephemeral achievements. there is no trade-off between development and peace operations, only an integrated approach. the un secretary-general kofi annan put it well when he spoke at the african union summit in maputo: we need a global approach that includes peace and security, human rights and democracy, reconstruction and development in a continuum. the first to realise this are the african governments themselves, who, already in the programming document for the new partnership for the development of africa, state that war and underdevelopment are two sides of the same problem, which feed off each other. in line with this assumption, they have proceeded to establish the necessary bodies to prevent, manage and resolve their crises, in particular the peace and security council and the joint committee of major african states. the new political element to be emphasised is this new determination of africans to assume their responsibilities also in the field of peace and security on the basis of the principle of ownership. it is an approach that the european union has always encouraged and supported, through action aimed at strengthening african capacities, both at the pan-african level and at the subregional level through ecowas, igad and sadc. in the face of this changing political landscape, the italian presidency has been active in promoting a european response that is up to the challenge. we did this by promoting theoretical reflection on the prevention, management and resolution of conflicts in africa, through a study seminar organised in rome on 28 july. we did so by reviving the eu-africa dialogue, which had been frozen after the postponement of the lisbon summit, through two troika meetings, the second of which was held in rome on 10 november. this revival was mainly centred on peace and security, where there was a significant convergence with the africans. we have done so through our constant support for the peace processes under way from côte d'ivoire to liberia, from sudan to somalia, from ethiopia/eritrea to northern uganda, from the democratic republic of congo to burundi. we have done so through constant diplomatic activity, including a series of missions to africa by the european union troika at ministerial level. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the results - at least in the short term - are largely positive. the real-time management of the liberian crisis, both at political-diplomatic and financial level, has made a decisive contribution to the cessation of the conflict, the conclusion of a peace agreement and the establishment of the current transitional government. in the same region, the recovery of sierra leone is consolidating, but the most difficult test is being faced by the ivory coast. the country is the real engine of the region's economy and the most important game is played here. the progress made so far is very good. the creation of a government of national reconciliation, the adoption of an amnesty law, the agreement of 4 july between the national armed forces and the rebels, are significant steps in a process that remains to be completed through the quartering and disarming of the militias and the extension of the state administration to the entire territory until the presidential elections scheduled for 2005. the european union has done and is doing everything in its power to ensure that the current impasse is overcome, reunification becomes irreversible and the linas-marcoussis agreements are fully implemented. the statements of 22 september and 9 december, the visit of a european ministerial troika in mid-october and the activities of the european union representative on the monitoring committee bear witness to this. the rapid intervention of the french armed forces and the ecowas contingents helped to avoid open conflict. however, the need remains for a larger peacekeeping force, under a un mandate, within which african contingents can continue to operate. it is the request made by ecowas in new york, a request which must be supported by the european union. these references to concrete conflict situations make it possible to appreciate, on the one hand, the determination with which africans show that they want to manage their conflicts and, on the other hand, the great work that needs to be done to strengthen operational capacities, especially those of subregional organisations. in this sense, the eu-africa partnership can only be resolved in a tripartite eu-un-africa cooperation, in which each component is complementary to the other. operation artemis - the first european-led military operation outside theatre - demonstrated the effectiveness of a rapid response, a prepared and well-organised force that can cushion the emergency of conflict to allow a larger and appropriately mandated un force to tackle broader stabilisation tasks. the forces of african subregional organizations can also have this value of rapid and decisive intervention, with the prospect of being replaced by the slower but better organized united nations machine. this could be the case in burundi, where the first all-african peacekeeping force is currently deployed and which, in no more than a year, could be replaced by the united nations. we have already mentioned the timely interventions of the european union in response to humanitarian crises and emergencies. the most significant innovation, however, is the creation of a peace fund - the peace facility - with a budget of eur 250 million and financed by edf resources - which was decided by the eu council on 18 november 2003. the european union thus has a predictable and rapidly deployable instrument that corresponds to its strategic partnership with africa and to the principle of african ownership. the peace facility will make it possible, with all the guarantees provided by the decision-making procedures, to finance a defined range of activities of peace operations conducted by african forces. the request to this end made at the african union summit in maputo has thus been answered by the european union in line with the commitments and promises it has repeatedly made. for at least a decade, together with the united nations, we have been urging africa to take its destiny into its own hands and break, with the support of the international community, the vicious circle of conflict and poverty. now that our appeal has been embraced by african leaders themselves, as evidenced by the new philosophy underlying the creation of the african union and nepal, it is a matter of political credibility to turn promises into decisions. if applied wisely, the peace facility can prove to be one of the most important instruments for the future of relations between europe and africa. in conclusion, i would like to stress that the field of conflict prevention, management and resolution in africa has undergone significant conceptual and operational developments. we are trying to fix this development by revising the basic document on which the overall action of the european union in this field has been based up to now: i refer to the european union's common position of 14 may 2001 on the prevention, management and resolution of conflicts in africa. the exercise we have started and which is under way proposes to complete the current common position by updating it, first of all with reference to the fight against terrorism and organised crime, which in conflict situations find fertile ground for expansion; the commission will continue to monitor the implementation of the new rules and to monitor the implementation of the new rules. the commission is also proposing to extend the scope of the directive to include the protection of the environment and the protection of the environment. finally, mention should be made of the seriousness of the situation in the so-called 'failed states', i.e. territories without control or public institutions capable of exercising the necessary authority and providing basic services. it is an open exercise, which we are handing over to the future irish presidency, and which will crystallize the overall approach of the european union to the great issue of conflict prevention, management and resolution in africa.
commission. – mr president, the commission shares parliament's concerns on the political situation in côte d'ivoire. even if some progress has been made in the implementation of the marcoussis agreement, the current deadlock has to be broken. the new forces have been boycotting the council of ministers for two months and this boycott, as well as the mutual lack of trust, makes it impossible training of the fisheries ministry and investment in the côte d’ivoire economy, mainly through the three tuna factories, are guaranteed only if the agreement is extended. bankruptcy of the tuna negative consequences and could only deepen the current crisis in côte d’ivoire, so i would not recommend pulling this element into a situation which is already problematic enough.

- question no 25 by mr newton dunn (h-0732/03): subject: heroin from afghanistan entering the european union via turkeycould the commission say what it is doing to convince the turkish government that before it can even dream of joining the union, it must stop the flow of the huge quantities of afghan heroin that turkish drug lords are smuggling into the union, using the latest technology and techniques, in order to enrich themselves while destroying the lives of young european citizens?
the commission is not prepared to accept the amendments tabled by the committee on budgets. the european commission shares your concern about drug transit through turkey. the association agreement with turkey provides for institutions which enable the commission to monitor very closely whether and how turkey adopts and implements community legislation on organised crime and drugs. in addition, turkey is currently being negotiated for observer status in the european monitoring centre for drugs and drug addiction. i think that turkey will be granted this observer status next year. a partnership will start on 1 january 2004 to establish a national contact point for the european information network on drugs and drug addiction and to promote the development and implementation of a national drug strategy. the commission also considers that a small dublin group should be set up in ankara as soon as possible. i am pleased to say that turkey has made and is making a great effort to combat drug trafficking. turkey is actively involved in international efforts to prevent heroin from entering the european union from afghanistan. it is the nature of the matter, mr president, that i cannot give you any information on the nature of these measures because they are partly intelligence operations. i can only tell you that the information available to the commission shows that turkey is fully cooperative and that the tone of your question is not justified. in 2002, the turkish authorities seized 2 124 kg of heroin. this is a decrease from previous years. this decline is due to the fact that international drug traffickers have changed their transport routes due to the tight controls in turkey. in 2003, turkish customs introduced state-of-the-art systems at three border crossings, where vehicles passing through the border are scanned. this has led to the discovery of large quantities of contraband drugs. as part of international cooperation, the turkish customs authorities organise monthly meetings with the anti-drug liaison officers posted to turkey. it goes without saying that the commission, in its cooperation with turkey, is pressing for full compliance with all existing agreements and provisions on the fight against drugs.
the commission. that is the question i asked myself when i was considering your question. i am therefore in a fortunate position to give you a very precise answer. first of all, you have to know what a dublin group is. the dublin group is the grouping of industrialised countries, i.e. all eu member states, the usa, canada and australia, which coordinates initiatives to combat drugs and drug trafficking. in cooperation with third countries not belonging to this dublin group, this group sets up so-called mini-dublin groups which have a regional scope, so a mini-dublin group in ankara would mean that the members of the dublin group and turkey in turkey themselves cooperate on these issues.
- question no 26 by mrs zabell (h-0765/03): subject: rules of competition applicable to sport in recent years, the commission has adopted several decisions on sport in the context of competition policy. most of these decisions, which take account of the specific features of sports competition, have led to satisfactory solutions from the point of view of community law. in view of the importance of these decisions and the doctrine they have given rise to, does the commission not consider it appropriate to draw up, before the end of its term of office, a communication on the application of the competition rules to sport, so that they can serve as guidelines for the future and enable sports organisations to draw up their regulations accordingly?
the commission. the commission is not currently planning a communication on the application of competition rules in sport. the commission considers that the longstanding and well-established case-law provides a good guide to the application of the competition rules. international sports federations, which are primarily responsible for the regulation of sport, are generally aware of this regulation anyway. the competition rules of the ec treaty apply only to economic activities linked to sport, and not to genuine sporting activities. there are borderline cases, and there may be borderline cases where it is difficult to separate economic and non-economic activities. the best way to deal with these problems is to deal with them in a case-by-case manner, so that the specific characteristics of the sport concerned can be taken into account.
(es) mr commissioner, thank you for your reply. i would like to ask you whether you do not think that the fact that the commission has had to take this series of decisions in recent years on sport in the field of competition policy and competition policy, if it is appropriate, highlights even more strongly the need to include an article on sport in the future treaty on european union.
commission. - madam president, this is an interesting reference to the current debate on the constitution. the commission can indeed imagine that sport will be given special consideration in the proposed constitution. however, if i understand the debate that has been held on this subject in the convention and in the public, it is not so much a question of the application of competition rules as it is a question of whether a 'soft' competence of the european institutions can be introduced in the field of sport. the commission is not ruling out the possibility of a definition in the future, which would then be reflected in a communication. but for the moment, i repeat our position that we believe that all parties are better served by reviewing the decision on a case-by-case basis, taking into account the decisions already taken, when doubts arise.

vice-president of the commission. (es) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the sections mentioned in the oral question form part of the priority project no 8, the portugal-spain-remainder of europe multimodal route, included in the commission's 1996 decision on community guidelines for the development of the transeuropean transport network. the growth initiative also considered that the vigo-oporto crossborder section met the conditions to be included in the so-called 'quick start list', where, as the honourable members know, in addition to being part of the transeuropean networks, it must have the crossborder component and the immediate start of the works, that is, in the next three years (2004-2006). in the period 2000-06, the cohesion fund is financing the line from the minho to the north of porto. decisions on the granting of aid totalling eur 87 million for the nine-braga-lousada-nine sections will be taken in the coming days. since 1987, studies on the galician atlantic railway line ferrol-portuguese border have benefited from community aid, which reached a total of almost eur 6 million in 2003. a further eur 5 million is planned for the period 2004-06 to finance studies on this railway axis, in response to a new request from the spanish authorities. as regards the spanish railway section between ferrol and the portuguese border, several technical studies have already been completed and many are still in the process of being completed. work has already begun north of vigo. according to information received from the national authorities - portuguese and spanish - the vigo-la coruña section is expected to enter service in 2007 and the vigo-oporto link in 2009, and the la coruña-ferrol section, which would complete the section of the line in spanish territory, is expected to be ready and operational from 2010.

(es) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, first of all i would like to say that i am pleased to think that we are about to complete the procedure for adopting the directive on the promotion of cogeneration. i would like to thank the rapporteur, mr glante, and the other rapporteurs and other responsible members of parliament who have worked hard on this directive, which is so important for energy policy in europe and at the same time so complex, in many cases from a technical point of view. the directive on the promotion of cogeneration is a step forward, which is intended to help solve the problems facing our energy sector in europe, such as the need to save energy and reduce greenhouse gas emissions. high-efficiency cogeneration is more efficient, as it involves energy savings and therefore reduced emissions. we are also looking at cogeneration with renewable energies, at a time when this helps us to increase security of supply and reduce the vulnerability of electricity transport, sometimes over long distances; indeed, cogeneration usually involves a greater proximity between electricity production and electricity demand and therefore brings generation closer to consumption. it also means greater flexibility in energy supply, since - i repeat - cogeneration can be produced on the basis of any fuel, including renewable energies. the european industry has been demanding such regulation for some time; it is following our work very closely and i think everyone appreciates the good deal - mr glante used to say that it 'does a little harm to everyone', perhaps partly because that is why it is a good deal - that we can get this evening and tomorrow, in the vote. there is a very important point, which mr glante has made, and that is that cogeneration has different concepts, which are hidden depending on the different countries. the debate has brought these different concepts together and has led us to something which seems essential: that cogeneration be genuine cogeneration and that it mean an improvement in the real global energy balance. the setting of targets for the promotion of cogeneration has been one of the key issues in the debate between the council and parliament, and to get the member states to be willing to identify and notify their potential, i think is a very important step forward, and the right one. these reports should be published and examined by all interested parties, and i have no doubt that viable capacities will be followed by the necessary measures to put into operation and use those capacities for more energy-efficient cogeneration. mr president, ladies and gentlemen, parliament's amendments have clearly improved not only the original directive, which we had submitted to parliament and the council, but also the common position and, most particularly, on this point to which the rapporteur referred, micro-generation, a new and promising technology. i welcome the initiative of this parliament in insisting on this issue and in making the amendments which allow it to be incorporated directly into our directive. parliament has also contributed to other improvements in the common position, such as the authorization of the committee responsible for the complex technical details and the adjustment of the thresholds for technical development, and i want to thank them once again for the work they have done, proving once again the seriousness and the good work of this parliament, even when very technical matters are being shuffled, dealt with and discussed, as in this case. i congratulate you on the magnificent standard you have demonstrated. i would like to thank the rapporteur, mr glante, all the other rapporteurs and the other participants in these debates for their contributions.
(es) mr president, ladies and gentlemen, commissioner, we have added a new floor to the building of the union's energy policy which the commission - and in particular the vice-president of the court - has been promoting since the beginning of this parliamentary term. this energy policy is based on the following principles: security of supply, reduction of our energy bill and preservation of the quality of the environment. cogeneration is a very valuable tool for achieving these aims and this directive was therefore timely and necessary. it has been clear in the discussion and drafting of this important legislative initiative that there are times when two interests, two sectors, are clearly at odds. in this case, the two interests to be harmonized were those of those who produce heat and those who use the heat in an industrial process. these two competing interests were represented curiously by two physical parameters: the energy efficiency of the installation and the saving of primary energy. what we have done in our joint work has been to try to achieve a balanced approach at the end, which would lay the foundations for the promotion of cogeneration, objectively considering all the interests that converge in this important activity. i believe, mr president, that we have achieved this thanks to the excellent work of the rapporteur, mr glante, and of the various colleagues who have contributed to this end, and in the end we have shown that consensus does not always get things wrong, but that there are occasions when consensus, in the end, achieves a result which we can all celebrate today. i would therefore like to conclude, mr president, by expressing my satisfaction at this achievement. we have certainly made a step forward in this energy policy which we all share and we hope that this directive will soon be translated into a harmonized method and a unified scheme for the promotion of cogeneration which will enable us to achieve the objectives which we have all been pursuing for some time.
(es) mr president, i would first of all like to congratulate the rapporteur, mr zimmerling, on his work, which has enabled us to agree on a good regulation on decentralised cooperation, which is necessary in the process of modernising community development policy. it is a consensus reached not only in parliament but also at interinstitutional level, which will enable us to have, as soon as possible and for the next three years, a renewed legal basis for implementing this policy. decentralised cooperation, i.e. the involvement of non-state actors and sub-state entities - both from european countries and from recipient countries - is a necessary condition for participatory development that responds to the needs and initiatives of the population to which cooperation is ultimately directed. it is an additional factor in the real democratization of developing societies, since decentralized cooperation strengthens the social fabric, and it is also a proven element of aid effectiveness and a vehicle for making the concept of ownership of development processes effective. development cooperation has long ceased to be only bilateral or multilateral and governmental or non-governmental. the european socialist group therefore enthusiastically supports decentralized cooperation which is becoming more and more perfect. we must therefore consider that those in europe who think that this line could be used to encourage strange movements outside the states or the authorities of the recipient countries who fear losing control over aid they consider their own are not right - from the perspective of sustainable and participatory local development. decentralised cooperation is more concerned with the actors than with the economic resources or the sectoral content of cooperation. as regards the financial resources mentioned by the rapporteur, we have given up our initial demand for more funds in the interests of the interinstitutional agreement, but we are confident that the commission will continue to implement the programme properly and we believe, however, that the decentralised cooperation line should be progressively increased and not be a minor line in the budget from which funds can be drawn to cover other gaps. we currently have eur 9 million for the first year and eur 6 million for the next two under heading b7-6002, without prejudice to the fact that resources from the geographical headings may be used for decentralised cooperation actions. we are not satisfied with that - we would like to have more - but, because of the consensus, we can reach that agreement. as this is a transversal line, it has no sectoral limits and the parliamentary group of the european socialist party has tried to open up as much as possible to the potential beneficiaries of this line, so that social articulation is actually favoured. it is made clear that local authorities are also considered to be municipal authorities and we welcome the extension of the regulation and the amendments that have been introduced, taking into account the references to the gemelli, carrilho and howitt reports and we hope that the commission will henceforth respect the deadlines for evaluation and presentation of results set by parliament so that we can analyse the effectiveness of this instrument in terms of development.

commission. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the european union has welcomed with great satisfaction the peaceful outcome of the political changes which have taken place in georgia following the parliamentary elections on 2 november and the resignation of president shevardnadze. georgia now has a unique opportunity to put the past behind it and build a better future for all its citizens, based on a clear commitment to democracy, the rule of law and the market economy. however, the challenges ahead cannot be underestimated. however, given georgia's commitment to reforms, mr patten wants me to assure parliament that the european union will do everything in its power to help georgia meet these challenges. the most immediate challenge for georgia is to hold democratic presidential elections on 4 january, followed by legislative elections at a later date that respect the commitments made in the framework of the osce and the council of europe. the commission intends to allocate a maximum of eur 2 million to the country to support the preparations for these elections. georgia is also facing a very difficult budgetary situation. the commission has just ordered the disbursement of €5 million under the food security programme under an accelerated procedure to enable the country to cope with its most urgent needs during the winter months. after democratic elections, the priority areas where reform is needed. combating the scourge of corruption will be of crucial importance if any reform programme is to deliver lasting results. the commission will examine how substantial resources can be mobilised in support of these reforms. i would also like to point out that the commission is already providing assistance to georgia to support respect for human rights and democracy in the framework of the european initiative for democracy and human rights. in particular, we are working with the council of europe to strengthen democracy at local level and human rights protection mechanisms. we intend to examine in the coming months whether these activities should be adjusted in the light of recent political developments in georgia. the european union has long expressed its support for georgia's sovereignty and territorial integrity. the search for solutions to the conflicts that are tearing the country apart will be important for the long-term stability of this region of the south caucasus. the establishment of good working relations between georgia and russia, based on mutual respect, will be of great importance in this respect. the european union is exploring new ways of supporting conflict prevention and resolution. the commission will be ready to support post-conflict rehabilitation efforts. mr president, in close cooperation with the european union special representative for the south caucasus, mr heikki talvitie, the commission is making a determined effort to contribute to the establishment of a broader european union policy towards the south caucasus region. our efforts to support georgia at this crucial moment are an important part of this process.

(es) mr president, the situation which inspired today's resolution shows that human rights and respect for life, as supreme values, are never fully acquired and that democrats everywhere must be ever alert. although the death penalty has not reduced crime rates in any country, we note with great concern that 83 countries in the world still maintain and apply it. today we must regret and denounce that president arroyo has changed her position on the death penalty in the philippines. we must not forget that in the republic of the philippines there are cases of juveniles awaiting a death sentence. the european union must draw certain red lines, which we must never cross. one of them is the death penalty. that a country like the republic of the philippines can retreat from what was a conquest through moratorium is a matter of great concern to all democrats in the world at this time and, very especially, to democrats in the european union. that is why, in this situation, we have inspired this resolution, which must absolutely be taken into account by the philippine authorities, so that we continue to consider that it is possible that the values we have defended as superior will never be put at risk. my group will vote in favour of this resolution today.
commission. - mr president, ladies and gentlemen, the european commission is extremely concerned by mrs arroyo's decision to lift the moratorium on the death penalty in the philippines. the european union is opposed to the death penalty in all circumstances, because it believes in the inherent dignity of every human being and in the inviolability of the human person. the european union therefore asked ms arroyo to reconsider her decision to no longer prevent executions, inviting her to maintain the moratorium in force since march 2000. we are also particularly concerned about the death sentence handed down by the supreme court to 15 minors in violation of article 6 (5) of the international covenant on civil and political rights. the commission supports this policy through specific actions. in its communication on the role of the european union in promoting human rights and democratisation in third countries of may 2001, it reaffirmed the priority given to funding projects for the abolition of the death penalty. it subsequently included the abolition of the death penalty among the thematic priorities of the european initiative for democracy and human rights for the period 2002-04 and allocated a specific budget of eur 12 million for actions in this area for 2000-04. in line with our commitment, we contributed around eur 500 000 to the fight against the death penalty in the philippines in 2002 as part of the european initiative for democracy and human rights. the commission's communication, 'a new partnership with south-east asia', states that new bilateral agreements with countries in the region must all contain the human rights clause as the essential element. in this context, this essential element clause, of which the death penalty is a fundamental aspect, will be a priority of any envisaged bilateral agreement between the european union and the philippines.
